en: Preface to the *Zuting shiyuan*:

Those throughout the world who hold the Buddha in the highest esteem do so because his words transcend the realm of the ears and eyes, and his principles exist beyond the six directions of the universe.
By believing and contemplating them within a single phrase, one may suddenly realize the truth without loss and perceive it with clarity.
One's original nature will undoubtedly achieve Buddhahood. Therefore, although the student lets the mind roam within words and letters, they do not become mired in those letters;
this is precisely what constitutes the Way. This Way was transmitted from Kāśyapa to Bodhidharma and only then reached China.
Five hundred years after Bodhidharma, Yunmen was born; he responded to questions according to the capacity of his interlocutors, guiding and receiving those who came to study.
Whenever there were spoken words or phrases, they vied with one another to record them privately; these accumulated until they formed a complete compilation.

Although its transmission and transcription were not permitted, it was secretly passed from hand to hand and preserved within book-cases. Later generations, lamenting that its circulation had not been widespread, eventually carved woodblocks to print and disseminate it at that time.
When I read it in my youth, I suspected there were omissions and errors in the text, and I wished to seek out other copies to collate it against.
I have not had the leisure. However, the printed and transcribed records of our school are generally full of errors and discrepancies.

This is because those in the lineage of Chan prioritize a pure mind and few affairs, never regarding written texts as their primary concern. In the spring of the second year of the Daguan era, I, on account of my role in assisting the Way, resided at...
The Chief Administrator (Dusi) of Hua-yan presented me with a very large volume he had transcribed by hand, which had passed through the hands of the Venerable Master Mu-an.

Its title was *Zuting shiyuan* (Garden of Affairs of the Patriarchal Hall). Having read it thoroughly, I observed that its editorial revisions and narrative style were consistently imbued with the methods of the masters.
All of these may be verified through historical records. I therefore inquired into the origins of his writings, and he said:

"In the past, while traveling among the monastic communities, I observed that in addition to the formal 'ascending the hall' and 'entering the room' [teachings] of the great masters, they also permitted students to recite from memory.

When those from the various Chan records—such as those of Yunmen and Xuedou—were brought forward by members of the assembly, the master would expound upon their context; this was called 'requesting instruction. Students..."
Some have obtained but scraps and remnants of these teachings and immediately transmit them to others.

Within these works, they frequently cite the causal conditions of Buddhist doctrine and the historical accounts of Confucian texts, yet they often fail to understand their origins and sources, instead offering reckless conjectures.

This not only invites derision from those with true knowledge, but the errors they perpetuate for future scholars are no small matter. You, Excellency, having extensively hunted through and immersed yourself in the various scriptures, have inquired everywhere.
Regarding knowledge: whenever I heard of a single condition or attained a single principle, I would record it in my mind and inscribe it upon bamboo slips.

Furthermore, I sought out ancient records to compare their points of agreement and divergence. Keeping this in mind at all times for nearly twenty years, I have compiled a total of over two thousand four hundred entries.
Although this deeply contradicts the intention of Bodhidharma’s transmission of the Mind from the West, it may perhaps serve to facilitate understanding.
The enlightened scholar deduces the one to reach the myriad things and integrates all affairs to return to the Truth.
Thus, the composition of this "Garden of Affairs" (*Shiyuan*) is by no means a minor contribution.

Should someone read this book and yet be able to criticize and revile it, establishing their own intent beyond words and letters to vigorously uphold our Way—would such a person not be both worthy of admiration and worthy of astonishment? This too is...
It was from my own *Shiyuan* (Garden of Affairs) that [this work] was initiated. I, Yu, admired his words and marveled at his resolve;
I have respectfully written this as a preface. The Master was born in Dongyue; his surname was Chen, his style name Shanqing, and his courtesy name Shijie.

He left home in his youth to serve as a disciple under Master Kaiyuan Cihui. He traveled to various regions to seek the Way. During the Yuanfu era, because his mother was elderly, he could not bear to be far away from her.
He traveled about and then returned to live in seclusion within his home village. Formerly, there was an elder in Muzhou surnamed Chen;

his parents were elderly and had nowhere to go, so he wove straw sandals and sold them to support himself. The Master secretly admired him and consequently named his residence "Muzhou Hermitage" (Muan).
His resolve and insight are truly commendable. Written by the Bhikṣu Faying of Siming.
Table of Contents for the *Zuting shiyuan* (Garden of Affairs from the Patriarchs’ Hall), Volume One:

Yunmen’s Record from the Room; Xuedou’s Record of Dongting;
Xuedou’s Later Record, Volume Two.
Xuedou’s Collection of Waterfalls, Xuedou’s Excerpts on Ancient Cases,
and Xuedou’s Verses on Ancient Cases,
Volume Three.
The Collected Verses of the Patriarch Xuedou,
Volume Four, Part One:
The Record of Xuedou’s Opening of the Hall from the Collected Verses of the Patriarch Xuedou.
Xuanshuo Shiyi,
Volume Five:
The Former Record of Chan Master Huai and the Later Record of Chan Master Huai.
The Sixth Volume of One Hundred Questions at Chiyang:
The Collection of the Roars of Fengxue and the Record of Fayan.
Volume Seven:
The Record of Lotus Peak, the Collection of Eight Directions' Pearls and Jade,
and Yongjia’s Song of Realizing the Way.
Volume Eight:
Ten Profound Discourses, Explaining Names, Interpreting Prophecies,
Distinguishing Phrases, and Miscellaneous Records.
Colophon to the Table of Contents of the *Zuting shiyuan* (Garden of Matters from the Patriarchal Hall).
End of Volume One of the *Zuting shiyuan*.
Compiled and Corrected by Muan Shanqing.
*Record of Yunmen*, Volume One.
The Master’s name was Wenyuan. He was born in Jiaxing, Eastern Wu, and his secular surname was Zhang. He received his monastic training at Doushuai Monastery.
Traveling to various regions to seek the Way, he first arrived at Muzhou to visit the venerable master Chen. Knocking on the door, Chen asked, "Who is it? He replied, "Wenyuan.
Chen opened the door, seized him, and said, "Speak! Speak! The Master was speechless. Chen said, "A carriage from the Qin dynasty has been drilled through!
Thereupon, he let go; as the door closed, it broke the Master's right leg. Because of this, the Master realized the Great Meaning. Chen pointed [to him].
He traveled to Xuefeng. Upon his arrival, it happened that Xuefeng had ascended the hall for teaching;

the Master stepped forward from the assembly and said, "Why do you not cast off this three-hundred-jin iron yoke upon your neck? Xuefeng descended from his seat, seized him, and asked, "For what reason have you come to such a state?
The Master rubbed his eyes with his hand. Thereafter, his Way flourished throughout the monasteries. He traveled again through various Zen groves until he reached Lingshu in Shaoyang Prefecture.

He occupied the first seat. After Lingshu passed away, the regional ruler of Guang, the Liu clan, commissioned the Prefectural Governor He Xifan to invite the Master to succeed him on the Dharma seat.
From this point on, he widely proclaimed the Way of Xuefeng throughout the world. He subsequently moved to Yunmen.

Students flocked to him from all directions. On the tenth day of the fourth month in the seventh year of the Qiánhé era of the Southern Hán dynasty—which was the second year of the Qiányòu era of the Great Hán dynasty—he sat upright and manifested his passing.
This was the first year of the Qián德 era of the present dynasty’s Taizǔ Emperor.
Moved by the dream of Ruan Shaozhuang, Li Tuo then presented a memorial to the throne. Upon opening the stupa, his entire body was found, its appearance and posture [intact].
He was received at the imperial palace as if he were alive and provided with offerings. Subsequently, having received imperial permission, he was returned to his native mountain for burial.
He was posthumously titled Great Master Kuangzhen Hongming of the Daciyun (Great Compassion Cloud) lineage. Alas!

Fourteen years after the Master’s passing, this title was again conferred during the era of the Founder of the Art (Yizu). That his Way has flowed forth so abundantly until this day—how could this be mere coincidence?
The Master [Laozi] said: "The good person is the teacher of the not-good person; the not-good person is the resource for the good person.
Commentators say: Only when there is a not-good person alongside a good person does the merit of the good person’s salvation become manifest; therefore, it is called a "resource" (zi).
The character for *bā* (筏) is pronounced with the *yue* (越) radical and the *qie* (切) phonetic; its correct form is *bō* (橃). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "A large ship on the sea.
It is also written as *bā* (筏). The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "The Tathāgata has often said to you: 'Preach the Dharma using the raft as a metaphor.
Even the Dharma should be relinquished, let alone what is not Dharma.'"
To stop crying is like when an infant cries; his parents immediately take yellow leaves from a *śiṃśapā* tree and say to him, "Do not cry, do not cry;
I will give you gold. Upon seeing this, the infant conceives the notion that they are real gold.
He then ceased crying. However, these willow leaves were not actually gold; this is seen in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. The "Easy Omission" section of the *Wangquan* says:
"Words are used to clarify the image; once the image is grasped, one forgets the words. The image is used to preserve the meaning;
once the meaning is grasped, one forgets the image. It is like a snare, which exists for the sake of the rabbit; once the rabbit is caught,"
One forgets the trap once the fish is caught; one forgets the fish-trap because the fish has been obtained.
Thus, words are the traps for images, and images are the fish-traps for meaning. Those who cling to words do not grasp the images;
those who cling to images do not grasp the meaning.
*Makkaṃsa* (in Sanskrit, *Magadha*), which here means "Land of Culture and Arts.
*Maṃśi* refers to the World-Honored One’s entering meditative concentration in the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā-dharmasabhā*). The *Record of the Western Regions* states:

"In the past, when the Tathāgata first attained perfect enlightenment in the kingdom of Magadha, the Brahmā King constructed a hall of seven treasures, and Śakra Devendra constructed a seat of seven treasures; the Buddha sat upon it."
Above this, he contemplated these matters for seven days; the meaning is the same as that of the *yan-shi* (the "closed room").
Vaidurya, which in Sanskrit is called *Vaiśālī*, means "Extensive Splendor" (*Guangyan*); it is the city where Vimalakīrti resides.

Du means "to close" or "to shut. In the "Entrance into the Dharma-Door of Nonduality" chapter of the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra, it says: Mañjuśrī asked Vimalakīrti, "We have each spoken for ourselves;
you, O Benevolent One, should now explain what constitutes the bodhisattva’s entrance into the dharma-door of nonduality."
At that time, Vimalakīrti remained silent and spoke no word. Mañjuśrī sighed in admiration, saying: "Excellent! Excellent!
Even to the point of being without words or speech—this is the true entry into the Dharma-gate of non-duality."
"Yi-tang" (異儻) should be understood as "yi-dǎng" (異黨). "Dǎng" (黨) means faction, cohort, or class. "Tǎng" (儻) is pronounced with the initial *t* and the final *-lang* (it-lang qie);

it does not carry a specific meaning here. Kāśyapa is called *Kāśyapa* in Sanskrit; this translates as "Drinking Light" (飲光). This refers to his bodily radiance being so supreme that it eclipses—that is, "drinks in"—the light of all the devas; hence the name.
The *Baolin Zhuan* of Caoqi: During the Yifeng era of the Tang dynasty, the local resident Cao Shuliang donated land to the Great Master, the Sixth Patriarch.
Because the site featured two peaks and a great stream, and was named after the surname of the Marquis Cao, it was called Caoxi.
Those from all under heaven who have studied the Way of the Patriarch are its branches and tributaries.
The character "lie" (烈) in "Lie-pai" (烈派) and "Lie-dang" (烈當) refers to the arrangement of a lineage.
According to the commentary by Hong of Shitou, Qiu Xuansu of the Tang dynasty composed a stele inscription for Chan Master Tianwang Daowu.
While Tianwang was a successor of Mazu and not a disciple of Shitou, upon examining that stele, it states that Daowu was born in Jingzhou and received the Dharma there.
At Jiangxi, he visited Master Mazu. The Master instructed him, saying, "If you take up residence as an abbot, do not leave your former location.
Consequently, he returned to Jingzhou and built a thatched hut atop Zhugong. Because the site was overgrown with wild brush, the Master of Jingzhou angrily threw it into the water.
Shortly thereafter, the spirit of the Heavenly King emitted flames from the master’s courtyard. The master was moved by this.
Wu established a temple for him; the present-day Tianwang Temple in Jingzhou still exists there. It is an error to claim that the current [emperor] is the Heavenly Emperor (*Tianhuang*).
Furthermore, upon examining the *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp), it states that the Master was a native of Dongyang in Wuzhou;

at the age of fourteen, he received the tonsure under a monk in Zhaozhou and received full ordination in Hangzhou. This is entirely different from the inscription in Jingzhou. Now, according to Qiu Xuansu...
Stele. It is clear that the Heavenly King (Tianwang) succeeded Mazu; it was not Shitou Hong who provided the commentary.

The character *zhòu* (胄) is pronounced with the *zhù* rhyme. It signifies lineage (*yìn*). Therefore, its radical is "flesh" (*ròu*). *Zhòu* refers to descendants. *Yì* (裔) is written with the "clothing" (*yī*) radical.
Regarding the term *yi* (裔) as meaning descendants: it is taken from the sense of a garment’s hem hanging downward. *Yi* is pronounced with the initial *yú* and the final *zhì*.
The *Saṃyukta Āgama* states: "There was a tortoise that fell into the hands of a jackal;

he hid his six limbs and did not emerge. The jackal became angry and departed. The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "You should be like the tortoise who hid his six limbs; you must conceal your own six sense faculties."
The Māra finds no opportunity. These three phrases are:
first, cutting off the myriad streams; second, the casket covers heaven and earth; third, following the waves and riding the currents.
The establishment of these three phrases began with the Great Master Yuandeng of De shan. Today, they are all referred to as the "Three Phrases of Yunmen."
This is likely due to a lack of careful investigation. Nevertheless, Deshan was indeed a successor of Yunmen, and he possessed these three phrases.
The "Biography of Lord Pingyuan" in the *Shiji* states: "When a worthy scholar dwells in the world, it is like a needle placed within a [sack of] grain."
[The sword] would have emerged with its point protruding long ago, not merely at the end. Mao Sui said, "If I had been placed in the bag early on, my blade would have thrust itself out;
it would not have been seen only at the very end."
Waiting for a Hare. Master Hanzi said: There was a man in Song who was plowing his field. In the field there was a stump. A hare ran into it, its neck broke, and it died.
Consequently, he abandoned his plowing to guard the stump, hoping to catch another hare again. He became a laughingstock to the whole state of Song.
The character 勉 (mǎn) should be read as 免 (miǎn). It means "to stop" or "to cease. It is not used in the sense of "exerting effort" (biànqiǎng).

The character 瘡疣 (chuāngwòu)—*wòu* being pronounced *yǔ* with the *qiú* tone—refers to a "knotted disease" or a wart. The *Shìmíng* states: "A *wòu* is like a *qiū* (a mound); it is a mass that protrudes high above the skin."
It is like a mound upon the earth:
although one has searched everywhere, one must still "search out and extract" (sōbyen kyeol dangjwa).

This means that because the Master would not permit copying, he traveled everywhere to search out and extract [the text] from other locations, and only now has he finally obtained it from Master Jin. *Kyeol* (抉): pronounced as in *juan-yue* (絹悅); it means to pick out or extract.
The *Xuanhe Xianghe Jing* (Classic on the Auspicious Characteristics of Cranes) states: "The crane is a bird of yang, born from the essence of metal.

At two years of age, its crown becomes red; at seven years, it flies to the edge of the Milky Way; after another seven years, it cries out throughout the twelve periods of day and night; and at sixty years..."

The large feathers fall off and downy feathers grow; their color is white as snow, and mud or water cannot soil them. After one hundred and sixty years, they conceive when the male and female gaze at each other.
At three hundred and sixty years of age, their color becomes pure black like lacquer; thus they are called "dark cranes" (*xuán hè*).
At two thousand six hundred years, they drink but do not eat, and are born through transformation from the womb. When they give birth, they become the *qí* (steeds) of the immortals.
Ji (referring to Shuai Kuang). Shuai Kuang was the music master of Duke Ping of Jin. The Duke ordered Kuang to play the qin. The Duke said, "Is there nothing more sorrowful than this on the qin?
May I hear it? [Kuang] replied, "Your Majesty’s virtue and righteousness are thin; you are not fit to hear it."
The Duke said, "This is the music that I delight in; I wish to hear it. Master Kuang, having no choice, took up his qin and played it.
Upon the first performance, six dark cranes gathered at the outer gate. Upon the second performance, they stretched out their necks and cried, fanning their wings and dancing.
Duke Ping was greatly pleased; he rose and offered a toast to Master Kuang for his longevity.
Regarding Ziqi and Boya, the *Lüshi Chunqiu* states: "Boya was skilled at playing the qin, and Ziqi was skilled at listening.
When Boya’s intent was set upon the high mountains, Ziqi said, ‘Majestic and towering, like Mount Tai.

When his intent was set upon flowing water, [Ziqi said], ‘Vast and expansive, like the Yangtze and the Yellow River. Whatever Boya contemplated, Ziqi invariably grasped it. Boya was traveling on Mount Tai..."

While traveling in the shade of a mountain, he encountered a torrential rainstorm and took shelter beneath a crag. Feeling sorrowful, he began to play the *qín*, composing the "Linyu" (Drenching Rain) piece and further creating the "Bengshan" (Collapsing Mountain) melody.
Every time he performed them, Zhongziqi invariably grasped their profound essence. Boya set aside his lute and sighed, saying, "How wonderful!
You have perceived my inner intent and visualized it within your mind; how could I ever conceal my sounds from you?"
"Shè lìlì" (涉瀝瀝) should be "lì" (歷), pronounced with the initial *l* and the final *di* (狼狄切). It means "to pass through. "Lì" (瀝) refers to water dripping;
it is not the correct meaning here. "Shēng táng" (昇堂) should be "shēng" (陞), meaning "to ascend. "Shēng" (昇) refers to the rising of the sun; it is not the correct meaning here.

Master Liu Yin usurped the title of Emperor of Han and occupied Guangzhou. He visited Shaoshi Mountain and, upon beholding the tree of the former spirit, learned of the final instructions left by the Great Master Zhi.
The Emperor issued an edict for the Master to receive purple robes and ordered the Prefect He Xifan to request that the Master open the hall for formal preaching.
The person referred to as "Lord He" in the record is Xifan.
Regarding the Tripitaka: first, the Sūtra Piṭaka, comprising the four Āgamas and other sūtras; second, the Abhidharma Piṭaka, including the *Abhidharmakośa* and so forth.
The *Vibhāṣā* and other treatises; three, the Vinaya Piṭaka, consisting of the five divisions of the Vinaya.

Regarding the five vehicles: first, by upholding the precepts, one attains the human vehicle; second, by practicing the ten wholesome paths of action, one attains the celestial vehicle; third, by cultivating the Four Noble Truths...

1. Attaining the Śrāvaka Vehicle; 4. Cultivating the twelve links of dependent origination, one attains the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle; 5. Being endowed with the practice of the six perfections, one attains the Bodhisattva Vehicle.
Regarding the four periods, the Tiantai school actually maintains five periods; thus, the mention of "four periods" is an error. As for the five, they are:
first, the period of the *Avataṃsaka*, which is like the rising sun first illuminating the high mountains; second, the period of the Deer Park, during which the Four Āgamas were taught.

It is like the sun illuminating a deep valley. Third, during the time of the Vaipulya [sūtras], he preached sūtras such as the *Vimalakīrti*, the *Saṃghāṭasūtra*, the *Laṅkāvatāra*, the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, and the *Śrīmālādevī*.
In terms of time, this corresponds to the mealtime. Fourth, during the time of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, he preached the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* and various other *Prajñā* sūtras;
this corresponds to the hour of the morning (yúzhōng). Fifth, during the time of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Nirvāṇa*, it was at noon.
At noon, the wheel [of the sun] is directly overhead, leaving no shadow or form.

Within the Tiantai school’s Eight Teachings (*bājiào*), there are the four teachings of transformation (*huàfǎ sìjiào*): first, the Tripitaka; second, the Shared; third, the Distinct; and fourth, the Perfect. There are also the four teachings of transformative method (*huàyí sìjiào*):
first, the Sudden; second, the Gradual; third, the Secret; and fourth, the Indeterminate. Among these, the One Vehicle is the Perfect and Sudden teaching. This is the system of the Teaching School.
This is the ultimate [term].
"Zhè" (這) is a word used for specific matters; it frequently appears as "zhè" in Chan records, though sometimes it is written as "zhē" (遮), neither of which carries the intended meaning.
Regarding "zhè," the *Sāncāng Gǔxùn* states: "In ancient texts, this was the character for 'shì' (適); it is no longer used in that sense today."
"Oblivion" (*wàngxiǎng*) should be read as "delusion" (*wàng*). [The character is pronounced with] the initial *qiè* of *wúfàng*.

It means "to disturb. "Sun-drying" (*shàiláng*): The upper character is correctly written as *shài*. [It is pronounced with] the *qiè* of *suòhuài*. It means "to expose to the sun. [The character] *shà* does not exist in the received texts.
"Yíng" should be written as "Yíng," pronounced "yíng. It means surplus profit from trade.
The "Three Vehicles" are: first, the Śrāvaka; second, the Pratyekabuddha; and third, the Bodhisattva. A "vehicle" (yāna) is so called because it carries one forward toward the infinite.
1. *Sūtra*: In Sanskrit, *sūtra*; here translated as "Scripture of Concordance" (*qìjīng*).
2. *Geya*: "Verses to be Chanted. 3. *Vyākaraṇa*: "Prophecy. 4. *Gāthā*: "Verses in Meter. 5. *Nidāna*:
"Causes and Conditions. 6. *Udāna*: "Spontaneous Utterances. 7. *Itivṛttaka*: "Past Occurrences. 8. *Jātaka*: "Birth Stories. 9. *Vaipulya*...
10. *Saṃkṣipta* (Abridged). 11. *Vaipulya* (Extensive). 12. *Avadāna* (Parables)—not yet [established]. 13. *Vyañjana* (Explanatory Verses). 14.
*Upadeśa* (Instructional Treatises). 15. *Upadeśa* (Discussions).
The *Zhengzongji* (Record of the Orthodox Lineage Outside the Teachings) states:

That which is called "the separate transmission outside the teachings" does not refer to the sounds, words, colors, or forms that manifest within the yellow scrolls and red volumes; it is simply identical to the treasure-mark and the formless.
Nor is it something distinct from the Buddha's teachings; rather, it is precisely that which the traces of those teachings do not reach.
Furthermore, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, "The Buddhas have severed attachment to dharmas; they do not establish scriptures, nor do they adorn their speech.
If this is so, how could the intention of the Great Sage ever necessarily reside in the teaching? As the Sūtra says:
"When I sat at the site of enlightenment, I did not obtain a single dharma that was real. With empty fists I deceived small children in order to deliver all beings.
Is this not proof that the Great Sage used the teachings as a provisional means (*upāya*) and did not intend for them to be taken as ultimate?

Furthermore, a sutra says: 'The teaching of the sūtras is like a finger pointing at the moon; if one sees the moon, one understands that what was pointed out is ultimately [the moon, not the finger].'"
It is not the moon. How could this possibly cause people to cling to the traces of his teachings? Furthermore, a sutra states:
"From the Deer Park until the end at the Bahudā River, during those fifty years in between, he never spoke a single word.

This is indeed what is meant by that which is outside the teachings (*kyōge*). Yet, this is extremely profound and esoteric; although it is recorded in the sutras, it is merely spoken of therein. The Sage—
People have verified this; therefore, it has been transmitted from mind to mind. This is precisely what the Chan practitioners refer to as the "separate transmission outside the teachings.
Furthermore, our Song Emperor Zhaosong composed a poem on the cultivation of the mind which says: "The First Patriarch sat in meditation at Shaolin;
He did not transmit scriptures or doctrines, but only the mind. If later generations awaken to the nature of True Suchness, [It will be] secret..."
The seals (mudrā) originate from the profound and wondrous principle.
The ten stages (*bhūmi*) are: first, Joy; second, Freedom from Defilement; third, Radiant Emission; fourth, Blazing Wisdom; fifth, Difficult to Conquer; sixth, Manifestation;
seventh, Far-Reaching; eighth, Immovable; ninth, Excellent Wisdom; and tenth, Dharma Cloud.

The *Huayan shu* (Commentary on the Avatamsaka Sutra) states: "The wisdom of a bodhisattva and the wisdom of a Tathāgata are like a person with clear vision looking at various forms and images through a thin gauze.
This statement indicates that the bodhisattva’s and the Buddha’s perception of the nature (*dharmatā*) differ.
*Śà* (pronounced with the initial *suo* and final *jià*) refers to a change in sound. It is now borrowed as the phonetic for *xià* (summer), carrying the sense of feigned doubt, as in [口*耶*].
Its original pronunciation was *xié*; it is now borrowed as the phonetic for *yé*.
[The character] 祝 (zhù) is pronounced with the radical 士 (earth) and the phonetic 側 (cè).
It means "to block" or "to obstruct. Where it says "yǒu xiàng" (有嚮), it should be read as "yǒu xiǎng" (有響); where it says "shàng xiàng" (尚嚮), it should be read as "shàng xiǎng" (尚饗).

Regarding the phrase "penetrating the Dharma-body" (透法身): I once read the *Ancient Records of Yunmen* (雲門古錄), in which a monk asked: "What is the phrase that penetrates the Dharma-body? The Master said: [text follows].
Holding up his staff, he asked, "Do you understand? A monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Hiding one's body within the Big Dipper.
Now, omitting this section on holding up the staff seems to have lost the original intent of that time.

*Gè* (upper character): Pronounced *gé*. The sound of a blade entering bone; also, dry bones are called *gè*. (Lower character): Pronounced *jí zhì* (cutting through). Bones that still have flesh upon them.

Also, the remaining bones of birds and beasts. Also, the sound of a blade entering flesh. *Yueling* (Monthly Ordinances) states: "To cover the *gè* and bury the *zì*. (The term *zì* refers to the flesh-covered remains.)
*Qi* (pronounced with the initial *jū* and final *qiē*) means to be stammering or speech-impaired.
Regarding "playing the lute for an ox," the worthy scholar Gongming Yi of Lu played the lute for an ox, performing the *Qingjujiao* (*Clearing the Horns*) piece.
The ox ate as before; it was not that the ox did not hear, but rather that its ears were not attuned.

When the sounds changed into those of mosquitoes and gadflies, or the lowing of a nursing calf, the ox would wag its tail, stamp its hooves, and pricked up its ears to listen; this was because its mind was attuned to them. (The character *xiè* [躞] is pronounced *xī xié*;
it denotes the manner of walking.)

*Yī kē*: "Kē" is pronounced with the *gě* (盍) rhyme. It refers to a *bíkē* (椑榼), which is the same as the modern *piānkē* (偏榼). It is used for holding wine. *Bí* (椑) has the phonetic value of *pí* (鼙).

The character *chúnwěn* (唇吻) should be written as *chúnlín* (脣); *chún* (脣) belongs to the *zhēn* (真) rhyme group and means "startled," which is not the intended meaning here. *Wěn* (吻) is pronounced with the *fěn* (粉) rhyme.
"Qi wu dangzuo qi wu" (Arising without doing, how could there be non-existence?).

"Jiliao" (吉嘹) has the lower tone "liao. This is a northern dialect; when two sounds are combined to form a character, it becomes "jiliao," meaning "to entangle" (jiǎo). "Jiǎo" means to twist or tangle.
To "entangle the tongue" is like drawing back the tip of the tongue. It is like calling a "kū-lóng" (cave-house) a "kǒng" (hole), or a "kū-tuó" (camel).
It is for the sake of [Song-Mu+Niao]. Furthermore, some take "jiliáo" (吉嘹) to mean auspicious speech. In Lingnan there is a bird resembling a magpie that is kept in a cage;
after a long time, it becomes able to speak, and the people of the south call it a jiliáo. At the beginning of the Kaiyuan era, Guangzhou presented one as an offering.
His speech and tone were as majestic and grave as those of a great man; he understood human nature with profound subtlety, far surpassing the likes of parrots or starlings.
It is likely that Yunmen, while residing in Lingnan, also employed this same principle.
"Solitary rock" (*tokuseki*) means a large rock. Just as one says "solitary ox" (*tokugyu*) for a bull, the *Shuowen* states: "A solitary ox is the father of oxen.
It is said that its simplicity and uniqueness are all the precious accumulations of the Buddha-dharma. The Buddha told Anantavyūha: "The Tathāgata constantly speaks of all..."
All phenomena are the Buddha-dharma. Because one is able to thoroughly understand all phenomena, they are called the Buddha-dharma.
The fundamental nature of all Buddhas is equal to the Buddha-dharma; therefore, all phenomena are the Buddha-dharma.
The character 性 (xìng) with the phonetic 僺 (pí) should be read as *sù* (cut by 到). It describes a coarse or sparse appearance.
The character 榼 (kē) with the phonetic 蔞 (lǚ) is a borrowed sound for 盦 (ān); it refers to excrement and soil.
"Wuyuan" (務原) should be "Wengyuan" (翁源). It is the name of a county located in Shaoyang Prefecture. This county possesses Ling Mountain;
there is a spring on its summit whose waters flow downward. Those who drink this water mostly live long lives, hence the name was given to it.
"Wu" (務) should instead be written as "Wu" (婺) with the "woman" radical, as in Wuxi County in Hexi Prefecture; it is not used here.
The term "Hu" (barbarian) was used to refer to those of Western India; this practice has been handed down since the Qin and Jin dynasties and is ultimately difficult to reform.
Consequently, there are those who call the Buddha the "Old Hu," the scriptures "Hu-language," and the Patriarch the "Blue-Eyed Hu.
Those who claim to be his descendants yet call themselves the "Hu-race"—being sons of Śākyamuni while bearing the name "Hu-race"—should not they clasp their chests in self-reproach?
This means that names must necessarily be rectified. Master Fushi said:

"I have observed that since the arrival of the scriptures in previous generations, whenever the virtuous and wise took up their pens to receive the teachings, they invariably referred to the process of transference as 'translating from Hu into Han.

Furthermore, 'Dongxia' (the Eastern Land), the 'Nine Provinces,' and 'Tianzhu' (India) for the Western Regions are all general names. Alternatively, it is called 'Shendu,' which corresponds to the Sanskrit name for this [land]."
It was then designated as Zhina and Zhendan. If one refers to it as Han, the Han dynasty comprised only two reigns under the Liu clan;

thereafter, with the succession through abdication, the Wei and Jin dynasties were distinct. One must rely on the titles of the emperors to distinguish their designations. Furthermore, there was the admixture of the Hu and the Rong.
This is merely a local custom of the western borderlands, similar to how this land has its own tribes such as the Qiang and Di who have undergone "barbarization.
How can it be that the scriptures are in the language of the Hu? The Buddha was born in India; there, the noble families and Brahmins are collectively called *Brahman*.
*Brahman* means "purity. They are descendants of the Ābhāsvara Heaven who came here at the beginning of the kalpa, feeding on the "earth-fat" (*pṛthivī-parpaṭaka*). Their bodies...
The character for "heavy" (chóng) was not removed; consequently, he became a human being and retained his original name, thus being called "Fan" (Brahman).
Wherever there were foreign (Hu) words, they were replaced with "Fan," so that future scholars who discuss these matters well might grasp their true meaning.
Today, Yunmen refers to Buddhas and patriarchs as "Hu"; this is also a case of following established tradition. Regarding "Shendu" (India): "Du" is pronounced like "du" (in "dǔ").
*Yězhì* (野榸) is pronounced with the *jiē* and *qiè* finals. It refers to the appearance of roots protruding from a withered tree. In the *Yuǎnfúshānjiǔdài* (遠浮山九帶), it is written as *yělí* (野狸).
This is because the characters [of the original] do not form a standard word; there are three explanations for this: first, that it consists of the two characters *ōu* (嘔) and *ā* (啊);

second, that it is a transliterated sound (*yīnzì*) that is not translated; and third, that it is the Sanskrit word for "heart" (*citta*). All of these refer to the title at the head of the sutra fascicle.

It is a word. Regarding the term *oṃ*, the Master of the *Qīngliáng* Commentary states: "The establishment of 'Thus' (*evam*) at the beginning of the Sūtra is intended to distinguish it from the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Thus, the sūtras of the non-Buddhists all begin with *oṃ*, or as some say, *ā-uṃ*, taking this to signify auspiciousness. Here, 'ā' means non-existence (*abhāva*) and 'uṃ' means existence (*bhāva*).
Although the myriad phenomena are numerous, they do not transcend existence and non-existence; this, however, is merely a calculation based on the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism."
The present "Thus" (evam) is precisely Suchness (tathatā). It serves to refute false doctrines by means of its wondrous presence, thereby manifesting the Middle Way.
Within the temporal teachings of a single lifetime, nothing exceeds these two characters, "Thus. In the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*, there are six new principles for translating scriptures.

First, the principle of translating words versus translating sounds, which is divided into four parts. First: translating words without translating sounds; this refers to *dhāraṇīs*. Second: ... [text continues] ...
1. Translating sounds but not characters: this refers to the *svastika* on the Buddha’s chest. 2. Translating both sounds and characters: this refers to the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras.
3. Translating neither sounds nor characters: this refers to the characters used for the titles of sūtras, such as "Ō" (嗚) or "A" (阿).

Furthermore, the opening formula "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) is not placed outside the text upon a marginal title; thus, it is said that both sound and character are not translated [in that specific sense].

It is unclear from whom this originated. Examining these two accounts, they both seem to lack foundation. Some have even recklessly identified it as the *hrdaya* (heart) syllable of the Sanskrit script;
yet since this claim does not even exist in the Sanskrit originals, such a view is especially erroneous.

When I once visited the Chuanfa Yuan (Dharma Transmission Court) in Xingguo, I privately obtained authentic palm-leaf manuscripts from India. Upon examining the titles of those scriptures that had not yet been translated, [I found...]
Since it has not yet been established, how could there be any textual evidence for its characters? It is likely that from ancient times, people have habitually propagated erroneous explanations;
the Dharma-gate of the former sages does not reside therein. Someone asked: "From what did the physical form at the beginning of the sutra originate?
It is certainly beyond doubt that at that time, a hired scribe was transcribing the text and inadvertently covered over the title. Nevertheless, the Master [Zhiyi] relied upon it...
This is intended to guide future students; how could it be something for the intellect to deliberate upon?
"Yufeng" should be read as "Gengfeng.
"Diaoti diao" should be read as "didi," meaning "to face" or "to confront."
"Ti-gang" (提綱) should be read as "ti-gang" (提綱), meaning to lift the main framework and shake the collar. All subsequent instances follow this pattern.
Regarding "piercing a wall," the *Xijing zaji* (Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital) states: Kuang Heng, courtesy name Zhigui, was a native of Dongyang. He was fond of reading books;
being poor at home and lacking oil for lamps, he pierced a hole in the wall of his neighbor's house to catch the light and read by it. He eventually rose to the rank of Chancellor (*xiang*).

The *Kūrmāpūpama-sūtra* (The Sūtra of the Blind Turtle) states: The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, "Suppose there were a blind turtle in the great ocean with a lifespan of immeasurable kalpas, which once every hundred years would raise its head above the water.
Floating upon it was a single piece of wood with exactly one hole, drifting and tossed by the waves of the sea, moving east and west with the current.
The blind turtle, emerging once every hundred years, might happen to encounter this hole. [If it did so] at the eastern edge of the sea..."
The floating wood may drift to the western side of the ocean; the same applies to its circling. Although their paths may diverge, they might nonetheless meet.
For an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) drifting in the ocean of the five destinies (*pañcagati*) to regain a human body is even more difficult than this. Furthermore, the *Vyūha-śāstra* states:
A young boy heard the Buddha say that a human body is difficult to obtain, like a blind turtle encountering the hole of a floating log.
A young boy bored a hole through a wooden board and placed it in the water of a pond. He tried to pass his head through it in and out repeatedly, yet he could never succeed.
He said, "A blind turtle that surfaces once every hundred years in the ocean—what day will it ever encounter this?
Now that I am a human being with eyes and a face, surfacing a hundred times a day, it is still difficult for me to find this hole in the wood."
"Lì" (利) should be read as "líng" (靈). The following instances are all to be treated in this manner.

Regarding "piercing the willow leaves," the *Shiji* (Records of the Grand Historian) states: Yang Shu, whose courtesy name was Youji, could shoot at willow leaves from a distance of one hundred paces; he hit the mark every time he released an arrow.

"Lingping" (伶俜) should be written as "lingping" (竛竮). The upper character is pronounced with the *lú* rhyme and the *jīng* initial; the lower character is pronounced with the *pāng* rhyme and the *dīng* initial. It means walking unsteadily. "Sapī" (撒披) should be written as "sàn pī" (散披).
The upper character is pronounced with the *sān* rhyme and the *dān* initial. "Sǎ" (撒) has the sound *sà*; it does not carry this meaning.
*Jíliáo*: the first character is pronounced with the *zi* and *qiè* finals; the second has the phonetic value *liáo*. Both are names for insects.
Regarding *Fúsāng*, the *Huáihuánzǐ* states: "Fúsāng is where the sun rises; it is within the Yang Valley (*Yánggǔ*). Its mulberry trees grow supporting one another.
The character *fú* (floating) should be read as *fú* (supporting).
A frog is currently acting as a *ma* (pronounced *ma*).
This is the "Song of Realizing the Way through the Five Natures.

Regarding the Western method of "severing the head and cutting off the arms": whenever one encounters a debate and their argument falls into error, they immediately sever their head and cut off their arms.
I apologize for my lack of proficiency.

After the Second Patriarch settled his karmic debts, he transmitted the Dharma to Kezang. Subsequently, at the Triple Gate of Kuangjiu Temple in Guan City County, he expounded the Unsurpassed Way, and those who listened gathered like a forest.
At that time, Dharma Master Bianhe was lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* at that same temple.
The *Pán jīng* (Discourse on the Bowl). When his disciples heard that their master was expounding the Dharma, they gradually drifted away.
Fǎhé, unable to contain his indignation, instigated a slander against the district magistrate, Zhái Zhòngkǎn. Zhòngkǎn was deluded by these claims and subjected the Master to unlawful treatment.
The Master remained serene and accepted it with resignation. Those who recognize the truth say this was him "repaying a debt. Hào Yuè Gōngfù asked Chángshā Cén: "To understand..."
"Karmic obstacles are originally empty; if one has not realized this, one must repay past debts.
Why, then, did the Venerable Siṃha and the Second Patriarch repay their debts? Cen said: "Virtuous One, you do not recognize that they are originally empty.

"How is it that they are originally empty? "It is because karmic obstacles are [empty]. "How is it that karmic obstacles are [empty]? "It is because original emptiness is [the nature of karmic obstacles]."
Chongfeng remained silent. Changsha then presented this verse: "Provisionally existent, it is fundamentally not existent; Provisionally extinguished, it is likewise not non-existent.
The meaning of Nirvana as the settling of debts— In its single nature, there is no further distinction."
The outer coffin revealed his feet with the double lotus position in the state of *nirvāṇa*.

At that time, Kāśyapa and his disciples were on Vulture Peak Mountain, having entered into right concentration (*samādhi*). While in this meditative absorption, their hearts suddenly leaped and their entire bodies trembled.
Emerging from concentration, they saw that the mountains and earth were all shaking violently; they immediately knew that the Tathāgata had already entered *nirvāṇa*. Thereupon...
Leading his disciples, he traveled swiftly along the road, proceeding with great sorrow. Exactly seven days later, they arrived at the city of Kuśinagara.
He circumambulated the precious coffin seven times to the right, his eyes overflowing with tears, and praised it by reciting verses, the gist of which was:
"World-Honored One, I am now in great agony; my mind is disordered, bewildered, and clouded. I now come to pay homage to the World-Honored One."
Is it that you weep in grief at the Tathāgata’s shoulders? Is it that you pay respectful homage to the Great Sage’s hands?

Is it that you mournfully pay homage to the Tathāgata’s waist? Is it that you respectfully pay homage to the Tathāgata’s navel? Or is it that you, with a profound heart, pay homage to the Buddha’s feet? For what reason do you not see the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa?
I only pray that you will show me the place where I may pay my respects. Out of great compassion, the World-Honored One immediately manifested a thousand [forms].
The marks of the thousand-spoked wheels emerged from outside the coffin and turned to show Kāśyapa.

From these thousand-spoked wheels, a thousand rays of light were emitted, illuminating all worlds throughout the ten directions. Thereafter, they returned and re-entered the coffin, which was sealed shut as before.
"Jǐn shāo" (緊梢) should be read as "jì" (帩), with the phonetic component "qiū" (七笑切). It means to bind. "Shāo" (梢) has the pronunciation "shāo" (音筲); it is not the correct meaning.
"Qì xūn" (氣勳) should be read as "xūn" (熏), with the phonetic component "yún" (許云切). It refers to the appearance of intense fire-gas. "Xūn" (勳) refers to merit; it is not the correct meaning.
Regarding "horizontal teaching" and "vertical teaching," Huangbo addressed the assembly, saying: "Under Master Mazu, there were eighty-eight people who sat in the place of enlightenment;
those who attained the True Eye numbered no more than two or three. Master Huineng of Mount Lu was one of them.
Those who have left the household life must know that there is a matter handed down from of old. For instance, under the Fourth Patriarch, there was Master Daorong, who taught horizontally."

This is the vertical teaching. One still does not yet know the pivotal catch that lies above; it is only with such an eye and brain that one can distinguish between the factions of the heterodox and the orthodox.
The character for "pivotal catch" (guān-lì) is pronounced lì (li4), meaning something that can be pulled or turned.
The character 狂 (kuáng) with the radical 犬 (dog) on top is pronounced jiè; it means scabies or leprosy.
The character 忙 (máng) should be written as 茫 (máng), meaning boundless or infinite. "Máng" [in its current form] denotes a state of mental urgency, which is not the intended meaning here.

*Mù* (謔) should be read as *huò* (諕). Pronounced with the initial *xǔ* and rhyme *yà*. It means to deceive. *Xū* (謔) is pronounced with the initial *xū* and rhyme *yuē*. It means to play or joke. These are not their primary meanings;

all subsequent instances follow this pattern. The character *guó* (國) above is identical to *hé* (盍). Pronounced with the initial *hú* and rhyme *là*, or it may follow *gài* (丐), with the pronunciation *hū*. These are not their primary meanings; the explanation is found under "Snow" (*Xuě*).
Regarding "竇頌古":
"躇蹰" (chúchú) should be written as "躊躇" (chóuchú), with the pronunciation *t'ou-ch'u*. It means to hesitate or be unable to proceed. "躇蹰" is not the correct meaning; "蹰" has the pronunciation *chú*.

"Zhuó rán" (酌然) should be read as "zháo rán" (灼然). [The character] zhǎo (隻) is pronounced with the *lue* (略) initial. It means "brightly shining. As for "zhuó" (酌), according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to pour wine and serve the cup";
this is not the correct meaning here.
"Míng méng" (冥濛) should be read as "míng méng" (冥蒙). "Méng" (蒙) means "obscure" or "dim."
"Jì (濟) in 木承 (木承濟) should correctly be written as Zhěng (拯). It is pronounced with the rising tone of 蒸 (zhēng); it means to lift up.

Āi qiáo (艾樵) should be written as Āi jiào (艾燋), pronounced with the *zi* rhyme group (*zǐ xiào*). It refers to a torch used for scorching tortoise shells. It is sometimes written as Jué (爝); Jué is the name of an official who managed fire.
When Tang obtained Yī Yǐn, he employed him as a Jué to manage the *guàn* fire; this merely refers to one who possesses a flaming torch. [The other reading] is not correct."

"Yūn-hú" (言*忽) and "zǔ-zǔ" (詛詛) are glossed as "ān-tiān-yī" (按天衣); the ancient text reads "kōng-kōng" (悾悾). The characters for "kōng" are pronounced "kōng" (孔) and "sōng" (熜). It signifies a state of being full or abundant.
The character below "dùnzhì" (鈍置) should be read as "zhì" (躓), pronounced *zhì*. It means to be obstructed and unable to proceed.

The five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). Having characteristics is form; experiencing is called feeling; grasping images is perception;
shifting and flowing are formations; and discerning is consciousness. "Aggregate" (*skandha*) has the meaning of accumulation; that is, the accumulation of births.
The faults and perils of death are also called the five aggregates (*skandhas*). "Aggregate" (*skandha*) takes the sense of "covering" or "obscuring.
It is obscured by the dark clouds of ignorance, which shroud the true nature and encompass all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).

"Bi" (擗) at the beginning of the phrase should be read as "pi" (劈), with the phonetic gloss *pì lì* (匹歷切); it means to split. "Bi" (擗) pronounced as *bì* (音闢) means to stroke; this is not the correct meaning here.

Regarding "seeing and hearing without sound," the Master of Old (Laozi) said: "When one looks at it, it cannot be seen; it is called the Subtle (*yí*). When one listens to it, it cannot be heard; it is called the Rare (*xī*).
When one grasps at it, it cannot be obtained; it is called the Minute (*wēi*)."

Regarding "the sound of the bell" (zhōngshēng): the ancient text reads "inside the sound of the bell" (zhōngshēng lǐ). "Wearing the seven-strip robe" (pī qītiáo) refers to wearing it over the bones and buttocks;
"gǔ" is pronounced "kuò," meaning "gǔmǐ" (the upper part of the thigh). It means [wearing it] upon the thighs.

The character 涕 (tì) above is correctly written as 洟 (tì); its pronunciation is *ti*. It refers to nasal mucus. The character below is pronounced with the initial *tǔ* and the final *wò* (i.e., *tuō*). It refers to saliva.
"Struck by an axe" should be written as "chopped by an axe," as seen in other editions.
"Han-qing" should be understood as "Han-lu. "Lu" means black; it refers to a black dog.
When people of Qi and those of Han were judging dogs in the marketplace, there was a dog that barked and howled, and the people of Han knew it was excellent. (See *Jianxuan* commentary.)
Regarding the verse hymns composed by Yunmen: none of them bear titles. Some extol the fundamental tenets, while others exhort future generations;

they are not like the works of secular poets who wait for a title before composing. Consequently, later scholars have offered diverse interpretations, many of which are mere conjectures that lose sight of the true Way.
I have often read the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Transmission of the Lamp) and the *Guang Deng Lu* (Extended Lamp).
Along with the *Extensive Record of Xuefeng*, there are only one or two verses concerning this karmic connection; I have not heard of any others.
I now record them below. The *Chuan deng lu* states: A monk asked Yunmen, "How can one ensure that the twelve periods of the day do not pass in vain?
Yunmen said, "Where would you place this question? The student did not understand and requested the Master's instruction.
The Case: When Jue was asked for his brush, he composed a verse, saying: "Jue does not look back; it is already a deviation. If you attempt to deliberate, when in kalpa will you awaken?
Furthermore, in the *Extensive Record of Xuefeng*, a monk asked: "What is the student’s own self? Xuefeng replied: "It hits your nostrils.
The monk looked up at Yunmen, who asked: "How do you understand this? While the monk was still reflecting, [the dialogue concluded].
The Gatekeeper also indicated this to him with the following verse. *Guangdeng* says: Upāśaka Fulang left home at a young age and frequently frequented lecture halls.
Having heard it said that a monk asked Yunmen, "What is the phrase that penetrates the Dharmakāya?
to which Yunmen replied, "Hide your body within the Big Dipper," Fulang was bewildered. He then went to visit him. Upon seeing him, Yunmen seized him and said, "Speak! Speak!"
Lang raised a query, and Yunmen then excused himself by opening the door. He subsequently composed the "Verse on Yunmen’s Sudden Piercing" (*Yunmen Songti*) to demonstrate this point;
Lang thereby attained awakening. Consequently, later students, upon seeing this anecdote, have given rise to groundless interpretations and forced constructions.
Yet, why must it necessarily be so?
To attempt to interpret ancient language is like holding a conch-shell to measure the ocean or grasping a tube to peer at the heavens.
Regarding the surname "Kang" (康), according to the biography of Senghui by Huijiao of the Liang dynasty: Dharma Master Senghui was originally the crown prince of the King of Kangju;
therefore, he was called by the surname Kang. The Master’s physical appearance was magnificent and imposing, and he was held in high esteem by the world.
"Jin feng ba bo jin feng" (The advancing point, the eight broads, the advancing point). This refers to the brush-point of Prince Jin Wang Yishao. "Ba bo" (the eight broads) is not clearly defined;
it is likely a phonetic corruption of "ba fa" (the eight methods). The *Jin jing* states: "The eight methods originated at the inception of the clerical script (*li*).
They were transmitted and employed by Cui, Zhang, Zhong, and Wang. As the supreme path of the brush, they must be understood."
The Sui monk Zhiyong elucidated its essential principles to Yu Shinan; from that time onward, the transmission was established and its existence made manifest.

Li Yangbing said: "In the past, when Yishao practiced calligraphy, he did so for many years. During fifteen years, he focused specifically on the character 'Yong' (永), because through the momentum of its eight strokes, one can master all characters.
These eight strokes are: [the vertical], [the left-falling stroke], [the right-falling stroke], [the hook], [the bend], [the left-tick], [the right-tick], and [the dot]. Yong...
A character consists of eight strokes: first, the dot is the *zè*; second, the horizontal is the *lè*; third, the vertical is the *nǔ*; fourth, the upward hook is the *tì*;
fifth, the upper-left stroke is the *cè*; sixth, the downward stroke is the *lüè*; seventh, the upper-right stroke is the *zhuó*; eighth, the downward stroke is the *zhé*.
This is *zé* (the slant). As for "slant," it means to be oblique; one must not keep the brush straight. 1. This is *lè* (the press). It is like a drill scraping stone;
the brush must not be laid flat. 〡. This is *shù* (the vertical). When drawing the vertical, it should be like a drawn bow; it must not be straight, for if it is straight, it lacks power.
[于-干]. This is *tiāo* (the lift). *Tiāo* is the same as *tì* (the kick); one must maintain the tip of the brush and emerge with momentum.
This is *ce* (策). One strikes the back of the brush, lifts it upward, and withdraws it; this is the character 丿. This is *lüè* (掠). The tip of the brush moves out to the left and must be harmonized;
this is the character [白-日]. This is *zhuó* (啄). It must be executed swiftly; this is the character 乀. This is *zhé* (磔).
It must be neither too swift nor too slow; this is the character 磔. (The pronunciation of *zhé* is *zhé-gé*.)
Regarding the three phrases: Yunmen once addressed the assembly, saying, "The box covers the sky;
the eye weighs the grain. Without ascending the worldly conditions, how do you take this up? He provided his own verse in response: "A single arrowhead pierces the three barriers.
Although he had this intention, he never formally established them as "three phrases. Formerly, Chan Master Puan Dao, because of Deshan...
He uttered three phrases and followed them with a verse, which is appended at the end of this volume. It is often the case that this verse is attributed to Yunmen;
however, such views all stem from a lack of careful examination. Dao was the direct successor of Deshan.
In every instance and every object, "shāng" (傷) should be read as "zǒng" (總). It is not "shāng. This is an error resulting from the similarity of the characters' forms.

In "zhěnhòu" (軫候), the upper character should be "zhěn" (診), pronounced with the initial *zhǐ* and the final *rěn*. It means "to examine" or "to diagnose. "Zhěn" (軫) refers to the horizontal wooden bar at the rear of a carriage; it does not carry this meaning here.
"Ophthalmology" (yǎnyīng) should be understood as "cataract" (yì); it means an obstruction.
"Deliberation" (shāngliáng) is like the measuring of merchants, ensuring that things do not deviate from the middle way so that each may obtain their intended purpose.
"Xiāodé gè fēiyáo" (消得箇非遙) should be read as "Xiāodé gè niàotóu" (消得箇搖頭). "Xiū" (休) and "tóu" (頭) share the same rhyme.
This concludes the various dialectal pronunciations; it refers to gestures and deportment.
“Shi” (什) should be read as “shifang” (十方, ten directions). “Shi” means “mixed”; it does not carry this meaning here.

“Dongyiyan” (同一眼, same eye) should be read as “kaiyiyan” (開一眼, open one eye). Following Yunmen’s *Duiji Lu* (Record of Responding to Occasions), appended are twelve verses composed by Chan Master Puan Dao.
The title of the three-verse sets of three lines originated with Deshan; the remainder [is as follows].
These nine titles and their accompanying verses all describe his own deeds; they are found together in the *Guangdeng lu*.
Regarding the entry for Yunmen in the lower volume of the *Lüshi chunqiu*: "A man of Chu was crossing a river by boat when he dropped his sword from the vessel. He immediately..."
He carved [his name] upon his boat, saying, "I dropped my sword here; when I search for it, I shall surely find it. Such is the nature of his delusion.
"Ju-jue" (舉覺) should be understood as "duo-jue" (搉覺). *Boya* (博雅) states that "yang-duo" (揚搉) means "general summary" (*dúfán*). "Duo" (搉) is pronounced *jué*.
"Death that is not *diào* (弔). Here, *diào* should be read as *dìào* (弔), with the phonetic component of *duō xiào* (多嘯). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "To inquire after the end [of life].

In ancient times, those who buried their dead would cover them thickly with firewood; the character is formed from a person holding a bow, signifying the driving away of birds and beasts. The *Liji* states: "There are three types of death that do not merit a formal visit of condolence (*diào*):
those who die of fear, those crushed by a collapse, and those drowned. Regarding "drowned," this refers to those who leaped into a river.

The city grounds should be made into moats and ditches. Within these moats and ditches is where the ruler resides. "Grounds" (*di*) is a scribal error; see other editions. *Rèn* (任) means "to allow" or "at one's disposal.
*Hé* (何) is pronounced with the final consonant *qie* (切); it means "to carry" (*dàn*). It is also pronounced *hé*. Xu Xuan said: "Danhé" (儋何) refers to... [text ends].
What does "carrying" mean?
At fifteen, while at Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai during the summer retreat, Hanshanzi saw a monk reciting the precepts during the fortnightly assembly.
The monk said, "You gather your heads together to form a faction; why do you let such matters drift by idly? He then struck and scolded him. It was then that he [Hanshan] met Shide.
Clapping his hands in loud laughter, he departed.
"Luofu" and "Tantuo" are the names of two mountains. Luofu is located in present-day Guangzhou. Tantuo is in the kingdom of Piṇḍa in the Western Regions;
it is the very place where the World-Honored One met Ārāḍa Kālāma.
*Cuò* (蹙) is pronounced with the *zi* (子) and *liù* (六) finals; it means to contract or shrink.
*Dǒu sǒu* (斗擻) should be read as *dǒu sǒu* (抖擻); it means to shake or toss up objects.
The *Móshāotù Dípó Púsà Shì Léngqiéjīng Zhōng Xiǎoshèng Nièpán Lùn* (摩[少/兔]提婆菩薩釋楞伽經中小乘涅槃論) states that the non-Buddhists... [text continues].
Regarding the treatise on female retinues, the masters of the Abhidharma explain that the deity Maheśvara created eight women:
first, named Atiñji, who gave birth to the devas; second, named Tiñji, who gave birth to the asuras; third, named Surasa, who gave birth to the nāgas;
fourth, named Vinatā, who gave birth to the birds; fifth, named Kapilā, who gave birth to quadrupeds; sixth... [text continues].
The seventh is named Mātaṅga; it gives birth to humans. The eighth is named Ilā; it gives birth to all kinds of grain seeds. The ninth is named Ketus;
it gives birth to all snakes, scorpions, mosquitoes, gadflies, flies, fleas, centipedes, millipedes, and so forth.
Regarding the *kāṅ* (鵝) and the *wěn* (吻): it is said that the Han Palace of Bailing (柏梁殿) frequently caught fire.
A sorcerer offered a ritual technique, taking the tail of a *kāṅ* fish and placing it upon the palace roof to ward off the flames. Today, these are made of tile;
they are traditionally called *kāṅ-wěn*, but the term *kāṅ-wěi* (鵝尾, "kāṅ-tail") is not used. This is likely an error among the common people.
"Zhuāngxiāngzhūāng": it should be read as "zhuāng," meaning to wrap or pack. "Dàshā":
the first character is pronounced with the *tā* and *gài* finals; it means "extreme. The second character is pronounced with the *suǒ* and *bài* finals; it means "fierce. "Móshē":
the correct form is "chāo," pronounced with the *sāng* and *hé* finals; it means to rub.
"Huangquan" (Yellow Springs) refers to where people return upon death; it denotes the profound depths of the underworld.
"Ri-xie" (Sun Pavilion) should be written with the "ice" radical (冫), as in *bīng-diào* (frost-withering). To use "xie" (pavilion) here—referring to a terrace or pavilion—is incorrect in meaning.
*Shēnkōng* (Deep Pit) is correctly written as *kēng*. [The character] is pronounced *qiūgēng* (cut by *gēng*).
*Bùtiào* (Tumbling) is correctly written as *bòtiào*. The pronunciation is *bèitiào*. It means to leap over or push aside.
*Xuánshū* (Profound Difference) should be written as *xuánshū*. *Xuán* means distant.
The name of the county, Jianghua, is located in Daozhou of Xiangnan. The character *shěng* (眚) is pronounced with the initial *jǐng* (景) and the final *qiè* (切);
it refers to a cataract or film appearing on the eye due to illness.

The character *bù* (不) in *bùnì* (不溺) should be read as *nì* (匿), pronounced with the initial *nú* (奴) and the final *lì* (力); it means to hide or conceal. To take it as "not drowning" (*ní* [沉溺]) is not the correct meaning.
"Ènmè" (恁麼): "Èn" (恁) means "to give. "Mò" (麼) is from "yāo" (幺). "Zuò mǒ" (作麼) and "yǔ mǒ" (與麼) are terms of indication.
It is also written as "ènmè. "Èn" (恁) is pronounced "rěn" (稔); it means "thought. "Ènmè" (恁麼) is a term of examination. It is also written as "shén mǒ" (什麼). "Dāng zuò shén mǒ" (當作甚麼):
"Shén" (什) is a miscellaneous character; it has no specific meaning. It is also written as "zé mǒ" (漝麼). "Zé" (漝) is pronounced "shí" (十); it refers to water.

"Mao" (貌) is also pronounced "xi" (習). "Chu" (滀) and "ze" (漝) are descriptions of water; neither carries the intended meaning here.
