"When one should cut, if one does not cut, one will instead suffer the resulting chaos. One day, while Baizhang was walking in the fields with Mazu, they saw a flock of wild geese. Mazu—
As he passed through the midst of them, the wild geese were startled and scattered. When Mazu followed behind, the geese were not startled.
Mazu then asked the Master, "When you passed through the flock of geese, why did they scatter? And when I passed, why did they not scatter?
The Patriarch replied, "I had a murderous intent; you had no murderous intent. They continued on their way and saw some water ducks. Pointing at them, the Patriarch asked, "What are these? Mazu said:
The Wild Duck. After a long silence, the Master said, "Where have you gone? Zhaozhou replied, "I flew over there.
The Master stepped forward, seized Zhaozhou by the nose, and pulled it. Zhaozhou let out a cry of "Aiya! The Master said, "You said you flew over there;
it turns out you were all along right here. He then released him. Zhaozhou was left with sweat pouring down his back.

At this point, there was an awakening. The next day, when the Patriarch entered the hall for the formal lecture, as soon as the assembly had gathered, Baizhang stepped forward and rolled up his sitting mat.
The Patriarch returned to his quarters, and Baizhang stood in attendance. The Patriarch then asked, "I have just now ascended the hall and have not yet preached the Dharma to the assembly;
why did you roll up your mat? Baizhang replied, "Haihai’s nose is still aching today."
The Patriarch asked, "Where did you come from yesterday? Baizhang replied, "Today my nostrils do not ache.
The Patriarch said, "You have thoroughly understood what happened yesterday. After Baizhang had prostrated in thanks, he went again to consult Mazu, as recorded in the *Zongpai Lu*.

Regarding the characters *diāo* (刁) and *dāo* (刀), ancient glosses state: "When the brush has grown weary from labor, one writes *diāo* as *dāo*. When affairs have passed through antiquity, one writes *yú* (魚) as *lǔ* (魯).
As for the character *cēnchā* (參差):
the upper part is pronounced *chǔ* (楚) with the initial *zhěn* (簪), and the lower part is pronounced *chǔ* (楚) with the initial *yí* (宜); it means "uneven" or "irregular."
*Mán* (in *mǎn*) should be read as *màn*; it means to deceive. The others follow this pattern.
*Yù* (in *yùmù*) has the upper tone; it means to corrode.
*Dàyě* (in *dàyě yángzhěqiè*) refers to a furnace or smelting works; *yě* means to melt or cast metal.
*Dèng* (凳): pronounced with the *dù* and *dèng* finals.

The character for "capable of subduing" (*fú*) in the phrase "capable of subduing the leopard" (*néng fú bǎo*) should be read as *fú* [with the radical *rén* minus *ér* plus *dāo*]. Pronounced with the *yú* and *jiào* finals; it means "obstinate" or "rebellious.
See Yuanshan Lu.
*Pīpǔ* (劈溥): pronounced *jīqiè*; to split or break. *Dèngmù* (瞪目): pronounced *zhàngzhèng*;
the appearance of staring fixedly. "Linji" (林際) should be read as "Linji" (臨濟);
it is the name of a monastery. The Master's name was Yixuan (義玄). He was a native of Nanhua in Caozhou and his surname was [Wu].
Xingshi left home at the age of seven and received full ordination upon reaching the age of twenty. From an early age, she admired the Chan school and first visited Huangbo.
There, the First Seat of the hall instructed her to go and inquire about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma. Huangbo struck her;
this happened three times as she entered his quarters, each time receiving sixty blows of the staff. When she wished to take her leave, the First Seat detained her, saying to Huangbo:
Yixuan said, "Although I am of later birth, I seem fit to be a vessel for the Dharma. Baizhang said, "I know this son. He is like a great tree in the wild;
he shall provide shade and coolness for the world. Just as the Master was about to take his leave, Baizhang said, "You should go to Daoyu at Ga’ān Tanchou;
he will surely clarify this matter for you. When Daoyu saw the Master arrive, he asked him:
For this reason, he recounted the previous conversation and asked: "Yixuan was beaten by Huangbo three times;
I do not know what fault I committed. Yunyu said, "Huangbo was so compassionate that he exhausted himself for your sake, yet you still ask whether there was a fault or not.
At these words, the Master realized his true home and cried out in realization: "So, Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma is..."
Wu Duizi. Yuyi grabbed him and said, "You bed-wetting ghost! Having seen what, do you speak thus? The Master struck Yuyi three times under the ribs.
Yuyi pushed him away and said, "Your teacher is Huangbo; it is none of my business. The Master returned to Huangbo.
When Huangbo saw him, he asked, "Coming and going like this, when will there ever be an end? The Master—
Baizhang said, "It was simply because his compassionate heart was so earnest. He then prostrated himself; only after rising did Huangbo ask, "Where have you been?
The Master then recounted the occasion of his meeting with Dayu. Huangbo said, "How can I get that old, garrulous fellow Dayu to come here?
The Master asked, "What would you do with him if you saw him? Huangbo replied, "Wait for him to arrive, and give him a thorough beating!"
"Dun! The Master said, "What are you talking about? Waiting for him to come? I shall give it to you right now. He then struck Huangbo with his palm.
Huangbo said, "A madman coming here to pull at a tiger’s whiskers. The Master then shouted. Huangbo said, "Go to the hall to practice.
Later, when the Master returned to his hometown, he accepted the request of the people of Zhao and resided at the Linji Chan Garden south of the city of Zhenfu.
As he was approaching his death, he ascended the hall and said, "After my passing, you must not extinguish my Treasury of the True Dharma Eye.
At that time, Sansheng was the head of the monastery, and he replied, "How would we dare extinguish it? The Master said, "In the future, if someone asks you, what will you say to them?
The head of the monastery then gave a shout. The Master said, "Who knew that my Treasury of the True Dharma Eye was right here in this blind eye?"

He said, "I shall pass away at the side of the donkey," and having finished speaking, he sat down to manifest his transformation. This was the tenth day of the fourth month in the seventh year of the Xian Tong era of the Tang Emperor Yizong.
He did not bow to Maitreya and gave a high salute to Śākyamuni. His failure to bow to Maitreya represents the Chan school’s severing of the distinction between the holy and the ordinary.
[This is] a statement. However, there is also a source for the reason why he did not prostrate. According to the *Tripiṭaka-avadāna* (Biographies of the Tripiṭaka Masters), it says:
"Four or five *li* south of the city of the kingdom of Mathurā is a small monastery; this is where the Master of Śāstras Guṇaprabha composed over a hundred treatises, such as the *Tattvasaṃdeśa*.
The Master was originally from the country of Pārvatīya; he initially studied the Mahāyāna, but later..."
Having renounced the study of the Hīnayāna, the arhat Deva-sena traveled back and forth to Tuṣita Heaven.
Guṇaprabha wished to see Maitreya to resolve his lingering doubts and entreaties; he requested Deva-sena to use his supernatural powers to transport him to the celestial palace.
Once he had seen Maitreya, he merely bowed to him but did not prostrate, saying: "I have now left the household life and am fully ordained; Maitreya dwells in heaven like a layman."
"It is not appropriate to pay him homage. Thus, during his three visits, he did not offer salutations on any occasion.
Since his pride was so great, his doubts remained unresolved; though his words were the same, his intent differed from this.

*Gǎn* (趕): read as *zhèng zuò hàn* (正作捍), with the phonetic component *gǔ* (古) and the rhyme *hàn* (旱). It means to push. This character *gǎn* does not exist in the received editions of the *Shūjīng* (Book of Documents).
*Táo* (苕): read as *tiáo* (條). A type of grass. *Lǚ* (菷): read as *zhǐ yǒu qiè* (止酉切). The correct form is *zhǒu* (帚), meaning a broom.

To "cut through the city" and see the excellence of the patriarchs, like a continuous string of jade, yet to cite Wuye’s response as "Do not engage in conceptualization" (*mò wǎngxiǎng*) is a failure of editorial skill on the part of the compiler. It should have been recorded as:

"Wuye," [then] the monk asked Wuye, "What is the Buddha? [Wuye] said, "Do not engage in conceptualization. The Master [Zhaozhou] said, "[That] blocks the nostrils. Furthermore, he cited: A monk asked Mazu...
"What is the Buddha? [The questioner] said, "This very mind is the Buddha. The Master said, "[I] block my tongue.
Wuye was a successor of Mazu; he was posthumously titled National Teacher Dada.
The character "fang" (妨) in the phrase "using oneself to obstruct others" should be read as "fang" (方), meaning "to compare. In the *Analects*, it says: "Zi Gong compared people.
The Master said, 'Ci, are you so very worthy? As for me, I have no leisure for such things. This shows that Confucius looked down upon Zi Gong’s practice of comparing people.
The character 簽 (qiān) in "signing the melon" (*qiānguā*) should be read as 籤 (qiān). It is pronounced with the *qī* and *lián* finals. It means to cut.

Only three people are Chan masters; this is from the poem by Pǔ of Dàguì. "The Son of Heaven of the Great Táng has only three [Chan masters]"—this is seen in Zhōu Pǔ’s commentary on the phrase "Wáng Cháo's speech" in the *Xiǎoshuō*.
The *Kuìtú* (Diagram of Shame) should be understood as the *Guìtú* (Diagram of Nobility).
The creation of the circular diagrams (*yuánxiàng*) began when National Teacher Nanyang transmitted them to his attendant Danyuan.

Danyuan, having received a prophetic record (*chènjì*), passed them on to Yangshan; thus, they have now come to be known as the "House Style" (*jiāfēng*) of the Weiyang lineage. —From Mingzhou Wufeng.
The Venerable Liang once composed forty cases. Mingben and Qianzi wrote a preface for them, extolling their excellence. Liang said: "The *yuanxiang* (perfect circle) comprises six names:
first, *yuanxiang*; second, *yihai* (ocean of meaning); third, *anjī* (dark trigger); fourth, *zihai* (ocean of characters);
fifth, *yiyu* (intentional speech); and sixth, *molun* (silent discourse). Furthermore, the lineage of the Weiyang school states that Danyuan said to Yangshan:
The National Teacher transmitted ninety-seven *yuanxiang* (circular diagrams) of the six patriarchs to this old monk.
As the National Teacher was about to pass away, he further said: "Thirty years after my extinction, a novice monk shall come from the south and greatly propagate this Way.
Transmit it in succession so that it does not become interrupted. I have carefully examined this prophecy; the matter lies therein.
"I entrust these to you; you must uphold them. Having received them, Yangshan proceeded to burn them with fire.
One day, Dongyuan again said to Yangshan, "The various *yuanxiang* (perfect circles) previously transmitted to you should be kept strictly secret.
Yangshan replied, "I have already burned them. Dongyuan said, "These were passed down by the successive patriarchs until they reached you; why did you burn them?"
Danyuan set it aside. Mount [Shishuang] said, "Huiji has glanced at it once and already knows its meaning; he simply uses it as it is, without clinging to the original.
Danyuan said, "You have attained it, but what about those who come after? Yangshan said, "If the Master wishes, I shall record another copy.
Thereupon, Shishuang recorded it again and presented it; there was not a single discrepancy. One day, while Danyuan was ascending the hall, Yangshan...
He stepped forward from the assembly and formed this *en* (circle) mudrā: he pressed his palms together in a gesture of presentation, then stood with his hands crossed.
Yuan [Zhaozhou] interlaced both hands, made fists, and showed them to him; he then stepped forward three paces and performed a woman’s bow.
Yuan nodded his head, and he immediately prostrated himself. This is the origin from which the *en-so* (circle signs) emerged. I have recorded it here to show future students.
Regarding "learning the Tang-step," consult the commentary on the *Zhuangzi*. Shouling was a commandery of Yan; Handan was a commandery of Zhao.
Being of tender age and not yet mature, he is called a "Yu-zi" (surplus son), which is equivalent to a child. In the region of Zhao’s commandery, the local custom was to be able to walk with grace;
thus, the youths of the state of Yan came to learn this step. Having already deviated from their own nature and failed to acquire the skill of the state of Zhao, they abandoned themselves.
He was attempting to emulate others and lost the reason for his own longevity; therefore, he crawled back on his hands and knees.
Xuedou said, "This monk was not a person from Handan. Why did he learn the 'Tang-step'? This statement is quite incorrect, and the facts are even inverted.
It was actually a person from Yan who learned the step from Handan, not someone from Handan learning the step from Yan.

According to the *Zhuangzi*, "the people of Yan learned the walking style of Zhao"; this text refers to it as the "Tang-style walk. This is likely a mistaken application of the phrase from Fengxue [Loyu]:
"Yue learned the Tang-style walk.

The character 籄 is correctly written as 簣 (*kùì*, pronounced with the *qiú* and *wèi* rhymes), meaning a basket for carrying earth. In the *Shàngshū*, "Lǚáo," it says: "One who does not take care of small matters..."
In the end, this will bring trouble upon the Great Virtuous One. When a mountain has reached nine *ren* high, its completion may be frustrated by a single basketful of earth.
"Tái" (擡) is pronounced with the upper tone as *tái*; it means to lift up. "Niè" (搦) is pronounced with the lower tone *niǎo* or alternatively *nì*; it means to grasp or hold.
The character "huo" (奯) in the name Huogong should be read as "huo" (豁). Yantou’s name was Quanhuo;
there is a record in the *Chanyu* of an Elder Huo who was a dharma heir of Linji, and he is not the same person as Yantou.
In the Western Han, Li Guang’s biography records that he did not receive a fief or rank as a marquis.

Although his official rank never exceeded that of a Nine Minister (*jiuqing*), some of his military officers and soldiers were enfeoffed as marquises. Once, while conversing with Wang Shuo, a diviner of omens, Guang said:

"Ever since the campaign against the Xiongnu, General Guang has never not been among them. Yet, while dozens of men from the rank of ordinary *jiaowei* downward—whose talents and abilities did not even reach the mediocre standard—were enfeoffed as marquises on account of their military merit, General Guang did not lag behind them. Nevertheless, in the end, he failed to gain even a foot or an inch of merit sufficient for a fief. Why is this? Is it that my physiognomy does not warrant a marquisate? Shuo replied: "General, you have indeed served with great distinction. However, when you first set out for battle, your horse was exhausted and your armor was worn; your troops were few and your weapons blunt. You led the vanguard to engage the enemy, yet you were unable to break through their formation. Your soldiers were weary and could not follow your lead. This was your first failure. Later, when you encountered the enemy at the White Tiger Post, you again led the vanguard. Your troops were exhausted and your horses spent; they could not advance. You were surrounded by the enemy and nearly captured. This was your second failure. Afterward, when you were stationed at Yiwu, you were ordered to guard the pass. The enemy army was vast and formidable, yet you were unable to repel them. You were forced to retreat and lost your position. This was your third failure. Finally, when you met the enemy at Maoji, you again led the vanguard. Your troops were exhausted and your horses spent; they could not advance. You were surrounded by the enemy and nearly captured. This was your fourth failure. It is because you have repeatedly committed these failures that you have not yet received a fief. Guang sighed and said: "I am truly unfortunate! Shuo then said: "If you can overcome these four failures, you shall surely receive a fief. Guang asked: "What are the four ways to overcome them? Shuo replied: "When you encounter the enemy, you must first ensure your troops are rested and your horses are fresh. Only then may you lead the vanguard to engage them. This is the first way to overcome failure. When you encounter the enemy, you must first ensure your troops are rested and your horses are fresh. Only then may you lead the vanguard to engage them. This is the second way to overcome failure. When you encounter the enemy, you must first ensure your troops are rested and your horses are fresh. Only then may you lead the vanguard to engage them. This is the third way to overcome failure. When you encounter the enemy, you must first ensure your troops are rested and your horses are fresh. Only then may you lead the vanguard to engage them. This is the fourth way to overcome failure. If you can do this, you will surely receive a fief. Guang thanked him and departed. Later, when he encountered the enemy at Gaixia, he followed Shuo’s instructions and was subsequently enfeoffed as a marquis. He then sent a messenger to thank Shuo, who declined the honor, saying: "This is the result of the General’s own resolve; it is not due to me. Guang replied: "If it had not been for your guidance, I would have perished long ago. It is entirely your doing. Shuo then accepted the title. The General thought to himself, "Have I ever harbored any resentment? Guang replied, "When I was the Governor of Longxi, the Qiang rebelled.
I lured more than eight hundred of their followers to surrender; then, through treachery, I had them all killed on the same day. To this day, my sole regret is this alone.
Shuo said, "There is no calamity greater than killing those who have surrendered. This is precisely why you, General, have not been granted a fief."

Also: *fùtóu* (the head-wrap). [The character] *fù* is pronounced with the rhyme *yù* (玉) and the tone *qiè*. It is a cloth (*pà*). It was the *fùjīn* (square headcloth) created by Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou dynasty;
because it had four corners that were folded over the head, it was thus named. Some write it with the pronunciation *pú* (蒲) and *wò* (沃), which is an error.

"Qiè cuō" should be read as "qiè cuō. The character "cuō" (磋) is pronounced with the initial *cāng* and the final *hé*. It refers to the fresh, bright whiteness of jade. In the *Shijing*: "As if cutting, as if polishing (*qiè cuō*).
[The character] "cuō" (蹉) means to stumble; it is not the correct meaning here.
"Yuánhài (遠害)"—the character for "yīn" (音) is read as "ruó" (挼); it means "to separate.

"Jiāngjūn zhìzhì" (將軍致致)—the first "zhì" (致) should be read as "zhì" (置); it means "to establish. "Zhì" (致) also means "to arrive. It is not [merely] "yi" (義). Furthermore, "zhì" (致) means "to obtain."
Follow this pattern. "觸悞" (chù wù) should be read as "觸忤" (chù wù). "忤" means to oppose; "悞" means to deceive. It is not correct [to use the former].
The *Eilan Guān Fó Sānmèi Jīng* (*Eilan-gandha-taru-buddha-samādhi-sūtra*) states: "The foul-smelling Eilan tree grows together with the sandalwood tree; yet its fragrance..."
The fragrances are distinct; their stench permeates forty *li*, like that of a corpse. As for those red-flowered trees, how can they be objects of delight?
To smell the stench and die—how utterly loathsome!
*Tuó* (the initial *tuó* is pronounced with the *kě* rhyme):
to drag or pull. *Niè* (pronounced *rě*): a term of respect; it should be written as [妳-女+口]. *Yìng*: to respond.
The Chan Master Dachi of the Chan School had two disciples: one was named Jingtong, who succeeded Yangshan;
the other was named Zhitong, who succeeded Guizong Chang.
*Chàn* (禪) is pronounced with the *qì* (慼) radical and the *shā* (砂) phonetic. It means to brush against or touch lightly.
*Bó* (伯) is a respectful title, like the *bó* in "Marquis" (*hóu bó*). Furthermore, during the Jin dynasty, there were eight *bó* established to correspond to the Eight Talents (*bā jùn*).
Just as those skilled in poetry are called "Poetry Masters" (*shī bó*), Du Gongbu’s [Du Fu] so-called "Great Talent" (*cái dà*) refers to this.
"Shībó" (詩伯):
"Dàn" (憚) is pronounced with the *tu* and *àn* finals; it means "difficult.
A tortoise shell (*guī*) is that by which doubts are resolved; a mirror (*jiàn*) is that by which things are distinguished.
*Bòtǎo* (勃趒) is pronounced *bèi*. It means to push aside or displace.
*Náo* (撓) should be written with the radical for wood; it is pronounced *rúzhāo* (如招切).
*Gé* (墼) is pronounced *gǔlì* (古歷切); it refers to a brick made of earth.

"Awakened" (*xīngxīng*) should be understood as "vividly alert" (*xīngxīng*). Its pronunciation is *xīng*. It refers to the clarity of wisdom. To interpret it as "sobering from intoxication" is not correct.
Addressing the assembly, he said: "In the sixteenth board, line twelve of the record concerning Master Juezhī, four characters have been omitted.
'Bao Ying Lao' (Old Man Bao Ying) should be 'Nan Yuan Lao' (Old Man Nan Yuan).
'Wu-shu' is pronounced *wu*; it is the name of a species of animal resembling a small fox, possessing bat-like membranous wings, and is also called a 'flying rat'."
Shengming was at the foot of a bright window when Furi left Yunju and arrived at Jiaoshan. During their exchange of questions and answers, Jiaoshan asked, "With whom do you travel?
Furi replied, "With Old Seat-Master Mu. Jiaoshan said, "Why do you not come to see this old monk? Furi replied, "The Master..."
Looking up at him, he said, "I have my share. Deshan asked, "Where is it? Zhaozhou then made the gesture of planting a staff upright in the earth.
Deshan said, "Did you get it from Mount Tiantai? Zhaozhou said, "It was not born from the Five Peaks. Deshan said, "Did you get it from Mount Sumeru?
Zhaozhou said, "Nor does it travel to the Moon Palace. Deshan said, "Did you get it from a human being? Zhaozhou said, "No."
"Even one's own self is like a born enemy; how much more so that which is obtained from others? Baizhang said, "A single bean popping in cold ashes.
Baizhang then said, "Attendant, call the rector to prepare at the bright window."
*Kan-on-ryō* (鎌音廉). The *Shì míng* (釋名) states: "It is called *ryō* (廉). That which is harvested is thin, resembling a blade.
It is also written as *ryaku* (鐮). *Ryū-mon* (龍門). This is a metaphor for fish. *Ryū-mon* is the mouth where the Yellow River descends; it is located in present-day Longmen County, Jangzhou.
The waters of the Dragon Gate are perilous and impassable; fish and turtles alike are unable to ascend. The Yangtze... [text ends]
Of the thousands of great fish that gather beneath the Dragon Gate, none can ascend; those that do ascend immediately become dragons.
Today, when a scholar is received with courtesy by a person of high standing, it is called "ascending the Dragon Gate. This is seen in the biography of Li Ying of the Eastern Han dynasty.
"A single phrase that hits the mark"—this refers to Yunmen’s "provisional response" (chu dai). An ancient said:
"A single phrase that hits the mark is a tethering stake for a donkey for ten thousand kalpas. How can one understand how to avoid this fault? An ancient referred to this as the "Boatman.
The Boatman asked Jia Shan, "Where did you learn this? Jia Shan replied, "It is not something reached by the ears or eyes. The Boatman—
Xiaoyou said: "A single phrase that fits the head is a tethering stake for ten thousand kalpas. Now Xuedou says:
"If Yunmen had suddenly said, 'A single phrase that fits the head,' this would have been the words of Chuanzi, not Yunmen."
*Erduō* (耳垛): pronounced *dingguò* (丁果); a small cliff. Sometimes written simply as *duǒ* (朵). *Lianjià dájì* (連架打架): should be read as *liánjiā dájì* (連枷打枷);
the character for "枷" (*jiā*) has the phonetic *jiā*. It means a flail. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*: "A flail used for threshing grain. As when a monk asked Puhua:
"What is it like when both light and darkness come together? He replied: "Striking with a flail. *Fù* (拂): pronounced *fú* (弗). A dialectal term.
It is said: "A flail is an instrument for threshing grain.

Regarding Xuedou’s *song* on an ancient case, the character 夥 (huǒ) has the phonetic value of 禍 (huò). According to local dialects, when things are abundant and numerous, the regions between Qi and Song call them 夥.
*Chǎn* (燀赫): The upper character is pronounced with the *shàn* rhyme; it means "to blaze. In the *Zuǒ Zhuan* of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*: "He kindled [the fire] with firewood. In Du Fu’s poem:
"The blazing brilliance of the old family's reputation.
The pronunciation of *yóu* (繇) is *yóu*.
*Xi* (翕): pronounced *xǔ jí qiè*. It means movement; it also means flourishing.
In the *Lunyu*, under the section on the transformation of Lu, the Master said: "Qi, after one transformation, will reach the level of Lu; Lu, after one transformation, will reach the Way.
Commentators say that Qi and Lu both possess the residual influence of the Duke of Tai and the Duke of Zhou. The Duke of Tai was a great sage, and the Duke of Zhou was a saint.
O people! Although the administration and teachings have now declined, if a wise ruler were to arise and promote them, Qi could be made like Lu;
and Lu could be made like the time when the Great Way was practiced.
Yáng (pronounced like yáng): In the *Lunyu*, it says, "How vast it is! It fills the ears.
Here it supersedes the sound of wài.
Xùn, with the phonetic component cí and the tone qiè, means "to follow."
"Zhèn" (朕) is pronounced with the initial *zh-*, the final *-in*, and the level tone; it refers to the omens of good or ill fortune (*zhèn*). "Fǎngfú" (髣髴):

the first character is pronounced with the initial *f-* and the final *-ai* (non-rain), and the second character is pronounced with the initial *f-* and the final *-uo*. "Fǎngfú" denotes a semblance or appearance.
The first-awakened Mencius awakened those who were later-awakened; he was inspired by the *Lunyu*, which states:
"If one is not indignant, I do not awaken them; if one does not struggle to express themselves, I do not reveal the meaning.
The character for "instant" (*shùn*) is pronounced "Shùn"; it refers to the movement of the eyes.
"Chāngqī" (昌期) refers to a period of flourishing prosperity.
"Tǐng" (挺) is pronounced with the initial *dǐng* (徒鼎切). It means to emerge.
"Cuì" (粹) is pronounced with the initial *suì* (雖遂切). It means pure.
Huī (恢): with the initial consonant of kǔ (苦) and the final rhyme of huí (回); it means to expand or enlarge. Chuíyù (垂裕):
with the initial consonant of zhāng (張) and the final rhyme of yángshù (羊戍); it means the Way or principle. Bǐfú (俾夫):
with the initial consonant of bìngmǐ (并弭); it means to cause or enable.
Zhì (zhì, with the initial of zhì and the final of lì):
to obstruct; to block. Ní (ní, with the initial of nú and the final of jì):
to be stuck; to be mired and unable to pass through. Néng (néng): a beast that possesses great strength and is skilled at climbing trees; therefore, one who excels in their affairs is called néng.
*Jiequ* (揭渠): pronounced with the *lie* (列) initial; it means to raise up high. *Jiaoji* (澆季):
pronounced with the *shang* (上) and *yao* (堯) finals; it means meager or thin. "The meager age" (*jiaoji*) refers to this degenerate and superficial end-period. *Xunxun* (循循):
as in the *Lunyu*, where it says, "The Master was *xunxun* and skilled at guiding people. *Xunxun* describes the manner of orderly progression. It refers to the Master... [text continues].
The Master himself used this very path to exhort and advance others in a systematic manner.
"Shenlu" (繕錄) means to transcribe; it is a form of copying. Furthermore, "zhi" (治) means to repair the old and create the new.
The name of the year *Caitra* (攝提格) is given when the Great Year (*tai-sui*) is in the branch of Yǐn (寅). It is called *Caitra*.
According to the *Erya*, the middle month of the eighth month is designated as "male" (*mǔ*). Guo Pu states that this is an alternative name for the sun;
however, the significance of the *sui-yang* (year-yan) reaching this point remains entirely unclear.

*Zai sheng bo zai*. The pronunciation of *zai* is "car" (cài). It means "beginning. It refers to the beginning of the waning phase of the moon. On the sixteenth day, the light fades and the dark phase (*bo*) begins.

In the year of the *Shètígé*, during the middle month of the male year, on the sixteenth day when the waning phase begins—this is the sixteenth day of the eighth month in the Year of the Tiger (*Yín*).
"Zhèn" (朕) is pronounced *zhí rěn qiè*. It refers to "I. In the twenty-sixth year of the Qin Shi era, this term was first adopted as the title for the Son of Heaven.
Regarding "Biàndià" (陛下), Ying Shao said: "A *biàn* is a step leading up to the hall. When a sovereign rules, there must be those holding weapons stationed at the side of these steps.
When the various ministers speak with the Most Honorable One, they do not dare to point directly at him; therefore, they address him as being 'under the steps' (*biàndià*)."

This is done to address them by means of their subordinate titles in order to convey the intent of reaching those who are honorable. Such is the case with current designations like "His Highness," "Your Excellency," "Attendant," and "Officer.
All of these belong to this same category.
The character 蓋 (gài) is also written as 盍 (hé). It is pronounced with the *hú* and *là* rhymes. According to the *Jiyùn*, it is also interchangeable with 蓋, likewise with the *hú* and *là* rhymes.

Nowadays, among the multitude, it is pronounced with the *jū* and *tài* rhymes; this is a corruption resulting from long-standing tradition. If it were pronounced as *gài*, it would mean "bitter" or "suffering," or it would be an interrogative particle.
Furthermore, how could there be any doubt regarding the character 國? For example, in the original records of Xuedou, this [character] is used four times.
Regarding the character 闔 (*hé*): there are those who derive it from 門 (gate) and those who derive it from 盍 (to cover). It is also pronounced *hú lè* (as in *húlà*).

As Yan Shigū of the Western Han dynasty explained the meaning of "the entire commandery" (*héxùn*) in his commentary on the *Hanshu*: "To *hé* means to close. Because it encompasses the entirety of a commandery, it is called 'the entire commandery' (*héxùn*).

Based on this evidence, what further cause for doubt remains? According to the *Nanshi*, Sengzhao and Dharmagupta were certainly not contemporaries. This is recorded in the biography... [text continues].
The Record states that Master Zhi was born at the beginning of the Taishi era of the Song dynasty and passed away in the thirteenth year of the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty.

Twelve years after Zhi’s passing, Bodhidharma first arrived in this land. According to the various records of Baolin, Bodhidharma actually arrived in Guangzhou on the twenty-first day of the ninth month of the first year of the Datong era;
however, the *Zuyuan* (Source of the Patriarchs) states it was the eighth year of the Putong era. This is what the history says.

The *Shu* (Book) states that [the era] lasted only until the seventh year. However, when calculated according to the *Huangyu Changli* (Extended Calendar of the Huangyu Era) starting from the *jiayi* year, there are eight years.

Now, upon examining the *Nanshi* (History of the Southern Dynasties), it indeed records eight years. In the third month of that eighth year, on the *jiaxu* day, the era was changed to "Dagong" (Great Penetration).
Bodhidharma arrived in the ninth month; thus, by the time of Bodhidharma’s arrival, the eighth year had already passed. Furthermore, it mentions Xiao Ang, the Governor of Guangzhou.
[This was] submitted for imperial review. Aṅ was a member of the imperial clan of the Xiao-Liang dynasty. His biography does not record his having governed this prefecture;
rather, it records two nephews named Lì and Bó who once served as Governors of Guangzhou. Furthermore, Aṅ was once summoned to serve as the Prefect of both Langya and Pengcheng.
In all these cases, I suspect there are errors in the transcription of the biographies. It is a pity that Yang Dainian, in his *Chuandeng lu*, failed to verify [the sources].

[The text] was collated. Consequently, later erroneous transmissions led other schools to harbor doubts and suspicions. The *Preface to the Transmission of the Lamp* states: "The year chronologies were compared to rectify discrepancies;
the historical records were consulted to eliminate errors; all [inconsistencies] were deleted, leaving only their words. Furthermore, the *Record of the Orthodox Lineage* states:
"Dharmatrāta actually arrived in the east on the twenty-second day of the ninth month of the first year of the Putong era, the Gengzi year..."
Come forward! As for the previously recorded national edition, since it contains both the correct and the incorrect, I dare not venture to delete it;

I have preserved its deficiencies and doubts out of respect. Alas! The accounts of the Patriarch’s life vary from one source to another, much like the differing dates for the World-Honored One’s birth and parinirvāṇa;
even the Sanskrit manuscripts from India often exhibit discrepancies, which cannot help but give rise to doubt among later generations.

To observe these anomalies in the biographies and discrepancies in the recorded deeds, which cause later generations to harbor doubts and slander—this is the error of those who composed the biographies;
how could it possibly be the intention of the Sage? Reflect upon this.

"Here" (zhè) and "this" (zhè): these are terms used to point to a specific object. Regarding "zhè," the *Sāncuāng* glossary states that its archaic form is identical to the character for "to reach" (*tóngshì*), pronounced with the initial *zhī* and the final *-e*.
Furthermore, the *Piānyùn* records two pronunciations, *dàn* and *yàn*. Only in Chan records is it written with the pronunciation *zhīyě*.
All of these are the result of successive transmission.
A monk asked Xiangyan, "What is the Way? Xiangyan said, "A dragon’s roar within a withered tree. The student said, "I do not understand. Xiangyan said, "An eye within a skull.
He then asked Shishuang, "What is an eye within a skull? Shishuang said, "It still carries consciousness. [The monk] asked again, "What is a dragon’s roar within a withered tree?
Shishuang said: "A withered tree without leaves— How could it have a dragon’s roar? A skull without an eye— How could it have an eye?"
The monk said, "It still seems to carry a trace of joy. The monk asked Caoshan again. Caoshan offered this verse: "The dragon’s cry from a withered tree is the true seeing of the Way;
When consciousness in the skull is exhausted, the eyes first become bright. When the consciousness of joy is exhausted, all news and signs vanish;
How can a person distinguish the clear within the turbid? The monk asked again, "What is the dragon’s cry from within the withered tree? Caoshan replied, "The life-blood."
"Uninterrupted. [The Master asked: "What are the eyes within the skull? The Mountain said: "Dried up. *Zhù yǔ* (著語): *zhī* (知) is pronounced with the *lüè* (略) rhyme;
it means to place or set down. *Xié fù* (挾複):

*xié* (挾) is pronounced with the *hú jiá* (胡頰) rhyme; it means to hold or carry. The lower character should be written as *fú* (幞), pronounced with the *fáng yù* (房玉) rhyme; it refers to a cloth or napkin. *Fù* (複) is pronounced [as above].
"Fú" (福) means "heavy. It is not [the character for] "righteousness" (義).
"Féiqí" (飛騎) refers to the General Li Zǔyīng.
"Lùtíngshàngláng" (虜庭上郎)—the second character is pronounced *gǔ*—is a title used by the Xiongnu.
*Róng*róng (pronounced *róng* with the second tone): the appearance of grass growing.
*Śūnyatā* (舜若多) is translated here as the "Deity Who Masters Space. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "The deity Śūnyatā has no body, yet perceives touch."
*Zhègū* (partridge): the first character is pronounced *shàng* with the *qiè* [rhyme] *zhé*; the second character is pronounced *gū*. Its shape resembles that of a pheasant;
it is born in Jiangnan. *Hù* (ladle): the *qiè* [rhyme] is *wán-gù*. It refers to a ladle, a vessel for scooping water.
The Poem of Bai Gui from the "Yi" (Suppression) chapter: "A flaw in white jade may still be polished away; but a flaw in these words cannot be remedied. Commentators say: "Dian" means a defect.
A defect in jade may still be ground and polished, but words once spoken must not be defective. "Lü" (in the term "polish") is pronounced like "lü" (as in "consideration");
it means to rub or grind with a file.
*Pī* (pronounced *pǐ* with the *pǔ* and *jī* finals): to split; to break. *Śakara*:
translated here as "vajra" (diamond/thunderbolt); it is also called "firm and solid.
*Lüèxū* (the first syllable pronounced with the initial *l* and final *lüè*): to seize; to snatch away.
The Two Blind Men Broadly Illuminating the Lamp. Venerable Master Shǒngniàn of Bǎoyìng ascended the hall and said:
"Venerable elders, you must not shout blindly or shout recklessly. Here, I have always told you: when there is a guest, it is a guest from beginning to end;
when there is a host, it is a host from beginning to end. There is no second guest, nor is there a second host. If there were two guests and two hosts, they would simply be two separate entities."
"Blind fellow.
*Kuāng* (匡) is pronounced with the initial *qù* and the final *shàng* (上); it means "correct" (*zhèng*).
*Huán* (寰) is pronounced with the initial *hù* and the final *guān* (關). A "kingdom" (*wáng*) refers to the counties within the royal domain; that is, the *huán* [world] is the interior of the seas.
"Emperor Dazhong. (Dazhong was the reign title of Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty.
When Emperor Xuanzong was still a hidden dragon [a prince], he was a śrāmaṇera and stayed at Yanguan together with Huangbo. One day, when the Emperor saw Huangbo prostrating, he asked:
"Do not seek by clinging to the Buddha; do not seek by clinging to the Dharma; do not seek by clinging to the Saṃgha. What is the use of prostrating?
Huangbo said, "One should prostrate to such matters as these. The Emperor asked, "What is the use of prostrating? Huangbo then struck him. The Emperor said, "That was quite crude.
Huangbo struck him again. The *Biographies of Song Monks* states: Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty was originally the thirteenth son of Emperor Xianzong, [son of] Emperor Muzong.
He was the half-brother of Emperor Wuzong. The Emperor often felt intimidated by and resented him, so he cast him into the palace latrines.

An official named Qiu Gongwu secretly provided rescue and protection, causing him to shave his head and become a monk; he was then released and allowed to escape. He traveled throughout the world, experiencing every kind of hardship and peril.
Eventually, through various circumstances, he was appointed as the Vice Governor of Jiangling—this was truly because [the Emperor] detested his presence at court. Thus it was with Emperor Wuzong.
The Emperor passed away. Yang Gongfeng, the Commander-in-Chief of the Left Shen-ce Army, led the ministers and officials to welcome and establish him on the throne.
[Yang] once resided among the assembly of Master An of Yan-guan. One day, Master An cautioned the administrators in advance, saying:

"A person of extraordinary character will arrive here. Prohibit idle talk and cease all disruptive matters; I fear they might bring reproach upon the Buddha-dharma. The next day, several wandering monks arrived.
When a person performed a prostration, Dao’an silently took note of it and subsequently ordered the *karmadāna* to place it in a high position.

As for the prayer beads and other such items, whenever Dao’an engaged in conversation with them, he would increase his display of humble demeanor, saying: "This poor monk has been mistakenly surrounded by a vast assembly."
Fearing that the vegetarian feast would not be provided, he requested from the *zhǔzàng* (abbot) a written invitation for a single offering.

The Emperor took up the brush and composed the text for him. When Hui'an read it, he was struck with awe and alarm; he knew that the offerings for the monks would be so abundant as to exceed all ordinary measure.

He then said to the Emperor, "The time has come. Do not delay; do not remain coiled like a snake in the mud. Having entrusted him with the future affairs of the Buddha-dharma, he departed. Upon reaching the salt... [text ends]

When Guān entered nirvana, the Emperor composed a poem in lamentation that read: "In this age of semblance, what calamity has befallen the teachings? The radiance of the Śākya gate is lost, like a dragon deprived of its pearl.
I am loath to tread upon the fresh grass of the fragrant steps; With palms pressed together, I sorrowfully behold your former countenance.

Your jade handle shall forever depart from the seat of the Three Teachings; The sound of the golden bell shall eternally guard your ten-thousand-year trace. I know that for you, Master, the karmic conditions of the lower realm have come to an end."
To which level of the heavens above should one ascend?
To manifest the task and respond to the occasion, Dongshan, a Grand Master of the religious school, successor to Yunmen, ascended the hall and said:

"The teaching tradition says that every dharma is its own essence and is never obscured. Is this truly so or not? If it is indeed so," he then pointed to a pillar and said: [The pillar is the Buddha.]
Furthermore, how do you understand this? If there is anyone who understands, come forward and speak before the assembly.
If you are fully conversant with it, then you shall not have brought Dharma to naught. At that time, a monk asked:

"When the successive patriarchs ascend the hall and are earnestly requested by humans and devas, they do not obscure the fundamental teaching; I beg the Master to proclaim it. The Master said: "The hair is disheveled; the ears are muffled. The monk said: [I do not understand].
"If it is so, then this single phrase circulates, making gods and humans prick up their ears. The Master said, "A black-dyed robe is being sunned in the daytime.
Question: "Whose song does the Master sing? To whom does the lineage of his school trace back? The Master said, "Repeated words do not deserve to be swallowed."
"What is the Buddha? The Master said, "Three *jin* of hemp. "What is the mind of the ancient Buddhas?
The Master said, "The nest knows the wind; the burrow knows the rain. The Master then said, "Words do not unfold the reality; speech does not meet the occasion. Those who rely on words perish."
Those who cling to words are deluded. One must clearly discern the view within these four propositions.
Only by becoming a liberated monk—regarding even a single beam or a shard of tile as a matter of sustenance—is one fit to be a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) for humans and devas.
If one does not understand this, one will ultimately remain muddled and confused. See the *Guanglu* (Extensive Record).
When the flowers bloom in dense clusters, this is the merit of the Venerable Xianhe. A monk asked, "What is the mind of the ancient Buddha?
The Master said, "Clustered flowers, clustered brocade. Xian was the successor of Dongshan.
Master Kuanghe of Zhushui in the Southern Land heard the story of Dongshan’s response to the question about the Buddha—“three pounds of flax”—and remarked, "To the south there are bamboos;
to the north there are trees."
Grand Master Lu Tang, Lu Xun by name, styled Jingshan, was a native of Wu Commandery.
He served as high as the Surveillance Commissioner of Xuan and She, with the additional rank of Censor-in-Chief. Initially, he asked Nanquan: "In ancient times, a man raised a gander in a jar.
As the gander grew larger, it could no longer get out of the jar. Now, one may not damage the jar, nor may one destroy the gander. What would you do, Master?"
"How did he get out? Nanquan called out, "Attendant! Guo Xuan responded. Nanquan said, "He has come out. From this, Guo Xuan attained realization.
After Nanquan had passed away, the head monk asked him, "Why do you not weep for the late Master? Guo Xuan replied, "If the head monk can speak, then I shall weep.
The head monk was speechless. Changqing spoke on his behalf, saying, "It would be appropriate to laugh, not to weep."
Xuedou spoke differently, saying: "The azure sky! The azure sky! Master Ya of Fuyan on Mount Nanyue once composed a verse on the "Three Pounds of Hemp," which says:
"Jade-colored markings on a bull's head, A golden dot upon its brow. On a clear spring day in the second month, All farmers take it as their model.
Celebrating the New Year at the Cold Food Festival, Iron coins worth three or five hundred. Ya was a high disciple of Dongshan.
"Brother, I once presented this verse to him. Dongshan deeply approved of it; those who speak of it later should not harbor divergent views.
Deva, the Great Being, was a native of South India. His family name was Viśāla, and he was the son of an elder."
The Master was by nature gifted with eloquence and delighted in cultivating meritorious deeds. He met the Great Being Nāgārjuna, and their minds were in perfect accord.
Having manifested the lunar sign, he was the very first to attain profound awakening; thus, the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye was transmitted to him as a preeminent disciple.
Nāgārjuna said, "I am now advanced in years; that you shall cause the sun of wisdom to shine brightly rests upon you. Thereupon, Deva avoided the multitude and performed his prostrations.
Zu said: "Though I am not quick-witted, I venture to accept your compassionate instruction. As for the school of Deva, some claim it is a non-Buddhist (tīrthika) school;
however, the Deva who established the banner [of this lineage] is none other than Deva, the fifteenth patriarch of the Chan school.
The *Xiyuji*, the *Fofazang zhuan*, and the *Baolin zhuan* record this in great detail, and none of them mention any connection to non-Buddhist matters."
For example, the thirteenth patriarch was formerly a non-Buddhist practitioner who possessed great illusory arts; the *Biographies* record this directly and without concealment.
It is said in the Western Regions that there are four suns in the world—one in the East, Mātr̥ceṭa; one in the West, Nāgārjuna; one in the South, Āryadeva;
and one in the North, Saṃgharakṣita—whose light can illuminate the deluded minds of sentient beings. Yet, when Āryadeva subdued the various non-Buddhists, the circumstances were quite [remarkable].
[Asanga] was frequent in his visits. At the beginning, he said to Nāgārjuna, "I now wish to demolish the mountain of false views and kindle the torch of the True Dharma.

Nāgārjuna replied, "You are not the right person for this; I have found the one. [Asanga] asked, "Does the Great Master establish the arguments of the non-Buddhists, while I refute their errors according to the texts?
We shall first examine their relative strengths and weaknesses, and only then plan our course of action. Thereupon, Nāgārjuna supported and established the doctrines of the outsiders.
Devaputra followed by refuting his arguments. After seven days, Nāgārjuna lost his position. He then sighed and said, "Erroneous words are easily lost;
false doctrines are difficult to support. You may go now. He subsequently went to the city of Pāṭaliputra.
[Therein he] 1) refuted the account of not striking the *gandhī* drum; 2) refuted the various non-Buddhists regarding the account of the Gaṅgā River being a river of merit; 3) refuted...
1. The Brahmin who followed the name to investigate the reality and turned back to question him until his arguments were exhausted. 4. The occasion of piercing the eye of the Great Lord Maheśvara.
5. The occasion of holding the long banner. 6. The occasion of establishing the meaning of the Triple Gem, refuting the various non-Buddhists, and transforming them so they left the household life.
7. The occasion of debating with the Arhat Māṇḍavya. *Māṇḍavya* means "Upper" in this context.

When he engaged in debate with him seven times, [the opponent] was defeated; his words faltered and he remained silent, unable to respond. [Deva] secretly employed his supernormal powers to go to Tuṣita Heaven and inquire of Maitreya.
Maitreya told him: "That Deva has practiced for kalpas beyond measure; in this Bhadrakalpa, he shall succeed to the rank of Buddha. This is not something you can know.
Because of this, his fame resounded throughout the Five Indias, and the followers of the non-Buddhist paths all looked upon him with awe.
Those who uphold the school of Deva refer to what we call our own orthodox lineage.

whenever he encountered the anniversary of Yun-men’s death, he would not offer incense or food. When people asked him the reason for this, he said: "I..."
I once had a dialogue consisting of three statements that were sufficient to repay the kindness and virtue of my former teacher. As for these three statements: A monk asked, "What is the Way?
He replied, "A man with clear eyes falls into a well. The Master asked, "Are the intent of the Patriarchs and the intent of the Teachings the same or different?

He replied, "When the rooster is cold, it climbs the tree; when the duck is cold, it goes down into the water. The Master asked, "What is the School of Deva? He replied, "Snow served in a silver bowl."

Adding to these six "nines," there are ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist paths, beginning with the Six Teachers. Each teacher produced fifteen varieties.

4. Sañjaya Vairaṭīputra; 5. Ajita Keśakambalin;

Hearing that various non-Buddhists intended to obstruct the Buddha-dharma, and having reflected upon this for some time, the Great Being took up his long banner and entered their assembly.
His banner was eight feet high, and its pole was twelve feet long. He stood there without taking another step. The non-Buddhists said, "You..."
"Why do you not come forward? he asked. [The outsider] said, "Why do you not come after me? "You resemble a lowly person," he said. "You resemble a noble person," the outsider replied.
"What Dharma do you understand? he asked. "You understand nothing at all," the outsider replied. "I wish to attain Buddhahood," he said. "I have certainly attained it," he replied.
"It is not fitting for you to attain it," the outsider said. "I originally knew that I would attain it; as for you... he replied.
"In truth, I have not attained it. The non-Buddhist said, "Since you have not attained it, why do you say you have? He replied, "Because you possess a self, you do not attain it;
because I am without self, I shall naturally become a Buddha. When the other was thus defeated in argument, he then asked:
"What is your name? he asked. He replied, "My name is Deva. The non-Buddhists had long heard of his reputation; they then repented their errors and offered their apologies.
In Sanskrit, *Deva* means "heavenly being" (*deva*).
*Qiē* (pronounced *qiān jié qiè*): A wooden wedge. *Jiānyóu*:
This is translated as "Supreme Gold" (*Jinsheng*).
*Āo* (pronounced *yú jiǎo qiè*).
The character "決" (jué) is derived from "water" and means "to open a channel.

Because the eighty-four thousand sentient beings possess eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*), the Buddha, wishing to sever them, established eighty-four thousand Dharma gates as means of subduing and counteracting them. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that this is *prajñā*.
The *pāramitās* can eliminate the root of the eighty-four thousand illnesses. These eighty-four thousand all arise from four types of illness:
first, greed; second, hatred; third, delusion; and fourth, the three poisons. These are further divided into four equal parts, each consisting of twenty-one thousand.
One eliminates the twenty-one thousand afflictions of greed through the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*). Through loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and compassion...

Through the contemplation of [the nature of] hatred, one eliminates twenty-one thousand afflictions; through the contemplation of causes and conditions, one eliminates twenty-one thousand afflictions of delusion.
By applying these remedies collectively, one eliminates twenty-one thousand afflictions of the "equal-parts" (sāmya) type.
Just as a precious gem can dispel darkness, so too can the Prajñāpāramitā eliminate the afflictions of the three poisons.

Fengmao (Phoenix Down) refers to Xie Feng of the Song dynasty. He was the son of [Xie] Lingyun. Feng’s son, Chaozong, accompanied his father to Lingnan and returned there at the end of the Yuanjia era.
He associated with the Daoist Huixiu; he was fond of learning, possessed literary talent, and enjoyed great renown.
By imperial selection, he was appointed Court Attendant to Prince Lin of Xin’an. When the prince’s mother passed away, Chaozong composed a eulogy for her.
He presented it [to the Emperor]. The Emperor greatly marveled at and praised it, saying to Xie Zhuang: "Chaozong truly possesses the 'phoenix feathers' (a sign of his father's literary talent);

Lingyun has appeared once more. Liu Daolun, General of the Right Guard, was seated near the Emperor; he went out to visit Chaozong and asked, "I have heard that you possess some extraordinary object; what is it?
Chaozong replied, "In a household as empty as a hanging bell, how could there be any extraordinary object? Daolun—
The military official was ignorant; he happened to utter his father’s name and said, "Earlier, while attending the banquet, His Majesty remarked that you possess 'phoenix feathers' (feng-mao).
Chaozong returned to the inner quarters barefoot. Dao Long, thinking he was searching for phoenix feathers, waited until nightfall without success.
He then departed.
Bān Chāo, styled Zhōngwài, was the son of Bāo and the younger brother of Gù. During the Yǒngpíng era, he was appointed as a *jiǎ sīmǎ* (provisional commandant) for his military merits.
Together with the official Guō Xún, he was dispatched to the Western Regions. Chāo arrived at Shànshān.
The King of Shanshan treated Faxian with great courtesy and reverence at first, but later he suddenly became negligent and distant.
Faxian said to his attendants, "Do you not perceive that the King's intentions have grown thin? This must surely be because an envoy from the Northern Barbarians has arrived;
he is hesitant and does not yet know whom to follow. A wise person perceives what has not yet sprouted, let alone what is already manifest. He then summoned a Huihu attendant and feigned—
He said to them, "The envoy of the Xiongnu has come several times asking, 'Where is he now? The attendant Hu was terrified and confessed the situation in full.
Chao then confined the attendant Hu and assembled all thirty-six of his officers and soldiers.
When they had finished drinking and were in high spirits, he took advantage of the occasion to incite them, saying, 'You and I are together in this remote frontier; we must achieve great merit.'"
"I seek wealth and honor. Now that the barbarian envoy has arrived for only a few days, King Guang’s respectful treatment has already ceased.
If the people of Shanshan were to seize us and send us to the Xiongnu, our remains would forever become food for jackals and wolves.
What can be done about this? His officials all said, "We are now in a perilous place; our lives and deaths depend on you, Sima. Chao said, "No..."
"If one enters a tiger's den and does not seize its cubs, it is a failure. Our current plan must be to use fire to attack the barbarian envoys at night.
They will not know our numbers and will surely be struck with great terror; thus they can be utterly destroyed.
Once these barbarians are eliminated, Shanshan will lose heart, and our mission will be accomplished."
*Biàn* (貶) is pronounced with the upper radical *shàng* and the phonetic *jiǎn*; it means to retreat. *Pō* (剝) is pronounced with the lower radical *běi* and the phonetic *jiǎo*;
it means to shave or pare away. As the verse of the Venerable Xiāngyán on the "Single Foot" states: "The child pecks and the mother cracks; once the child is aware, there is no shell."

The mother and child are both three; their conditions should not be mistaken. They chant in harmony along the same path. "Miao" (妙) and "xuan" (玄) are solitary feet. "Ming" (邈) is the same as "ming" (詺);
the upper radical is *mi* (彌) and the lower is *zheng* (正). It refers to observing all things. The lower part should be "miao" (皃); it is pronounced with the *mo* (墨) and *jue* (角) finals.
It means appearance. "Miao" (邈) means distant; it does not carry this meaning here.

*Jiǎoduō* (角馱): the character *tuó* (馱) is pronounced with the initial *dú* and the final rhyme *gè* (箇). It means "to carry a heavy load," referring to a donkey or horse carrying goods; it should be written with the radical *dà* (大).
As for *jiǎoduō*, the character *tuó* (馱) is pronounced with the initial *dú* and the final rhyme *hé* (何); it means "to ride" and is not the correct meaning here.
In the *Zihu Ben*, it is written as "Zihu. This is the name of a cliff located in Quzhou. [She was] the nun Liu Tiemo;
at that time, people of the age referred to her as "Liu Tiemo. She visited the Venerable Lizong of Zihu Cliff in Quzhou.
As soon as the Master saw her, he asked, "Are you not Liu Tiemo? She replied, "I dare not say so. The Master said:
[The Master] turned left, then turned right, saying, "Preceptor, do not be mistaken. The Master then struck him.

Emperor Suzong consulted the *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp), which states that National Teacher Nanyang, sensing that the time for his nirvana had arrived, took leave of Emperor Daizong and established the conditions for the construction of a stupa.
To say it was Emperor Suzong now is an error. The National Teacher lived ten years after Emperor Suzong.
Two years later, he finally entered nirvana. Daizong was the eldest son of Suzong. Regarding "xiang" (相), it should be pronounced with the departing tone (*xiàng*);
it refers to "se-xiāng" (色相, physical appearance). Regarding "tan" (譚), it is pronounced *tán* (with the initial *dú* and the rhyme *nán*);

it should be written as "tán" (談), pronounced *tán* (with the initial *dú* and the rhyme *gān*), meaning "discourse. Some versions read "south of Xiāng and north of Tán," but that interpretation is forced. He once...
In reading Yuan’s *Nine Bands of Mount Fushan*, it was previously stated that "South of Xiang" and "North of Tan" were incorrect; rather, they refer to South of Niutou and North of Matou.
Nevertheless, Old Master Yuan was a master craftsman who profoundly penetrated the essential tenets; students of later generations should reflect upon this with careful discernment.
"Receiving the blind turtle" refers to the "blind turtle" entry in the *Yunmen Lu*.
The character *jiao* (勦) is pronounced with the small-cut (*xiaoqie*) tone;
it means "to sever. As for "fox-doubt," the nature of a fox is to be indecisive in its advance; hence it is called "fox-doubt."
*Cuān* (pronounced *cuān*, with the second tone): to throw; to cast.
Master Huìléng of Chángqìng, whose courtesy name was Sūn Gōng, was a native of Yánguān in Hángzhōu. His surname was Sūn.

He was registered as a monastic at Kāiyuán Monastery in Sūzhōu and traveled through various Chan centers. Later, upon meeting Xuěfēng, his doubts were completely resolved. His fellow practitioners... [drum]... beat.
The mountain was always called "Master Sun.
Master Xiang of Lianhua Peak on Mount Lu succeeded Master Fenshan Daochen; he was the grandson of Yunmen.
When the Master was about to pass away, he held up his staff and showed it to the assembly, saying: "Tell me, when an ancient Buddha arrives here, what does he do?"
"Why do you not consent to stay? The assembly had no reply. [Dongshan] said himself, "It is because on that road one cannot gain strength.

He spoke again, "How does one go so as to gain strength? Then, slinging his staff across his shoulder, he said, "Carrying my staff crosswise, heedless of others, I go straight into a thousand peaks and ten thousand peaks," and then he passed away.
If one possesses these conditions, only then will one understand the meaning of this verse.
"Divine horse colt, divine horse colt. This refers to Master Ma. His name was Daoyi; he was a native of Shifang in Hanzhou and surnamed Ma.

Because the Patriarch had issued a prophecy stating, "In the future, there shall emerge a horse colt who will trample the people of the world to death," and as the Master happened to fulfill this prophecy, everyone called him Mazu (Ancestral Master Ma). He was thus known as the Divine Horse.

"He is indeed a 'thousand-li colt' (a horse of great potential). The *Han Shu*, 'Account of the Western Regions,' states: In the kingdom of Daxi Yüan there is a high mountain; upon it there are horses that cannot be captured.
Consequently, they took mares of five colors and placed them below [the mountain] to mate with them. The resulting colts all had blood from their foreheads when sweating;
thus they were called 'Heavenly Horse Colts. A horse two years old is called a colt (*jū*). 'Yuan' (*wǎn*) is pronounced in the level tone."
"Feeling the tiger's whiskers": when Confucius saw the robber Zhi, he withdrew and said, "What I, Qiu, have done is like applying moxibustion to oneself when one is not ill.
To rush forward to stroke a tiger’s head and comb its whiskers—how nearly did I fail to escape the tiger’s jaws? This is from the "Robber Zhi" chapter of the *Zhuangzi*.
The character 料 (liao) is pronounced liao.
*Shou* (攸) is pronounced with the *zhou* rhyme; it means "place" or "that which.
*Zu* (鏃) is pronounced with the *mu* rhyme; it refers to the tip of an arrow.
Baizhang Baizhang Niepan was the successor of Guishan; he was the great-grandnephew of Hai and Zheng. However...
Hai and Zheng were both successors of Mazu. Under Mazu, there were two hundred *zhang* (fathoms).
Therefore, when the *Chuan deng lu* refers to Nanquan as "the Master-Ber" (*shibo*), this is none other than Baizhang of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
To now instead attribute this anecdote to Zheng is an error in the *Baizhang Lu*.
*Dàshā* (大煞) is synonymous with *shā* (殺). It is pronounced with the level tone of *jiè* (戒).
It means "fierce. "The kalpa-fire blazes intensely; the kalpa-fire blazes intensely. The great trichiliocosm is utterly destroyed.
Mount Sumeru and the vast oceans are obliterated without remainder," as seen in the *Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
The term "yù" (浴) should be pronounced as "gǔ" (谷). Regarding the method for water, the *Xī* (溪) says it is called "gǔ," meaning the place where one dwells.

The *Shí èr mén xī zhàng jīng* (Twelve-Gate Staff Scripture) states: "This staff has three compartments (*gé*). One should contemplate the three miserable realms (*sān tú*) and cultivate precepts, concentration, and wisdom;
therefore, three compartments are established. Furthermore, there are four prongs (*gǔ*), used to sever the four modes of birth and to contemplate the four [truths]."

The four corners represent the contemplation of the Truths (*satya*), the cultivation of the four immeasurables (*brahmavihāra*), and the entry into the four dhyānas; thus, the four corners are established. The height from the center to the top is five units, signifying the severance of the five destinies (*pañcagati*).
The revolving [structure] represents the cultivation of the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) and the possession of the five powers (*pañcabala*).

The twelve rings signify the mindfulness of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), the realization of non-attainment (*anupalambha*), and the practice of the twelve gates of meditation (*dvādaśa-dhyānamukha*), whereby the mind remains free from affliction. There are three layers and four corners.
Combined, these numbers total seven. By recollecting the Tathāgata’s seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*), one employs the eight applications subsumed under mental phenomena (*dharmas*).
By recollecting the eightfold path, one attains the eight liberations; therefore, eight are employed.
Hǎo (好): The initial radical is 虍 (hú) and the phonetic is 到 (dào). It means "to love.
See the *Jùlíng jiàn hòu lù* (Record of the Subsequent Revelations of Jùlíng).
Shānshān (珊珊): The initial radical is 艹 (cǎo) and the phonetic is 干 (gān). Selected [from literature]: "Pearls and jade ornaments jingle and shimmer (*shānshān*)."
"Cuo" (駝) should be read as "duo" (馱). Pronounced with the initial of *tang* (唐) and the rhyme of *xiang* (向). It refers to a donkey or horse carrying a load. "Juan" (捲) should be read as "quan" (圈).
Pronounced with the initial of *qu* (去) and the rhyme of *yuan* (爰). It refers to the bending of wood. The character below is pronounced with the initial of *lü* (呂) and the rhyme of *yuan* (員).
The character on the right, 眄, should be read as *pàn* (composed of 普 and 莧). It means "to look around" (*gùpàn*).
The pronunciation *miǎn* (as in 沔) is incorrect. A poem by Hanshanzi says: "If you wish to find a place of rest, Hanshan may be preserved forever.

A gentle breeze blows through the secluded pines; Listening closely, the sound is even more pleasing. Below are men with graying hair, Muttering the teachings of Huang-Lao. After ten years, they return..."
It is not permitted. One must not forget the words spoken upon arrival.
Regarding the "Three Threes Before" and the "One Extended Purity," the *Chuanqing Lu* states: "The monk Wuzhuo, surnamed Dong, was a native of Yongjia."
At the age of twelve, he left the household life under the Vinaya Master Yi of Ryūsen-ji Temple in his home province. He recited several hundred thousand verses of Mahāyāna sūtras.
In the eighth year of the Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty, he received full ordination due to his excellence in these studies.

At twenty-one years of age, he first studied the *vinaya*, and subsequently traveled to Mount Niútóu in Jīnlíng to attend upon Chan Master Zhōng and receive the essentials of the mind. Master Zhōng said to him:
He said: "Sentient beings and Buddhas have fundamentally no different minds. It is like the sky: when the clouds and veils are removed, its original purity is revealed.
At these words, his Dharma-eye opened instantaneously. Later, in the fifth month of the summer during the third year of the Dali era, he arrived at the foot of Mount Tai.
As the sun was about to set, he suddenly beheld a temple complex of such exquisite beauty that it surpassed all in the world. He thereupon knocked on the door and requested entry. There...
The youth Kūṭi opened the door and came out to meet him. Asaṅga invited the youth inside and said, "I wish to stay here for the night.
Having received this message, the youth extended an invitation for Asaṅga to enter. A monk asked the Master, "From what direction have you come? Asaṅga answered in detail.

The monk asked again, "How is the Buddha-dharma in that region? He replied, "It is currently the age of the Semblance Dharma (śāsanapratirūpaka), and the precepts and discipline are observed according to one's capacity. He was asked once more.

"How many people are there? He replied, "Sometimes three hundred, sometimes five hundred. Zhao said, "What is the state of the Buddha-dharma here? He replied, "Dragons and snakes are intermingled; ordinary people and sages dwell together. Zhao asked again, "How many people are there?

He replied, "Three before, three after, three more after that. Zhao remained silent for a long while without answering. The monk asked, "Do you understand? Zhao replied, "I do not understand. The monk said:

* *The monk said:* "Do you understand? * *Zhao replied:* "I do not understand. * *The monk said:* [He did not speak further. (Note: The final "曰" (said) indicates the end of the dialogue or the monk's concluding remark.)
Since you do not understand, you must leave immediately. As the youth escorted the guest out the gate, he said, "What is the name of this temple?
He replied, "Qingliang Temple. The youth asked, "Regarding what I previously asked about 'three times three in front and three times three behind,' does the Master understand it?"
He said, "I do not understand. The youth said, "You may look behind the Vajra. The Master then turned his head, and the temple immediately vanished.
He remained deeply sorrowful for a long time, and then spoke a verse: "The holy monastery pervades the entire realm of sand-like worlds; ... [the rest of the verse is omitted in the source]"
With Maṇjuśrī filling the eyes, he engages in conversation; in that moment, one does not know how the Buddha-seal is opened.
Turning the head back, one sees only the cliffs of Mount Huán. "Fúqú yīn fúqú"—it is the lotus leaf.
The character *yíng* (嬴) should follow the radical for sheep (*yáng*). It is written as *lí* (羸), pronounced with the *qì* rhyme of *lì*. It means exhaustion.
*Wā* (哇) is found in the *Fēngxué Lù* (Record of the Wind Cavern).

Regarding the Three Mysteries (*sān xuán*), the Linji school possesses the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials (*sān xuán sān yào*): namely, the Mystery within the Essence (*tǐ zhōng xuán*), the Mystery within the Mystery (*xuán zhōng xuán*), and the Mystery within the Phrase (*jù zhōng xuán*).
Xuán used this to receive scholars.
The City of King Chu is the present-day province of Yǐng. The *Jiānglíng Jì* states: "King Wén of Chu first moved the capital from Dānyáng to Yǐng;
the southern city to the north of the present province is it."
*Mánhàn* (pronounced *màn hán*) means "broad-faced. *Yàojì* is a colloquial expression for "speech.
Regarding the five ranks of Dongshan—Orthodox and Deviant:
first, the Orthodox within the Deviant; second, the Deviant within the Orthodox; third, Coming from within the Orthodox; fourth, ... [fifth, Returning to the Source].
"Simultaneously Reaching the Center. Five: "Simultaneously Arriving at the Center.
As seen in the Yunmen Lu (Record of Yunmen), Hanqing states:
"The *Heishan Baozang Lun* says: 'Now, there are three kinds of students. The first is called the True [Student].'"
The third is called "hearing" (*wen*). To study and practice is called "hearing"; to sever learning is called "neighborhood" (*lin*).
That which transcends these two is called "the Real. [Note: The original text has the character *guo* (exceed/transcend) twice;

commentators say this is like a person hearing of events in another land—merely believing them without personally witnessing them—which is "hearing. Not following after birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), and not relying on nirvāṇa.]
Thus, the cessation of study is called "the neighbor. "Neighbor" means proximity.
To realize that the two limits of birth-and-death and nirvana are equal, neither grasping nor rejecting them—surpassing the previous two stages—is called the Unsurpassed Right and True Way.
Yunmen’s “dragging stones” is what Xuefeng called “rolling the ball,” and Guizong’s “dragging stones.
When any new arrivals reached the master Shandao of Yuanzhou, known as Master Muping, they were not permitted to pay their respects before being first ordered to carry three loads of earth.
He showed them this verse: “The eastern mountain path is level, the western mountain is steep; New arrivals, do not [proceed]!”
He declined the three layers of mud-brick roofing. Alas, you have been on the road for many days; though you face the Way clearly, you have instead become lost.
"Gǔnqiú" (Rolling the Ball) refers to seeing the Patriarch's excellence.
"Mǎnglǜ" (Rough and crude): the first character is pronounced as *mò* (cut by *jīng*); the second is pronounced as *lánggǔ* (cut by *gǔ*). It describes an appearance that is not distinct.
"Biàn-pì-pì. This should be read as "bì," meaning to press or constrain.
"Āi" (乙諧切) means to push; it also means to carry on one's back.
There is no mention of Zhaozhou’s saying: "If someone comes from the north, I load them up; if someone comes from the south, I... [The text appears to be incomplete.]
He downloaded this:

the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi* and the Perfect Penetration of Avalokiteśvara. Entering the *samādhi* through hearing, reflection, and cultivation, he first, within the process of hearing, entered the flow and forgot the object.
Once that which was entered had become still, the two characteristics of motion and stillness clearly ceased to arise.

*Pānghuài*: The first character is pronounced with the *bó* (薄) and *láng* (郎) finals; the second is pronounced with the *pù* (鋪) and *gài* (蓋) finals. *Pānghuài* describes the appearance of heavy rain.
"Forming wind" (*chéngfēng*) should be read as "receiving wind" (*chéngfēng*).
The "One-Eyed Dragon" refers to Chan Master Mingzhao Deqian of Wuzhou, who received the seal of approval from Luoshan and was not hindered [by fixed views].
In a single corner, he struck out and proclaimed the profound essence of the teachings; everyone feared his quick-wittedness, and few dared to meet his edge.
Because he had lost his left eye, he was thus called the "One-Eyed Dragon."
*Liè* (pronounced with the *liáng* and *shè* initials): A beard; a mane. From the poem by Hanshanzi:
"Without trousers, I am constantly beset by the six extremes of suffering; the nine dimensions of the world are discussed by others.

I have no means to leave the wild marshes, nor the skill to dwell idly at my thatched door. Looking up at the crags, it is still dark; the smoke has vanished, yet the valley remains shrouded in gloom. Within this...
"O son of a householder, each and every one of them is entirely without trousers.
Regarding the etymology of *lìzhè* (略彴): it refers to a wooden bridge. Furthermore, the *Guǎngzhì* states that a bridge consisting of a single log is called a *què* (榷).
It is also called a *zhé*, referring to a single log laid across water to serve as a crossing.
*Què* (pronounced *jué*). In the *Guàn-xī Zhìxián Chán-shī Lù*, a monk asked: "I have long heard of Guàn-xī; having arrived here, I see only a pool for soaking hemp.
The Master said, "You recognize only the hemp-soaking pool, but you do not yet know Guàn-xī. The monk asked, "What is [Guàn-xī]?"
Guankui said, "As swift as a split arrow. When Xuansha heard this, he said, "Even after thirty more years of study, you will still not have understood Chan.
(The character *òu* is pronounced *hòu*; it means long-immerse or steeped.)
*Niǔ* (rhyme with *jiǔ*): the appearance of hands turning.
*Diào* (rhyme with *xiào*): to inquire about misfortune.
Regarding the question asked by Linggu at Shishuang to Master Wogu: "A single piece of bone, when struck, rings like bronze. Toward what [does it ring]?"
"Where have you gone? I am calling for the attendant. The attendant responded. The Master said, "In the year of the donkey, you will go.

In the ninth month of the ninth year of the Dàhé era of the Táng dynasty, the Master manifested illness. On the eleventh day, as he was about to depart, he addressed the assembly, saying, "I shall now proceed to the West."
"Principle does not shift eastward. Having finished speaking, he entered a state of silence. He was cremated, and several fragments of sacred bone were obtained.

A stupa was erected on the southern slope of Shishuang Mountain. Furthermore, the *Song Gaoseng Zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Song Dynasty) states that several fragments of "ashless bone" were recovered;
one section from the crown of his head was particularly extraordinary and translucent, its color like gold and its resonance like bronze.
*Hào miǎo* (浩渺): pronounced with the *miáo* rhyme of *miǎo*. "Vast and boundless" describes the appearance of distant waters.
Nine years after the First Patriarch, Bodhidharma, had personally transmitted the Dharma and the robe, he manifested his entry into *nirvāṇa* and was buried at Wuban on Mount Xionger.
Three years later, the Wei envoy Song Yun was dispatched on a mission to the West.
Fayou returned and saw his master at the Pamir Mountains (Congling), who was holding a single shoe in his hand. He said to Song Yun, "Your sovereign has already grown weary of this world;
I am returning to the Western Kingdom. Yun initially did not understand this. Upon his return, the Emperor had indeed passed away.
He subsequently reported this to Emperor Xiaozhuang of the Later Wei, who then ordered the stupa to be opened. Inside, only a single shoe was found, which was then taken by imperial decree.
The offering at Shaolin Monastery was stolen from there in the fifteenth year of the Kaiyuan era and subsequently lost within Huayan Monastery on Mount Wutai;
its whereabouts were never again known.
Xiansha had said: "In my humble view, this verse precisely employs the words of Chang Guizong; its meaning is quite detailed. Now...
It is said that Xuan Sha had these words; furthermore, he attained [realization] under Gui Zong. Both verses are recorded here; one should understand their chronological sequence.
**Chan Master Guizong Chang’s Verse:** In Guizong, phenomena and principle are cut off. The sun is at its zenith at midday.
Free and easy like a lion, He does not rely on external things. He strides alone atop the four mountain peaks.
Strolling leisurely along the three great paths, a yawn causes birds to fall; a frown strikes terror into all the heterodox. When the trigger is set, the arrow is easily caught;
when the shadow vanishes, the hand cannot cover it. Its deployment is like a skilled artisan; its cutting and shaping are like the use of a ruler.

Though there are ten thousand kinds of clever carvings and names, they return to their source as mere earth. Speech and silence, sound and voice—all are cut off; the subtlety of the sound is such that the mind finds no place to rest. Cast this aside!
The eyes are dim; take this, and the ears are deaf. A single shaft pierces the three barriers—clearly visible is the path behind the arrow.
Piteous indeed is the great man, whose primal nature is the ancestor of the mind. Xuan Sha’s verse says: One, two, three, four, five.

The sun is precisely at its zenith. How pitiable, this so-called "Great Man. He takes the "Pre-Celestial" (*xiantian*) as the patriarch of the mind. [This is marked by a circle. Regarding "Pre-Celestial":

those who were fond of such matters collected them and carved woodblocks for printing. Subsequently, due to the inquiries of Chan practitioners entering the inner quarters, these teachings were further disseminated.
