The character for "to contend" (zhēng) is correctly written as [口*爭]. It is composed of "claw" (爪) and "xī" (虒). It signifies the way of dragging along and contending.
There are many instances in the Zen school where non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) question the Buddha, citing various sources from the *Āgamas* and the *Mahāyāna*.
It is by no means rare for individuals to attain realization through such causes and conditions. For example: Ānanda overturned the banner pole at the gate;
the non-Buddhist did not ask whether [the Buddha] existed or not; the World-Honored One held up a flower; Mañjuśrī struck the gavel; and the World-Honored One spoke of the "unfixed" (*aniyata*).
When the Dharma was preached, flowers rained from within a rocky cave; the Five Supernatural Powers questioned the Buddha; and two women evaluated a corpse.

Regarding such instances as these, those who merely lecture on and study the teachings often claim that there are no records in the sutras and treatises, immediately harboring doubts and refusing to believe.

Yet, when our Patriarch first arrived, he certainly did not regard language and written words as his primary concern; rather, it was those of later generations who transmitted his Way who [relied upon them].
In order to gain the trust of those who have come to study, he frequently cites the *Āgama* and *Yāna* scriptures as evidence; this misses the essential point by a great distance.

Nevertheless, regarding the Way of our Patriarchs and the Buddhas, these two do not obstruct one another. As stated in the *Ten Gates on Discerning Delusion*: "Vimalakīrti is the Tathāgata Suvarṇapuṣpa.
Master Jizang says that [this] appears in the *Cintā-vimokṣa-samādhi Sūtra*, and he himself states: "I have not yet..."
One sees its origin. Now, according to various catalogs of the scriptures, this title does not appear. Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "Innumerable sacred teachings have been lost;
since the Sthavira has not heard them with his own ears, he then dismisses them, saying, 'These are not the sacred teachings.
The treatise cites a sūtra which says: 'Although what you have spoken is not my original intention, that which was spoken [is indeed the teaching].'"
All of these are well consistent with correct reasoning and can be accepted and upheld. How much more so for those who attain realization through these words!

Those who serve as teachers in future generations need not be overly preoccupied with the distinction between the *Hīnayāna* and *Mahāyāna* (or *Āgama* and *Yāna*) to the point of bringing reproach upon their own ancestors.
The character 塵 (dust) should be derived from 土 (earth). It is written as 挨 (ái). 挨 refers to fine dust.

The Ten Continents are all attached to various kingdoms beyond the sea. First is Zu Zhou, where *fanhun* incense is produced. Second is Ying... [text continues]
1. Zhuzhou (Island of Mushrooms): It produces *zhicao* fungi and jade stones; its springs have the taste of wine. 2. Xuanzhou (Mysterious Island): It yields elixirs of immortality;

Regarding the "Dragon and Snake Array" among the Six Arrays of the *Wu Tão*: King Wu asked Grand Duke (Tàigōng), "In the Green Dragon Army, what serves as the vanguard and the rear?

"Śuddhāpa! The minister immediately presented the horse. Zu Zhimen once composed a verse on Mañjuśrī striking the gavel:

"Why do you not see the place where I do not see? If you were to see my non-seeing, it would naturally cease to be that characteristic of non-seeing.
The commentator says: "This refutes a further conceptualization. If you insist on saying, 'I also see the Buddha’s essence of non-seeing,' what fault would there be?
Therefore, it is said that if one sees non-seeing, it is immediately subverted; thus it is called 'naturally not [that]."

Regarding the phrase "the characteristic of not seeing": the intention is that since the substance of not seeing has already been seen by you, how can this constitute the characteristic of not seeing?
This is because the substance of not seeing has already been perceived. As the Sūtra says: "If you do not see the ground of my non-seeing, it naturally is not a thing;
how could it not be you? The commentator says: The meaning of this passage unfolds as follows...
The conclusion returns to the main point. Altogether there are five layers to reveal Ānanda’s seeing-nature.

since you do not see the place where I see, my seeing is naturally not a thing. If my seeing were not..."
This is an object; your seeing is also not an object. Since your seeing is not an object, how could it not be your true seeing?
This passage was translated by the Master with such skillful brevity that its meaning is difficult to clarify through a mere summary; therefore, I have recorded it in detail.

The *Xiàngxiàng liùdù jīng* (Sūtra on the Elephant Simile and the Six Perfections) states: King Ādarśamukha ordered a group of blind men to feel an elephant. The king asked them, "Have you all seen the elephant?

"O King, the elephant is exactly as I have described. At that time, the king laughed loudly and said to him, "Blind! Blind! You still do not see," and then he spoke this verse:

"I have seen the whole ox. In the present moment, I encounter it with my spirit rather than viewing it with my eyes.

There, he again encountered the Chan master Ziyu, who further clarified his understanding of the Way. He composed the *Fuxing Shu* (Treatise on the Restoration of Human Nature) in two parts, upper and lower.
In essence, it asserts that the original nature is inherently luminous, yet it becomes defiled by the six emotions; thus, one becomes lost and fails to return. Now, he seeks to restore it, just as...
The reappearance of the *Leidi* (Book of Earthly Treasures) manifests the Will of Heaven; it is precisely the inner teaching’s return to the root and restoration to the source.
Its text is manifest yet hidden, concealed yet revealed. Its writing follows the patterns of the *Xici*, the *Zhongyong*, and other classics—hidden yet not hidden.

As for the principles of the Buddhist teachings, one abandons delusion by following the truth and manifests one's own mind; they are not expressed through words, but are realized solely through the awakening of intention.

When Han Yu and Liu Zongyan saw this, they sighed and said, "Our Way has withered and declined; we shall flee. This is recorded in the *Song Gaoseng Zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Song Dynasty).
The *Tianguan Shu* (Book on the Heavenly Officials) in the *Shiji* (Records of the Grand Historian) states: "In the Taiwei Palace is the seat of the Five Emperors;
behind it, twenty-five stars cluster densely, which are called the 'Ranks of the Lang. During the reign of Emperor Ming of the Han, the Princess of Guantang sought for her son the position of a Lang.
The Emperor did not grant the request, but bestowed upon her ten million coins, saying: 'The office of the Tianlang corresponds above to the arrayed stars; its officials govern the hundred li.'"
It was not the right person; the people suffered the calamity. *Yàoqiáo* (藥嶠):
the character *qiáo* is pronounced with the *miàochuǎn* (廟切) rhyme; it refers to a mountain that is sharp and high. *Miǎn* (緬):
the character *miǎn* is pronounced with the *míyuǎn* (彌遠) rhyme; it means "distant."
The *Tai fu chun qiu* states: "The Three Dukes correspond above to the Three Terrace Stars; therefore, they are called 'Terrace-Aids' (*tai fu*). 'Fenwei' (藩維):
'fen' is pronounced with an initial *fan* and a final *chan*; it means a fence. According to the *Rites of Zhou*, those outside the Nine Provinces are called 'fence-states' (*fan guo*)."
The name of the mountain where the Immortal resides is traditionally said to be the place where the Yellow Emperor ascended to heaven.

The Regional Inspector (Taishou)—the title "Regional Inspector" having been changed from "Commandant of the Commandery" by Emperor Jing of the Han dynasty—was Jia Zong of the Eastern Han, styled Mengjian. He was a native of Liaocheng in Dongjun. Formerly, the land of Jiaozhi...
The region produced many rare treasures. Successive Regional Inspectors (Cishi) were mostly devoid of upright conduct; consequently, the officials and populace resented and rebelled against them.

In the first year of the Zhongyuan era, the garrison troops in Jiaozhi rose in revolt, seizing both the Regional Inspector and the Governor of Hepu. The authorities nominated Zong to serve as the Regional Inspector of Jiaozhi.
Upon arriving in his jurisdiction, Zong interrogated them regarding the nature of their rebellion, and they all stated that it was because tax levies had become excessively heavy. Hundreds...
There were none among the surnames who were not destitute. The capital was far away, and there was nowhere to appeal one's grievances.

With no means of livelihood, the people were forced to survive by their own wits; thus, they gathered together as bandits. [Wang] Zong immediately sent a letter to inform them, ordering each to settle into their own occupations.
He executed the ringleaders, and the common people were at peace. The people sang this song along the streets: "Father Jia arrived late, leaving us to suffer first."
On the contrary, he was now seen to be upright and impartial; the officials did not even dare to accept his hospitality. He was subsequently summoned and appointed as the Inspector of Jizhou.

According to established custom, the official carriage was drawn by three horses and draped with red curtains when the inspector was welcomed at the boundary of the province. When Zong reached his jurisdiction, however, he ascended the carriage and said:
"An Inspector ought to look far and listen widely, scrutinizing both the good and the evil. How can one instead hang up curtains [to hide oneself]?"
He himself had covered and blocked it; thereupon he commanded his charioteer to lift it up. When the people of the hundred cities heard the news, they were naturally struck with awe and trembled.
Regarding the "Six Articles for the Inspection of Governors" (*huàtiáo*) in the *Hànshū*: Yán Sīgǔ states that the *Hànguān Diǎnzíyí* says:

"The Inspectors (*cìshǐ*) proclaimed their mandates and traveled throughout the commanderies and kingdoms, inspecting the conditions of governance, demoting those who were incompetent and promoting those who were capable, and adjudicating legal cases."

Regarding wrongful imprisonments, matters were to be investigated according to six categories; anything not included within these categories was not to be examined. First: Powerful clans and influential families exceeding the prescribed limits for land and dwellings;
using force to oppress the weak and relying on numbers to exploit the few. Second: District Magistrates (Dierqianshi) failing to implement imperial edicts and follow established regulations;
turning their backs on the public good to pursue private interests, secretly issuing orders to secure personal gain, and plundering the common people through excessive taxation and extortion.

3. Those of the rank of two-thousand-stone officials do not investigate doubtful cases with care; they encourage murder, meting out punishments arbitrarily when angered and bestowing rewards excessively when pleased.

They are vexatious, oppressive, and cruel, stripping and mutilating the common people until they are loathed by the populace. Consequently, mountains collapse and tiles crack, while portents and false rumors arise. 4.
Those of the rank of two-thousand-stone officials are unjust in their selection and appointment of subordinates; they merely curry favor with those they love and conceal the worthy.
1. I have favored the obstinate. 5. The children of those holding the rank of two-thousand-shi rely on their illustrious power and influence to solicit favors from their superintendents. 6.

Those holding the rank of two-thousand-shi violate public duty by forming cliques with subordinates, sycophantically aligning with the powerful and strong, universally distributing bribes, and undermining the correct ordinances.
"Jingwei" (經緯): the lower character is pronounced as *yú* (于) and *guì* (貴). In civil affairs one can span the heavens (*jing*), and in military affairs one can weave across the earth (*wei*).
Without military power and only civil culture, there is no means to win over distant lands; without civil culture and only military power, there is no means to resist disorder.
A "jian" (箋) refers to paper with colored edges; such paper is called *jian*.
The Dharma Master Ying, a Bodhisattva, stated that the Sanskrit term *bodhisattva* translates here as "Kaisi" (開士). This means a person who guides others by means of the Dharma.
During the Former Qin dynasty, Fu Jian bestowed the title "Kaisi" upon virtuous and learned śramaṇas.
*Huī* (pronounced *huǐ*) means "great" or "vast. It also means "to stretch out.
*Dì* (pronounced *dí*) means "to see.
Regarding the "night-light" in the *Shiji*: Zhù Yuánchàng of the State of Suí was traveling toward Qi. On the road, he saw a snake that was about to die.
He then sprinkled water upon it and departed with the divine medicine he had applied. Suddenly, one night, the middle courtyard was brilliantly illuminated by light.
Thinking there might be a thief, he grasped his sword to investigate; he then saw a snake crawling away across the ground, carrying a pearl in its mouth.
Thus it was known that this was the karmic retribution for the previous snake. Because the luster of the pearl could illuminate the night, it was called "night-light" (yèguāng).

Jiaotong (Crisped-Tongue Lute): Cai Yong of the Eastern Han, styled Bojie, was a native of Chenliu. While he was seeking refuge in the regions of Wu and Kuaiji, there was a man in Wu who was burning a *tóng* tree for fuel.
Hearing the crackling sound of the fire, Cai Yong recognized it as fine timber.
He requested the wood and had it fashioned into a lute, which indeed produced exquisite tones; however, its tail remained charred. Consequently, people of the time called it the "Charred-Tail Lute."
Furthermore, while he was in Chenliu, he heard his neighbor playing the *qín* behind a screen one day.

Cai Yong listened secretly and said to the neighbor, "Sir, why does your playing of the *qín* contain such a murderous intent? The neighbor replied, "Just now as I plucked the strings, I saw a praying mantis crying out;
a cicada was nearby but had not yet flown away. The mantis moved forward and then recoiled for its sake. My mind—"
He stood tall, fearing only that the mantis might miss its prey. How could this have been an expression of a murderous intent manifesting in his voice?
He was profoundly moved; such was the subtlety of his listening.
"Pai-bu" (排步) is read as qiè. It means to push or drive away.
"Wǎngxiàng" (罔象) should be written as "Xiàngwǎng" (象罔). When the Yellow Emperor traveled north of the Red Water, ascended Mount Kunlun, and looked out, he returned and lost his dark pearl (xuánzhū).
He sent Zhì (智) to search for it, but he could not find it; he then sent Lízhu (離朱) [to search].
He searched for it but could not find it. He sent Ke-hou to search for it, but he too could not find it. Then he sent Xiang-wang, and Xiang-wang found it. (See *Zhuangzi*). Ke (喫):
the initial consonant is *kʰ* with the level tone; Hou (詬): the initial consonant is *kʰ* with the departing tone.
*Sai* (塞) is pronounced with the initial *shang* (上) and the final *su* (蘇) and *ze* (則).
Regarding the four rivers: first, the Gaṅgā; second, the Nairañjanā; third, the Sindhu; and fourth, the Śītā. These are the four great rivers of the four heavens.
*Ku'e* (枯枿): "e" is pronounced with the fifth tone (*ge*). It refers to the remains of felled trees. *Zōng héng* (蹤橫):
the upper character should be *zòng* (縱).
*Huangtóu* (黃頭): in Sanskrit, this is called *Kapila*; here it means "Yellow Head. This is because the Buddha was born in the kingdom of Kapilavastu. [End of entry].
In his place of birth, he was called the Buddha, the Great Being of Yellow Head.
As for the First Patriarch, Master Bodhidharma, his eyes were a deep blue-black color; therefore, the Patriarch was called "Blue-Eyed."
The *Treatise on the Precious Treasury of Detachment and Subtlety*: Its emergence is subtle; its entry is detached. Knowing entry as detachment, external objects have nothing upon which to rely.
Knowing emergence as subtlety, the internal mind has nothing for which to act. When the internal mind has nothing for which to act, various views cannot shift it.
When external objects have nothing upon which to rely, the myriad existents cannot bind it. Furthermore, "detached" means that the essence does not unite with things, nor does it...

It is detached from all things; the five colors cannot defile it, and the five notes cannot disturb it. As for "subtle" (zhēng): its essence is wondrous and formless, possessing neither color nor appearance.
Yet its application extends to ten thousand ends, while its form remains unseen. The two characters "detached" (lí) and "subtle" (wéi) constitute the wondrousness of the Way.
*La* (闌) is pronounced *luògān* (落干); it means "late.
Shaolin refers to Shaolin Temple, which was constructed by the Wei dynasty śramaṇa Buddhabhadra.

Bodhidharma arrived in this land by sea in the first year of the Datong era of the Liang dynasty. Upon meeting Emperor Wu, their dialogue did not reach accord, so he subsequently traveled to Luoyang in the Wei territory.
Bodhidharma stayed at Shaolin Monastery on Mount Song. He sat facing a wall, remaining silent all day long for nine years.
Thus he was able to find the Second Patriarch, Huike, to whom he transmitted his Dharma. The traditional account that this occurred in the eighth year of the Putong era is an error.
The phrase "flower-wood" (*huamù*) should not be read as "flower-tree.
At the Sixth Patriarch’s Lu Ridge, the Layman Lu was secretly entrusted with the robe and the Dharma. That night, he fled in secret.
A man named Daoming, along with several dozen others, followed his tracks in pursuit. Upon reaching Dayu Ridge, Daoming was the first to see him; the Patriarch then—
He placed his robe and bowl upon a flat rock and said, "This robe represents my faith; can it be taken by force? You may take it as you please.
When Ming tried to lift it, it was as immovable as a mountain.
Zhongni and Bo Xueshen. Bo Xueshen was a man of virtue from the southern states. He traveled to Qi and stayed in Lu; Zhongni saw him but did not speak with him.
Zilu said, "Master, you have wished to see Master Bo Xueshen for a long time. Now that you have seen him, why do you not speak?
Zhongni replied, "As for such a person, the Way is present in a mere glance. There is no need for further words."
"It can accommodate sounds. This is seen in the *Zhuangzi*.
"Tilting the Canopy"—this was not Wen Bo Xue, but rather Chengzi. In the *Jia Yu*, it is recorded that when Confucius was traveling to Tan, he encountered Chengzi on the road;
they tilted their carriage canopies to converse all day long, becoming very intimate. Confucius then looked back and said to Zilu, "Bring a bundle..."
He offered silk to present to the Master. Zilu responded with an air of disdain, saying, "I have heard that a scholar does not grant an audience to those who do not come through an intermediary.
When a woman marries without a matchmaker, she remains unmarried; you, sir, do not follow the rites of introduction.
After a pause, he looked back at Zilu again, and Zilu answered as before. Confucius said, "Zilu, does the *Shi* not say: 'There is a beautiful person, bright and radiant'?"
Ah! To meet unexpectedly is to find what my heart desires. Now, Master Cheng is a man of great virtue in the world;

had I not presented this gift to him here, I might never have seen him again for the rest of my life. *Qinggai* (inclining the canopy) means to stop the carriage. *Qing* means to lean or tilt. *Tan* is pronounced as *tan*.

The *Linfeng Ruìyìng Tú* (Illustrations of the Auspicious Responses of the Qilin, Phoenix, Tortoise, and Dragon) states: "The qilin, phoenix, tortoise, and dragon are the four auspicious omens of the state.
The qilin is a benevolent beast and the foremost among the Four Spirits (*sìlíng*). The phoenix is the auspicious omen of a sovereign and the chief among birds.

The tortoise is the spirit of the aquatic realm and the chief among shelled creatures. The dragon is the chief among scaly creatures; they are also called the Four Spirits. Furthermore, it is said that the qilin possesses five colors."
Its belly was yellow; it stood one zhang and two chi high.
According to the *Traditions of Recluse Scholars Xu and Hu*, Xu You, whose courtesy name was Zhongwu, was a native of Yangcheng in Yingchuan. He lived in seclusion on Mount Ji.
The Master [Shun] lived among Qiè Què; he ate what the mountains provided and drank from the rivers. When Yao recognized his worthiness, he offered him the imperial throne.
Upon hearing this, [Qiè Què] went to the river and washed his ears. There was also Náo Fù, who was tending a calf;
when he heard of it, he led the animal away to avoid the area, saying, "I loathe the water [of such a man]. Later, when he died, Yao established a tomb for him and titled him Lord Jī.
*Chán* (蟾): pronounced with the initial *lián* and final *qiè*. It refers to the moonlight. *Gāodào* (高蹈):
pronounced with the initial *tú* and final *dào*. It means to tread upon or step on.
Regarding "not knowing [this] as noble," Zào said: "If one says they do not know it, then one is truly noble."
The *Record of the Western Regions* states that the Sanskrit name for this mountain is Gṛdhrakūṭa-parvata, which translates here as "Vulture Peak.

It is the site where the World-Honored One Śākyamuni preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Because it rises most prominently above the city of Rājagṛha, it symbolizes the transcendence of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
It is named thus because many vultures dwell there; furthermore, it is said that the shape of the mountain resembles the head of a vulture.
It is also called Vulture Peak. "Tattered robes, tattered robes" refers to Kāśyapa.
Kāśyapa was foremost among those who practice *dhūta* (ascetic virtues); he wore tattered robes. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"There are ten benefits to tattered robes: first, they are counted among coarse garments; second, they require little seeking; third, [they follow...]"
1. It is suitable for sitting. 2. One may lie down at will. 3. It is easy to wash. 4. It is rarely damaged by insects. 5. It is easy to dye. 6. It is difficult to destroy. 7.
No further clothing is required. 8. It does not cause one to lose the pursuit of the Way.
Xiongling is the site of the Dharmatrāta Stūpa. The stūpa record states: "The Great Master’s work for the sake of sentient beings was completed;
having found the one to whom he would transmit the Dharma, he sat upright and passed away. This was on the fifth day of the twelfth month of the second year of the Datong era.
He was buried at Mount Xionger, and a stūpa was erected at Dinglin Monastery. Yan Shiguo states that Mount Xionger is located in Shunyang.
To the north, east of Yiyang County, there is a mountain whose two peaks resemble the ears of a bear; it was named accordingly.
It is over three hundred li from Shaolin. Based on this, it is not the place where the Second Patriarch stood in the snow;
that is merely an error regarding the facts.
*Suo* (索): pronounced with the initial *suo* and the final *xié*. It denotes the appearance of fear; it also means to disperse.
*Wǎn* (菀) should be read as *wǎn* (宛). *Píngtián* (平闐):
the first character is pronounced *fánglián* (房連) and the second has the sound *tián* (田). *Píngtián* denotes abundance.
“Biàn” should be written as “biàn. It means to distinguish. “Biàn” (皮變切, pí biàn qiè). This is the name of a crown of the Zhou dynasty; it does not carry this meaning here.
The following entries follow this pattern. “Hùxī” (虎兕): the second character is pronounced “xùmèi qiè” (徐妹切). It is a blue-colored, single-horned animal resembling an ox, weighing one thousand *qīn*.
The *Shichuang Siming Ji* (Record of the Stone Window of Siming) states: "Upon this mountain there is a natural stone window that is transparent on all four sides;
therefore, it is called Siming.

[The phrase] "Severing the golden chain" is from the *Chan Yue Lan* (Chan Yue’s Survey), citing a poem from the collection of Li Bai: "I often think of Li Taibai, who drove away the immortal *zhū*..."
The Creator’s work: the Emperor of the Mysterious Source placed him upon a bed of seven treasures; whether in the Tiger Hall or the Dragon Pavilion, there was nowhere he could not go.
But once the martial guards stripped his boots, a green fly settled upon the jade. Before the Purple Sovereign’s desk, the five-colored qilin suddenly snapped its golden chains.
The great waves of the Five Lakes were like mountains of silver; with a boat full of wine, they beat the drums.
It is past. O Elder, you have become a thing of another age; who would dare to join in your wild rants? Who would know that by the riverbank grave, you are not yet lying there drunk and asleep?
(The rhyme word *qīng* [輕] is pronounced *shūyě* [書冶] in the *Qièyùn*).

The "Seven Stars" (qīxīng) refers to the seven-star ornamentation on a sword. The *Xījīng zájì* states that the sword with which the Gāozǔ (Emperor Gaozu) slew the white serpent was adorned with seven-starred pearls and nine-flowered jade.
It was further encased in a sheath made of various five-colored lapis lazuli.
The sword was kept within its inner chamber, yet its radiance still shone forth outside; it was no different from having the blade drawn.

Every twelve years it was once polished and sharpened, so that the edge always appeared as if covered in frost and snow. When the case was opened and the scabbard removed, a wind-like breeze would immediately arise, and its brilliance would strike those who beheld it.
"Intending to give to the traveler" should be read as "intending to take and give to the traveler.
Bian He was a man of Chu; Bian He presented jade to King Li of Chu. The king said, "It is stone," and dispatched an envoy to cut off one of his feet.
When King Wu ascended the throne, Bian He presented it to him again. King Wu was again enraged, and [the envoy] cut off another foot.
His feet were cut off. When King Wen of Chu ascended the throne, Bian He went to the foot of Mount Jing and wept while clutching the jade.
King Wen summoned him and said, "Why do you resent having your feet cut off? He replied, "I do not resent having my feet cut off;
rather, I resent that true jade is treated as common stone, and loyal service is treated as negligence. This is why I weep. King Wen then ordered a craftsman to split the stone.
"It is indeed genuine jade. King Wen sighed and said, "How tragic! Our two former rulers found it easy to cut off a man's foot, yet difficult to split a stone.
If this pear-shaped object is truly a jade disc, it is a national treasure. This is recorded in the *Hanzi*.
In the third line of the first section, three characters were omitted due to a slight touch or lack thereof. *Mí* (靡):
the initial is *mǔ* (毋) and the final is *pǐ* (彼); it means "none" (*wú*). *Kǎngkǎi* (慷慨):
the upper character is pronounced *kǔ* (苦) and the *láng* (郎) rhyme, while the lower character is pronounced *kǔ* (苦) and the *ài* (愛) rhyme; it means to exhaust one's sincerity.
Regarding "a crooked piece of wood occupying its place," Master Yunmen of Shaoyang said: "Those old bald monks everywhere sit upon crooked meditation benches seeking fame and profit.
When asked about the Buddhas, they answer regarding the Buddhas; when asked about the Patriarchs, they answer regarding the Patriarchs.
It is like passing the spittoon from one person to another, or like old women in a village of three houses playing word games. What do they know of good and evil? They are all like this."
For one of such a kind, even water is difficult to digest. What fault would there be in cutting down hundreds of thousands of millions of them with a sharp blade?
"Chǔdiàn" (楚甸): "diàn" is pronounced *liàn* (切); it refers to the suburban fields.

*Lei-lei* (pronounced *li-zhui-qie*). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*: "To join together so as to form a coherent pattern. One interpretation says it means "creeper. It also refers to a "net" or "mesh.
*Chi-li* (pronounced *li-zhi-qie*): ten *hao* are called one *li*.
The compass is called *gui* (the round) and the square is called *ju* (the square).
The *Zhouxing Ruiying Jing* states: "When the Bodhisattva manifested his birth, he immediately took seven steps; with one hand he pointed to heaven and with the other he pointed to earth, declaring:
'In all that is above heaven and below heaven, I alone am the most honored.'"
"Hónggāng" (宏綱): "Gāng" is pronounced as in "gǔláng" (古郎); it refers to the large rope of a net.
"Gào" (郜) is pronounced as in "gào" (告).
"Spring rain, spring rain, like fat (gāo)" (膏)—the hundred grains look up to it.
The *Chunyun yitong fengyan* states: At the commencement of spring (*lìchūn*), the clouds of azure radiance emerge from the constellation Fang, appearing like accumulated water.
At the vernal equinox (*chūnfēn*), the clouds of true yang emerge from the constellation Zhang, appearing like white cranes.
*Kugai* (枯荄): "Gǔ" and "āi" are pronounced with the *qièyùn* [rhyme categories] of *gǔ* and *qiē*. It refers to the roots of grass.
*Lílí* (離離) should follow the radical for "grass" (*cǎo*). When written as *lí* (籬), it denotes a light and fine appearance.
*Wéi fēng wéi* (維風維): *wéi* is an auxiliary particle used for metrical cadence.
The *Gongyang Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals* states: "Clouds touch the rocks and arise;
they coalesce in a span of a few inches and, before the end of the morning, pervade the whole world—such are the clouds of Mount Tai."
One day, Bodhidharma said to his successor, Huike: "Internally, I transmit the Dharma-seal to accord with and realize the mind;

externally, I entrust the kashaya robe to establish the fundamental principle. In future generations, when the world becomes degenerate and doubts arise in abundance, simply produce this robe along with my Dharma-verse to clarify the matter.
Listen to my verse: 'I originally came to this land / To transmit the Dharma and save those lost in delusion.'"
Sentiment: One flower opens and five petals unfold; the fruiting occurs spontaneously.
(In the third board, line thirteen, the character "yun" [to operate] is missing from "du yun" [solely operating].
Having traveled through the Wei and visited Liang, he beheld Shaolin.
*Zhu* (pronounced *yù qiè*): to gaze; to look.
*Ji* (pronounced *yí qiè*): a tether; a halter.
*Tài* (pronounced *tāi dài qiè*): demeanor; graceful appearance; beauty.
"Clouds hanging from the sky" means clouds suspended in the heavens. Master Zhuang took this to compare with the wings of the Peng bird.
*Yī* (pronounced *yú* in its radical form) is a sound of regret, pronounced *qì*.
*Ōuyōu* (pronounced *yí* in its radical form) means "distant."

"Han-dan" (菡萏): the first character is pronounced with the *hu* and *gan* rhymes; the second is pronounced with the *tu* and *gan* rhymes. It describes the appearance of a lotus flower about to open. "Wan-hui" (萬卉):
the second character is pronounced with the *xu* and *gui* rhymes. It is a general term for all plants.
*Cu*: pronounced with the *zi* and *liu* finals; it means "to press. *Zhou*: pronounced with the *ze* and *jiu* finals.

"Enemy" (*di*) should be written as "recompense" (*chou*). This refers to responding from afar to inquiries and answering according to the various capacities of beings. "Recompense" (*chou*) means "enmity"; it is not [the intended meaning here].
Regarding the meaning [of the name]: Old Hanshan of Mount Tiantai was known as Hanshanzi. He originally had no clan or family name.

Seventy li west of Shifeng County, there were two cliffs, Hanshan (Cold Mountain) and Anshan (Dark Mountain). Because he once resided within Hanshan Cliff, he was named after it. His appearance was withered and emaciated.

His clothes were tattered and falling apart; he wore a crown made of birch bark and dragged large wooden clogs. He would occasionally come to Guoqing Temple to approach Shidi and eat vegetable scraps.
Sometimes he would stroll slowly along the corridors, and at other times he would shout and clamor.
When the temple monks chased him away with staffs, he would turn around, clap his hands, and laugh loudly. Although his speech was like that of a madman, it possessed a certain profound meaning.
"White clouds embrace the secluded rock," says the poem by Hanshanzi: "I have chosen my dwelling among the layered cliffs; The bird-path is cut off from human tracks.
What is there within my courtyard? White clouds embrace the secluded rock. I have lived here for years beyond counting; I have seen spring and winter pass again and again.
Send word to those who dwell in the bronze and bell [of nobility]: Empty fame is surely of no benefit."
Regarding "orchids and *zhǐ*," Zuo Si’s *Du Fu* states: "As for its plants, there are *du ruò*, *héng jú*, *shí lánn*, *zhǐ xī*, and *lán zhǐ*.
These are what the ancients used to compare with the gentleman. The *Jia Yu* says: "Mushrooms and orchids grow in the deep forest."
It does not fail to be fragrant simply because there is no one present.
"Kong-seng" (Empty Birth) is the Indic name Subhūti, also called Supoditika. This has three meanings in its translation.

The first was named Śūnyatā-ja (Born of Emptiness). This signifies that at the time of his birth, his entire household became empty, manifesting the characteristic of the realization of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
The second was named Sudarśana (Good Manifestation). This signifies that at the time of his birth, various auspicious omens appeared. The third was named Svastika (Auspiciousness).

This signifies that after his birth, physiognomists divined that this child would possess only goodness and only auspiciousness. The *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions) states that he originally came from the East.

The Buddha Qingluntuo (Śākyamuni) manifested a shadow-body within the assembly of Śākyamuni; today, this serves as a general designation for those who practice Chan—referring to practitioners who investigate the profound mystery and understand emptiness.
At Huangmei in Lingnan, the Dharma was secretly transmitted to Lu (Huineng), who then traveled far and wide, becoming the spiritual home for those in Lingnan.
In the *Analects*, it is asked regarding Zi Xi: Confucius said, "He! He!
The commentators say this means there is nothing worthy of mention.
I, Yu, am still this very same person. An ancient had a saying:
"Guanxiu imitated 'The Noble Man’s Thoughts on the Passing Year'. I admire Yin Jifu for composing the *Shang Song* (Eulogies of Shang) out of his longing for worthy men;
I admire Yang Xiong for whose principles and governance all things were like the phoenix. Shaking my robes, I rise in the middle of the night; the dew...
The fragrant flowers sway and flutter; they strike against the bright moon pearl of the black dragon. Striking it forth, one produces the five-colored marrow of the phoenix.
In the desolate lanes, amidst the whistling and rustling sounds, I yearn for this person who excels jade and璧 (bi). In silent stillness, through the passing years, we have not met.
Infinite floating lives are all cast away in vain. Have you not seen Shen Yue say: "The fair lady is not here;
for whom does the spring light care?
How urgent is the Black Dragon! This refers to the black dragon.
Yunyan Cheng frequently snapped his fingers. Having first studied under Baizhang Hai, he attended him for twenty years without awakening to the profound essence.
He snapped his fingers in frustration and descended the mountain. Later, upon visiting Yaoshan, he finally attained realization.
Regarding the "Eight Horizons" (*bāhóng*), the *Huáinánzǐ* states: "Heaven has nine divisions and eight coordinates; Earth has nine provinces and eight cassia trees.
Beyond the nine provinces are the eight boundaries (*bāshān*); beyond the boundaries are the eight horizons. The horizon in the northeast is called the Wilderness Land (*huángtǔ*)."
The eastern extremity is called Sangye (Mulberry Field). The southeastern extremity is called Zhongan (Many Peaceful).
The southern extremity is called Fanhū (Turning Door). The southwestern extremity is called Huotu (Fire-Earth). The western extremity is called Woye (Fertile Field).
The northwestern extremity is called Shasu (Sand Place). The northern extremity is called Weiyu (Leaning Wing). Therefore, it is said that there are four directions and four [extremities].
The corners are called the Eight Horizons (bāhóng). Beyond the Eight Horizons are the Eight Extremes (bājí).
Furthermore, the nine Yi, eight Di, seven Róng, and six Mán are called the Four Seas.
Liao-chén (寥沈): "liao" is pronounced with the *hu* and *jué* finals; it describes the appearance of empty space.
Ā-ài (藹藹): pronounced with the *yú* and *gài* finals; it describes abundance. Tiān-jì (天驥):
pronounced with the *jiǎ* and *lì* finals; it refers to a celestial horse. For details, see the "Eulogies on Ancient Cases" (*Sònggǔ*).
*Zòu* (pronounced *chú yòu qiè*): the rapid pace of a horse.
*Dàpéng* (pronounced *bù dēng qiè*): In the Northern Ocean there was a fish; its name was Kūn. As for the size of Kūn, one could not know how many thousands of *lǐ* it measured.
It transformed and became a bird; its name was Péng. As for the back of Péng, one could not know how many... [thousands of *lǐ* it measured].
"It spans a thousand *li*. When it flies in a rage, its wings are like clouds hanging from the sky. This is seen in the *Zhuangzi*.
"Zhanlu" is the name of a sword belonging to the King of Wu. The *Bitian* states: "Among ancient swords, those named Zhanlu were so called because they were a deep, lustrous black (*zhan-zhan*)."
Regarding the shooting [of the bow] at the Ox and the Plow (the constellations Beidou and Niuxi) in the *Book of Jin*: Lei Huan was skilled in celestial phenomena.

Because Zhang Hua observed that there were often extraordinary vapors between the Ox and the Plow, he invited Huan to ascend the tower at night to look upward. Huan said, "I have observed this for a long time;
it is the essence of a precious sword ascending to heaven, located within the borders of Fengcheng County in Yuzhang. Hua then recommended Huan for the post of [Magistrate of] Fengcheng.
The magistrate of the city, Wang Huan, arrived and was repairing the prison foundations when he unearthed a stone casket containing a pair of swords.
Their radiance was exceedingly brilliant. He sent one to Lord Zhang and kept the other for himself to wear. Later, Hua was executed, and the sword was lost.

When Wang Huan died, his son became an official (Chengshi) of the province. While wearing his father’s sword at Yanping, it suddenly leaped from his waist and fell into the water. He sent someone [to retrieve it].
They cast them [into the water], but saw only two dragons several *zhang* long, brilliant with patterns. Those who had cast them down were terrified and retreated.

The *Dian’e Shuijing* (The Water Classic of the Marked Foreheads) says: "The *zhān* and *wěi* fish emerge from the Gǒng Cave; in the third month, they ascend to cross the Lóngmén Gate. Those that succeed in crossing become dragons;
otherwise, they return with their foreheads marked. *Zhān*: pronounced *zhāng-lián*; *wěi*: pronounced *yǔ-guǐ*. These are two types of fish.

"Name. *Yunluo* refers to *nülüo*. The *Bowuzhi* states: "It grows by attaching to plants and trees; its roots do not touch the ground, yet its branches and leaves are lush and dense as if it were planted.
This is precisely *tusi* (dendrobium).

"Zhōu" (洲) in the upper character is pronounced "zhōu. The *Erya* states: "That which can serve as a place of rest within the water is called a zhōu. In the lower character, it is pronounced with the *yǔ* rhyme.
The *Shiming* states: "It means 'to block' (*zhē*). It is able to block the water so that it flows sideways. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* says: Subhūti addressed the Buddha.
"How does a bodhisattva set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening in order to act as an island for the world?
The Buddha said: "It is like the great ocean; amidst the vast rivers, there is a high and prominent land that can be inhabited, surrounded by water on all sides."
It is called an island. Thus, Subhūti, the prior and posterior limits of form are severed;
likewise, up to the prior and posterior limits of the perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas are severed. Because these prior and posterior limits are severed, all phenomena are severed.
This severance of the prior and posterior limits of all phenomena is itself quiescence, itself sublime, itself reality—namely, emptiness.
There is nothing to be attained. Form is severed, craving is exhausted; through the remainderless fading away of passion, there is eternal extinction in *nirvāṇa*.
Yet, the Bodhisattva, desiring to reveal the subtle and sublime Dharma of cessation to sentient beings, sets out for enlightenment in order to act as an island for the world.
In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva replies to the Bodhisattva Prajñāprabhāsa: "O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of groves for bodhisattvas.
They are as follows: Birth and death are the grove of a bodhisattva, because they never grow weary of or abandon them.
Teaching and transforming sentient beings is the grove of a bodhisattva, because they never become exhausted."
*Dàn* (dàn tú àn qiè): To fear; to dread; to find difficult.
Regarding the "Ten Shadow Divine Horses," Prince Wangnian’s *Shiyí* states: "The twenty-second year after King Mu of Zhou ascended the throne..."
He traveled throughout the world, driving eight magnificent dragons. The first was named Juedi; its hooves never touched the ground.
The second was named Fanyu; it moved faster than flying birds. The third was named Benxiao; it could travel ten thousand li in a single night.
The fourth was named Yueying; it ran alongside the sun. The fifth was named Yuhui; its coat was brilliantly radiant. The sixth was named Chaoguang; it cast two forms and ten shadows.

The seventh is named Tengwu (Leaping Mist); it gallops upon the clouds. The eighth is named Xieyi (Clasping Wings); its body possesses fleshy wings with which it flies everywhere. The *Buddha-benxing-jing* states:
"I recall that in the past there was a horse-king named Jishi, whose speed was like the wind.
At that time, five hundred men entered the sea to seek jewels; they suddenly encountered a violent wind that blew them to the realm of the rākṣasas."
In that country, there were many rākṣasī women. [The merchants] went there to rescue and assist them, and they enjoyed themselves with those women.
At that time, the women said to the merchants, "You must not go from here toward the south of this city. One merchant leader conceived a doubt in his mind:
"What fault is there that going south is forbidden? He immediately took a sharp knife and went to the place where he was prohibited.
At that place, he saw a narrow path that was most terrifying, appearing like a hell. Near the city stood a tall tree, so he climbed it to observe.
He saw many dead people within that city; some were half-eaten, while others were nothing but sinews and bones.
These suffering beings looked up at him on the tree and spoke these words: "Please rescue us now!"
"I was once a merchant. When my ship was wrecked, five hundred companions and I reached the shore. There we encountered rākṣasīs who first gratified us with the five desires;
having entered this city, half of us have already been devoured. The merchant leader asked, 'Is there any expedient means by which we might escape this suffering?
The suffering man replied, 'There is one expedient means. On the fifteenth day, a horse-king will come here.'"
At the seashore, a voice spoke out, saying: "Who wishes to cross this great salt sea? I shall now safely reach the other shore.
If you encounter the Horse King, you will immediately be freed from this suffering. Upon hearing this, the merchant leader immediately told the people, "Be careful not to be heedless;
let us go together to that place to see the Horse King. Then, the Horse King spoke to the merchants.
"O people, do not give rise to defiled attachment. You may mount my back, or grasp my body, feet, or limbs.
The horse will then fly upward and travel as swiftly as the wind, crossing to the other shore of the ocean."
The *Benxing jing* (Sūtra on the Original Acts) concerning the five-colored auspicious qilin states: In the past, the Bodhisattva was the king of deer.
His body was tall and large, and his fur was five colors. Thousands of deer followed him in a herd. Once, when the King went out hunting, the herd of deer scattered;
they threw themselves off cliffs, fell into pits, dashed against trees, and pierced through thorns. They were crushed, broken, killed, or wounded—the slain were not few. The deer...
When the King beheld this, he choked with sobs. "As the leader of the multitude, I ought to have exercised clear foresight. That these small creatures were brought to ruin was my fault.
He immediately entered the kingdom and went before the palace hall, where he knelt and said: "These small animals, greedy for life, entrusted their lives to the borders of your realm.
Suddenly encountering hunters, the flock fled in terror; some lost one another while alive, and others lay scattered in death."
"The Emperor treats all creatures with benevolence and compassion; they are truly pitiable. I pray that you will select yourselves by rotation to provide for the Imperial Kitchen daily.
I beg that you inform him of the number, so that I may not dare to deceive him on high. The King found this most extraordinary and said, "The Imperial Kitchen uses no more than one [deer] per day;
I did not know that you were being slaughtered in such great numbers. If it is indeed as you say, I swear never to hunt again. The Deer King then withdrew and returned.
He summoned all the deer and explained his intention to them. The deer listened attentively and each took their place according to rank.
Whenever it was the turn of one to go to his death, he would approach the king to take leave. The king would weep for him and instruct him, saying:

"Such is the nature of this transient world; who can escape it? As you proceed, keep the Buddha and his benevolent teachings in mind, direct your heart toward that human king with compassion, and be cautious."
They were free from resentment. Day after day it was thus. Among them was one who was due to go on his rounds but whose body was pregnant with a child.
He said, "I dare not avoid death; I beg that you draw me aside and take another in my place.
The next man bowed his head and wept, saying, "I must certainly face death; yet I still have one day and one night of life, even if only for a brief moment."
When the time arrived, he felt no regret. The deer king could not bear to see his life unjustly taken; the next day, he left the herd and went in person to the Grand Cook’s office.
The cook recognized him and immediately reported this to the King. When the King asked for the reason, he replied as before. The King was moved with grief and shed tears for him, thinking:
"How can there be such a beast that sacrifices its own body to save others? As a ruler of men, I slaughter [animals] daily."
Sentient beings! The King sent the deer away, returning it to its original dwelling, and issued a decree throughout the realm: "If anyone offends the deer, they shall be punished as if for a human.
As for the auspicious qilin, the current citation of the Deer King's karmic conditions is merely the flowery rhetoric of those who seek to embellish; the deer was not a qilin.
*Língqì* (瓴甋) means *pínmó* (頻磨), which refers to dripping water. The *Erya* states: "Língqì is called *bì* (甓). Guo Pu says: "It is a brick.
Formerly, Mazu once lived in a hermitage, devoting himself solely to seated meditation. One day, Master Rang said to him:

“What do you hope to achieve by sitting in meditation? the Patriarch asked. Nanquan replied, “I hope to become a Buddha. Nanquan then took a piece of brick and began polishing it in front of the hermitage.
The Patriarch asked, “What are you doing, polishing a brick? Nanquan said, “I wish to make a mirror. The Patriarch said, “How can polishing a brick produce a mirror?
Nanquan replied, “If polishing a brick cannot produce a mirror, how can sitting in meditation produce a Buddha? At this, the Patriarch was suddenly enlightened.

Nanyue rose and asked, "How is it that this is so? Nangxiao replied, "It is like a person driving a carriage. If the carriage does not move, one may strike the carriage; one may also strike the ox. The Patriarch had no reply.
Nangxiao spoke again, "Are you studying seated meditation, or are you studying the seated Buddha?

If you are studying seated meditation, meditation is neither sitting nor lying down. If you are studying the seated Buddha, the Buddha has no fixed form. At these words, [the Patriarch] was enlightened.
Abiding in the Dharma, one should neither grasp nor reject. If you were to sit as a Buddha, that would be to kill the Buddha; if you cling to the form of sitting, you have not realized its principle.
During the early years of the Shenglong era of Emperor Zhongzong, Master Lu sent the inner attendant Xue Jian with an imperial decree summoning the Sixth Patriarch to the court. The Patriarch—

He declined on the grounds of illness. Xue Jian then asked the Patriarch, "The Chan masters in the capital all say that if one wishes to realize the Way, one must practice seated meditation and cultivate concentration.
They claim it has never happened that anyone attained liberation without relying on dhyāna and samādhi.
What do you make of this principle? The Patriarch replied, "The Way is realized through the mind; how could it depend on sitting? As a sutra says, 'If one sees..."
Whether the Tathāgata sits or lies down, he practices the way of deviance; therefore, he comes from nowhere and goes nowhere.
If there is neither arising nor ceasing, this is the Tathāgata’s pure dhyāna. All dharmas are empty and quiescent; this is the Tathāgata’s pure sitting.
Since there is ultimately nothing to be realized, how much less can there be "sitting"?
*Dì* (蒂) is correctly pronounced *dǐ* (音帝). It means "root.
As for "rare sound" (*xīshēng*), the Master of Lǎozi said, "The Great Sound has rare sound.
*Yì* (翳) is pronounced *yì* (於計切), meaning "an obstruction arising in the eye."
The *Zizhou* chapter of the *Shiji*. Zizhou, whose courtesy name was Zhifu, was offered the empire by Yao after Yao had declined to accept it from Xu You.
When Yao again offered it to Zizhou, Zizhou said, "It would be acceptable for you to consider me the Son of Heaven;
nevertheless, I am currently afflicted with a deep-seated melancholy and am in the midst of treating it. I have no leisure to govern the world."
Juanjuan (Juanjuan), surname unknown. Scroll title: "Juanjuan. Shun offered the empire to Juanjuan, who said: "I stand within the universe;
in winter I wear skins and furs, in summer I wear hempen and fine linen. In spring I plow and sow, my body sufficient for labor;
in autumn I harvest and gather, my body sufficient for rest and nourishment. I rise at sunrise to work and rest at sunset, wandering freely and at ease."
"Amidst heaven and earth, my mind and spirit find their own fulfillment. What need have I for the world?
Thus did Tao Qian of Jin return to his former life after serving as the Magistrate of Pengze. At that time, the Prefectural Inspector arrived on an official tour.
It was the custom for county officials to don their formal belts and pay their respects to the inspector; however, Qian sighed and said, "I cannot stoop my waist for the sake of five pecks of rice."
Facing the children of his village, he then personally unfastened his seal and ribbon and returned to his fields and home;
consequently, he composed a piece entitled "Return Home" (Guiqulai Ci), as seen in the *Collected Works of Tao Qian*.
"Zhēnbié" (甄別): The first character is pronounced with the *jū* and *yán* finals; it means "to observe. The second character is pronounced with the *bǐ* and *liè* finals;
it means "to discern. "Kuàngpáiyóu" (曠排猶) means "to depart far away.
"Gūdài" (沽待) refers to selling. As the saying goes: "Shall I sell it? I am one who waits for a buyer (*gù*)."
"Hu zhì zhì" should be read as "hu zhì". It means to cast aside or discard. "Zhì" means to arrive at. This is not the correct meaning.
"Jī" (譏) is pronounced *jǐ* in the first instance and *bó máo* (博毛) in the second. "Jī" (譏) refers to censure; "bāo" (襃) refers to praise. [Note: The character 誽 is a variant of 譏.]
*Yīgè* (衣裓): *gùdé* (古得) in transcription; it refers to the front lapel of a robe.
One *xún* (尋) equals six *chǐ* (尺).
*Tāoguāng* (韜光): *táodāo* (它刀) in transcription; it means to conceal.
The Eight Steeds from the *Mùtiānzǐzhuan* (Annals of Emperor Mu). The Emperor’s eight steeds were:
first, Chìyāo; second, Dàolì; third, Bái xī; fourth, Huálóu; fifth, Lù’ěr; sixth, Qúhuáng; seventh, Yúlún; eighth, Shānzǐ.
*Lì* (in the character 驪) has the pronunciation *lí*; it refers to a horse of deep black color. *Lù* (in the character 騄) has the pronunciation *lù*.
The Fourth Patriarch, the Great Master Guanding, said to the assembly: "During the Wude era, I traveled to Mount Lu and ascended its summit.
Looking toward Mount Poutou, I saw a purple vapor like a canopy, beneath which was a white vapor divided into six paths. Do you understand this?
The assembly remained silent. The Fifth Patriarch said, "Is it not that after the Upadhyaya’s passing, a separate branch of the Buddha-dharma will emerge?"
"Is that so? The Patriarch said, "Indeed; it was Niutou Lanrong.
Later, when Sheng of Yunyan went to visit Yaoshan, Yaoshan asked him, "I have heard you are skilled at performing the lion dance;
is this true? He replied, "It is. "How many times have you performed it? "I have performed it six times. "I too am skilled at performing it. Yaoshan said, "Master..."
[The Master] said, "I have performed one instance. [He asked: 'One is six; six is one. Later, Daosheng went to Mt. Guiyang.
The Mountain [Master Guishan] said, "I have heard that you, Elder, perform the lion at Yaoshan—is this true? He replied, "It is. [Guishan asked: "Do you perform it constantly?
Is there also a time to set it aside? He replied, "When I wish to perform it, I perform it; when I wish to set it aside, I set it aside. At the moment of setting it aside, the lion is within."
"Where? [The Master] said: "Set it aside; set it aside. *Ze* (置) should be read as *ze* (厇);
*sù* (愬) is pronounced *shè* (陟革切). *Yì-sù* (厇愬) refers to the appearance of ears flapping like those of a wild horse (*yì*, 野馬).
Alternatively, the pronunciation *zhuó-shuò* (卓朔) is incorrect in meaning.
*Tí* (pronounced with the *lì* tone) means "to explain.
When the layman Pangyun first visited Mazu, he asked: "Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as a companion?
Mazu replied: "Wait until you can suck up all the water of the West River in a single mouth, and then I shall tell you."
*Dào* (robe):
the character is pronounced with the *pī* and *yì* finals; it refers to a monk’s outer robe (*cīvara*).
*Kòu*: the phonetic is *kǒu*; it means to strike.
The character "shàng" (上) in the term *língshǎn* (凌晨上) should be read as *líng* (陵). This is because it carries the sense of "encroaching upon.
All subsequent instances are to be understood in this manner. *Quǐxiàn* (屈眴) refers to the *kāṣāya* robe transmitted by Master Bodhidharma; it was eventually left at Caoxi by the Sixth Patriarch.
*Kuṣṇa* (屈眴). A Sanskrit term; here it means "coarse fine cloth. It is woven from the heart of the *śālmalī* cotton flower. Its color is dark blue-black, and it is lined with green silk.
At the beginning of the Shangyuan era of Emperor Suzong of the Tang dynasty, an imperial edict was issued requesting that robes of this material be brought into the palace for veneration.

This lasted for a total of six years. On the night of the fifth day of the fifth month in the early part of the Yongtai era, Emperor Daizong dreamed that Master Huineng requested his robe and returned to Caoxi.
On the seventh day, he dispatched the imperial messenger Yang Chongjing to respectfully enshrine it there. At dawn, [the robe] was found.
"Yinshun. This refers to the verse concerning the "One Flower and Five Petals" of the Dharma transmission from the First Patriarch Bodhidharma.
"Liu Yang Seng" (Master Liu Yang)—it should be read as "Liu Yang," referring to the name of a county; it is Shichuang Qingzhu of Tanzhou.
The Chan Master received the Dharma-seal of Dao Wu and withdrew into seclusion. At that time, he had only recently completed his second summer retreat as a monk.
Seeking to avoid the world, he lived incognito among the common people at Táojiā Fáng in Liúyáng, Chángshā; no one recognized him.
Dōngshān Jià visited him and discovered his whereabouts, whereupon the Master invited him to reside on Mount Shīshuāng.
*Hījì* (希冀): pronounced *hī-jì*, meaning "to hope" or "to look forward to.

*Gùntiān* (貫天): "To move heaven and earth. From *Gùnlí* (貫休)'s "Imitating the Ancients: Parting": "The resentment of parting is like fine wine; those who drink it, ancient and modern alike, are all intoxicated."
I only fear that the waters of the Yangtze River are all the tears of sons and daughters. I am not of their kind; as I see someone off, I merely clasp their arm in vain.
Should we meet again in another day, a pure wind shall stir heaven and earth.
Péng-dǎo (Island of the Tangled Grass) is Penglai Mountain. Its description is detailed in the "Twelve Tortoises.
*Xiāozhēng* (journeying at night): *xiāo* means night; *zhēng* means to travel. As the *Shijing* says: "Solemnly journeying at night, from dawn till night attending to public duties."

In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* concerning the hundred cities, the youth Sudhana, starting from the site of the six stūpas east of Puṇḍravardhana, together with the five groups of followers, paid homage to Mañjuśrī.
Having resolved his mind upon Bodhicitta, he traveled southward by stages, passing through one hundred and ten cities and meeting fifty-two spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Upon arriving before the pavilion of Maitreya, he addressed him, saying: "O Great Sage..."
"Open the door of the pavilion so that I may enter. Then Maitreya Bodhisattva went before the pavilion and snapped his fingers;
the door opened immediately. He commanded Sudhana to enter, and once he had entered, it closed again.
"Huilin" (惠理) should be read as "Huili" (慧理). Lu Hongjian’s record states:

"The foreign monk Huili of the Western Regions during the Jin dynasty pointed to the Feilai Peak at present-day Lingyin and said, 'This is a small peak of our country’s Vulture Peak (Gṛdhrakūṭa); when did it fly here?
The title of the verse, "Sent to Guang Huayan Returning to Vulture Peak," refers precisely to Lingyin; therefore, the name "Huili" is employed here.
The "pavilions" (lóu gé) allow one to see the hundred cities;
"kàng" (pronounced with the initial *k* and the rhyme *làng*) means to resist or oppose.
The "nine wilds" (jiǔ yě) refers to the ancient Nine Provinces. According to the *Erya*: the region between the two rivers is called Jizhou; south of the Yellow River is Yuzhou.
The region west of the River He is called Yongzhou; south of the Han River is Jingzhou; south of the Yangtze River is Yangzhou;
between the River Ji and the Yellow River is Yanzhou; east of the River Ji is Xuzhou; Yan is called Youzhou; and Qi is called Yingzhou.
"Yin" refers to a mat; it means a cushion.
Regarding the thirty-four patriarchs—twenty-eight from the Western Regions and six from China—it is because Bodhidharma came to this land as the first patriarch that the total is indeed thirty-four.
*Tuí* (頹): The first character is pronounced with the *dù* and *huí* rhymes; it means to fall downward to the ground. *Xí* (襲): Pronounced with the *sì* and *rù* rhymes;
it means to join or come together. *Qióng* (瓊) and *Jiǔ* (玖):

The first character is pronounced with the *qú* and *yíng* rhymes; the second is pronounced with the *jǔ* and *yǒu* rhymes. These are names for jade. In the *Shī* (Odes), it says: "He throws me a wooden peach; I shall repay him... [The text continues with the verse].
To adorn it with *qióng* and *jiǔ*.
"Lóngqì" (dragon-riders) should be understood as "lóngjì" (dragon-steeds). See its source.
"Pìnì" (to look askance): the upper character is read as *pǐ* (切), the lower as *nù* (切); it means to gaze upon.
Regarding the shooting of tigers: Li Guang of the Western Han was out hunting in Beiping when he saw a stone among the grass.

Thinking it was a tiger, he shot at it; the arrow entered the stone so deeply that the shaft was lost. Upon looking at it, he saw it was indeed a stone. He then tried to shoot it again, but in the end, he could not penetrate it.
Furthermore, the *Han Shi Waizhuan* records that while Xiong Quzi was traveling at night, he saw a stone lying in his path that resembled a tiger. He drew his bow and shot it;
the arrow penetrated the stone so deeply that the feathers were soaked in its marrow.

The *Xijing Zaji* by Ge Zhichuan states that Li Guang and his brothers were hunting north of Mount Ming when they encountered a sleeping tiger. He shot it with a single arrow, which killed it instantly, and he cut off its skull.
He used it as a pillow to demonstrate his subduing of the fierce. He cast a bronze image of its form to serve as a vessel for urine, demonstrating his loathing and contempt for it.
On another day, he again hunted on the southern slope of Mount Ming and saw a tiger lying down; he shot at it, and the arrow’s feathers drank the blood (penetrated to the bone).
Looking at it more closely, it was a stone; its shape resembled a tiger. He withdrew and shot again, but the arrowhead shattered, the shaft broke, and the stone remained unharmed.
I once asked Yang Xiong about this, and he said, "When one’s utmost sincerity reaches its peak, even metal and stone will open.
I replied to him, "In ancient times, there was a man traveling upon the Eastern Sea. After some time, the wind grew violent and his boat drifted uncontrollably..."
He was able to control it, but the boat followed the wind and waves, and no one knew where it was going. After one day and one night, they reached a solitary island. His companions were overjoyed;
they cast anchor with stones, climbed onto the island, and began to cook their food. Before the food was cooked, the island submerged.
Those on the boat cut their mooring lines, and the vessel drifted again. That which had been the solitary island was actually a great fish, which angrily lashed its tail.
It raised its mane, sucked up the waves and spat out the surges as it departed, swift as wind and clouds. More than ten people died on the island.
Furthermore, I know a man named Chen Gao, who was a person of simple and rustic character. He entered Mount Zhongnan to gather firewood and returned late.
On his way, before he had yet arrived at his destination, he saw a stone horse in front of the tomb of Chancellor Zhang. Thinking it was a deer, he struck it with his axe;
the axe head was shattered and the handle broke, yet the stone horse remained unharmed. These two instances [of the broken axe and the unharmed horse] were also due to the power of utmost sincerity.
Since there was the incident of Shen Ni’s drowning and the broken axe, why is it that the resonance of metal and stone is so partial? Master Ziyun had no reply.
"Zi" (子) means "to die," pronounced *bi* (弊), referring to sudden transformation. "Shou" (溲) is pronounced *sōu-liú* (所留切);
it refers to urine. Regarding the story of the horse: Duke Mu of Qin sent Bo Le to seek out horses. Bo Le recommended Jiu Fang Yin to seek them.
After three months, he returned and said, "I have found a horse; it is at Shaqiu, a stallion, yellow in color. When the horse arrived, however, it was—
It was a mare and black in color. Duke said to Bole: "In the horse you seek, you do not distinguish between coat color, sex, or age;
you are finished. Bole sighed deeply and said: "Has it come to this? What I observe is the heavenly mechanism (tianji)."
To grasp its essence while forgetting its coarseness; to perceive its interior while forgetting its exterior. Indeed, he obtained a horse from a thousand li away (as recorded in the *Huainanzi*).
Regarding the "Woman of the Rice Pot":
the consort of the King of Chu once sat in the summer heat, embracing an iron pillar and conceiving; subsequently, she gave birth to an iron [child].
The King of Chu commanded Gan Jiang to cast two swords for him; after three years, they were completed as a pair, one female and one male.
Gan Jiang secretly retained the male sword and presented the female to the King. The King stored it within a casket, where it frequently let out a mournful cry.
When the King questioned his ministers, they replied, "Swords have both female and male aspects; that which cries is merely longing for its mate. The King was greatly incensed.
He immediately seized Ganjiang and killed him. Ganjiang, knowing his destiny was fulfilled, concealed the sword within a pillar of his house and instructed his wife, Moye, saying:
"When the sun rises over the northern door and the pines grow upon the southern mountain—pines that sprout from stone—the sword shall be found therein.
Later, his wife gave birth to a son with eyebrows a foot apart. At the age of fifteen, he asked his mother, "Where is my father? His mother [replied].
He then recounted his previous history. Having reflected upon it for a long time, he had split open a pillar and found a sword;

day and night he desired to take revenge on King Chu. The king, in turn, sought after this man, proclaiming: "Whoever finds the 'Inch Between the Eyebrows,' I shall reward them handsomely. The Inch then fled.
Shortly thereafter, a guest arrived and said, "Are you not the Inch Between the Eyebrows? He replied, "Indeed. The guest said, "I am a man from Zengshan."
He was able to take revenge for his father’s enemy. Guǐchí said, "My father was formerly innocent, yet he was unjustly subjected to cruel torment.
Now that you have shown such benevolence toward me, what is it that you require? The guest replied, "I must have your head along with your sword. Guǐchí then gave him both the sword and his head.
Having obtained them, the guest presented them to the King of Chǔ. The king was greatly pleased. The guest said, "I wish to cook him. Thereupon, the king threw [the head] into the cauldron.
At the cauldron, a guest deceived the King, saying, "His head has not yet been cooked. While the King was looking on, the guest raised his sword behind him and struck;
the King's head fell into the cauldron. Thereupon, the two heads began to gnaw at one another. Fearing that he would not survive the encounter, the guest then slit his own throat to join them.
The three heads gnawed together until they were all eventually consumed. This is recorded in the *Xiaozizhuan* (Biographies of Filial Sons). [Note: *Dǎi* (紿) is pronounced *dài*.]
Dài (待): To deceive. Chéngróng (崢嶸):
The first character is read as gēng (耕) and the second as hùméng (戶萠); it describes a steep and lofty appearance.
Zēngxián (曾閒): The first character is read as gǔxiàn (古莧).
*Pā* (pronounced with the *bǔ* and *pō* initials): the calyx of a flower.
One day, while Juanshi Baizhang Hai was strolling in the mountains with Mazu, they saw a wild duck. Mazu asked:
"What is it? Baizhang said, "A wild duck. The Patriarch asked, "Where has it gone? Baizhang said, "It flew away.

The Patriarch then reached out his hand and pinched Baizhang on the bridge of his nose. Baizhang let out a cry of pain. The Patriarch said, "When did it ever fly away? At this, Baizhang attained great enlightenment.
On the following day, when the Patriarch ascended the hall, Baizhang came forward, folded up the cushion in front of him, and prostrated.
The Patriarch then descended from his seat.
Chan Master Danxia Tianran first visited Shitou; their karmic conditions were in accord, and he personally performed menial labor, such as tending the hearth, for three years.
One day, Shitou addressed the assembly, saying, "Tomorrow, clear away the weeds in front of the Buddha Hall."
When the next day arrived, the assembly and the novice trainees each prepared spades and hoes to clear away the grass;
only the Master filled a basin with water and washed his head, then knelt before the Abbot Heshang. Seeing this, Shitou laughed and proceeded to shave his hair.
Just as he was about to explain the method for reciting the precepts, the Master covered his ears and departed. Later, the Master went to visit Mazu.
Upon entering the Sangha hall, he mounted the neck of the Holy Monk (Śākyamuni). The assembly all cried out in alarm. Seeing this, Mazu said, "My son is naturally gifted.
The Master descended, prostrated himself, and said, "I thank you, Master, for bestowing my name."
The Preface to the Yunmen Lu: Seeing the Flow at Caoxi.
Regarding "stilled water," Zhuangzi said: "A person reflects in stilled water but does not reflect in flowing water;
only that which is still can bring rest to all things that move. The meaning of this verse reverses the words of Zhuangzi.
When the Great Master Bodhidharma was about to return to India, he addressed his disciples, saying, "The time has come;

why do you not each speak of what you have attained? At that time, Dao Fu said, "As I see it, one does not depart from words and letters, yet one does not cling to words and letters, taking them as the functioning of the Way. The Master said, "You have attained my skin. Nizi Tongzhi said:
"What I have now understood is like Ānanda seeing the land of Akṣobhya Buddha: having seen it once, he never saw it again. The Master said, "You have attained my flesh.
Daoyu said, "The four great elements are fundamentally empty; the five aggregates do not exist.
In my place of vision, there is not a single dharma to be obtained. The Master said, "You have attained my bones. Finally, Huikě prostrated himself and followed him.
He stood there. The Master said, "You have attained my marrow," and he subsequently transmitted the robe and bowl to him.
Shitou had previously said that Qingyuan Si sent Shitou Xiqian with a letter to the Venerable Nanyue Huairang, saying, "Wait for you to return;
I have a small adze for you to use while living in the mountains. Xiqian arrived at that place.
Before the letter had been presented, [Nanquan] asked: "When one does not admire the sages and does not prize one's own spiritual nature, what then?

Nanquan said: "Your question is directed toward those who are exceedingly lofty; why not ask about those below them? Xuefeng said: "I would rather sink into the depths for eternal kalpas than admire the liberation of the sages.
Nanquan then ceased speaking. When Xuefeng returned, he thought to himself: "Did my letter reach him? Xuefeng said: "The letter did not even reach him."
Dashi reached [the gate], but his message was not passed on. Xianshou thought, "What shall I do?
Qian then recounted the previous conversation and added, "When you left, you promised me the 'rusty axe'; I now request it. Dashi lowered one leg, and Qian immediately prostrated himself.

In ancient times, when people were being sent off on their way, Zi Lu was about to depart and took his leave of Confucius. The Master said, "Shall I present you with a gift of a carriage, or shall I present you with words of counsel?
Zi Lu replied, "I beg for your words. The Master said, "If you are not diligent, you will not achieve success;

if you do not toil, you will have no merit; if you are not loyal, you will have no close kin; if you are not trustworthy, you will have no return; if you are not reverent, you will lose the Way of Ritual. Be careful of these five things."
As for this, Zilu said, "I, You, request to serve him for the rest of my life. This is recorded in the *Jia yu*.
Shan Jia of Qudong Mountain in Xinfeng lived on Mount Xinfeng at the end of the Tang Dynasty Daizong era; he was known by the name of the mountain.

One day, he addressed the assembly, saying: "Brothers, at the end of summer and the beginning of autumn, whether you go east or west, you must go to a place ten thousand *li* away where there is not even an inch of grass before you will succeed.
He further asked: "As for that place ten thousand *li* away where there is not even an inch of grass—how does one go there?
When a monk reported this to Shishuang, Shishuang heard it and said: "Stepping out the door is it."
"Grass. When Dongshan heard this, he said: "How many people can there be within the Great Tang?
'Gao' (杲) is pronounced with the *lao* (老) and *qie* (切) finals. It means the sun rising. Because it depicts the sun atop a tree, it is called 'gao' when situated above."
That which is below is called "the profound" (yǎo); that which is in the middle is called "the eastern" (dōng).
Regarding this, Tao Kan of the Jin dynasty said to people: "The sages cherish every inch of time; ordinary people should cherish every fraction of time."
Gu Yue of the Jin dynasty was of the same age as Emperor Wen, yet his hair turned white prematurely. When the Emperor asked him why this was so, he replied:
"The nature of the pine and cypress grows even more luxuriant after enduring the frost; the substance of the *púliǔ* tree, however, begins to wither before the autumn."
"Mu" (毋) is pronounced "wu. It is a prohibitive term.

[The story of] Dui Xue (奪席) concerns Dai Ping (戴憑), courtesy name Cizhong, a native of Pingxing in Runan during the Eastern Han dynasty. On the first day of the New Year, he attended the court audience for congratulations.
When the hundred officials had assembled, the Emperor commanded those among the ministers who were able to expound the sutras to engage in mutual debate and cross-examination.

Whenever one’s interpretation was found to be不通 (unconvincing or inconsistent), the Emperor would immediately strip him of his seat to bestow it upon the one who excelled. Daoping eventually sat upon more than fifty seats in succession.
Consequently, a proverb arose in the capital: "In the exegesis of the sutras, no one can defeat Dai Shizhong."
Regarding the recitation of *zhǔ* (broom), it is correctly written as *zhǔ*. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "The Venerable Cūḍapanthaka was by nature dull-witted and slow.

The Buddha instructed him to recite the word 'sweeping broom' (*sǎozhǔ*). He would remember 'sweeping' (*sǎo*) and forget 'broom' (*zhǔ*), and he would remember 'broom' (*zhǔ*) and forget 'sweeping' (*sǎo'). This continued for six years."
He concentrated his mind on this meaning and attained realization. He then reflected to himself: "The broom (*sūci*) is the brush; 'to sweep' (*mārjana*) means to remove.
The removal-brush is a metaphor for the Eightfold Noble Path, while the filth is a metaphor for the defilements of the three poisons.
To sweep away the filth of the three poisons with the broom of the Eightfold Noble Path—this is precisely what the meaning of 'broom' signifies. As he contemplated this principle deeply, his mind...
He attained understanding and realized the path of Arhatship. *Sui* (篲): pronounced as in *sui* (似歲切), meaning a broom.

From the *Famu* (伐木) ode: "Cutting Wood" concerns the fellowship of friends and old acquaintances. From the Son of Heaven down to the common people, there are none who do not require friends to achieve fulfillment.
One should be harmonious through affection for kin, not abandon the virtuous in friendship, and not neglect old acquaintances.
Thus, the virtue of the people will turn toward substantiality. The woodcutters’ axes ring out with *ding-ding*; the birds cry out with *ying-ying*.
Emerging from the dark valley, they move to the lofty trees. They cry out their song, seeking the voices of their companions. Look at those birds; even they seek the voices of their friends.
How much more so for this person! Not seeking out companions.
*Dingding* (pronounced with the initial *zhōng* and rhyme *gēng*) is the sound of hewing wood.
*Mōngmōng* (pronounced with the initial *mēng*) describes the appearance of fine rain.
The words of the ancients are the very eye of the Great Dharma. A verse sent to Elder Fu says: "Qú qú qú. Wǒ wǒ wǒ.
North, south, east, and west—all are acceptable. Whether acceptable or unacceptable, it is simply that for me, there is nothing that is not acceptable."
Huo (cut by Hu and Kuai): A particle used for emphasis.
Zeng (cut by Bi and Bao): To feel ashamed; it means shame.
Yi (cut by Yu and Gui): To leave behind or bestow upon me.
The Elder Xinghuo once composed a verse and sent it to Xuedou, saying: "Ten thousand transformations and deeds are not bound by time;
Why need the pure breeze be restricted to the east or west? If someone asks me about the meaning of the Westward Journey, A stone tiger swallows the wooden sheep."
From the *Lunyu*, "On Not Being a Vessel": The Master said, "The gentleman is not a vessel. Baozi said, "A vessel is that which is limited to its specific function;
as for the gentleman, there is nothing he does not apply. Xuedou remarked that the Perfected Person is one who reaches everywhere.
*Zuàn* (賺) should be read as *zhàn*. Pronounced with the *zhù* and *xiàn* finals. It means to be deceived. Other instances follow this pattern.

In *xiāo shuò* (銷爍), the lower character should be *jīn* (金); it is written as *shuò* (鑠). Pronounced with the *shū* and *yào* finals. It means to melt metal. *Shuò* (鑠) also means *zhuó shuò* (灼鑠), meaning brilliance or radiance.
This is not the meaning.
Regarding "matters" (shì), some speak of them as "matters of the monastic grove" (cónglín shì). Often, people falsely discuss the trivial, mundane affairs of that day;
how could this be so? When a patriarch proclaims the Way, there are no instances where his words do not arise from these very matters.
Verses and hymns are intended to guide and attract learners; how could they be meant to embody ultimate truth?

If a master, relying on conventional truth, were to declare "that is wrong" and "this is right" merely to instruct gods and humans, what would such a teaching be worth as a standard for future generations?
To begin with, Dongshan, on account of a certain matter, spoke in verse: “On Mount Wutai, clouds steam rice; Before the Buddha Hall, it is a ‘dog-urine sky.
Atop the flagpole, *zhuanzi* are being fried; Three monkeys toss coins at night. Furthermore, Ciming, on account of a certain matter, spoke in verse:
“When the time comes, open the bowl and spread the mat; When the meal is finished, put away the bowl and sleep when weary.”
The stone man claps his hands and laughs "he-he"; the wooden woman plays the zither—you play the zither yourself. Furthermore, Shao Jiupeng composed a verse on account of an incident:
"Having caught it, he immediately removes its four legs; Two ears are hung with golden rings. How excellent it is, in the deep night under the bright moon:
A single sound, clear and penetrating, passes through the pine gate. All of these were composed in response to specific events; how could they harbor attachment to matters of right and wrong?
