It lies in the interval between movement and stillness.
"Luoluo" (落落) and "lulü" (碌碌)—*lù* should be read as *lù* (jade); *lù* is stone. This is not the correct meaning.
The Master Lao said: "Do not be *lùlù* like jade; be *luoluo* like stone. Commentators say: "Jade that is *lùlù* is merely precious; it is not [the way of the sage]."
"It can be base; stones fall one after another—base and nothing more. It cannot be noble. The word "sī" (斯) means rapid;
its pronunciation is like "xī," and its sound is a vibration. One interpretation says it is a groan or sigh, referring to the frequency and speed with which one groans and sighs.
This expression appears in the *Pratyaya-nidāna* concerning the passing of the summer retreat in vain; therefore, Xuedou cites it here.
Regarding "White Water Lily" (*báipín*) in Song Yu’s *Fu on the Wind*: "The wind arises from the earth, rising from the tips of the green water lilies (*qīngpín*).
It spreads through the streams and valleys, winding along the slopes of Mount Tai, and dances beneath the pines and cypresses.
It is called "white water lily" because its stalks are green while its flowers are white. The *Fengtu Ji* (Records of Local Customs) by Zhou Chu states: "Píng and pín are names for celery."
The larger is called *pín* (duckweed), and the smaller is called *píng* (duckweed).
Regarding the twelve tortoises: in the "Tángwèn" chapter of the *Lìzǐ*, it is said that within the Guīxū (Vast Abyss) there are five mountains. The first is called Dàiyù.
The second is called Yuanqiao; the third, Fanghu; the fourth, Yingzhou; and the fifth, Penglai.

These mountains are each thirty thousand li in circumference at their base, and their level summits are nine thousand li across. The distance between them is seventy thousand li, such that they serve as neighbors to one another.
The palaces and towers upon them are all made of gold and jade, and the birds and beasts there are all pure [in color].
There are trees of white silk and of pearl and jade that grow in dense clusters; their flowers and fruits all possess flavor, and those who eat them neither age nor die.
The people dwelling there are all of the lineage of immortals and sages; those who fly back and forth between them day and night are beyond counting.
However, the roots of these five mountains have no firm attachment, and they constantly rise with the tides and waves.
The five mountains drifted downward and back and forth; they could not remain stationary for even a moment. The immortals and sages were distressed by this and petitioned the Emperor.

Fearing that the mountains would drift to the western extremity and cause the dwellings of the various sages to be lost, the Emperor commanded Yuqiang to dispatch fifteen giant tortoises to lift their heads and support the mountains.
These were divided into three shifts, with a change of rotation every sixty thousand years. Only then did the five mountains begin to stand firm.
It moved. Now, in the Land of the Great Dragon-Lords, there were giants who could reach the five mountains in less than a few steps with a single stride;
they would hook six giant tortoises (*āo*) at once with a single line, carry them all together back to their land, and burn their bones to calculate [the distance].
Consequently, the two mountains of Daiyu and Yuanjiao drifted toward the North Pole and sank into the great ocean. The sages and immortals...

Those who were dispersed and migrated numbered in the billions. The Emperor was filled with indignation; he encroached upon and diminished the land of the Dragon-Ber (Lóngbó) so that it became cramped, and he encroached upon and shortened the people of the Lesser Dragon-Ber.
By the time of Fuxi and Shennong, the inhabitants of those lands were still several tens of zhang tall.
According to this account, there were only six *āo* tortoises; yet the hymn (*sòng*) speaks of twelve. Thus, various regions have established differing numbers. Therefore—
It is difficult to verify with certainty; however, one must follow only the principle.
Several times I have earnestly inquired about the characters *chízhú* (踟躅):

the first character is pronounced with the initial *zhí* (直) and the final *lí* (離), while the second is pronounced with the initial *zhí* (直) and the final *zhū* (誅). As for the word *chízhú*, I have not yet seen its source.

The "monkey" refers to the monkey of the Lingguang (Numinous Light) Temple. It clings to the crossbeam (*yuan*) and pursues [its mate]. *Yuan* is pronounced like *chuan*. "Chen-yuan" means to gallop and pursue.
This is the explanation of Sima Zheng.
The "Two White Cranes Flying Over" (雙白鶴篇) says: "Every five li they look back; every ten li they linger.
Furthermore, the *Wenxuan* states: "They spread their wings toward Penglai and Fuzhou, and raise their voices gazing at Kunlun and Langfeng."
Master Wang, the Chan Master Nanyuan Puyuan of Chizhou, was a native of Xinzheng in Zhengzhou. His surname was Wang.
Having received the Dharma from Mazu, he propagated the Way at Nanquan and frequently referred to himself as "Master Wang. He once addressed the assembly, saying:
"Throughout the entire world, one cannot find a single person who is dull-witted and simple-minded."
"Golden Gates, Golden Gates. These are the national gates. Cui Bao’s *Notes on Ancient and Modern Times* states: "A *que* (gate-tower) is located beneath the ruler's gate.

It is so named because when ministers arrive here, they reflect upon their own deficiencies; or the ruler himself reflects upon his own failures and seeks to remedy them. They are coated with vermilion and white plaster.
Beneath them, clouds, vapors, transcendents and spirits, and various wondrous birds and strange beasts are painted to instruct the myriad people. Furthermore, as for the term *que*:"
"Què (Deficient). The two sides of the gate are deficient; "I" [the character 我] is hidden within it. This is from the Self-Preface.
Regarding "treading upon water," the *Han Shi Waizhuan* says: "Now, water follows principles in its flow and leaves nothing behind, as if possessing ritual propriety (*li*).
It is heavy yet yields to what is below, as if possessing wisdom (*zhi*). One may tread upon its depths without hesitation, as if possessing courage (*yong*). It provides embankments and defenses..."
Yet it was extinguished; he seemed one who knew his destiny. He traversed perils to reach distant lands; he seemed one possessed of virtue.

Perhaps his original composition was "Treading on Ice," yet when we met under the overturned carriage-canopy, I saw before me the verse on the "Overturned Canopy. We traveled the same road, yet followed different tracks.
"Summer Clouds," from Tao Qian’s *Poems on the Four Seasons*: Spring waters fill the four marshes; summer clouds abound with wondrous peaks.
Autumn moonlight casts forth its brilliant radiance; winter ridges display the elegance of solitary pines. In antiquity there was the poem "Spring Clouds Arising Everywhere":
The spring colors pervade the vast clarity; spring clouds arise everywhere. Entering the wind, the robe briefly gathers; following the carriage canopy, they grow light. [End]
The leaves still cling to the trees; as the tower approaches the city, one ascends it with sorrowful thoughts, facing its reflection as if possessed by the sentiment of parting.
Master Yuànchéng of the Yìfǎ Temple said: "Gandharva" is translated here as "City of Seeking Fragrance.

This refers to the musical deities named Gandharvas who dwell among the ten jeweled mountains. When the various devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven desire music, these deities manifest their bodies [to provide it].
There are distinct signs by which one may know the will of the gods and go there to enjoy themselves. For this reason, in the Western Regions, musicians are called *gandharvas*.

These musicians often use illusions to create cities and palaces that vanish in an instant and reappear as before; consequently, the cities manifested by dragons and vapors are also termed "Gandharva Cities.

Furthermore, the *Wùlèi xiānggǎn zhì* (Records on the Mutual Resonance of Categories of Things) states: [The text continues with further details regarding the nature of these illusory manifestations.]
It is said: one theory holds that the *shen* is simply the *ge* (clam). The *che-ao* is a large clam capable of exhaling vapors to form towers and terraces;
these vapors frequently emerge from the sea amidst the islands. Another theory identifies it as a dragon, while yet another calls it a *shen*.

As for the appearance of the *shen*, it resembles a *chi-long* (a hornless dragon), possessing ears, horns, and a mane; when viewed from the rivers and seas, it appears like a blazing fire and undergoes many transformations.
Transformation: When it is about to rain, the heavens emit vapors between morning and evening that coalesce into pavilions and terraces with distinct roofs and railings.
In the space of a single glance, these manifest as broad or narrow, high or low; thus, they cannot be fixed with certainty.
"Where does the rain come from? When Senior Official Liu Yu asked this while seeking rain at Yunju Mountain, he received a response.
He then asked Yunju Yingshan, "Where does the rain come from? Yingshan replied, "It comes from where Senior Official you ask. The official was delighted and thanked him.
Yingshan, however, turned the question back on him, asking, "Where does the asking come from? The official was left speechless.
"What color is the wind? asked Xichan while sitting with Dongping and several officials. Dongping remained silent.
Xichan then asked a monk, who picked up his cassock and said, "It is being sold in the market in the prefectural seat. Xichan asked, "How much silk cloth does it require?
The monk said, "It has nothing to do with that. Xichan was speechless. Yunmen spoke on his behalf, saying, "Tsk!"
This is the talk of one who has fallen into the abyss. See the *Record of the Master Huaihe* and the *Recorded Sayings of Yunmen*.
In the *Recorded Sayings of Xuedou*, every phrase and sentence was never uttered at random; there was always a basis for them.
For instance, regarding the expression "pō pō léng léng," it refers to when a monk asked Qingping: "When [the waves] are pō pō léng léng..."
"How is it? Ping said, "It is because you do not understand. The monk asked, "What is it like after one has understood? Ping said, "Do not further heap up layers upon layers.
This is like the saying: "A great merit is not rewarded with a banner. Thus, a monk asked Fengxue: "The 'carving a boat to seek a sword' is far off;
what is the matter of the immediate body? Fengxue said: "A great merit is not rewarded with a banner; the thatched gate is overgrown with weeds. Furthermore...
"A head three feet long—know who this is? This refers to when a monk asked Dongshan, "What is the practice of a śramaṇa?
Dongshan replied, "A head three feet long, a neck two inches long. Furthermore, it is like now throwing [it] into West Lake;
this refers to when a monk asked Yantou, "What is the Way? Yantou said, "Throw your worn-out straw sandals into the lake. It is also like...
"What are the Five Emperors and Three Sovereigns? Who says that gold is like dung and soil? The heavenly colt within the White Moon Palace.
These are all words from the songs and poems of Chan Yue.
In the third year of the Tianxi era (989), a monk asked Yunmen, "What is the uppermost orifice? Yunmen said, "Nine times nine is eighty-one.
Another monk asked, "What is the very first phrase? Yunmen said, "Nine times nine is eighty-one.
Yet another monk asked, "The character 'yi' (one) is not it; the character 'ba' (eight) does not form it. I wonder what word this is? Yunmen—
It says: "Nine times nine is eighty-one. The character *xiáo* (詨訛) is correctly written as *xiáo* (殽).

It is pronounced with the initial *hú* and the rhyme *jiāo*. It means "to confuse" (*hùnxíáo*) or "to mix. The second character is pronounced with the initial *wǔ* and the rhyme *huó*. It means "to err" (*miù*).
*Míng* (冥) should be read as *mìng* (瞑); it means to close one's eyes.
*Shǔ* (曙) is pronounced with the initial *cháng-shù* (常恕); it means dawn.
*Chuì* (毳) is pronounced with the initial *chǔ-shuì* (楚稅); it refers to fine hand-sewn patchwork.
Xianggu (Elephant Bone) Laoshi was a separate mountain of Xuefeng, so named because its shape resembled that of an elephant’s bone.

"The vast expanse of mist and water" contains a profound meaning inherent to the genre of verse (song). Furthermore, when inferred from the momentum of the text, it merely initiates a sense of distance;
there is no necessity to engage with specific affairs, which makes it particularly concise and appropriate. Nevertheless, in our teaching, we discuss the process of taking birth.
The sūtras and śāstras record this in full detail. When three conditions coincide like a chick pecking at its shell and a parent tapping from without, there is no way to alter it.
How could it be that this body has not yet perished while he has already been entrusted to another realm for three years?

Even if one were a Bodhisattva who takes birth at will and possesses mastery over the one and the many, why would such a person as you need to weep upon seeing a brocade apron? Consider this carefully: this was merely a matter of idle curiosity.
This was done for that purpose, yet the underlying principle cannot be examined.
"Yi" (遺) is pronounced with the *qu* (余) and *gui* (貴) finals.
Presenting this to you, I request you to explain the final phrase. These five characters should be written with the *zhu* (注) radical; see other editions.
"Difficult to deceive" (nán-mán-mán) means one should act with deceit; it signifies to cheat. The following cases are to be understood in this manner.
"Golden hammer" (jīn-chuí): it should be written with the "metal" radical (金), as in 鎚. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Iron is black gold"; therefore, it is called a "golden hammer."
Regarding the *chui* (hammer): the interpretation that it is a curved support for silkworms is incorrect.
The *Zhinan* and *Gujin zhu* state: "When the Yellow Emperor fought against Chiyou at Zhuolu, Chiyou raised a great mist that confused the four directions.
The Emperor, standing in his chariot, pointed southward with his finger to show the way to his soldiers, and thus finally captured Chiyou."
And he cut it down. It was subsequently called the "South-Pointing Chariot.
My Buddha’s response-body (nirmāṇakāya) is subsumed within the True Reality; ultimately, not a single characteristic can be apprehended.

From that True Reality, the response-body arises, manifesting as bodies of a thousand feet, sixteen feet, or three feet. Extending even to the forms of monkeys, deer, and horses, he manifests transformation-bodies according to the various classes of beings.
The phrase "three feet more" (*sānchǐ duō yǐn*) refers to the Elder Kuśinātha; it has not yet been seen in which sutra this appears.
*Chéng* (懲) is pronounced with the initial *zhí* and the final *líng* (切).

It means to demonstrate or to admonish. *Gè* (革) is pronounced with the initial *gǔ* and the final *hé* (核); it means to change. *Zhé* (轍) is pronounced with the final *zhí* and *liè* (列); it refers to a track or path.
Master Futi was a native of Yiwu, Wuzhou. On the eighth day of the fifth month in the fourth year of the Jianwu era of the Qi dynasty, he was born into the family of Fu Xuanci in Shuanglin Township;
his given name was Xi. In the eleventh year of the Tianjian era, he took Liu Shi as his wife, whose name was Miaoguang, and they had two sons, Pucheng and Puguang.
He once sent a letter to Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty. From himself—
He was titled the Great Being of Future Liberation, Shanhui (Good Wisdom).
Later, he met the monk from the Western Regions, Seng Shoudou, who said, "I and you both made vows before the Buddha Vipaśyin. The robes and alms bowl currently in the Tuṣita Palace remain there;
when will you return? Thereupon, he ordered [the monk] to look at his reflection in water. Seeing a halo and a jeweled canopy, he realized it was indeed Maitreya Bodhisattva.
In the *Gandavyūha*, the youth Sudhana traveled south by stages toward the land of Suprabha.

He ascended Mount Sumerukalpa, and from its summit, he surveyed the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir, searching everywhere out of longing and yearning to see the bhikṣu Meghashri.
After seven days had passed, he saw that bhikṣu walking slowly upon another mountain peak.
He walked on foot. Having seen him, he went up to him and prostrated at his feet. Master Qingliang’s Commentary states:
"Only when one forgets the station where they abide can they be said to have attained the essential meaning."
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra of the Poison-Coated Drum* states: The Buddha told Kāśyapa, "For example, it is like a skilled physician who compiles various medicines and coats a drum with them.
If there are those wounded in battle, upon hearing the sound of that drum, all their wounds are completely healed."
Except for those whose lives have ended and those who are destined to die, it is likewise with this sound of the Dharma drum of the Mahāyāna:
when all sentient beings hear its sound, the arrows of lust, anger, and delusion cease to afflict them.
Even those who have not yet resolved to attain enlightenment, or who have committed the four pārājika offenses or the ānantarya crimes, are all healed and cured—except for the icchantikas.
*Bei* (輩):
pronounced with the *yu* and *jiao* finals; it means "desire.
*Vaiśālī*, here translated as "Extensive Splendor" (*Guǎngyán*), is the city where Vimalakīrti resides.
The fowler yearns for the crane; this is from the "Inquiry into Clarity" (Wenming). Someone asked about the gentleman in times of order, to which [the Master] replied:

"He is like a phoenix. When asked about him in times of chaos, he said: "He is like a phoenix. Someone did not understand, so [the Master] said: "It is because you have not reflected upon it. He said: "In times of order he appears; in times of chaos he hides.
The wild goose flies into the boundless void; what can the fowler yearn for? Commentators sometimes cite this passage, asking: "If that is so, what would the fowler yearn for?"
It is said that one must not harbor longing. The intent of the verse is that the hunter harbors longing; this is indeed the opposite of the aforementioned meaning.
This passage from the *Yunmen Lu* (Record of Yunmen) reveals the Dharma-body and concerns the karmic conditions of Elder Fulang.
*Lǎodǎo* (潦倒): The first character is pronounced with the *yún* and *hào* rhymes; the second is pronounced with the *lú* and *kǎo* rhymes. It describes the state of being old. *Jiūqiū* (啾秋):
The first character is pronounced with the *jí* and *yóu* rhymes. An ancient verse says: "Boiling water will not cease its bubbling;
the Patriarch comes and goes, adding firewood. The chirping continues as before in its clamor; each person claims they are practicing the Way."
The *Biemo yan Song zhuan* states: His name was Changyu, his surname Yin, and he was a native of Fanyang.
He left the household life at An Guo Temple in northern Yan and came to reside at Biemo Rock on Mount Wutai, which is the place where Mañjuśrī subdued the dragon.
He took this as his name. He always carried a wooden fork. Whenever he saw a monk coming to pay his respects, he would immediately thrust the fork under the monk's neck and say:
"Which demon enticed you to leave the household life? Which demon taught you to travel on pilgrimage? If you can speak, you shall die under the fork;
if you cannot speak, you shall die under the fork. Speak quickly! Few among the students were able to respond.
There was one who could respond to him: Jingtong of Huoshan in Jinzhou, who was none other than Dajian Chanbuddha.

As soon as he arrived, he leaped into the Master’s embrace and sat there. The Master patted Huoshan on the back three times, whereupon Huoshan ran out, saying, "From three thousand li away, you have come to mock me!"
Baofo Deceives People: Chan Master Congzhan of Baofo in Zhangzhou deceives people in four ways. First: He asked a monk, "What Buddha is in the hall?
The monk said, "Wait for the Master to decide. The Master said, "Śākyamuni Buddha. The monk said, [“... (The text continues with the monk's response).
1. “Do not deceive others. The Master said, “In fact, it is you who are deceiving me. 2. He asked a monk, “What karma have you performed to eat so much?
The monk said, “The Master is not small either. The Master then crouched down. The monk said, “Master, do not deceive others.
The Master said, “In fact, it is you who are deceiving me. 3. He asked a monk, “What is your name?”
The monk said, "Xianze. The Master said, "What if you suddenly encounter one who is parched and dried up? The monk said, "Who is the one who is parched and dried up?
The Master said, "It is I. The monk said, "Master, do not deceive people. The Master said, "In fact, it is you who are deceiving me. 4.
He asked the bath attendant, "How wide is the cauldron for the hot water? The attendant said, "Please let the Master measure it. The Master then made a measuring gesture.
Shi said, "Master, do not deceive people. The Master said, "In fact, it is you who are deceiving me.
'Dependent arising, dependent arising' refers to the twelve links of dependent origination; it is also called the twelvefold dependent arising. The *Vimokṣa-śāstra* states:
1. Ignorance (*avidyā*): not knowing the Four Noble Truths. 2. Volitional formations (*saṃskāra*): the actions of body, speech, and mind. 3. Consciousness (*vijñāna*):

the single moment of mind at the time of entering the womb is called consciousness. 4. Name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*): the mental factors arising together with the continuous stream of mind, as well as the material form of the *kalala*.
5. The six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*): the six internal sense bases. 6. Contact (*sparśa*): the six groups of contact. 7. Feeling (*vedanā*): the six [feelings].

8. The body of sensation (*vedanā-kāya*). 9. Craving (*tṛṣṇā*): the six bodies of craving (*ṣaṭ-tṛṣṇā-kāya*). 10. Grasping (*upādāna*): the four graspings (*catvāry upādānāni*). 11. Existence (*bhava*):

this karma is capable of giving rise to existence in the realms of desire, form, and formlessness. 12. Birth (*jāti*): the arising of the aggregates (*skandha*) within existence. 13. Old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).

The maturation of the aggregates (*skandha*) is called aging; the disintegration and scattering of the aggregates is termed death. Furthermore, within a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) are established.
For example, when the eye perceives a form, a deluded person gives rise to craving. At that time, the mind of one who pursues purity and pleasure is deluded; this is called ignorance (*avidyā*).

The volitional engagement (*saṃskāra*) based on attachment to this [craving] is "conditioned by ignorance. The consciousness (*vijñāna*) that adheres to this [volitional engagement] is "conditioned by volitional engagement," being associated with cognition.

Because of the mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) and the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) as conditions, the sense faculties (*indriya*) become purified; this is called "conditioned by form, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*).
Ignorance (*avidyā*) and contact (*sparśa*) are the conditions for the six sense bases. Contact associated with joy (*saumanasya-sparśa*) conditions feeling (*vedanā*).

Feeling conditions craving (*tṛṣṇā*), which clings to pure pleasure. This craving conditions grasping (*upādāna*); through clinging to volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), grasping conditions becoming (*bhava*). The arising of those phenomena is becoming.
Dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*): having gone [into existence] is aging; the dissolution of mindfulness is death.
Fu Gu (布鼓) was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Han and served as the Chancellor of Dongping. He said to the King’s Grand Tutor: “Do not carry a cloth drum toward Leimen.
The commentator says: Leimen is the gate of Kuaiji in Yue. There was a great drum there. Yue—
He struck it; the sound was heard as far as Luoyang. "A cloth drum" (bùgǔ): a drum made of cloth, which has no sound. "Mǔ": pronounced *wú*.
Regarding the iron contract (*tiěquàn*), a monk asked Xuedou, "What is the meaning of dependent origination? The Master said, "A diamond-cast iron contract."

The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "A signpost in the middle of a bustling marketplace. The monk said, "In that case, when the path reaches the end of the water, one sits and watches the clouds arise. The Master said, "Lià (pronounced with the *quàn* and *qù* finals). The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "A signpost in the middle of a bustling marketplace.
The monk said, "In that case, when the path reaches the end of the water, one sits and watches the clouds arise. The Master said, "Lià. (The character is pronounced with the *quàn* and *qù* finals.)
"Names and realities do not correspond. Master Zhao said: "If one seeks objects by means of names, there is no reality that corresponds to the name.
If one seeks names by means of objects, there is no efficacy in the name to apprehend the object. That an object has no reality corresponding to its name means it is not truly an object."
A name has no power to grasp an object; it is not the name itself [that grasps it]. Therefore, the name does not correspond to the reality, and the reality does not correspond to the name.
When name and reality do not correspond, where are all phenomena? Master Qingliang said: "If the reality were the name, then upon seeing a face, one should immediately know its name.
If the name were the reality, then upon calling out 'fire,' it should immediately burn one's mouth."
Spring rice should be pounded. The character for "accommodating" (*shū*) denotes merit. *Cuíwéi*:
the first syllable is pronounced as *cú* (with the *lú* and *huí* finals); the second syllable is pronounced as *wú* and *huí*. It means "greatly high.
"Empty space arises within the crags" refers to Subhūti being seen within a rock cave, as recorded in the *Hòulù*.
The character "tu" (圖) [as in "tushu"] should be understood as meaning "pictorial representation.
The *Record of Mount Wulao* states: "At Qixian Temple, to the northeast of the monastery, there is the Five Elders Peak (*Wulao Feng*)."
Everything can be clearly counted. Among them is Lion Peak, which appears as if carved from stone; when clouds and mists veil it, its resemblance is particularly striking.
Of all the wonders of Mount Lu, this is the most excellent.

A layperson (upāsaka) who possesses four virtues is entitled to be called a layperson: first, not seeking official office; second, having few desires while accumulating virtue; third, possessing great wealth;
and fourth, upholding the Way and attaining self-awakening. Furthermore, the *Bodhisattvacaryā-sūtra* states:

"There are those who dwell in wealth, those who dwell in the home, those who dwell in the Dharma, and those who dwell in the court or in the mountains; these are all collectively termed [laypersons]."
"Jushi" (居士): "Wei" (隈) is pronounced *wū huī* (烏灰切); it means to lean against.
Regarding Taihu (太湖), the *Wudi zhi* (吳地志) states: "Taihu is forty *li* southwest of Wuxian County. Its circumference is three... [The text continues with the measurement of the lake].
It covers sixteen thousand *qǐng*. It is also known as the Jūqū Marsh (*Jùqū Zé*).
During seven hundred sexagenary cycles, Chán Master Cóngshěn of Zhòuzhōu lived to the age of one hundred and twenty. Once, someone asked him:
"Master, how old are you? The Master replied, "A single string of prayer beads has not yet been fully counted. The *Record of the Pagoda at Zhentufu* states:
"The Master attained seven hundred cycles of the sexagenary calendar. This "seven hundred cycles" is a general reference to the large number of one hundred and twenty;
in reality, it was one hundred and sixteen years plus eight months, totaling forty thousand and two days.
Regarding the "City-Bridge Jade" (*Lianchengbi*) from the *Records of the Grand Historian* (*Shiji*): The state of Zhao possessed the Bianshi Jade. Qin wished to exchange it for fifteen cities.
Zhao dispatched the Grandee Xiangru to present the jade. When King Zhao of Qin obtained the jade but did not cede the territory, Xiangru feigned that there was a flaw in the jade;

he took it up and pointed to it, then leaned against a pillar and refused to return it, saying: "I request that you first purify yourselves and prepare the ground [for the sacrifice] before you cede the territory."
Only on the fifth day did he receive the jade disc. The King thought that if he were to press the official too hard, both his head and the jade would be shattered.
Fearing the destruction of the jade, the King did not dare to inflict further harm upon him, and the jade was eventually returned to Zhao.
"Bi-feng" (Sorrowful Wind) and "Liu-shui" (Flowing Water) are the names of two ancient melodies. Chen Zuan’s *Qin Shu* (Book of the Lute) states that they were composed by Zhongni (Confucius).
"Wu-ye" (Wailing): when the heart harbors something loathsome, it is as if one is vomiting it out. "Yan" (Throat): this refers to the obstruction of the voice.
"Rare Sound" is seen in the *Record of Yunmen*, Volume One.
Regarding the "Sentence that Settles Heaven and Earth": when the Great Master Yunmen was traveling on pilgrimage, an official asked him, "Do you have a sentence that settles heaven and earth?
Yunmen said, "Suru suru siri svāhā."
*The Selection of Orchid Boats*. Commentary: "Orchid boats" refers to boats with cassia oars;

this is chosen for their fragrance and purity. *The Eight Rhapsodies* by Shen Yue of the Tang dynasty: "Ascending the tower to gaze at the autumn moon; gathering in the garden to face the spring breeze; autumn arrives and I lament the withered grasses;
the cold comes and I grieve for the fallen paulownia; traveling at dusk, I hear the night cranes; setting out at dawn, I listen to the morning wild geese. [End of excerpt]
Wearing [the robes] to leave the marketplace, he donned coarse cloth to guard the lands east of the mountains.
At sunset, the azure clouds gather; the beloved has still not arrived. Many senior scholars of the Confucian and Buddhist traditions have often attributed this to the poetry of Tang Huixiu.
Xuedou frequently employs this same sentiment; for instance, in his "Sending Off a Monk," he writes: "The azure clouds flow back to their source..."
This is a poem by the poet [Wan]. Furthermore, he harmonized with the record of the monk Wan Shuji, saying: "How could the words of Tang Huixiu be easily heard?
At evening, the wind blows away the azure clouds from the stream. According to the *Wenxuan*, this is actually Jiang Yan’s "Imitating Huixiu:
A Poem on Parting Sorrow," which was indeed composed by Jiang Yan.

Danxia Ruian began his studies while selecting candidates for the imperial examinations. While he was preparing to take the exams in Chang’an, he encountered a Chan practitioner who asked him, “What are you doing?
Ruian replied, “Selecting officials. The guest said, “How does selecting officials compare to selecting Buddhas? Thereupon, Ruian inquired about the method for selecting Buddhas;
he was joyfully enlightened by this, and later he received the Dharma from Shitou.
"Difficult elder brother, difficult younger brother" refers to Chen Changwen, the son of Chen Yuanfang of the Eastern Han dynasty; this was Chen Qun.
He and Xiaoguang, the son of Chen Jifang, each debated the merits and virtues of their respective fathers.
Unable to reach a decision, they consulted Taichu—Chen Shishi, the father of both Yuanfang and Jifang. Taichu said, "For Yuanfang, it is difficult to be an elder brother; for Jifang..."
It is difficult to be a younger brother to Nanwei. Furthermore, there was Wang Min of the Jin dynasty, whose courtesy name was Xiujie.

From his youth, he possessed talent and artistry, and his reputation surpassed that of his elder brother, Wang Xunzhi. A saying goes: "Fahu is not without merit, yet Sengmi makes it difficult to be an elder brother.
Fahu was the childhood name of Xun, while Sengmi was the childhood name of Min.
Fāngfēi (Fragrant and Luxuriant): *fāng* refers to fragrant herbs; *fēi* describes the lush appearance of grasses. Xuánshā (Mysterious Sand): His name was Shíbèi.
He was the son of the Xiè family of Míncóun County, Fúzhōu. In his youth, he made his living as a fisherman and angler.
At the beginning of the Xiántóng era of the Táng dynasty, he suddenly developed a resolve to transcend the mundane world and followed Língxùn of Fúróng Mountain to receive instruction.

At thirty, he shaved his head and received the precepts from Vinaya Master Daoxuan. He wore coarse hemp robes many times over, ate at midday while practicing breath-holding, and remained in meditative seclusion throughout the day.
Later, he visited Xuefeng, who rejoiced that he had thoroughly shaken off all karmic burdens and designated him as a *dhūta* (ascetic).
Having received the Dharma from Xuefeng, he never departed elsewhere; he later resided at Xuansha for four years.
Those who were just beginning their studies flocked to him like spokes converging at a hub. Those who succeeded to his Way became quite numerous;
for instance, Luohan Chen and Anguo Qiu were both the most eminent among his disciples.

Nevertheless, as for the number of his followers who mastered his methods and retired in seclusion to cherish the Way, they cannot be detailed exhaustively—how could the *Monk Biographies* or the *Chan Records* possibly enumerate them all? I once passed through Kang...

Outside [the monastery], he visited the *śarīra* of his preceptor at Heshang Temple and paid homage to the Preceptor’s true body (*dharmakāya*). An inscription on the stone reads: "The Master’s name was Daolin. He was the son of the Li clan of Minyue.
He shaved his head under a teacher and received full ordination at the age of twenty. He obtained the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye from Xuansha Shiguan.
At the beginning of the Jianlong era, he entered Wuyue and arrived at Puan Temple in Qiantang. Although he did not open a formal hall for teaching,"
He performed [these] songs and chants. Those who had entered the chamber to study the mysteries of the Way constantly numbered five hundred.

In the sixth month of summer in the Bingzi year of the Xingguo era, the Master suddenly said to his attendant monk, "I am returning to my hometown. The monk did not understand this. Consequently, the Master sought out a brush and wrote a verse, saying:
"Returning to my hometown, silent and still, leaving no trace; Unmoored on the solitary sail, I pass through both water and land. Suddenly I reach the old pass—"
The ground was firm; there was no longer north, south, east, or west. Three days later, he passed away while sitting upright.
He was sixty years of age and forty-five years since his ordination. His entire body remains solemnly intact today in the northern corner of the monastery.

Although the halls and buildings have fallen into ruin, those who come to pay their respects continue without interruption. This is because the Master’s “Verse on Returning Home” was widely circulated during his time.
Therefore, he did not manifest himself by name, but was instead titled the "Retired-to-Hometown Upādhyāya.
As for *kāṣāya*, it is called *kāṣāya* in Sanskrit; this means "improper color" (*apraśasta-varṇa*). The Vinaya states: "One must not possess robes of superior colors;

one should instead make them into *kāṣāya*. The *Yejieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) says: "The original character was written as *jiāshā* (迦沙). During the Liang dynasty, Ge Hong composed the *Ning*..."
*Yuan*. Below, "adding clothes" refers to monastic robes.
Regarding the "engraved night lamp": Prince Ziliang of Jingling once held a gathering of scholars at night. They would carve a candle to compose poetry;

for every four-line verse, they would carve one *cun* of the candle, using this as their standard. They all considered this no great difficulty, until he struck a bronze bowl and stood [to challenge them].
The resonance fades and the poem is complete; all may be observed and appreciated. See the *History of the Southern Dynasties* (*Nanshi*).

Regarding "reeds sprouting from his knees," see the *Sutra on the Ocean-like Samadhi of Contemplating the Buddha*. At that time, the Bodhisattva sat beneath a tree and entered the *Samadhi of Extinct Thought*.
The realm of this samadhi is called "the Quiescence of All Faculties. The devas wept and their tears fell like—
It rained. [The gods] exhorted the Bodhisattva, saying, "Please arise and partake of food. When they made this request, the sound pervaded the trichiliocosm, yet the Bodhisattva remained unaware.
There was a devaputra named Manojña who saw grass sprouting from the ground and piercing the Bodhisattva’s flesh, growing up as far as his elbow.
He addressed the devas, saying, "How extraordinary! This man’s asceticism has reached such a state."
He had not eaten for a long time; his cries went unheard, and he was unaware that grass grew over him.
He composed a poem for Emperor Wen of the Wei dynasty: In the northwest there are floating clouds, Lofty and upright like carriage canopies.
*Śāla* is translated here as "high and remote" (*gāoyuǎn*). This is because its trees grow tall and dense, rising above all other trees; alternatively, it may be translated as "firm and solid.
The latter is an error, arising from the phonetic proximity between *śāla* and *sāra*. If one were to call it "firm and solid," [it would be incorrect].
Then one turns the tongue to pronounce it. If calling out to something high and distant, one pronounces it according to the level tone.
*Háng* (頏): the second character is pronounced with the *làng* rhyme.
*Lín-lín* (磷磷): the first character is pronounced with the *lì* rhyme; it refers to stones amidst rushing waters.
Tang Huixiu: "Tang" is his surname. In antiquity, śramaṇas were often referred to by their secular surnames or the surnames of their teachers;
examples include Zhu Daosheng, Bo Daoyou, and Zhu Fatai. It was from the time of Dharma Master Dao’an onwards that they began to be called "Śākya" (Shishi).
While translating the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, he encountered the passage stating that when the four rivers enter the sea, they no longer retain their names as rivers.
There were four castes among those who had left the household life, yet they were all of the same Śākya lineage. Huīhuì, whose courtesy name was Mǎoyuǎn, resided at Chánggān Temple.

He was fond of wine and women, looked down upon his fellow monastics, and harbored worldly inclinations. He took up the pen to compose documents and essays; his literary style was elegant and refined.

His talent emerged with great brilliance, and his reputation rose rapidly. During the reign of Emperor Xiaowu of the Song dynasty, the Emperor issued an edict ordering him to return to lay life and appointed him as the Director of Literature for Yángzhōu.
Tang Zongshi was a man of high spirit who felt profound indignation at his circumstances. He subsequently served as the Magistrate of Jurong, where he died in frustration.
Having read the writings of Shen Yue, Zhu Xi, and Yan Yanzhi, he consistently disparaged Tang Huixiu’s compositions, dismissing them as nothing more than the folk songs of the common streets.
He lamented that such works were destined to mislead future generations.
In the *Hōyō Shikan* (Verses on Autumn Leaves and Tranquility), it is said: "In the life of a monk, there is nothing more secluded and leisurely than this.
Facing green pines nearby and mountains afar, I have never inscribed a verse upon fallen leaves, Fearing they might follow the flowing stream into the human world.

Furthermore, when Zheng Qian served as the Guangwen Doctor, he suffered from a lack of paper while practicing calligraphy. Knowing that Ci'en Temple possessed several rooms filled with persimmon leaves, he... [proceeded to use them].
I borrowed a monk’s quarters for my residence and took up red leaves to practice calligraphy; over many years, I have nearly mastered them.
Regarding the phrase "ancient and modern sentiments should be made to harmonize," I have seen another version of this text.
*Kǎo-mù* (with *kǔ* and *hào* as the phonetic components). From the *Zhuangzi*: "The physical form can indeed be made like withered wood.
*Yīngmén*: Kong Rong of the Eastern Han, courtesy name Wenju; a native of Lu. He was the twenty-second descendant of Confucius.
At the age of ten, he accompanied his father to the capital. At that time, Li Ying, the Governor of Henan, maintained an air of dignified reserve and did not—
He would not casually receive guests; he commanded his attendants that unless they were famous men of the day or members of his own family, no one was permitted to announce themselves.
Yang Rong wished to observe the man, so he went to Ying’s gate and said to the gatekeeper, "I am a descendant of a family related to Master Li.
The gatekeeper informed Ying, who invited Rong in and said, "Your illustrious grandfather once had a [connection] with me..."

"Is this not a matter of old affection? Rong replied, "Indeed. Your late father, Confucius, and your ancestor, Lord Lao, shared the same virtue and compared their righteousness, acting as teacher and friend to one another.
Thus, Rong and you have been related by marriage for generations. Those present could not help but sigh in admiration.
Chen Wei, the Grand Master of the Palace, arrived later; someone informed him of what had transpired at the gathering. Chen Wei said, "That man is small-minded."
He was quick-witted, yet being large does not necessarily imply extraordinary talent. Rong replied immediately, "Judging by what you have said, will you not be precociously wise?
Ying laughed heartily and said, "One of such lofty brilliance must surely become a great vessel."
*Zhēnzhào* (眹兆): The first character is pronounced *zhǐyǐn* (直引切). It refers to the omens and signs of good or ill fortune.
According to the *Hèshù Nìpán Jīng* (The Sūtra on the Nirvāṇa under the Śāla Trees): "At that time, the World-Honored One was reclining upon a jeweled couch beneath the śāla grove.
During the middle watch of the night, he entered the fourth dhyāna; all was silent and without sound. At that very moment, he attained parinirvāṇa. [He entered...]
After the parinirvāṇa, the two pairs of śāla trees to the east and west merged into a single tree, and the two pairs to the south and north merged into a single tree.
They hung down and covered the precious couch, sheltering the Tathāgata.
At that moment, the trees suddenly turned a dismal white, like white cranes; their branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, bark, and trunks all burst apart and fell away, gradually...
Withered, decayed, and utterly ruined.
The account of his double lotus-position is found in the *Yunmen lu*, volume one.

This is like the student from Shouling who attempted to imitate the gait of Zhuangzi’s "Autumn Floods" chapter; having traveled to Handan to learn the local stride, he had not yet mastered the native way.
Yes. Furthermore, he has lost his former conduct; he simply crawls back on his belly.
A "Great Sacrifice" (Daxiang) should indeed be a grand banquet. According to the *Zhouli*, the *Zhengkeshi* (Director of Guests) presides over the assembly of various states.

When performing a Great Sacrifice, one prepares twelve vessels and a hundred articles. When a feudal lord acts as a guest at a Great Sacrifice, it is considered sufficient to merely refine the offerings. This means that—
"Enjoying flavor. *Xiá* (暇): read as *dīngguàn* (丁貫). "To insert a bamboo splinter [into the mouth].
Regarding "fragrant food," the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* says: At that time, Śāriputra thought to himself, "The time for the meal is approaching;
where shall these bodhisattvas eat? Then Vimalakīrti, knowing his thoughts, spoke to him, saying: "The Buddha has said..."
"Enter into liberation; O worthy one, receive and practice it. How can you listen to the Dharma while preoccupied with the food of desire?
If you desire food, wait but a moment, and I shall cause you to obtain a food never before experienced.
Thereupon, Vimalakīrti, without rising from his seat, manifested a bodhisattva before the assembly and addressed him, saying, "Go to the world-system above."
[He] crossed over as many buddha-fields as there are sands in two *gaṅgā* rivers. There was a land named Saṃghagandha; the Buddha there was named Gandhottamakūṭa.
Having arrived there, [he] spoke these words on my behalf: "Vimalakīrti bows his head at the feet of the World-Honored One.
He wishes to receive the remains of the food consumed by the World-Honored One, so that he may perform the work of a Buddha within the Sahā world. Thereupon, the Tathāgata Gandhottamakūṭa...
He filled a bowl of various fragrances with fragrant food and gave it to the manifested bodhisattvas.
At that time, those nine million bodhisattvas merely uttered these words: "We wish to go to the Sahā world. The Buddha said, "You may go. In an instant, they departed.
Accompanied by the manifested bodhisattvas, he went to the house of Vimalakīrti. Vimalakīrti immediately manifested nine million lion thrones, and all the bodhisattvas sat upon them.
The manifested bodhisattva presented a bowl filled with fragrant food to Vimalakīrti.
The fragrance of the food pervaded the city of Vaiśālī and the trichiliocosm. He spoke to the household...
"Reverend Śāriputra and all you great śrāvakas, you may eat this delicious ambrosial meal of the Tathāgata, which is permeated by great compassion.
Do not harbor limited thoughts, lest it fail to digest. There was another śrāvaka who thought to himself, 'This food is too little.'"
The manifested bodhisattva said: "Do not, with the minor virtues and limited wisdom of a śrāvaka, attempt to measure the immeasurable merit of the Tathāgata.
The four oceans may run dry, but this food is inexhaustible. Even if all people were to eat from it, each person’s portion would be as vast as Mount Sumeru;
yet even for all beings, it could never be exhausted. Thereupon, the food in the bowl satisfied the entire assembly, and those who ate it—
His body was at ease and he was joyful.
Śāriputra—*Śāri* in Sanskrit means "śārikā crane"; this is translated here as "son of the śārikā crane.
He received his name from his mother because her eyes were like those of a śārikā crane; thus he is called Śāriputra. He was foremost in wisdom, and his eloquence was peerless.
The *Udraka Rāmaputra-prabhāsa Sūtra* states: "The World-Honored One left the city to become a renunciant and went to Mount Tāṇḍya.

There, he first stayed with Ārāḍa Kālāma for three years, where he studied the concentration of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-samādhi*). Realizing it was not the final goal, he abandoned it.

He then went to Udraka Rāmaputra for another three years, where he studied the concentration of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana-samādhi*). Realizing this too was not the final goal, he abandoned it as well. — *Puji jing* (Sūtra on the Universal Assembly).
It is said that on the eighth day of the second month, beneath the Bodhi tree, the Bodhisattva raised his head and saw the morning star;
he awakened to the Way and attained Buddhahood. Desiring first to go and repay his debt of gratitude, a divine being informed him that Ārāḍa had already been dead for seven days.
After Udraka Rāmaputra had died, the Three-Eyed One [the Buddha] went to the Deer Park to deliver the five *pāñcavargika* monks.
"Dí" (昳) is pronounced with the initial *d* and the final *tue* (結切); it means the sun has declined.
"Bū" (晡) is pronounced with the initial *b* and the final *mu* (謨切); it refers to the hour when the sun reaches the *shēn* (申) position.

Regarding the story of the non-Buddhist (Tīrthika) with a fire-sheet belly who was offered a "burning bell" (*shāozhōng*) as a head-covering in the midst of the assembly, the circumstances seem quite incongruous.
I once heard a monk from Shu say that this is a local dialect term. When people in the Sichuan region mock someone for being ignorant, they say, "A burning bell has covered your head.
It is often called "the gradual heat of early summer" (*méngxià jiàn rè*). This was indeed spoken by Xuedou, a native of Sichuan.
"Yuhua" (Rain of Flowers): "Yu" (rain) is pronounced with the *wang* and *yu* finals. To descend from above is called "rain.

The elder wished to purchase the grove to build a vihāra.

Prince Jeta said, "If you can cover the ground with gold until there is no empty space between the coins, then I shall grant it to you. Sudatta replied, "I shall certainly pay whatever the price may be.
The prince said, "I was only joking. Sudatta said, "A prince should not speak falsely," and he immediately dispatched his men on elephants.
He went out carrying gold. Within eighty *qǐng* of land, it was almost full; only a small portion remained.
Sudatta thought to himself, "What treasury of gold will suffice—neither too much nor too little—to take and fill this? Jeta asked, "Do you regret the price and wish to abandon it? He replied, "No.
I am simply considering which treasury of gold might suffice to obtain enough to complete the purchase. Jeta said:
He thought to himself: "The Buddha must possess great virtue, for he has caused this man to regard his treasures as so insignificant. Let us agree to stop; do not provide any more gold.
The garden grounds shall belong to you, and the trees shall belong to me. I myself will offer them to the Buddha, and together we shall establish a vihāra."
The Venerable Master Jia Shan spoke these words in a bustling marketplace: "Recognize the Son of Heaven within the marketplace;
realize the old monk upon the tips of the hundred grasses.
*Za* (pronounced *zé*, with the second tone) means to press or constrain.
Kauśika is Śakra, the Lord of the Six Heavens of Desire. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Formerly, in the kingdom of Magadha, there was a brahmin named Māgata, whose family name was Kauśika. He possessed great merit and profound wisdom."
He had thirty-three close friends with whom he jointly cultivated merit. When their lives ended, they were all reborn on the second heaven atop Mount Sumeru;
the brahmin Māgha became the lord of the devas, and the thirty-two others became his ministers.
Juzhi (Kubjita) was the Venerable Juzhi of Mount Jinhua in Wuzhou. Initially, he lived in a hermitage;
it was only after being exhorted by the nun Shiji that his resolve was stirred, and he first conceived the aspiration for the Great Way. Shortly thereafter, Tianlong arrived at the hermitage.

Juzhi recounted the circumstances of Shiji’s visit to the hermitage and questioned him. Tianlong held up a single finger to indicate the truth. At that moment, the Master [Juzhi] attained manifest realization.
Wu, on the eve of his passing, said to the assembly, "I obtained a 'finger-pointing Chan' from Tianlong;
I have used it throughout my life and it is not yet exhausted. Having spoken these words, he suddenly passed away. Tianlong was the successor of Damei Chang, who was a direct grandson of Mazu.
*La-jié-jie* (in Sanskrit, *laṅgula*). This means "staff. The Song of the Essential Tenets by the Venerable Zhimen Zuohé says:

*La-jié-jie, yè-lù-bù;* *The spiritually sharp monk traverses this single path;* *A lion does not seize a qilin’s cub;* *How could a fierce beast deign to look beneath the bed?* *La* (or written as *là*) is pronounced with the initial *l* and the final *dá* (as in *láng-dá*).

*La-jié-jie, yè-lù-bù:* *The staff, the trailing robe.* *The spiritually sharp monk traverses this single path;* *A lion does not seize a qilin’s cub;* *How could a fierce beast deign to look beneath the bed?* *La* (or written as *là*) is pronounced with the initial *l* and the final *dá* (as in *láng-dá*).
Lu Mian (Unveiled Cap) refers to Guo He of the Eastern Han dynasty. His courtesy name was Qiaoqing; he was a native of Luoyang. He was appointed as the Inspector of Jingzhou (*Jingzhou Cishi*).

Upon his audience with the Emperor, he was granted rewards and honors, receiving exceptional favor and distinction. When he arrived at his post, he implemented extraordinary governance, bringing great benefit to the common people.
They sang of him: "His virtue is benevolent and enlightened, Guo Qiaoqing; loyal and upright in court, high and low are at peace. Later, Emperor Xianzong visited the south on a tour of inspection.

Yang was frequently seen by the people, who sighed in admiration. The Emperor bestowed upon him the robes of a high minister, complete with *fu* and *fu* patterns, the ceremonial cap, and the hanging pendants.

He issued an edict that when Yang traveled through the provinces, he should remove his curtains and canopies so that the common people might behold his appearance and attire, thereby manifesting his virtue.
Wherever he passed, officials and citizens would point him out to one another, all of whom felt great honor at the sight.
"Vast and azure, vast and azure—this is the color of heaven. Lofty and vaulted—this is the form of heaven.
It is by means of the great virtue of Heaven and Earth that it is compared to impartial governance."
"Yipi" (倚毗) is synonymous with "bīyǐ" (毗倚).

A "living shrine" (*shēngcí*) was established for ancient figures who possessed virtuous governance; because their benefits reached the common people and they left behind enduring affection, people erected living shrines upon their departure from office out of longing for them.

Within these, they painted portraits and fashioned statues, making offerings to them during the four seasons. During the Eastern Han, there was Wang Tang, whose courtesy name was Jingbo. Guang— [text continues]
He was a native of Qi in the Han dynasty. During the Yongchu era, the Western Qiang tribes raided Ba Commandery, causing great distress to the people.

By imperial decree, General-in-Chief Yin Jiu was dispatched to attack and suppress them, yet he failed to achieve victory for many years. The Three Courts recommended Tang for this difficult task, and he was appointed as the Governor of the commandery.
Tang Chui led his troops against the rebels and decapitated more than a thousand captives. The regions of Ba and Yong were thereby purified; officials and commoners established shrines for him.
"Yong" refers to Shangyong County. "Qi" is pronounced with the *qian* and *si* initials combined.

The character 蒱 (pú) should follow the pronunciation of 浦 (pǔ). To write it as 蒲 (pú), meaning "water grass" which can be used to make mats, is incorrect; furthermore, 蒱 (pú) refers to the game of *chūshú* (backgammon), which is not the intended meaning here.
The characters 猿 (yuán) and 猱 (náo)—the latter being pronounced with the *nuó* radical and *dāo* stroke (i.e., *náo*)—refer to the monkey.
The *Liji* (Book of Rites), "Siyi" (Silken Robes), records that the Master said: "The words of a king are like a single strand of silk; once they issue forth, they are like a plied thread (*lun*).
When the words of a king are like a plied thread, once they issue forth, they are like a thick rope (*fu*). Therefore, a great man does not initiate idle speech. 'Idle' (*you*) means floating;
it refers to speech that cannot be put to use. *Fu* is pronounced *fu*.

The *Sengshi* (History of Monks) concerning the purple robe is something esteemed by antiquity; it is both a name and an insignia. When bestowing ceremonial robes upon others, the highest rank is that of crimson and purple.
The yellow and green ribbons constitute the descending grades; thus it is said that one who is conferred the purple ribbon must necessarily receive the golden seal.
Today, monks merely receive the purple [robe] without the gold. The square-cut robe is not a ribbon. Examining various histories, the robes of monks were red.
Regarding colors such as yellow, black, and blue, one does not hear of vermilion or purple.

According to the *Jiu Tang Shu*, during the reign of Empress Wu Zetian, monks such as Falang retranslated the *Dayun Jing* (Mahāmegha Sūtra) and presented its prophetic signs, claiming that Empress Wu was Maitreya descending to birth as the sovereign of Jambudvīpa.
Because the House of Tang contained the subtle [signs], they consequently underwent a revolution and styled themselves Zhou. [The figures involved were] Falang and Xue Huaiyi.

The nine men were all enfeoffed as County Dukes, and they were granted various gifts according to their rank; each was bestowed with purple *kāṣāya* robes and silver tortoise-shaped pouches (*qiudai*).
This was the beginning of the practice of bestowing purple robes. Furthermore, during the reign of Emperor Xuanzong, his affection for them was profound.

When Prince Ning fell ill, imperial messengers and court physicians were dispatched in such numbers that they crowded the roads. Only the monk Chongxian’s medical treatment proved effective; the Emperor was delighted and granted him a vermilion fish-pouch (*yudai*).
Furthermore, during the Yongtai era of Emperor Daizong, the monk Chonghui of Zhangjing Temple outshone a Daoist in a contest of supernatural arts.
Consequently, the eunuch Gong Tingyu was granted a set of purple robes and the removal of his fish-bag (the official rank insignia).
Today, on the anniversary of the Emperor's birth, these are bestowed; if the monks of the inner chapel already wear purple, they are further granted three robes of purple silk.
This matter is called "Valuing Purple.
The Protector-General of the Western Regions during the Western Han, Zheng Ji, was a native of Kuaiji. He followed the army as a common soldier and traveled repeatedly to the Western Regions.

Consequently, he was appointed as a Lang (Court Gentleman). When Ji first defeated the Kingdom of Che-shih and further brought the King of Jichu to submit to the Han, his prestige shook the Western Regions.
He subsequently oversaw both the northern and western routes of Che-shih; thus, he was titled the Du-hu (Protector-General). This was the establishment of the Du-hu.
"It began with Ji. Yan Shigu said: "Because they jointly protected both the northern and southern routes, they were called 'Duhu.

The *Baiyue yuetu jing* (Classic of the Maps of the Hundred Yue). "Hundred Yue" (*Baiyue*) is a specific designation for the Yue people; "hundred" (*bai*) is a term used because their lineages were not uniform.

It is also called *Yuejue* (Extinguishing Yue), which refers to the fact that the evil of the Yue was severed when they destroyed Wu. Some call it *Lingyue* (Numinous Yue), meaning that it is the source from which numinous wonders emerge within the mountains and seas.

The tiger represents the North and the Black Warrior (Xuanwu). Within the imperial borders, the yellow dragon also serves as a sign of good faith. Currently, the Jin dynasty employs only the white tiger to signify good faith;

In the *Treatise on the True Nature of the Three Jewels* (*Sanbao Shixing Lun*) by Xuedou Zu Ying, it is asked: "Why are the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha called the 'Three Jewels'? He replied: "Because they possess six meanings."
1. Rare, like precious jewels and the like; 2. Stainless and undefiled; 3. Possessing power to eliminate greed and remove poison; 4. Adorned; 5. Most supreme; 6. Unchanging.

The Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) are called the Dharma Jewel. The merit of the Śrāvaka’s No-more-learning..."

Virtue and wisdom are called the Jewel of the Sangha. Regarding the Three Jewels of Common Characteristics: first, within the essence of the Buddha, the sense of awakening and illumination is named the Buddha Jewel;
from the perspective of the sense of normative rules, it is named the Dharma Jewel; and the exhaustion of all faults of contention is named the Sangha Jewel.
These take the merit of the untainted realm as their essence. Second, within the Dharma, that which possesses the nature of awakening is...

The Buddha Jewel. The upholding of the norms is the Dharma Jewel. The non-deficiency of the essence of the Dharma is the Sangha Jewel. Third: regarding the Sangha, the superior contemplative wisdom is the Buddha Jewel; the norms are the Dharma Jewel; and because they abide among the multitude without conflict with sentient beings, it is named the Sangha Jewel. Regarding the Three Jewels of Identical Substance: True Suchness possessing the nature of awakening is the Buddha Jewel. True Suchness possessing... [the nature of] phenomena is the Dharma Jewel. True Suchness... [abiding] without conflict among the multitude is the Sangha Jewel. Thus, these three are identical in substance. Furthermore, the three jewels are identical in substance because they all take True Suchness as their essence. Why? Because True Suchness possesses the nature of awakening, it is named the Buddha Jewel. Because True Suchness... [possesses the nature of] phenomena, it is named the Dharma Jewel. Because True Suchness... [abides] without conflict among the multitude, it is named the Sangha Jewel. Therefore, the three jewels are identical in substance. Furthermore, the three jewels are identical in substance because they all take the Tathāgata as their essence. Why? Because the Tathāgata abides without conflict among the multitude, he is named the Sangha Jewel. Therefore, the three jewels are identical in substance. The meaning of "upholding the path" (*mārga-dhara*) is called the Dharma Jewel; True Suchness (*tathatā*) in its state of union is called the Sangha Jewel.

Regarding the Three Jewels as distinct entities, there are two schools of thought: First, the Mahayana teaching holds that the Tathagata of the three bodies (*trikāya*) is the Buddha Jewel; the teaching of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is the Dharma Jewel;

and the three stages of worthiness (*tri-kṣānti*) and the ten stages of sainthood (*daśa-ārya-bhūmi*) are the Sangha Jewel. Second, the Hinayana teaching holds that the golden body of sixteen feet (*ṣoḍaśahasta-pramāṇa-kāya*) is [the Buddha Jewel].

As for the character *jiào*, it means that one should clearly announce the facts of the matter. It takes the radical "wood" (木) because, in antiquity, paper did not yet exist; [the document] was written on wood.

The characters were inscribed upon wood, and bird feathers were further inserted atop them to signify speed. Furthermore, a *xíshū* (proclamation) is a document that accuses those who ought to be punished.
It also enumerates the evils of the other side and proclaims the virtues of one’s own; it is a letter intended to inform and console. *Jiǎo*: its pronunciation is the same as *jī* (to strike).

Han Yu, styled Tui-zhi, was a native of Changli. His father, Zhongqing, held no official rank or title. Han Yu was orphaned at the age of three and was raised by his paternal uncle.

From childhood, he applied himself with diligence to the study of Confucianism without waiting for encouragement. He subsequently passed the jinshi examination and was appointed as an aide to a regional military governor.
His speech was straightforward and sincere, free from hesitation or avoidance; his conduct was firm and upright, yet he was unrefined.
In worldly affairs, he held successive offices until reaching the rank of Vice Minister of the Ministry of Personnel. He died at the age of fifty-seven.

It was kept within the imperial palace for three days before being sent to various temples. Princes, dukes, officials, and commoners rushed to offer their gifts as if they could not wait.

Han Yu submitted his "Treatise on the Buddha’s Bone," in which he spoke most vehemently regarding its evils. Emperor Xianzong was extremely incensed. One day later, he presented the memorial to his ministers and intended to impose the ultimate punishment upon him.
Pei Du and others remonstrated, stating that Han Yu’s offense was too grave, and consequently, he was demoted to serve as the Prefect of Chaozhou.

"Leading the sheep, leading the sheep, and presenting the jade tablet" refers to the ritual of surrendering to an enemy. according to the regulations for the Dukes and Marquises, their territories are one hundred li square; for the Earls, seventy li; and for the Viscounts, fifty li. This refers to that.
