According to the *Shiji*, Zhu Rang was a man of righteousness. He first served the lords Fan and Zhongxing of Jin;
later, when they were destroyed by Zhi Bo, Rang transferred his service to Zhi Bo.

When Zhi Bo was in turn destroyed by Zhao Xiangzi, Rang fled to the mountains and marshes, changed his surname and name, and took the form of a criminal to enter the palace of Zhao Xiangzi as a sweeper.
He was in the latrine, clutching a dagger, waiting for Xiangzi with the intent to kill him. When Xiangzi went to the latrine, his heart felt uneasy;
he inspected the latrine and saw Rang inside the latrine hole. His attendants requested that he kill him, but Xiangzi did not permit it. He sighed and said:
"He is a man of righteousness. Let him go; I shall carefully avoid him so as to escape death.

He fled again to the mountains and marshes, lacquering his body to appear like a leper and swallowing charcoal to alter his voice. He returned home in secret, unrecognized by his wife and children, known only to his friend.
His friend urged him, saying, "Why not serve Xiangzi instead? You would have the fortune of being close enough to kill him. He replied, "I serve..."
If one were to kill him, it would teach future generations of ministers to serve their sovereigns with divided loyalties;
this must not be allowed. Later, when Xiangzi went out on an excursion, Yu Rang hid beneath a bridge to wait for him.
Before Xiangzi had even reached the bridge, his horse became startled. Xiangzi said, "Could this be Yu Rang? He sent someone to search for him and indeed found Rang there.
Xiangzi called out to him and said, "Previously you served Fan and Zhonghang, yet Zhi Bo destroyed them.
You did not seek revenge for them, but instead pledged your fealty and served him. Now that Zhi Bo is dead, you alone seek to avenge his death so deeply."
"Why is this? Let asked. "Your servant previously served the Fan and Zhongxing houses.
They treated me as a common man, and I repaid them as a common man. Zhibo, however, treated me with the courtesy due to a state minister, and I repaid him as a state minister.
Lord Xiangzi sighed and said: 'You have already established your reputation for Zhibo; my pardoning you fulfills the requirements of righteousness. Thereupon, he was released.
He devised a plan for himself. Yang Rang said, "I have heard that an enlightened ruler does not conceal the beauty of others, and a loyal minister dies for his sovereign according to righteousness.
Since Your Majesty has previously pardoned my crimes, there is no one in the world who does not praise Your Majesty’s virtue.

As for today's matter, I am indeed prepared to submit to execution; however, I wish to request Your Majesty’s robe so that I may strike [the enemy] with it. Only then shall I die without shame or regret."
Xiangzi considered this righteous. He then removed his own clothes and presented them to Rang; he drew his sword, leaped three times, and struck him.
He sighed, saying, "I can now go below to repay Zhi Bo. Thereupon, he lay down his sword and died.

A *ge* (spear) was positioned before the hall. The Emperor questioned Amoghavajra, who replied, "This is the second son of King Vaiśravaṇa, Dujan.
He accords with Your Majesty’s heart and has gone to rescue Anxi. On the eleventh day of the second month, at the hour of *si* (9–11 a.m.
that year’s fourth month, it was reported that thirty *li* to the northeast of the rear city, amidst darkening clouds and mist, there was a deity. It could...
They were over ten feet tall and all clad in golden armor. At the hour of You (5–7 p.m.), drums and horns resounded loudly; the earth shook and the mountains trembled.
After two days, the barbarian raiders were routed and dispersed. In an instant, a brilliant light appeared atop the city tower and the Heavenly King manifested his form.

We have respectfully depicted his likeness and submitted it with this memorial. Consequently, an imperial edict was issued for all provincial and prefectural governments to establish a [statue of] the Heavenly King in the northwest corner of each.
The image of the King was also ordered by imperial decree to be enshrined in a separate hall within a Buddhist temple;

it is the very image that appeared at that time, holding a stūpa in its hand. Nowadays, it has become customary to fashion such images atop the city walls of prefectures and counties, or amidst the enclosures of monasteries.
*Chángxiào* (long whistle): pronounced with the *sū* and *diào* finals. It refers to the sound of blowing. Cheng Zian’s *Xiàofù* (*Rhapsody on Whistling*) says:
"It issues forth following the movements of the lips and mouth, borrowing fragrant breath to travel far away."
In the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* (The Great Ornament Sutra), it is said that in the past there was a bhikṣu who, while begging for alms, came to the home of a pearl-driller.

At that time, the bhikṣu’s robes were red; as he stood over the mani-jewels being strung, his robes reflected their color, making them appear crimson. Then, the pearl-driller entered his house to fetch food.
Suddenly, a goose swallowed it. The pearl-worker immediately searched for the pearl but did not know where it was.
He said to the bhikṣu, "Have you taken my pearl? Fearing that the goose would be killed to retrieve the pearl, the bhikṣu then spoke this verse:
"For the sake of another's life, I now undergo suffering in my own body. There is no other means; I shall substitute my life for theirs."
Although he heard these words, [the jeweler] immediately bound him, beat him, and throttled him tightly with a rope until blood flowed from both his mouth and nose.
That goose came to eat the blood; the jeweler, filled with rage, struck the goose to death. The bhikṣu then spoke this verse:
"I have endured all these sufferings in the hope that this goose might live. My life has not yet ceased, and the goose remains."
"I shall die first. The jeweler asked, "In what way, then, are you related to this goose? The bhikṣu explained everything in detail.

When they opened the goose's belly, they found the jewel. The jeweler raised his voice and wailed, "It was because you protected the life of this goose that I was forced to commit such an unrighteous act.
[The text reads] *xue*, which refers to the color of the goose; this is merely an inversion in the composition of the verse.

Regarding "wax person" (*làrén*) and "ice-wax" (*bìnglà*), *là* should be understood as *là* (the ritual of the season). This refers to the *là* of the year. According to the *Zēnghuī jì* (Record of Increasing Radiance):

"*Là* means 'to join' (*jiē*), referring to the junction between the old and the new. In common parlance, the day after *là* is called the beginning of the year. This is because the year arrives once *là* has ended;
thus, it is correct that the *Shìshì* (Ritual Manual) designates the day of receiving the *là* at the conclusion of the retreat as the "Dharma Year" (*fásuì*). Heaven... [text ends].

As for the claim that the *zhú* (monastic seniority) serves as a criterion for verification: since these individuals vary in their seniority according to their years of ordination (*lǎ*), one must further verify whether their conduct is defiled or pure.
To say that a person is "ice-like" in their *lǎ* is to say that their conduct is as pure and clear as ice.

Now, some within the assembly falsely claim that the regulations established in the Western Heaven (India) consist solely in observing whether the "wax-person" is frozen or melted, and only then knowing whether their conduct is defiled.
This is incorrect. There is no such text in the Buddhist sutras, nor is there any regulation in the Vinaya rules. It is unclear from what source this statement was derived.
In this current compilation, "lâ" (臘) is taken as "là" (蠟), which has deeply misled later generations; it is truly lamentable.
Yuan Shi saw the record of Ding Lake regarding the "Cao Fu" (Whetting the Axe). It says:

"To *zhenfen* (shake and rouse) sounds means to cleanse. It is composed of the radical *da* (great) and the character *jia* (home) above the character *tian* (field); this is its symbolic form. "Shaking and rousing" (*zhenfen*) was a phrase of great gravity in antiquity.
Emperor Gaozu was conceived after a single night’s gestation. His name was Bang, his courtesy name was Ji, and he was a native of Zhongyang Village in Fengyi.
His surname was Liu. His mother, Lady Wang, once rested by the embankment of the Great Marsh. She dreamed of encountering a deity; at that time, thunder and lightning filled the darkness.
When the Grand Duke went to investigate, he saw a dragon and a serpent above her. Thereafter, she became pregnant and subsequently gave birth to Gaozu.
The Patriarch (Zu). The High Ancestor (Gaozu) was a man with a prominent nose and a dragon-like countenance; he had beautiful whiskers and a beard, and his left thigh bore seventy-two black moles.
*Mǎo* (pronounced *wū lǎo qiè*) refers to a woman; *shēn* (pronounced *shēn*) means to be pregnant.
The Verse on the Single Shaft Returning to the Source says: A single shaft pierces the three barriers; clearly visible is the path behind the arrow.
How pitiable are those great men who take the primordial sky as their mind-source.
"Luoyueyue" should be read as "Luo Yue. Luo Yue is the name of a city in Western India;
it is what the *Pinfen Gongde Lun* (Treatise on the Analysis of Merit) calls the Eastern Mountain of the City of Luo Yue, the very place where Subhūti folded his patched robe.
Learning the "Tang step" also carries the same meaning as learning the "Zhao step" from Yan.
Ten times Yunju Deng addressed the assembly, saying: "A person who truly knows 'there is' never acts recklessly.
Ten times he intends to speak, yet nine times he desists. Why is this? It is because he fears it will be of no benefit.
If one has realized the essence, their mind is like a fan in midwinter, and white mold grows upon their lips."
This is merely you forcing things to be spontaneous in such a manner.
As for the horizontal halberd in the front hall, some frequently cite the precedent of Emperor Taizong of the Tang; however, such statements generally lack authoritative evidence.

This will surely invite the laughter of the wise. I have carefully recorded from the "Annals of Emperor Taizong" that when the High Ancestor first raised the Banner of Righteousness, he established his eldest son, Jiancheng, as the Crown Prince.
At that time, the achievements of the Second Son (Taizong) were flourishing daily, and the High Ancestor privately promised to establish him as the Crown Prince.
Jiancheng learned of this in secret and, together with Prince Yuanji of Qi, secretly plotted to...
In a fit of madness, he invited Emperor Taizong into the palace for a night banquet, intending to administer poison.
Shortly thereafter, Taizong suffered a violent pain in his heart and spat out several pints of blood. Prince Shen Tong of Huai’an hurriedly supported him back to the Western Palace.
Gaozu visited his residence to inquire after his illness and consequently issued an edict forbidding nocturnal gatherings. He then said to Taizong, "From the time we set out from Jinyang..."

The conquest and pacification of the realm was your great achievement. When you were about to ascend the throne of the heir apparent, you firmly declined and would not accept it, thereby fulfilling your noble resolve.
Jiancheng has occupied the Eastern Palace for many years; now, we cannot bear to deprive him of it.
"I observe that you brothers are not in harmony. Although you reside together in the capital, there must surely be contention and strife between you.

You should return to the Imperial Chancery and settle in Luoyang. Just as he was about to depart, Jiancheng secretly instructed several men to submit a memorial to the throne; consequently, [the Emperor] stopped him from leaving.
Thereafter, day and night, he conspired with those in the inner palace, his slanderous accusations becoming increasingly vehement. Gaozu was deluded by him.
In the ninth year, when the Turks invaded the borders, an edict was issued for Yuanji to lead an army to repel them.
Yuanji, taking advantage of the assembled troops, made an appointment with Jiancheng to rise in rebellion. Changsun Wuji, Fang Xuanling, Du Ruhui, and Weizhi Jingde [were informed] daily...
Yegù argued insistently, "The situation is urgent. If you do not employ expedient means, the state will surely be in peril.
If Your Majesty fails to act decisively at this critical juncture and remains passive while facing slaughter, what purpose will be served by such conduct? Emperor Taizong approved of his plan.

On the third day of the sixth month, he secretly memorialized that Jiancheng and Yuンジ had committed lewd acts within the inner palace, and then addressed him personally, saying, "As for my relationship with my elder brother..."
"Your younger brother owes me not the slightest debt. Now he wishes to kill me; I am about to die an unjust death and shall forever be separated from my sovereign and my kin.
When the High Ancestor (Gaozu) examined this, he said in astonishment, "Tomorrow I shall interrogate him. You should attend court early.
On the fourth day, Taizong led nine attendants to Xuanwu Gate, where he personally summoned Gaozu and ordered Li Qiong to investigate the matter.
Jiancheng and Yuji perceived the change of events and immediately turned their horses to return home. Taizong followed after them, calling out to them.
Yuji drew his bow several times from atop his horse, but could not string it. Taizong then shot him; Jiancheng fell dead at the sound of the bowstring.
Yuan Ji was struck by an arrow in the midst of battle and fled; Yu Zhiji killed him. On the day of Jiazi, Tai Zong was established as the Crown Prince.
In the eighth month, an edict was issued to transfer the throne to the Crown Prince, and Gaozu was honored with the title of Taishang Huang (Retired Emperor).
"Holding a halberd" refers to Taizong; "donning the ceremonial robe" refers to Shendiao. Although the expressions are not identical, their underlying meaning may be similar.
"Riding the raft" refers to seeing the ancestral brilliance upon the celestial raft. A *cha* (raft) is a piece of wood floating on water; it is pronounced as *chú* (as in *chú-rú*).
Gan Jiang, Gan Jiang—was a man of Wu. Together with Ouyezizi, he studied under the same master for King Helü, who commissioned them to forge two swords.
One was named Gan Jiang; the other was named Moye. Moye was the name of Gan Jiang’s wife. When Gan Jiang was forging the sword, [he...]
The essence of the gold and iron was unwilling to flow. The husband and wife then cut their hair and severed their fingers, casting them into the crucible;
only then did the metal become malleable, and thus the sword was completed. The male blade was named Ganjiang, upon which a tortoise-shell pattern was wrought; the female blade was named Moye.
Yet they employ fallacious reasoning. The sword Ganjiang conceals its male [blade] and brings forth its female; it was presented to Helu, as seen in the *Wuyue Chunqiu*.
The sword Tai'e is recorded in the *Dongting Lu*.
*Jū'ér* (蛆兒): pronounced *jū'ér* (with the second syllable having the *yu* rhyme).
It means a fly. *Vajra*: in Sanskrit it is called *vajra*; here it is translated as "diamond" or "thunderbolt. It emerges from within the seven golden mountains and is near Mount Sumeru.
The joints of the *vajra* tree are like those of the *qióngzhú* (bamboo used for canes); there is nothing it cannot destroy.
The term "rǒuyáng" (羺羊) should be understood as referring to the *śarabha* (a mythical antelope). The *Prajñā-śāstra* states: "The principle of nirvāṇa and buddha-nature is like a diamond (*vajra*);
there is nothing that cannot destroy it, except for the horn of the *śarabha*, which can destroy it. In the same way, the buddha-nature can only be destroyed by the *icchantika*."
"Flower-crowns withered" means that the flowers have withered. This refers to the five signs of decline for devas: first, their garments become soiled and greasy;
second, the flowers upon their heads wither; third, their bodies emit a foul odor; fourth, sweat breaks out from beneath their armpits;
and fifth, they no longer find pleasure in their own seats.
*Móu* (upper radical): pronounced *mò fú qiè*. It refers to the pupil of the eye. *Zhǎ* (lower radical): pronounced *zè jiá qiè*. It refers to the movement of the eyes.
The celestial eye (*tianmu*) originally does not blink; when the eyes move, it is [the manifestation of] the *bāo-gòng* (the divine gaze).
Songshao (Mount Song and Mount Shao) is the collective name for these peaks. To the east of this mountain is Taishi (Great Chamber), and to the west is Shaoshi (Lesser Chamber);
thus they are called the "Two Chambers. It is among the Five Sacred Peaks. As it is said: "Lofty is Mount Song, a sacred peak reaching to the very heavens."
In the past, when you were the sea, your waters covered the level plains; Yu carved through Longmen to channel them.
Today, they have become prefectures and counties. A monkey wearing a straw hat is not a poet. I see the new Jinshan at Huyang.
"Collected. It is like Yang Xiu seeing the "young lady"; he knew her excellence at a single glance.
"The radish in the twelfth month goes back into the cellar"—these are all words from Jinshan.
Mount Ziling is its name; it is located in Jingshan County of Ying.
The White Snow Tower stands atop the western city wall of Ying. It originated when Song Yu addressed King Xiang of Chu, saying: [the following].
The "Yangchun Baixue" (The Spring Breeze and the White Snow) had few who could harmonize with it; thus it was named accordingly.
Yu was a native of Ying, serving as a high minister to King Xiang of Chu and a disciple of Qu Yuan.
*Tāyìn* (塔印) should be read as *dāyìn* (搭印). [The character] *hé* (合) is pronounced with the *qùe* (切) tone; it means "to strike.
Regarding *wābù zhǎnní wā* (蛙步[馬*展]泥蛙), it should be written as *wā* (洼). This refers to the "Horses of Wawa" (*wòwā shuǐ*).
During the reign of Emperor Wu of the Han, there was a man named Bào Lì who lived beside the Wawa waters. He saw a strange horse among a herd of wild horses that came toward him.

He drank this water. Consequently, he fashioned a clay figure holding the bridle and reins by the water’s edge. The horse became accustomed to this as its regular practice and eventually allowed a person to take over holding the bridle and reins.
[The Emperor] captured the horse and presented it [to the throne]. Desiring to manifest the horse's divine and extraordinary nature, he claimed it had emerged from the Wawa Waters.
This is what is meant by the "Zhan" mentioned in the *Fengxue*: that a fine horse emerges from clear water, yet is instead called a "Zhan."
"Lying amidst the mud and sand" is its intended meaning. Now, the term recorded as "wa" (臥) refers to a *xīnmā* (蝦蟆), that is, a frog.
How could it possibly stretch out to lie down in the manner of a horse's stride? [The character for] "zhǎn" (展) is pronounced with the initial *zhān* and the final *shàn*.
The Great Dances were established by the former kings. For the civil dance, they used feathers and flutes (*yuè*); for the martial dance, they used shields and axes.
In the minor martial dance, there was the shield but no axe; in the minor civil dance, there was the shield but no flute.

The use of feathers, flutes, shields, and axes constituted the great dances of both the civil and the martial. *Yùe* (flute): the pronunciation is like that of *yào*; it is like a flute with three holes, but shorter.
Regarding the shield: *qī* (戚) means *shù* (戍). Regarding the falcon on the banner:

according to the *Zhouli*, in the districts and neighborhoods, the falcon-banner (*yú*) is established. A falcon-banner refers to the skin and feathers of a bird of prey being stripped and placed atop a pole.

The *Yinyi* (Phonetic Explanations) to the *Hanshu* states: "A banner painted with a bird-falcon is called a *yú*; one painted with a tortoise and snake is called a *lí*. The term "falcon-banner" (*yǔn yú*) is pronounced [as such].
Sūn yú. *Qiāo juànzhui*: “Juàn” is pronounced as *jù hán qiè*; “zhui” has the phonetic value of *dì*. This is translated as "sound-echoing. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
After the World-Honored One’s parinirvāṇa, Mahākāśyapa manifested great supernatural powers and ascended to the summit of Mount Sumeru, where he spoke this verse: "As..."
"Come, disciples! Do not yet enter *nirvāṇa*. Those who have attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) should attend the council.
Having spoken this verse, he immediately struck the bronze *ghaṇṭā* (bell). This verse was transmitted through the *ghaṇṭā*, and its sound pervaded the trichiliocosm.
There were four hundred and ninety-nine who had attained supernatural powers; they all entered Rājagṛha.
At that time, Ānanda was unable to enter the assembly because his outflows (āsrava) were not yet exhausted.
He thought to himself: "I have served the Tathāgata without any transgression, yet because of my own remaining outflows, I am not included among the number of the assembly.
Having reflected thus, he practiced walking meditation day and night. When the dawn appeared, his body was utterly exhausted; as he was about to lean down and lie down, [the Buddha appeared].
Before his head had even reached the pillow, he attained the fruit of Arhatship. With a heart full of joy, he immediately went to the cave and struck upon its stone door.
At that time, Kāśyapa asked, "Who is this knocking at my door?
He replied, "It is the Buddha’s attendant, the bhikṣu Ānanda. Kāśyapa said, "Your outflows (*āsrava*) are not yet exhausted; you may not enter. Ānanda said:

Having already realized the state of outflowlessness (*anāsrava*), Kāśyapa said, "Since you have realized the state of outflowlessness, you should manifest supernatural transformations (*ṛddhiprātihārya*) to dispel the doubts of the assembly.
At that time, Ānanda immediately exercised his supernormal powers and entered through the keyhole of the door, thereby joining the assembly and completing the count of five hundred.
*Piṇḍola* is also called *Bipala*; in full it is *Pippalā*, which means "lofty and eminent."
The character *chòu* (簉) should be read as *zòu* (揍), with the phonetic *qiānhòu* (千候). It means "to insert. The character *chòu* (簉), with the phonetic *chūjiù* (初救), means "an attendant" (*cuì*).
This is not the correct meaning here. The term "pierced-ear guest" refers to the Patriarch Bodhidharma. However, piercing the ears was not established by the Buddha;
he merely adopted it to manifest the physical characteristics of a Brahmin.
The "carver of the boat" is found in the *Yunmen Lu*.

"And the blind man's perverse complaint" (*he mang bei su*) should be read as "and like the blind" (*ru mang*); "perverse complaint" (*bei su*) should be read as "perverse [strike]" (*bei su*). It means "to be in disorder."
"Su" (索) means to take an object in the dark. "Beisu" (捾索) is also a dialectal term; it refers to groping or searching by touch. See Yuan Fushan’s *Nine Bands* (Jiudai).
The *Yaśas-saṃyukta-āgama* states: King Aśoka fashioned eighty-four thousand caskets of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal to enshrine the Buddha’s relics.
He further fashioned eighty-four thousand precious vases to contain those caskets, and commanded various spirits and deities to each hold and make offerings to the relics.
He gave detailed instructions to the spirits, saying: "In Jambudvīpa..."
Proceeding to the shores of the ocean, through cities, towns, and villages where there were ten million households, he erected stūpas for the relics of the World-Honored One.
At that time, there was a senior elder (sthavira) in the city of Pāṭaliputra named Yaśas.
The king went to his place and said to the elder, "I wish to erect eighty-four thousand Buddha-stūpas throughout Jambudvīpa within a single day."
“Tī. His intention was thus. The Elder said, “Excellent, Great King!

On the fifteenth day of the next month, at the time of the lunar eclipse, cause these Jambudvīpa lands to erect stupas for all Buddhas; in this manner, let eighty-four thousand stupas be established within a single day.
The people of the world will experience immeasurable joy. Yaśas—this word means “praise. Furthermore—
The phrase "called Ren-cheng" (Yun-ming-cheng) should be read as "served as attendant" (zhang-shi) according to the original text;
see the *Yun-men-lu*, Volume I.
"Emerging from the sleeve" should be understood as "achieving through engagement. Xuedou’s commentary on the "Waterfall Spring" is extremely detailed.

Daguang once composed a verse on the "Four Modes of Concealing the Apex," which I have recorded here for verification: The first: When engaging with a matter, the apex of concealment is fully present;
One does not seek verbal explanations within the principle. If the golden dragon did not swallow the fragrant bait, It would wag its tail and shake its head, sporting in the azure depths.
The River. II. Entering the Concealed Point of the Principle: The principle is most subtle; how could it be established through phenomena by even a hair’s breadth?
A hawk from Silla flies beyond the heavens; would it deign to seize a dead sparrow in the woods? III. Entering the Concealed Point of Both Principle and Phenomena:

Principle and phenomena are both encompassed. In the azure pool, movement stirs like wind and thunder. At the Dragon Gate in the third month, the peach-blossom waves surge; they bear horns and uphold...

The head is spared from exposure and the gills are hidden. Fourth: emerging to manifest while concealing the point; principle and phenomenon both vanish. The vast sky and blazing sun cause no further hindrance.
Thunder-god and Lightning-mother speak clearly: amidst the roar of thunderbolts, it is but a flash of fire in stone.
The "Fujian Beads" are not clearly detailed.
Li Su’s *Great Expedient Means Sutra on Repaying Kindness* states:

When Prince Shan’you went out of the city to observe, he saw the matters of plowing and sericulture, the killing of living beings, and how people in the world sustain themselves through food and clothing—these being the roots of various evils. His heart could not bear it.
Enduring this, his eyes filled with tears of compassion. Thereupon, he entered the sea to gather *maṇi* jewels in order to relieve sentient beings.
His younger brother, Evil Friend, also wished to accompany him. Prince Good Friend went together with his brother;

by the power of his compassionate heart and merit, they reached the abode of the Dragon King. The King came forth to welcome them, and the Prince preached the Dharma, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening him. The King—
He said, "I have traveled a long distance to visit you; what do you require? The Prince replied, "I now wish to beg from the King the *cintāmaṇi* jewel from within his left ear.
The King said, "I shall grant it to you. Thereupon, the Good Friend took the jewel and returned to Jambudvīpa.
At that time, his younger brother, Evil Friend, conceived feelings of jealousy. While his elder brother was lying down to sleep, he immediately rose.
He sought two dry bamboo stalks, pierced his elder brother’s two eyes, and seized the pearl and departed.
At that time, the Good Friend called out to his younger brother, saying, "A thief here has pierced my two eyes and taken the precious pearl away! But the Evil Friend did not respond.
The elder brother then lamented in a loud voice, "My younger brother, the Evil Friend, has been killed by a thief! He cried out thus for a long time, but there was no response. At that moment...
The tree deity then raised its voice and said, "Your younger brother, Evil Friend, is your wicked enemy. Upon hearing this, Good Friend was despondent and sighed deeply.
Later, he encountered a cowherd and returned home to provide him with offerings.
After one month had passed, the household grew weary and distressed, and they said to their master, "I wish to depart now. If you love me, make for me a lute that can play melodies."
"Send me to a place where there are many people. The host immediately fulfilled his wish. The Prince was skilled at playing the lute;
its sound was harmonious and elegant, delighting the hearts of all who heard it, so that everyone felt fully satisfied.
*Ge*: pronounced with the *gu* and *wo* initials. In the state of Chu, a large boat was called a *ge*.
Zhang Xingman’s *Baolin Zhuan* records that when the Great Master, the Sixth Patriarch, was about to enter *nirvāṇa*, he said to the assembly:
"After my passing, there will be someone who steals my head. Listen to my prediction: 'Raising one's parents upon the head; in the mouth..."*
He was about to take his meal when he encountered the disaster of being struck by a falling beam. A disciple of his, fearing for his safety, had previously secured the Master’s neck with iron plates.
During the Kaiyuan era, at midnight, the sound of dragging iron was heard from within the stupa. The assembly started up in alarm and saw a filial son emerge from the stupa;
they then discovered that the Master’s neck bore a wound. They reported the matter in full to the authorities.
The County Magistrate Yang Liu and the Regional Inspector Liu Wutian captured him at Shijue Village. Upon interrogation, he told the officials:
"My surname is Zhang and my given name is Xingman. I am a native of Liang County in Ruizhou.
I received twenty thousand coins from the Silla monk Kim Daebi of Kaiyuan Temple in Hongzhou, intending to take the head of the Patriarch back to the sea."

He made offerings to the east. When Liu the Governor heard of this, he realized that the ancestral prophecy had been fulfilled; he subsequently pardoned the Zhang family and treated them with great respect.
"Xin-lü" (舋閭) should be read as "Dié-lü" (疊閭), as seen in the *Guǎngdēng* (廣燈). "Dié-lü" means "connected villages," expressing their great number. "Xin" (舋) [is pronounced] xǔ...
[The character] *jìn* (覲) [is pronounced with the initial *qie*.

It means "not right. Regarding the phrase "a bag of wisdom" (*zhináng*): Zhang Xingman was a man from Hai. Because the people of Hai frequently suffered from goiters, he was called a "bag of wisdom" by referring to those with goiters.
According to the *Shiji*, Qin Chulizi had a goiter but possessed great wisdom; thus, his contemporaries nicknamed him "the Bag of Wisdom. *Chū* (樗) [is pronounced *chōu*].]
The character *ju* (居) is pronounced as *qie*. The Chan master was astonished; "ya ya" should be read as "wen" (question). See its original text:
*Sanjian Jiayu* (The Three Silences: Family Sayings). When Confucius visited Zhou, he entered the ancestral temple of the Great Ancestor Houji. To the right of the temple hall...
Before the steps stood a golden man with his mouth bound by three seals. Inscribed upon his back was this: "He was an ancient man who was cautious in speech.
Be on guard! Do not speak much; much speaking leads to many failures. Do not involve yourself in much business; much business leads to many calamities.
One must be cautious even in times of peace and joy, so that there shall be no cause for regret later. Do not say, 'What harm can it do? for its consequences will be long-lasting. Do not say—"
What harm is there? The calamity will be great. Do not say you have not heard: the spirit watches over man. If a spark is not extinguished, how can its flames be contained?
If a trickle is not dammed, it will eventually become a river. If a thread is not cut, it may eventually form a net.
If one does not nip things in the bud, they will soon require the handle of an axe. Truly, those who can be cautious reach the very limits of fortune;
those whose mouths cause injury enter the gateway of calamity. The violent and overbearing do not meet their natural deaths; those who love to triumph must inevitably encounter their adversaries.
After Confucius had read this text, he looked toward his disciples and said, "The words of the small man are well-known to me. These words are substantial and hit the mark;
they are sincere and trustworthy. As the Odes say: 'Trembling and cautious, as if standing on the brink of a deep abyss, as if treading upon thin ice.'"
If one conducts oneself with the body in this manner, how could there be any fault in speech? "Shi" (識) is pronounced "zhi" (志).

I once read the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp), where there is an anonymous monk who composed the "Inscription on Ceasing the Mind" (*Xixin Ming*). Its literary style was modeled after this [work].
However, while the man of gold kept his mouth sealed, this anonymous monk sealed his mind; the latter's principle is somewhat superior. Students should examine it.
Observe this:
when the plum and willow trees arrive at the time of spring, it is not because they possess human surnames; rather, it is a matter of successive transformation and change.
(The character "di" is pronounced as "te" with the "ji" and "qie" finals; it means "to change" or "to replace.")
The character 朕 (zhèn) should be written with the radical 目 as 眹 (zhèn), pronounced *chǐng* (丈忍切). It means "the mark on the eye. The character 眹 (zhèn), pronounced *zhǐn* (直稔切), means "self" (*wǒ*).
This [usage of 朕] is not correct in meaning.
The *Tongxuan Jian Zapiyu Jing* (Sutra of Miscellaneous Parables on Penetrating the Profound) states: Suppose there is a person who gives three coins as an offering and requests three vows:
first, that he shall become a king in the future; second, that he shall understand the speech of sentient beings; and third, that he shall possess great wisdom.
When that person’s life ends, he is reborn into the family of a commoner. His physical form is upright and handsome, and the king admires him and appoints him as his left-hand attendant.

Thus it was. This man, having sought refuge in the King’s favor, was granted the privilege of attending by his side. Seeing a swallow in its nest, he looked up at it and laughed. The King asked why he laughed, and he replied:
"The swallow says, 'I have obtained the daughter of the Dragon King; her hair is ten *zhang* long. I called my companions to come and see her."
The king said, "If it is truly so, that is well; if not, you shall be put to death. He sent him off with the command: "Go and find her.

The king desired to take the dragon maiden as his wife and said to the boy, "Since you understand the language of birds, you must surely possess many stratagems. I shall provide you with provisions; go and seek this woman.
If you find her, you shall be richly rewarded; if you do not, I will kill you along with your family. The boy, braving death, set out.
They headed toward the shore of the eastern sea. There they saw two men quarreling over an invisibility cap, water-treading boots, and a staff that could kill or bring to life.
A young boy said, "What need is there for such contention? I shall release an arrow; you two follow it, and whoever reaches it first shall have it."
He gave him two kinds of objects. The man replied, "Excellent," and drew his bow to release an arrow. The two men raced toward it;
the boy took the cap, put on the boots, grasped the staff, and went straight into the sea. Upon reaching the dragon's abode, he removed his cap so that the dragon maiden could see him.
Women are full of desire, so she gave the boy a piece of gold and sent him back to his own country. The king there dispatched an envoy to welcome him.
The King commanded his daughter to enter alone. The girl then stepped forward, and the boy, wearing an invisibility cap, followed her inside.
When the girl saw that the King was ugly, she threw a piece of gold at him; his forehead was split open and he died. The boy removed his cap and ascended the dais together with the girl.
He cried out in a loud voice, "I shall be king, and you shall be my queen; together we shall rule over all under heaven.

As for the "three corpses" (sānshī) or "three dregs" (sānshī guǐ), these do not appear in the Buddhist scriptures. They were spoken as a response to a specific inquiry and thus cannot avoid conforming to worldly conventions;

they are merely words for a particular occasion. Furthermore, what are called the "three dregs" derive from the Daoist practice of guarding against the *gēngshēn* spirits, as seen in the *Yǒu* [month].
Yang Lu. According to the *Piyu jing* (Sutra of Similes) now available, the "lost seductive ghosts" specifically refers to the two ghosts by the seashore.
The present mention of "three corpses" (sāśi) is likely an error resulting from a confusion with related categories, such as the "five peaks" or "paired eyes."
Buddhabhadra—translated as "Jue Xian" (Awakened Virtue)—was born in India.

In his youth, he studied under the Great Dhyāna Master Buddhasvāmin and became thoroughly proficient in the sūtras and śāstras. At the invitation of the Qin monk Shi Zhiyan, he came to Chang’an to study under Kumārajīva.
While Xian maintained a life of quietude and did not associate with the crowds, he later spoke to his disciples:
[He] said: "Yesterday I saw five ships from my native region set sail together.

My disciple reported this to outsiders, and the monks of Guanzhong, such as Sengfu and Daoheng, all claimed that [this man] was displaying wonders to delude the masses and that his actions violated the Vinaya; they felt it was unreasonable for him to remain here."
"It would be appropriate for you to depart at once. Daoyuan said, "My body follows conditions; it is very easy to flow along with them.

Having long been renowned for his mastery of the *Vibhāṣā*, he met [Huiyuan] as if they were old acquaintances upon first meeting.

He then requested the translation of various sutras on meditation and Abhidharma, and subsequently resided at Mount Lu, staying there in accordance with conditions. "Qiè" (契) is a phonetic abbreviation.
*Zhì huò* (炙輠): "Huò" is pronounced with the initial *hú* and the final *wǎ*. It refers to the appearance of the hub-head turning.
*Zhì* means to grease the hub (*huò*). *Hù* (扈) has the initial sound *hù*; it was the fief bestowed upon those of the same surname as the Xia dynasty. The battle at Gan took place in Hù;
there was the Gan-ting (甘亭) in the valley of Hù. *Hù* is pronounced *hù*.
*Yáo'āng* (搖鞅): "yáo" is read as *liǎng* (兩); "āng" (*dà*) is read as *dá* (怛), meaning supple leather. *Shuā huángjiàn* (刷黃犍):

The first character, *shuā* (刷), is read as *shù huá* (數滑), meaning to scrape. The second character, *jiàn* (犍), is read as *jiū yán* (居言). *Jiàn* (犗) refers to a castrated bull; its pronunciation is *jiè* (戒).
*Mùng* (目瞪): pronounced *zhàng zhèng* (丈證), meaning the appearance of staring fixedly. *Kǔqié* (口呿):
pronounced *qiū qié* (丘伽), meaning the appearance of the mouth being agape.

*Tì* (殢): should be read as *ní* (泥) with the phonetic *nài jì* (乃計); it means to be obstructed or stuck. Alternatively, *tì* may have the pronunciation *dì* (第), meaning "extreme," but this is not the correct sense here.
"Chángyòng" (常用) means that which is used as the actual substance; see the *Guǎngdēng* [commentary]. "Shǎngláo" (賞勞):
the second character is pronounced with the *láng* and *dào* finals;

it means to encourage or reward. Regarding the *Prātimokṣa* of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it says: "One should instruct others regarding good and evil by means of the three-fold invitation (*pravāraṇā*). The *Chāo* [commentary] states: "During the ninety-day [rain retreat]..."

Within this [community], many people are deluded regarding themselves and do not recognize their own faults. It is only right that they rely upon the pure assembly to bestow compassion and instruction;

they should openly confess their own transgressions and allow the Sangha to freely point out their errors. Thus, internally there shall be no concealment of private failings, and externally there shall be the exposure of manifest defects.
Because one entrusts body and speech to others, it is called *pravāraṇā* (self-indulgence). Regarding the "three statements," these refer to what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
The *Mūla-ekottara-karman* of the Bhikṣu states: "The bhikṣu who receives the invitation (*pravāraṇā*) should provide living *kuśa* grass for the Saṃgha to serve as a seat;
all the bhikṣus shall sit upon this grass. Furthermore, the *Hetuphala-sūtra* states: "All..."

When the Tathāgata attained the Unsurpassed Way, he used grass as his seat; therefore, the youth Śrī gave soft grass to the World-Honored One, so that he might act according to his own will and at his pleasure.
The *Suvarṇasūtra-mūla-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states: A bhikṣu went begging for food and entered deeply into a householder’s quarters, which subsequently invited censure and slander.
The bhikṣu informed the Buddha, who said, "You should make a sound to alert them. He then made a clamorous noise by shouting "ha-ha," which again invited ridicule and reproach.
The Buddha prohibited this, so he then struck the door with his fist. The family members asked in astonishment, "For what reason [did you do this]?"
They broke down his gate, but he remained silent and offered no reply. The Buddha said, "You should make a mendicant’s staff (khakkhara). The bhikṣus did not understand;
the Buddha said, 'Attach rings to the head of the staff, circular like the rim of a cup, and fix small bells upon them so that they produce sound when shaken to serve as a warning.
Shake it two or three times; if no one asks anything, you must then depart. "
The character 措 (cuò) is pronounced as 口 (kǒu). It means "to place.
The character 劒 (jiàn) should be read as 劒 (jiàn), and 梁 (liáng) should be read as 良 (liáng).
The character 膊 (bó) should be read as 髆 (bó); it refers to the shoulder blade.
When Foyi Xingjiao was traveling on pilgrimage, he arrived at Jia Shan. One day, during a communal work session (*pǔqǐng*), the *vina* (chant master) ordered him to deliver tea.
Xingjiao said, "I have come for the sake of the Buddha-dharma; I have not come to deliver tea. The *vina* replied:
The Upādhyāya instructed Yunju to invite the Senior Seat (the Abbot). Yunju said, "The Upādhyāya has already received [his share].

Yunju then took the tea to the work area and saw Jia Shan. He shook the tea bowl to make a sound, but Shan paid him no heed. Yunju said, "I have brought three or five bowls of tea; my intention lies with the side of the hoe.
Shan said, "The pitcher has the appearance of pouring tea; how many bowls are there in the basket? Yunju—
Jianzhi said, "The pitcher has the appearance of being tilted, yet there is not a single bowl in the basket. He then poured out the tea, and the entire assembly watched him with their eyes.
Yangshan said, "The assembly gazes upward like cranes; I beg the Master for a word. Dongshan said, "If you encounter a dead snake on the road, do not strike it;
take it up in a bottomless basket. Yangshan said, "Holding a night-bright talisman in his hand—how many would recognize it?"
At dawn, the Mountain (the Master) summoned the assembly, saying, "There is already someone here; go back. He then remained for the communal labor (*pǔqǐng*).
In the Eastern Hall, Jìn Quèxīn was appointed as the Governor of Yōngzhōu by Liáo. The Emperor held a farewell banquet for him in the Eastern Hall and asked Quèxīn, "How do you rate yourself?
Quèxīn replied, "I have been selected a hundred times for the 'Worthy and Good' examination and have provided responses for the empire."
"First: like a single branch of the Gui-lin cypress, or a fragment of jade from Mount Kun. The Emperor laughed at this.
[This passage] appears in the *Huishen Chanshi Houlu* (Posthumous Record of Master Huishen).

"Qiān náo" (thousand monkeys) should be read as "qiān nóng" (thousand *nóng*); "nóng" is pronounced with the second tone (*nu*) and the initial *dāo*. It refers to a long-haired, vicious dog. "Náo" means monkey. This is not the correct meaning.
*Jiān* (pronounced yá): the appearance of dogs fighting.
[This term appears in] the *Vaiśālī City* [section of the *Lengqie shizi ji*], where Xuedou’s verse on the "Ancient Case" is found;

it refers to the event of Emperor Taizong of the Tang dynasty returning to life after gazing upon the dragon throne. This has been cited by various monastic communities to transmit to students. However, the underlying intent...

Some may find this plausible; however, it is not recorded in the *Annals of the Tang Emperors*. It seems that Fengxue believed this based on hearsay and composed these words without any historical verification.
This is similar to such statements as "The three peaks of Mount Hua sit in court without being questioned."
The preceding term "shi" (事) is in one version written as "shi" (使). The *Jingying Lü* (景影律) states:
"Measuring the shadow" (*liang-ying*) is the method for assembling the community to know the time. There are seven methods for assembly in total:
first, measuring the shadow; second, splitting bamboo to make a sound; third, producing smoke; fourth, blowing on a mirror; fifth, beating a drum; sixth, striking a *gandi*.
7. Striking the gong: When the time has arrived, the one who measures the shadow uses a wooden staff one chi long. At midday, he sets it upright and marks its shadow to measure it;
by calculating the celestial inches, he determines the length of the shadow at that specific hour.
*Nirgrantha* is a Sanskrit term; here it means "unbound," signifying that one is free from all attachments.
Regarding "should be gathered" (*yīng shōu*), it should be read as "difficult to gather" (*nán shōu*). See the original text.

On the first day of the first month of the fourteenth year of the Yongping era of the Later Han dynasty, during the formal audience for the New Year, the Daoist masters of the Five Peaks and various mountains, including Chu Shanxin and others, addressed one another, saying: "The Son of Heaven has abandoned our Way and its teachings to seek afar for the barbarian doctrine.

Since we have gathered here for the court assembly, we may submit a memorial to oppose this. They subsequently submitted a petition requesting a comparison of their respective merits and shortcomings.

"If there is indeed a victor, we beg that falsehoods be eliminated. An imperial edict was issued for Song Xiang, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, to escort [the winner] into the Changle Palace;
it was decreed that on the fifteenth day of this month, they should assemble at Baima Monastery, where the Daoist masters and others were to establish three altars.
Each person brought five hundred and nine scrolls, including the *Lingbao Zhenwen*, to the eastern altar.
Two hundred and thirty-five scrolls, including those of Maoshengzi and Laozi, were placed on the central altar. The Emperor occupied his mobile palace at the south gate of the monastery.
Buddhist relics, scriptures, and images were placed to the west of the Daoist area. On the fifteenth day, after the vegetarian feast was concluded, the Daoists used firewood and reeds to...
Using agallochum and sandalwood for torches, he wept and said, "Now the barbarian deity has brought chaos to the Xia dynasty, and the sovereign believes in heterodoxy.
Let us take fire as the test to distinguish the true from the false. He then set fire to the scriptures; the scriptures were consumed by the flames and turned entirely to ashes.
At that moment, the Buddha’s relics emitted light of five colors that shot straight upward, outshining the sun. Dharma Master Mātanga rose high into the air.
He flew and sat or lay amidst the air, extensively manifesting supernatural transformations. He further preached on the merit of renouncing the world, stating that its blessings are supreme.
Liu Jun, the Minister of Works, along with over a thousand officials, scholars, and commoners, renounced the world.
Six hundred and twenty people, including the Daoist Lü Huītōng and others, also renounced the world; this is recorded in the *Hàn Fǎběn nèi zhuàn*. Pómò and Wàngqīng both [did likewise].
This is the location. There is no textual record for this in the sutras or commentaries;
"the hundred limbs flowing with sweat" should be read as "a fine drizzle [of sweat] flowing. This is seen in the *Chuan deng lu*.
Regarding "the *kāṣāya* covering the face," the *Mahāsannipāta Kṣitigarbha-daśacakra-sūtra* states: "In the past, there was a country named Pañcāla..."
In that land, there was a king named Jayasena who ruled over the kingdom. At that time, there was a great mountain cemetery there called Kalandava, which was most terrifying;
yakṣas and rākṣasas dwelt there in great numbers, and if anyone were to enter it—
His heart was terrified and his hair stood on end. At that time, there was a man in the kingdom whose crime merited death.
The king commanded the jailer to bind him at five points and send him to the great charnel ground of Khaḷamba, ordering the various malevolent spirits to devour his body.
Upon hearing this, the criminal, in order to protect his life, immediately shaved off his beard and hair and sought a *kāṣāya* robe; he happened to find a single fragment. By himself—
They bound his neck. Then, following the king’s command, the jailers sent him into a burial mound.
When night fell, a great rākṣasī named Sword-Eye arrived at the cemetery with five thousand attendants.
From afar, the sinner saw them, and his body and mind were struck with terror. At that moment, the rākṣasī saw this man, his five limbs bound.

Having shaved off his beard and hair, and fastening a fragment of saffron-colored cloth around his neck, he immediately circumambulated his venerable teacher to the right, prostrated with palms joined, and spoke these verses with reverence: "May you find comfort within yourself; I shall never harm you."
Seeing one with shaved hair and dyed robes causes me to recollect the Buddha. Qie (pronounced with the *qie* of *qiūjié*).
Bo Le (Li Bo Le), whose courtesy name was Sun Yang, was skilled at appraising horses. While traveling on the mountain slopes of Mount Yu, a salt cart also arrived;
upon it was a dragon-horse that people did not recognize, yet it was being used to pull the salt cart. From afar, it saw Bo Le.
It then neighed. Bǎilè traded his sitting horse for it; the horse could travel a thousand *li* in a day.
"The white ox without horns" refers to a horse. The *Puyao jing* (Lalitavistara Sūtra) states:

"At that time, the kings of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven and the various devas of the desire realm filled the void. They then spoke with one voice to the Prince, saying: 'All internal and external kinsmen...'"
They were all fast asleep. "Now is precisely the time for renunciation. At that moment, the Prince went to Chandaka’s place;
by the power of the gods, Chandaka woke up of his own accord, and the Prince said to him, "You must bring me Kanthaka.
Having heard this, Chandaka’s entire body trembled with fear, thinking, "How can this be in the final watch of the night?"
Suddenly he asked for his horse, intending to go somewhere. The Prince said, "I wish to subdue the thieves of the fetters of affliction for the sake of all sentient beings;
therefore, you must not disobey me. Thereupon, the various devas supported the four hooves of the horse and took hold of Chandaka.
Śakra-devānām-indra followed behind, holding a parasol. They arrived at the forest of asceticism belonging to the seer Bhārgava.
Upon arriving there, he immediately dismounted from his horse and sent Chandaka back.

He knit his brows—*pín* (the character is read as *pín*; the phonetic component is *pín*, and it also means to frown)—and frowned, the latter being pronounced with the *zi* and *liù* initials, meaning to contract or draw together.
In the *Wuwei Huayan Shu* (Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra), the Master says:
"Wei" means "to act. To act is [the realm of] arising and ceasing. That which is tranquil, profound, and empty, abiding eternally and serenely, is devoid of such contrivance;
therefore, it is called "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*). Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "It is without arising or ceasing..."

That which is not bound by causes and conditions is called unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Because there is nothing to be attained, it is named unconditioned.
Moreover, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "Because it does not fall within the realm of numerical reckoning."
The character *qiān* (籤) should be understood as a pickaxe (*chā*). It signifies "to honor" (*chǒng*).
Regarding the "Prince’s Precious Sword," the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "For example, there were two men who were close friends; one was a prince."
The first was poor and lowly. These two men traveled back and forth together.
At that time, the poor man saw that the prince possessed an excellent sword, the most pure and exquisite of all; his heart became greedily attached to it.
Later, the prince took hold of this sword and fled to another country. Thereupon, the poor man subsequently sought lodging for the night at another house. Immediately—

While in the midst of his sleep, he muttered, "Sword! Sword! When those nearby heard this, they took him into the presence of the king. The king then asked, "As for that 'sword' you spoke of, where was it obtained?

The man answered the king in full regarding the aforementioned matter, saying, "Even if Your Majesty were now to butcher my body and sever my hands and feet, if you wish to obtain a sword, it truly cannot be found; I merely..."
The Prince had long been his close friend; they had previously stayed in the same place together.

Although he had seen it with his own eyes, he did not even dare to touch it with his hand, much less take it intentionally. The King asked again, "What was the appearance of the sword when you saw it?
He replied, "Great King, what I saw was like a sheep's horn. Upon hearing this, the King smiled with delight.
[He] spoke: "Go now wherever you wish; do not give rise to anxiety or fear. In my treasury, there is no such sword at all.
[His] nature (*xìng*)—the character *sù* pronounced with the *qiè* of *dào*—is coarse and callous."
*Qixi* (隙骸): *qi* is pronounced as *ji* (戟).

It refers to a cloth for covering the face, as recorded in the *Wuyue Chunqiu* (Spring and Autumn Annals of Wu and Yue). When King Fuchai of Wu died, he said, "I am ashamed to appear before Zi Xu," and thus covered his face with a kerchief (*jin*).
What people today call a "face towel" (*mianjin*) is still the same as what the King of Wu first used. *Fu* (夫) is pronounced as *fu* (扶); *chai* (差) is pronounced as *chui* (楚宜).
