At that time, as the World-Honored One was traveling toward the city of Rājagṛha, Piṅgala-bhāradvāja was residing in that city.
He was widely known and had a large following of disciples who received abundant offerings of ghee, fresh butter, honey, and rock sugar.
When his disciples received these, they accepted them and accumulated them until their storehouses were full.
Large jars, *kuṇḍikā* water flasks, *vāraka* bowls, large alms bowls, and small alms bowls; or within net-bags or water-strainers;
or placed upon pegs in the ground; or upon ivory curved hooks; or between the windows—[these items] were suspended in every place.
The [medicines] overflowed and spread about, and the rooms became foul-smelling and filthy. At that time, various elders came to enter the rooms and inspect them;

they all criticized and disapproved. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha assembled the community and, through skillful means, rebuked them. "From this day forward, I establish a rule for the bhikṣus who are ill:
regarding leftover medicines—ghee, oil, fresh butter, honey, and rock sugar—they may be consumed for a period of seven days. If...
Regarding "exceeded": it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. If that bhikṣu possesses [medicines] that have exceeded seven days—such as ghee or oil—he should smear them on the door hinge;
or, if it is rock honey (*śarkarā*), he should give it to the park-keeper (*ārāmika*). "Kuang" (攩) is pronounced with the *tang* rhyme; it refers to a wooden bucket.
Regarding "eating honey," it should be understood as eating "stone-honey" (śarkarā). The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "The dregs of sugarcane are as hard as stone;
this is called 'stone-honey'.

Regarding "guarding the enclosure," it should be understood as "guarding the garden," meaning one who guards a Buddhist monastery (*vihāra*). In India, a Buddhist monastery is referred to as a *saṃghārāma*.
"Lányuán" (藍園). "Yuán" (垣) means a wall; it is not used here in its standard sense.
"Zhǐyuè" (指月) refers to the story of Xuedou’s waterfall and the moon.

"Mùluó" (汨羅): "Mù" is pronounced with the *mo* and *bi* finals combined (*mòbì*). It is the name of a river located in Luó County of Changshā; hence it is called Mùluó. *Shījì* (Records of the Grand Historian).

Qu Yuan, courtesy name Ping, served the state of Chu as the Grand Master of the Three Tribes (Sanlü Dàfū). Gao Shan Shang slandered him to the King, causing him to be exiled to the region south of the Yangtze River.
As the King of Chu ultimately failed to show him favor, he threw himself into the Mù Pool and died. *Qu* is pronounced with the *jiù* and *wù* finals;
*Jìn* is pronounced with the *jū* and *jìn* finals.
The character for "deaf" (聵) should be written with the radical "ear" (耳) on top; it is pronounced *kuài* (five-guǎi-cut) and means "deaf.

The place name "Mèngtín" should be written as "Mèngtín. According to the *Shū* (Book of Documents), *Tàishì*: "When King Wén passed away, King Wǔ went to observe his troops at Mèngtín," which is located north of Luò.
Because it was where all the capital roads converged, it was designated as a "ferry-crossing" (*tín*).
*Bào* (pinyin: bào): A compound of *jiào* (教) and *qiè* (切). It means to be split open by fire.
See "The Subtle Manifestation of the Patriarch" (*Líwēi Jiàn Zǔyīng*).
Regarding "whipping a corpse": King Bùpíng of Chǔ killed the loyal minister Wǔ Shē along with his son Wǔ Shàng. Shē’s son was Yuán, whose courtesy name was... [text truncated].
Wuzi Xu was both brave and wise. Having fled to Wu with the sole intent of avenging his father, he encountered the death of King Ping and the accession of King Zhao.
When the King of Wu conquered Chu and entered the capital of Ying, Wuzi Xu, failing to capture King Zhao, dug up the tomb of King Ping, extracted his corpse, and whipped it three hundred times.
He trampled upon the king’s belly with his left and right feet, while his right hand tore open [the chest].
His eyes glared at him in reproach, saying: "Who allowed you to use your mouth of slander and flattery to kill my father and elder brothers?
Are you not a traitor?
'To leave Luo and build a fence' refers to the village fences and hamlets."
"Without silk" should be understood as "without partiality.
*Xi* (兕) is pronounced with the initial *xú* and the final *jiè*. It resembles an ox; it is blue in color, has a single horn, and weighs a thousand *qīn*.
Regarding the Three Chu: Jiangling was Southern Chu, Wu was Eastern Chu, and Pengcheng was Western Chu.
The Five Tombs refer to the five imperial mausoleums of the Han dynasty, locations where wandering knights-errant (youxia) resided. They are:
Changling of Emperor Gao, Anling of Emperor Hui, Yangling of Emperor Jing, Maoling of Emperor Wu, and Pingling of Emperor Zhao.
Pig’s Head was once teaching in the marketplace at Mount Pan in Youzhou.
Arriving at a butcher’s shop, he saw a man selling pork and said to the butcher, “Cut me one jin of the finest meat. The butcher set down his knife and replied:
"That one was not refined. At these words, the Master attained realization. Later, his disciple Puhua came forth and said:
"When Mañjuśrī wielded his sword, five hundred bodhisattvas attained the knowledge of past lives.

Because they knew of the grave sins they had committed over many hundreds of millions of kalpas, they were overcome with remorse and thus failed to realize the non-arising of phenomena. At that time, Mañjuśrī, knowing their thoughts, [proceeded]..."
Within the great assembly, someone took up a blade to harm the Buddha. The Buddha said, "If you wish to harm me, do so for the sake of goodness.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying, "What is meant by 'if you wish to harm me, do so for the sake of goodness'?

The Buddha then explained at length that all phenomena are like illusions and transformations. "If one can act in this way, that is to harm me for the sake of goodness. It was because of this that the Bodhisattva [acted].
He perceived that his past offenses were all like illusions and transformations, and he attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Five hundred bodhisattvas, with one voice and in unison, spoke these verses: "Mañjuśrī, the Great Sage of Wisdom, has profoundly penetrated the very source of the Dharma.

With his own hand he grasped a sharp sword and held it against the body of the Tathāgata. As is the sword, so too is the Buddha; they are of a single characteristic and not two. They are without characteristics and without..."
Regarding what is produced therein, how is there killing? See the *Baoji* (Precious Accumulation), fascicle 105.
Once, while Baoshou of Xichan in Zhenzhou was ascending the hall, the senior monk Siming asked: "When you come having trampled through the 'City of Transformation' (the provisional stage), what then?
Baoshou said: "I do not execute this dead man. Ming said: "Execute him! Baoshou then struck him. Ming continued—
Dàozhǎn uttered several shouts, and Shòu followed by striking him several times with his staff. Shòu spoke again, saying, "This monk is using his raw flesh to meet its dry stick;
what kind of desperate urgency is this? He then descended from his seat. At that time, a monk said, "The monk who just asked the question came from Dàjué’s place;
there is also a fellow practitioner there who has the same understanding."
"Baṇ. If you wish for future generations to fully understand the Dharma-way of the Upādhyāya, it is necessary to drive out those two monks;
only then will it be possible. If they are not driven out, I fear it will be difficult for anyone to succeed the Upādhyāya in the future.
Shòu then drove out the monks who had reported the matter. Sīnmíng resided at Xīchán Monastery in Rǔzhōu and was a Dharma successor of Bǎoshòu.
Holding up a sheep’s horn is the story of the Prince’s Precious Sword at Nirvāṇa.
Master Sita received a message from Baozhi which said: "Why do you not go down the mountain to teach and transform sentient beings?
Why do you gaze at the clouds and the Milky Way? Sita replied: "The Buddhas of the three periods of time have all been swallowed by me in a single mouth. Thereupon [Baozhi] said: "There is..."
"What sentient beings can be saved? He split and analyzed them away;
"split" and "analyze" should be written with the radical for silk (糸) and the phonetic *pì* or *xī*. According to the *Bóyǎ*, it means "extreme.
One says it is the appearance of being about to die. Yuan Fushan’s *Jiùdài* writes "pútiao" (to fall and leap) as entering the Tiger Gorge; "broken leg" refers to climbing onto a fisherman.

Regarding the "Venerating the Heavenly King" (Lì Tiānwáng): many monasteries of the Conglin tradition cite National Teacher Nanyang as having performed this veneration; however, this is incorrect. I have frequently encountered it in the sutras and commentaries.

For instance, in the *Buddhacarita* (The Sutra of the Original Deeds), it is recorded that after the Prince was born, according to the custom of the Western lands, it was appropriate to venerate the heavenly deities.
His name was Maheśvara. This deity was extremely malevolent yet possessed great spiritual power. He took the Prince and went to his shrine;
the deity left his seat and descended the steps of his own accord to first prostrate before the Prince. The deity said, "This is the Great Holy Prince; you should not prostrate before me.
Anyone else who receives my prostration shall have their head split into seven pieces. [Furthermore, there are five accounts regarding why he did not bow to the King.]

A lay devotee who observed the precepts did not pay obeisance to a deity. The king asked, "Why do you not pay obeisance? He replied, "I fear it will damage the deity. The king said, "Just pay obeisance.
When the devotee finally paid obeisance, the form of the deity was shattered into pieces.

Furthermore, when King Kaniṣka received the five precepts from the Buddha, he once paid obeisance in a shrine to a deity, and the image of that deity fell over by itself. Later, the guardian of the shrine...

A Buddha image was fashioned within his ceremonial crown. When the king prostrated before him, it did not fall. Finding this strange, he questioned him. [The man] replied, "There is a Buddha image within the crown.
The king was greatly pleased; recognizing that the Buddha was supreme, he pardoned him. ○ Furthermore, the *Gantong lu* (Records of Spiritual Resonance) states:
The monk Baojing of Shuchuan during the Tang dynasty was pure and simple in his monastic life. He recited the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and resided in the vicinity of Shifang;
the local inhabitants were all of the Mi clan and had never before honored the Buddha, such that śramaṇas did not enter their villages.

Consequently, many of the elderly women there did not even know who a monk was. Baojing, wishing to deliver them, waited for a gathering of the community and then went to join them. He did not prostrate.
[The Daoist] sat down. The Daoist faction all said, "To not pay homage to the Celestial Honored One is not the way of a śramaṇa.

Sengqiong said, "The heterodox and the orthodox differ; what each venerates is distinct. Even Heaven still pays homage to me; how could I possibly pay homage to Laojun? The assembly’s discussion was tumultuous.
Sengqiong said, "If I were to bow down in prostration, I would surely bring disgrace upon myself. He then performed a single bow, and the Daoist image immediately rose from its seat.
He shook uncontrollably and was restless. He prostrated once more, falling over in a disheveled heap upon the ground.

Thereupon, the entire assembly prostrated before the statue of [the deity] Qiong, and at once received a response. I have examined all the various accounts and thus learned that those who sincerely believe in the Buddha should not worship spirits.
To worship them brings no benefit to the spirits. Upon reading the *Nanyang Guanglu* (Extensive Record of Nanyang) in detail, I found no such account; therefore, I have omitted it.
The questioner identified him as the National Teacher; this was likely due to a lack of careful scrutiny.

Regarding this anecdote of the boy’s playful inquiry, tradition holds that once, while Fengxue was bathing with the assembly during a communal work period, a monk tied a hand-towel around his head like a topknot.
The monk did this as a joke to provoke laughter. When the Master saw this, he departed without saying a word.

The following day, the scholar consequently raised this question. Furthermore, when Fengxue was showing a look of anger, he placed a vajra on the ground, which was then touched by a wild sheep’s horn;
his question further asked: "Since these are the marks of a Great Man, why are they not complete?
It is also like the phrase regarding the red furnace with its fierce flames reaching out to seize the moon while making sesame cakes. It is similar.
The sources for these accounts are numerous; however, as they are all transmitted orally within the monastic communities, they are difficult to verify and trust.

Even if these accounts were not cited, it would not have detracted from the essential meaning. It is simply because there was such deliberation among the assembly that later generations have spread these as worldly conventions, taking them for granted.
Consequently, when a sense of grievance arises, they immediately [challenge] the assembly of humans and devas.
In the presence of a vast multitude, relying solely upon ignorance, you have openly mocked [the Dharma]. With such a state of mind, what benefit is there for yourself or others?
You do nothing but increase the slander of the shallow and vulgar. Truly, as it is said: "Though the cause be virtuous, it brings forth an evil fruit"—is this not tragic?
I once read the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, which asks: "For what reason is it called 'Dharma-offering'? Regarding the Dharma...
What is the meaning of "offering" (*pūjā*)? The answer is: the meaning of being able to serve as a condition (*pratyaya*) is the meaning of offering.

Because this takes the Dharma as primary, it is called "Dharma-offering. If one preaches the Dharma for others in order to benefit them, and those others, having heard the Dharma, give rise to unprecedented, skillful, and awakened wisdom (*buddhi*), this is called "giving" (*dāna*) and is also called "offering. Alternatively, if the listener does not... [text fragment ends]
Faith alone is called giving (*dāna*), but it is not called worship (*pūjā*).

If, for the sake of causing harm, one speaks words of derision regarding another's Dharma, and that person, upon hearing this, abides in right mindfulness, joyfully accepts it, does not enumerate its faults, and gives rise to a sense of wonder and wisdom—this, although not giving, is called worship.
If, for the sake of causing harm, one speaks words of derision...
Another person, having heard this, gave rise to a mind of resentment and anger, thinking: "This is not called giving, nor is it an act of offering.

He superficially examined the intent of the treatise; yet the scholar’s mind was not set on the Path. Attached to sensory dust and turning his back on awakening, he immediately brought disgrace upon his own house.
"What benefit is there in oneself or others? Are you not being heedful? Are you not being heedful?

While the bhikṣu Śāṭī was performing bathing duties and splitting firewood for the sake of the community, a large black snake emerged from a hole in a rotten tree and bit the big toe of that bhikṣu’s right foot. Ānanda informed the Buddha, and the Buddha—
He was cured by being given the Peacock King Incantation (Mayūrarāja-mantra).
Xiong’er saw Zu Ying.
When one sees an "in" guest, it should be treated as a "diao" guest; see Guangdeng.
The white tortoise should be understood as the blind tortoise. The story of the blind tortoise appears in the *Yunmen Lu* (Record of Yunmen), Volume One.
Regarding the invocation of "Awakening" (*jue*) and "Teaching" (*jiao*), the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: Once there was a king who ordered a messenger to travel far to purchase wisdom with gold.
The messenger obeyed his command and went everywhere. Later, while he was beneath a tree, someone questioned him.

"Where have you come from? he asked. "To buy wisdom," he replied. "I have some," [the other] said. "Give me gold and I will sell it to you. The messenger gave him the gold and received only this verse:
"Examine and reflect with careful discernment; Be cautious not to act rashly or wrongly. Though there is no use for it now, There shall surely come a time when it is needed.
The messenger took the verse and returned to present it to the king. The king inscribed it upon the window of his chamber and constantly recited it to himself.
Later, the princess fell ill. Wearing men’s clothing, she lay in the palace bedchamber sleeping with her mother. When the king entered and suddenly saw her, he drew his sword, intending to kill her.
Only when he woke her did he realize who she was; it was because of her wisdom that this occurred.
The Swordsman saw the *Later Record* of Xuedou:
"If you wish to cut it off, you must cut it off. "Cut" (*duàn*)—the initial rhyme is *guǎn*; it means to sever. See the *Chuan Deng Lu*.
The Red Eyebrows saw this in the *Former Record* of Master Huai:
"The leopard transforms into the sage-tiger. This distinguishes its brilliant markings; the "leopard of the gentleman" distinguishes its luxuriant markings;
and the "discerning man-leopard" distinguishes its gathered markings. When a wildcat transforms, it becomes a leopard; when a leopard transforms, it becomes a tiger. This is seen in the *Yangzi*.
*Páo xiāo* (咆哮) means to roar. The upper character (*páo*) is pronounced *báo* and means to kick. The lower character (*xiāo*) is pronounced with the *xū jiāo* rhyme;
it means to cry out. Once, there was a man in Lu who shared the same name as Zeng Shen. When he committed a murder, someone reported it to Zeng Shen’s mother.
The mother did not believe him and continued weaving as before. He told her this three times. The mother threw down her shuttle and started up in alarm;
she mistakenly thought he was saying "do not weave," but upon seeing the lamp, she realized it was "weave. She then transmitted the lamp.
Aṅgulimāla is translated as "Finger-Garland. The *Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish* states:
A son was born to the family of the prime minister of King Prasenajit; he was handsome and powerful, capable of matching a thousand men.
He was named Anupama (The Untroubled). He studied under a Brahmin for three months, during which time only his wife remained at home. That wife was unchaste.
The Brahmin desired to engage in unchaste conduct without causing distress, but because his resolve was firm, she did not comply.
The wife felt ashamed and, instead, proceeded to slander him. When the Brahmin returned home, his wife immediately began weeping and told him:
"Since you left, Ananda has repeatedly attempted to violate me. Just now, when I refused him, he tore my clothes and bruised my head and body. The Brahmin...
The gatekeeper said, "The son of a high minister is difficult to subdue; you must devise a special stratagem.

He then said to Anupama, "If, within seven days, you can sever the hands of a thousand men and take one finger from each—collecting a total of one hundred fingers—to fashion them into a garland for adornment, then Brahmā himself will descend to you.
At the end of your life, you will certainly be reborn in the Brahma Heaven."
He then uttered incantations and planted his sword in the ground; immediately, an evil intent arose within him, and whenever he encountered a person, he would kill them.
Within seven days, he had obtained ninety-nine fingers, lacking only one person. Though he searched for this last victim, he could not find him.

At that time, his mother brought food to give to him, but he immediately sought to kill her. Then, the World-Honored One saw this from afar and manifested himself as a bhikṣu, walking along beside him.
He then abandoned his mother and rushed toward the bhikṣu. When the Buddha saw him approaching, he walked away slowly.
Aṅgulimāla ran with all his might but could not catch up; he then called out, "Stop for a moment! The Buddha said, "I always abide in stillness; it is only you who do not abide.
Aṅgulimāla asked again, "How is it that you abide and I do not? The Buddha replied, "My faculties are tranquil..."
"By means of meditative concentration, one attains mastery. You have followed an evil teacher and distorted your mind, so that you have failed to attain stable abiding.

Upon hearing these words, his mind was opened and he attained awakening; he took refuge in the Tathāgata, who immediately manifested his body for him and preached the Dharma. He then left the household life and realized the fruit of enlightenment.
Wanhui the Mad Monk, Wanhui by name, was surnamed Zhang and was a native of Wenxiang in Guozhou. While still in his tender years, he appeared white and foolish, remaining mute.
His parents grieved over his dull nature, and he was mocked by the daughters of the neighborhood; yet he never displayed any competitive spirit.
He would call himself "Wanhui" (Ten-Thousand Returns), and thus he gained his name. At the age of ten, he saw his elder brother...
Wan Hui was stationed in Liaoyang. For a long time there had been no news, and his parents grew anxious for him. They prepared a vegetarian feast and offered prayers on his behalf.

Suddenly, Wan Hui said to his mother, "Your brother is very easy to find; why do you worry about him? Then, during the time of the monastic meal, Wan Hui took his leave of his mother and went out the door.
When evening arrived, Wan Hui returned holding his brother’s letter and presented it to his mother. When his mother asked him about the circumstances of his departure, he gave her no reply at all.
It was true. He had traveled from Mianxiang in Guozhou to Liaoyang, a journey of over ten thousand li there and back.

One day, when his elder brother returned, he recounted in detail the conversation he had with Hui on that day, mentioning how they had taken bread and rice to eat together before departing. His parents were greatly astonished;

everyone changed their opinion of him, and his reputation reached the imperial court. Emperor Zhongzong summoned him for an audience and treated him with considerable honor and respect. Shen... [text fragment]
In the second year of the Long era, an imperial edict was issued to grant special ordination to one Huí, bestowing upon him the title Gōng Fǎyún.
He was rarely seen by outsiders and possessed many miraculous powers. Furthermore, he was granted garments of silk embroidery, and palace attendants were assigned to serve him.
The verses and hymns composed by the Master circulated among the people; those who heard them were few, as they were seldom obtained. The *Zōngjìng lù* once cited a verse which begins: "Black..."
White forgets both, opening the Buddha-eye; unattached to a single dharma, emerging from the lotus grove. True emptiness does not destroy the nature of numinous wisdom;
wondrous function is eternally constant, without the effort of action. Holy wisdom originally constitutes the path to Buddhahood;
the light of stillness is not a reflection, but is spontaneously perfect and pervasive. *Han* (pronounced as in "hu-tan-qie") means delusion. *Wei* (phonetic: *wen*).
*Qiūshuài* (酋帥): "Qiū" is pronounced as *zì qiū* (自上秋切); it means "chief" or "leader. *Nàbì jiànzǔ* (納璧見祖):
"Offering jade and appearing before the ancestors.

*Yīngqiānyáng* (英牽羊): "The leader leads a sheep. *Qūyì* (曲䚄) should be read as *qūlù* (曲[跳-兆+彔]); the pronunciation is *lù*. It means "walking with reverence. *Yì* (䚄): "To look with a smile. This is not [the correct meaning].
The *Shiji* records that the dog of a thief can be made to bark at Yao; it is not that Yao was unkind, but rather that the dog barked at one who was not its master.
"Qi-han" (祁寒)—the first character is pronounced with the initial *qí*, meaning "great"—refers to what is called the "severe cold of winter," when the common people lament and complain.

Xuantou Cigu (Suspended Head and Pierced Thigh) was Sun Jing, courtesy name Wenbao. He frequently stayed shut in his room to study; whenever he fell asleep, he would tie his head with a rope and suspend it from a beam above.
Once, he went into the marketplace, and when the market folk saw him, they all called him "Mr. Closed-Door. The Emperor specially summoned him, but he did not accept the appointment.
This is recorded in the *Biographies of Former Worthies*. *Sū Qín* was a native of Luoyang. He studied under the same teacher as Zhāng Yí of Wèi.
When Master Guiguzi was reading and fell asleep, he drew a needle to prick his own thigh until the blood flowed down to his ankle;

later, he served as a minister to the six states, as recorded in the *Zhan Guo Ce*. During the Sui dynasty, the eminent monk Zhishun specialized in the study of the Way and contemplation, refusing to concern himself with worldly karmic conditions.
Whenever deluded thoughts suddenly arose that could not be restrained, he would immediately prick his thigh until it bled, or sometimes embrace a stone.
He circumambulated the stupa, his mind never for a moment wandering from its focus. Thus, the spots where his thighs were pierced appear like a brocade spread out;
this is recorded in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* by Huìjiǎo.

The character for "biting" (*niè*) is correctly written as 齧 (pinyin: niè, with the radical 齒), meaning to bite or gnaw. During the end of the Sui dynasty, there was one named Dū Jūnmó who was skilled at locking doors.
He aimed at the eyes; when he fixed his aim on the eyes, he hit the eyes. When he fixed his aim on the mouth, he hit the mouth.

There was a man named Wang Lingzhi who studied archery under Mo, believing that he had mastered every subtlety of the art. Desiring to kill Mo so as to monopolize its excellence for himself, he took up his bow.
Mou held a single short sword; whenever an arrow came, he would intercept it with his blade. There was only one instance where he missed; he opened his mouth to catch it and bit the arrowhead.
He laughed and said, "You have studied archery for three years, yet I have never taught you the method of biting off an arrowhead."
I have seen this in the *Taiping Guangji*. "Dí" (鏑) is pronounced "dí"; it refers to the arrowhead. "Yīngjùn" (鷹俊) should be read as "yīngsǔn" (鷹隼), meaning hawk and falcon.
I have seen this in the *Chuandeng Lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp).
"Mènglàng" (孟浪) is synonymous with "shuàilǜ" (率略), meaning hasty or reckless.
*Chīxiāo*: The upper character is pronounced *zhī* (cut by *chēng*); it refers to an owl. The lower character is pronounced *jiāo* (cut by *jiāo*); it is a bird of unfilial nature.
The "ghost" (gui) should not be treated as a mere spectral entity.
It reveals its original nature: the "whipped fox" (bianhu). This is a beast of aberration ridden by a ghost; see the *Shuowen Jiezi*.

[The character] "shou" (head) has the phonetic "jiao"; it refers to an inverted head. The character "jia" (賈) explains this as a severed head hanging upside down. [This was noted by] the Palace Attendant (Shizhong).
"Zèngrén" (甑人) appears in the *Zǔyīng* (祖英).
"Biānzhēng" (鞭征) should be read as "biānzhēng" (邊征); see the *Guǎngdēng* (廣燈).
"Pèixié" (佩攜) should be read as "pèixuī" (佩觽), pronounced *huī*. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is a sharp-pointed object used for untying knots. [Cited from] the *Pénglán* (芃蘭) of the *Shī* (詩).
Chapter: "The Youth Wears a Hairpin. The commentators say: "The hairpin (xī) is used for untying knots; it is the ornament worn by an adult.
Since the ruler manages the affairs of adults, even a youth wears the hairpin so as to cultivate his virtue early."
"At the age of twenty, his voice was penetrating. 'Guan' refers to the cap that binds the hair; a man at twenty is said to be 'at the age of the weak cap.
The 'Venus Star' is the Chang-geng star in the west. The *Tianwen zhi* (Record of Astronomy) states:
'The Chang-geng star is as broad as a bolt of cloth stretched across the sky. When this star appears, war breaks out.'"
*Jiong* (扃) is pronounced *yǎng* (上古螢切). It refers to the closing bolt of a door outside. *Xià* (鐍) is pronounced *jué* (古穴切); it is a ring with a tongue.
Regarding the severing of his arm, Guifeng Mihuai’s disciple Taigong severed his own arm as an expression of gratitude for the Dharma he had heard from his master.

Some within the monastic community point to the circumstances involving the Second Patriarch at Shaolin, but this is because they do not understand the meaning of that dialogue. How could the Second Patriarch...
One who seeks the wisdom that discerns the distinctions of illumination!
"Lùbù" (露布) should be understood as "exposed proclamation. An unsealed imperial edict or memorial is called a *lùbù*.
Regarding the "ringing of bells," the *Xīyùjì* (Record of the Western Regions) states: "In India, the *caṇḍāla* are called 'evil persons,' just as the *guǐ* (魁, leaders/ogres) are in this land."
Huai lived separately from others. Whenever he entered a city or market, he would shake a bell to distinguish himself;
people, recognizing him, would avoid him and not collide with him by accident.
[The author] greatly disparages the *Rituals of Zhou* (*Zhōu Lǐ*). Four *lǐ* make one *zuǒ*; five *zuǒ* make one *bǐ*. A *bǐ* is a small state.
"Great *bǐ*" refers to the royal city.
*Caṇḍāla*: the character is pronounced *tú*; it is also called *caṇḍāla*, which here means "killer," or "fierce and blazing."
Furthermore, it is said that one should revere those who commit evil deeds;

it is also said that one should refrain from killing. Regarding the certainty of attaining Buddhahood, the *Śūramgama-samādhi Sūtra* states: "At that time, Upāli rose from his seat and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'World-Honored One, in the past, within the Vinaya and the various scriptural collections (Sūtrapitaka), you spoke of Ajita as the next [Buddha]...'"
"He shall become a Buddha. This Ajita possesses the body of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and has not yet severed the outflows (*āsrava*).

Where will this person be reborn when his life ends? Although this man has now left the household life, he does not cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) nor sever the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Yet the Buddha has prophesied that this person will undoubtedly attain Buddhahood. To which land will this person be reborn at the end of his life? The Buddha told [them]:
Upāli, listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon this well. This person will, twelve years from now, certainly be reborn in Tuṣita.
"Night produces light" should be treated as "black produces light.
See the *Chuan deng lu*. Guang'e saw Chiyang ask;
Fushi Xianyi saw Xuedou's verse on the ancient stone.
The character for *hrī* (懞[怡-台+羅]) should be read with the first part as "muo" (毋果切) and the second part as "lao" (郎可切). *Hrī* means shame (*lajjā*).
*Chu* (麈) is pronounced with the *yu* rhyme. It refers to the "dust-whisk deer" (*chulü*) mentioned in Xuedou’s *Songgu* (Verses on Ancient Cases).
*Wúliáo* (無憀) has the phonetic *liáo*; it means reliance.
*Kharaskandha* (佉羅騫馱) is translated here as "roaring like thunder"; he is one of the four Asura kings, two *zhang* in height.
It is eighteen thousand *li* in height. It has nine heads and a thousand eyes, with fire issuing from its mouths.

It possesses nine hundred and ninety-nine hands and eight legs, standing in the midst of the ocean with the water reaching only to its waist. With its hands, it upholds the sun and moon and rubs and strokes heaven and earth.
When Taiwei Sima Qinyi was departing for his provincial command, he took leave of Baozhi. Baozhi drew a tree with a bird perched upon it.
At first, Qinyi did not fully understand its meaning; later, however, Qinyi indeed encountered an emergency and climbed the tree.
His pursuers saw a bird shrieking on the tree and concluded that there was no one there, whereupon Qinyi managed to escape. This is recorded in the *Baozigong Zhuan* (Biography of Master Baozhi).
"Yim-xiao-wen, Yim-xiao-wen; after Yim-xiao-wen, one likes to hear [it]. One should say 'Yi-gen-xiao-hou-hao-gu-wen'.
This is because I have seen another version."
One should polish an inch of gold until it becomes worth ten pieces of gold.
During the Tianbao era of the Tang dynasty, An Lushan, the Regional Inspector of Fanyang, achieved great military success on the frontier.
The Emperor held him in high favor. When Lushan came to court, the Emperor ordered the sisters of the Noble Consort Yang Dazhen to form a brotherly bond with him.
Brother, when An Lushan’s mother served the Noble Consort and An Lushan’s rebellion was exposed, the imperial edict enumerated the crimes of Yang Guozhong.

As bandits rose up in Hebei and Emperor Xuanzong intended to lead a personal campaign, he appointed the Crown Prince as Supreme Commander of the Armies of the World to oversee and pacify the affairs of the military and the state.
Yang Guozhong was greatly terrified; the various members of the Yang clan gathered to wail, and the Noble Consort [attempted to] offer earth from her mouth in petition.
The Emperor did not, however, proceed with the abdication of the throne. When Tongguan fell, he followed the imperial procession to Mawei.
There, the commander of the imperial guards, Chen Xuánlǐ, secretly petitioned the Crown Prince to execute Guózōng and his sons. Subsequently, the four armies refused to disperse.
The Xuanzong dispatched a *lìshì* (eunuch attendant) to inquire into the matter; they replied, "The root of the rebels still remains," referring specifically to the Noble Consort.
The strongman reported this again. The Emperor, having no other recourse, took leave of the consort; she subsequently hanged herself in the Buddha chamber.
She was thirty-eight years old at the time and was buried on the road to the left of the post station.

The numinous tortoise dragged its tail [through the mud] as Zhuangzi fished in the Pukui River. The King of Chu sent two high officials to summon him, saying, "I wish to trouble you with the affairs of my realm.
Zhuangzi replied, "In Chu there was a divine tortoise that died three thousand years ago.

The King wrapped it in silk, placed it in a bamboo case, and enshrined it upon the hall of his ancestral temple. As for this tortoise, would it rather have its dead body preserved as a skeletal relic?"
Which do you consider more noble? Would you rather live out your days dragging your tail through the mud?
The two officials replied, "We would rather live with our tails exposed in the mud. Zhuangzi said, "Go then; I shall drag my tail through the mud."—Pu.
Yīnbo (音卜): Borrowed from 借;

As for the "willow whip," it refers to Liu Kuan, courtesy name Wenyao, a native of Huayin in Hongnong during the Eastern Han dynasty. In the eighth year of the Yanxi era, he served as the Governor of Yingchuan. His character was mild and his demeanor gentle; he governed the people with benevolence and compassion. He would not strike anyone with a staff, nor did he ever raise his voice in anger. It is said that when his attendants once struck a servant who had spilled wine while serving him, he merely took a willow branch and lightly whipped him on the back. The servant, weeping, remarked, "I have been whipped by the willow branch today. Upon hearing this, Liu Kuan immediately felt remorseful and apologized to the servant. His wife, Lady Xu, was also exceptionally virtuous and kind. Once, while she was cooking, her mother-in-law accidentally dropped a meat bone onto the ground. The lady picked it up herself and returned it to her mother-in-law. Her mother-in-law, surprised, asked, "Is it because you are afraid I will scold you? The lady replied, "I am not afraid of being scolded; rather, I thought that since it was my own hand that dropped it, I should pick it up myself. Hearing this, her mother-in-law sighed in admiration, saying, "My daughter-in-law is truly a woman of great virtue. Thus, the people of Yingchuan were moved by his kindness and affection, and even those who harbored resentment toward him could not bring themselves to bear ill will. When Liu Kuan passed away, the people of Yingchuan erected a stone monument at the crossroads to commemorate him. The inscription read: "The Governor of Yingchuan, Liu Kuan, was a man of profound virtue and high integrity. He governed the people with benevolence and compassion, and never raised his voice in anger. Even when a servant spilled wine, he only used a willow branch to strike him. He was a true father to the people, and the people regarded him as their father. When he died, they erected this monument at the crossroads to honor his memory. This account appears in the *Hou Hanshu*, "Biographies of the Eminent Women. Furthermore, the *Shishuo Xinyu*, "Discourse on the Way of the World," records that Liu Kuan’s son, Liu Xun, was also a man of great virtue. When he was the Governor of Yuzhou, he governed with such benevolence and compassion that he never punished anyone with a staff. "Stopping poison" (*ting du*) should be read as "pavilion" (*ting*). "Pavilion-poisoning" (*ting du*) refers to the vital energy of Heaven and Earth by which all living beings are sheltered, sustained, and nurtured.
This is identical to the *Ṣaḍdhātuvibhaṅga-sūtra* (Lengyan jing). As the verse of Mañjuśrī states: "Once a single faculty returns to its source, all six faculties attain liberation."

Furthermore, originally based on a single luminous intelligence, it divided into six harmonious combinations. When one locus becomes quiescent and returns to its source, the functions of the other six are all suspended.
Without trace, they should serve as body and land; when the traces have faded, [the true nature remains].
The three turnings of the wheel of Dharma are: first, the turning that demonstrates characteristics, which means demonstrating the characteristics of the dharmas of the Four Noble Truths;

second, the turning that exhorts practice, which means exhorting the cultivation of these Four Noble Truths; third, the turning that provides testimony, which means declaring "I have realized them" so as to inspire faith and acceptance.

On that mountain there is a creature called the *chī*. It resembles an ox; it has no horns, is azure in color, and moves on one leg. Its roar is like thunder.
When the Yellow Emperor fought against Chiyou, he used its hide to make a drum whose sound could be heard for five hundred *li*.

"But look at the puppets performing on the stage; all who pull the strings are people from within."

The six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) are: 1. The power of the body (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna*). In a single moment, the body follows the activity of wisdom, pervading the ten directions and manifesting physical forms (*rūpakāya*) in accordance with the faculties of beings, responding skillfully to them.
2. The power of the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*). The faculty of hearing constantly hears all sounds throughout the ten directions.
3. The power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). The faculty of sight constantly sees all forms—whether coarse or subtle—throughout the ten directions. 4. [The power of knowing others' minds...]

1. The supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*). Wisdom follows all sentient beings as they die here and are born there; it is able to fully know the causes, conditions, and karmic actions performed by them.

5. The supernormal power of knowing the minds of others (*paracitta-jñāna*). In a single thought-moment, one can know the mental intentions and desires of all sentient beings throughout the three periods of time.
6. The supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna*). Following wisdom, one universally knows all phenomena (*dharmas*) without any worldly passions or attachments.

*Yǎn zǎo* (罨棗) should be read as *yì zǎo* (腤棗). *Niǎo hán* (鳥含) is the phonetic transcription; it means to boil. *Yǎn* (罨), with the phonetic transcription *wū dá* (烏答), means a net; [in this context] it is not the correct meaning.
*Náo* (聱), with the phonetic transcription *wǔ jiāo* (五交), means that speech does not enter [the ears].
The *Śata-rasa-jñāna-śāstra* states: Regarding "a hundred flavors" (*śata-rasa*), some say that being able to provide a hundred kinds of offerings is called "a hundred flavors.
Others say that there are five hundred varieties of cakes, and their flavors number one hundred; this is called "a hundred flavors.
Still others say that medicinal herbs of a hundred kinds are made into *modaka* (joy-pills); this is called "a hundred flavors. Yet others say it refers to rice, food, and soup.
"Cakes" (*piǎng*) generally comprise a hundred flavors. Some say that because various kinds of food and drink are fully provided, they are called "the hundred flavors.
"Grinding ointment" (*mògāo*) is not clearly explained.

*Biǎobǔ* (杓卜) refers to divining good or bad fortune by casting a ladle; this is called *biǎobǔ*.

The Dharma-eye [Master] Fayan, whose taboo name was Wenyi, was born in Yuhang. His surname was Lu. At the age of seven, he followed Chan Master Quanwei to receive his training.
He attained the Dharma from Luohan Chen. Later, he traveled to Linchuan, where the regional governor invited him to reside at Chongshou Monastery. [This occurred during the] Jiangnan Kingdom...
The Emperor, having heard of the Master’s reputation for the Way, welcomed him to reside at Baen Temple and bestowed upon him the title of Chan Master Jinghui. Later, he moved to reside at Qingliang.
He passed away in the fifth year of the Xiande era of the Zhou dynasty; his posthumous title was Chan Master Dafaian.
Subsequently, because of the request of his disciple Xuyan, who designated him as the Guiding Master Xuanguo, he was granted a second posthumous title: Great Wisdom Treasury, Great Guiding Master.
“Nengren” (能仁) is the Chinese translation of Śākya, which means “Capable Sage. The *Vinayakṣudrakavastu* states:
In ancient times there was a king named Ikṣvāku who had four sons: first, Mukhacūḍa; second, Kharakarṇa; third, Hastipṛṣṭha; and fourth, Pādapiṇḍika.
When these four sons committed transgressions, they were all banished. At that time, the four youths went forth...
They went to the side of the Snowy Mountains and, by the bank of a river, each constructed a thatched hut for their own rest.
There the husband and wife married and each gave birth to sons and daughters. At that time, King Ikṣvāku, longing for his sons, asked his ministers:
"Where is my son? His attendants related the preceding events in detail. The King said, "My son was capable of such a deed.
They replied, "He was indeed capable. Because of this, his clan was named Śākya (釋氏). [Note: *Jiàn* (玔) is pronounced with the initial *chǐ* and the final *juàn*.]

it means the tip or end. *Xie Zhao* (謝肇): *Xie* refers to Xie Lingyun, the Marquis Kangle of the Jin dynasty; *Zhao* refers to the Dharma Master Jiekong of Later Qin.
Sengzhao’s *Verses on the Vast and Unattached Mind* states: "Vast, foremost, and eternal, its mind is not inverted;
abiding in a profound mind of benefit, the merit of this vehicle is fulfilled. Vasubandhu’s *Śāstra* asks: "What is meant by the vast mind of benefit? As the Sūtra says:"
All Bodhisattvas give rise to such a thought: "How can I bring about the foremost benefit for all sentient beings?
As the Sūtra says: "I shall lead them all into *nirvāṇa* without remainder and deliver them. How is it that they bring about constant benefit? As the Sūtra says:
"In this way, although immeasurable and boundless sentient beings are delivered, in truth no sentient being has been delivered."
Regarding "nirvāṇa": Why is this? Subhūti, if a bodhisattva perceives the mark of a sentient being, he is not a bodhisattva.

How then could there be non-perverted benefit? As the sūtra says: "Subhūti, if a bodhisattva gives rise to the mark of a sentient being, the mark of a person, or the mark of a life-span, he is not called a bodhisattva."

*Nirvāṇa* is here translated as "Great Perfect Quiescence" (*dàyuánjì*). According to the *Jiǎndìng zhǔnshí lùn* (Treatise on the Determination of the Standards for Consciousness), there are four kinds of *nirvāṇa*: 1. *Svabhāva-viśuddhi-nirvāṇa* (Nirvāṇa of Innate Purity).

This is possessed equally by both ordinary beings and sages. 2. *Sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (Nirvāṇa with Remainder). This refers to the state where one has emerged from the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
There is suffering because it relies upon the body. Third, there is the "remainderless" (*anupadhiśeṣa*); because one has emerged from birth and death, suffering no longer has a basis.

However, the Hīnayāna considers the extinction of the physical form and the cessation of cognition to be "remainderless. There are three types of remainder: first, the remainder of afflictions (*kleśa-śeṣa*); second, the remainder of karma;
and third, the remainder of karmic retribution (*vipāka-śeṣa*). In the Mahāyāna, however, the ultimate jewel-treasure site is taken as "remainderless. Thus, the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states:

It is taught that the exhaustion of the afflictions of the four stages of abiding is called "nirvana with remainder. Because the four types of non-abiding compassion and wisdom are combined, one does not abide in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa;
this is precisely the "nirvana without remainder" of the Mahāyāna. Among the four kinds [of nirvana], it refers to non-abiding nirvāṇa:
namely, not abiding in the transformation-death (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*) of Bodhisattvas, nor abiding in the extinction-annihilation of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
Nirvana is precisely true non-abiding; it is called "without remainder" (*anupadhiśeṣa*).

Regarding birth from eggs, wombs, moisture, or transformation—birth as a deva or in hell is by transformation; birth as a *preta* admits of both womb and transformation; humans and animals each have all four. The *Kanding* (Determination of Difficulties) asks:

"Birth from eggs is the most inferior; why is it placed first? This is answered by considering the general scope of the realms: it is said that birth from eggs necessarily involves [the presence of] a womb and moisture.
Transformation is manifold due to conditions; therefore, we trace the mind back to its origin. This means that sentient beings originally give rise to karma through their fundamental cause.
The karmic consciousness is the fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*) in union with the original nature (*prakṛti*); subject and object are not yet differentiated, being as chaotic as an egg.

"Egg" refers here to the embryonic membrane (*kalala*). Thus, the *Bhaiṣajyaguru-sūtra* says: "Break the eggshell of ignorance, dry up the river of afflictions (*kleśa*). It is from ignorance that karma is initiated.

Birth: being in the *ālayavijñāna* constitutes birth from a womb; receiving birth [from external conditions] constitutes birth from moisture; and arising suddenly from non-existence at the moment of birth constitutes birth by transformation.
For these reasons, they are arranged in this order.
The realms of emptiness consist of the six heavens of the desire realm; the realms of form consist of the four dhyānas:
the three heavens of the first dhyāna, the three heavens of the second dhyāna, the three heavens of the third dhyāna, and the nine heavens of the fourth dhyāna; and the four formless attainments:

the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Furthermore, there is the sphere of emptiness and the sphere of consciousness.
There are two states: the state of perception is called "floating," while the sphere of nothingness and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are "sinking.
*Sattva* is fully explained as *bodhisattva* or *mahāsattva*, which has three interpretations. First, *bodhi* is...
1. "Buddhahood" (*buddha*) refers to the fruit sought; "sattva" refers to the sentient beings to be transformed, who are the objects of compassion and wisdom.
The name is established based on these objects. 2. "Enlightenment" (*bodhi*) is the fruit to be sought; "sattva" is the person who seeks it.
Because the means and the end are conjoined, one is called a *bodhisattva*. 3. *Sattva* here means "valiant. This refers to [the resolve] toward great enlightenment.
Because of seeking with valor (*vīrya*).
*Jing* (晶) is pronounced as *ying* (盈); it means light.
From a verse in the *Agnirāśi-jñāna-śāstra*: "If a person sees Prajñā, they are thereby bound; if they do not see Prajñā..."
If one does so, one is likewise said to be bound. If a person perceives *prajñā*, they attain liberation;
yet if they do not perceive *prajñā*, they also attain liberation. The *prajñāpāramitā* is like a great flame: it cannot be grasped from any of its four sides;
there is no grasping, nor is there anything to be grasped.
Later, upon seeing the *Zuying* (Anthology of the Patriarchs), it says:

"Grasping at the self-substance of the four marks of self and person constitutes the conception of a self (*ātman*). My transmigrating through various realms of existence constitutes the conception of a person (*pudgala*).
My continuity through various transformations of prosperity and decline, suffering and pleasure, constitutes the conception of a sentient being (*sattva*). My..."
The retribution of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) remains uninterrupted and persists; this constitutes "longevity" (*āyus*). Regarding the term *jilong* (羈籠):
the first character, *ji*, is pronounced with the initial *ch* (宜切); it refers to a head-halter for a horse.
As for the term *fangzhang* (方丈), it is now used to designate the principal quarters of a Chan monastery. This is likely modeled after the Vihāra in the city of Vaiśālī.

Regarding the chamber of King Mahāsudarśana: within a chamber measuring only one *zhang* (ten feet), he was able to accommodate thirty-two thousand lion thrones because of its inconceivable and wondrous nature.
When the Tang envoy Wang Xuance traveled through the Western Regions, he passed by his residence and measured it with his hand-tablet (*shouban*) both lengthwise and crosswise;
it measured ten *hu* (cubit-widths). Consequently, it was named after this measurement.
The inscription’s sounds are profound, recounting his meritorious achievements so that they may be extolled by name; it is also a record of his aspirations.
He planned the abode of Master Hou for the long term, not as a private residence.
Therefore, those who could dwell in that place for a long time were not merely one person; thus, that location may be called "Hou" (Thick/Abundant).
Xiaoyin (Minor Seclusion) by Kang Ju, Prince of Jin, in his "Poem on Returning from Seclusion" (*Fanzhaoyin shi*) says: "The minor recluse hides in marshes and thickets;
The great recluse hides in the capital and the marketplace. Bo Yi went into exile on Mount Shouyang; Lao Dan remained hidden as the Grand Historian."
The Great Obscurity of the Old Master says: "While worldly people are bright and clear, I alone appear as if obscured. Commentators say:
Because one has forgotten both things and self, and does not give rise to discrimination, one is thus as if obscured.
Yǎo'ài (窈靄): the first character is pronounced with the *zhào* rhyme group, the second with the *gài* rhyme group;
it describes the appearance of clouds. Chányán (孱顏): the first character is pronounced with the *shān* rhyme group; it means uneven. See the commentary on the Western Han [Annals].
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* states: "Citta, manas, and vijñāna—though these three are one in essence—differ in their etymological definitions and semantic categories.
That is to say, it is called 'citta' because it accumulates and gives rise [to phenomena]; it is called 'manas' because it cogitates; and it is called 'vijñāna' because it discerns."
"Accomplishment" (chéngbàn) [is pronounced with the second tone on 莧].

It means "to possess. The *Six Aspects of the Golden Lion* states: "The lion is the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). The differentiation of the five faculties is the specific characteristic (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*).

Sharing a single dependent origination is the common characteristic (*sabhāgalakṣaṇa*). That the eye and ear do not know one another is the distinct characteristic (*asabhāgalakṣaṇa*). The various faculties meeting together is the collective characteristic (*samudāyalakṣaṇa*)."
This is the characteristic of formation (*siddha-lakṣaṇa*). That all conditions each abide in their own positions is the characteristic of destruction (*bhaṅga-lakṣaṇa*).

This reveals that within the *dharmadhātu*, there is no solitary phenomenon; whichever single phenomenon is cited, it possesses these six characteristics. Through the integration of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), each lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Within each individual characteristic, inexhaustible characteristics are contained; within each individual phenomenon, inexhaustible phenomena are present. Furthermore, the verse says: "In total..."
If taken as a whole, the body is undivided; if distinguished, the various conditions are each separate. If they are the same, the various conditions are in harmony;
if they differ, their functions are distinct. If established, they mutually pervade and support one another; if disintegrating, each abides in its own position.
Within the body, one definitely perceives the *cittotpāda-samādhi* (the samādhi of the arising of the mind).

Regarding the word *lúluó*: the first character is pronounced with the *láng* and *hóu* initials; the second is pronounced with the *liáng* and *hé* initials. According to the *Fāngyán* (Dialectal Dictionary), it means "to illuminate" or "wisdom."
*Cuòdà* (措大): pronounced *cù dà* (with the first syllable having the *gù* radical). It means "to place" or "to arrange. It refers to those who manage the great affairs of the world.
"The Harmonious Ruler should act as a recompense for his Ruler"—this is seen in another edition.
*Dōngdōng* (鼕鼕): the drum. In the capital's streets, drums were placed atop small towers to signal the transition between dusk and dawn. This was the practice of our dynasty.
During the reign of Emperor Taizong, Zhang Gongji composed the names for the wards and displayed the plaques upon the towers.

According to the records, it was Sima Zhou who first proposed the establishment of the *dong-dong* drum; this institution existed only in the two capitals. Later, the *dong-dong* drum also appeared in the Northern Capital (Luoyang), which followed the precedent of the imperial capitals.
Recently, the sound of the street drums has ceased to be made, as the duties of the Jinyu Command have fallen into disuse.
[This is] so. See the *Chunming ji* (Collection from the Eastern Capital). "Dong" (鼕): pronounced with the initial *tu* and the final *dong*.
"Su" (宿): pronounced *xiù*; it refers to the fixed stars.

The *Liujie shidao zhi* (Record of the Six Streets and Ten Roads) states: "In Chang'an there are six streets, nine thoroughfares, and nine markets, thereby [receiving] the products of the Nine Provinces."
"Person. Therefore, the Dharma-eye (Fayan) took Jinling as the name for the capital city; its broad thoroughfares were the six main streets (*liùjiē*).
"Jù" (即) means to reside, with the phonetic component *chǔ*.
"Qí" (芰) is pronounced with the initial *qì* (cut by *jì*); it refers to water chestnuts (*líng*). "Hé" (荷) refers to the leaves of the lotus flower.
*Pùbù* (Water-cutting Cascade): Refers to suspended water and flying springs.
*Dāoshǔ* (Eagle-mouse) should be read as *diāoshǔ*; it rhymes with *liáo*. It is large and yellowish-black, originating from the country of Hudingling.
The nineteenth, the response body (nirmāṇakāya), refers to Baozhi, who was an emanation of Avalokiteśvara.

That he is the nineteenth specifically points to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the "Universal Gate" chapter, which describes the nineteen bodies beginning with "Those who should be delivered by means of a Buddha-body... and so forth.
"Gongchen" (拱宸) should be read as "Gongchen" (拱辰). The *Analects* states: "For example, the North Star dwells in its place, and the myriad stars revolve around it.
Yuan Fa'er (遠法師), who knit his brows in distress, established the White Lotus Society; he once sent a letter summoning Tao Yuanming (陶淵明), to which Tao replied: "Your younger brother..."
Zi was by nature fond of wine. If the Dharma Master would permit him to drink, he would go at once. Huiyuan granted his request, and Zi consequently went to visit him.
Huiyuan then urged him to join the monastic community, whereupon Tao Yuanming knit his brows and departed. This is recorded in the *Jilu fuzaji* (Miscellaneous Records of Mount Lu).
The "Treatise on Translators" states: The peoples of the five regions have unintelligible languages and differing desires.
To convey their intentions and facilitate their needs, there are those called *ji* in the east, *xiang* in the south, *diti* in the west, and *yi* in the north.
Zheng Xuan says: "These are all common names based on their respective functions; *diti* means 'to know'."

The Dharma Master of Wuxing said: "Those who now translate by communicating through Western (Indic) languages did so because during the Han era, affairs were mostly centered in the north, yet the official translators were also proficient in Western tongues;
thus, when Dharmakāla first arrived, he translated the *Sūtra of Forty-two Sections*.
Furthermore, regarding the term 'fan' (to turn/translate), the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Song* states: 'It is like turning a brocade or silk over to see its reverse side.'"

Both flowers exist, though they differ in their left and right positions; for this reason, both names have been preserved in the translations. Regarding *ṭi* (pronounced *ti*), the *Nanshan Chao* on the ritual of the drum states:
"In the usual method of assembling the congregation, at the very beginning of striking the mallet, one must gradually initiate [the sound]."
The sound gradually diminishes and then gradually increases until the sound ceases, at which point one full stroke is struck.
This is repeated three times; this is called "three strikes. During the Buddha’s lifetime, there were only these three strikes; thus, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states, "strike three times.

It was only later, due to invitations from others, that the "extended striking" (chángdǎ) came into being. The initial commencement of the extended striking was also the same as the three strikes; in the middle...

There is an interval of four *zhuī*. Only when the sound has ceased does one break [the rhythm]. In this way, one gradually withdraws the *zhuī*, making them increasingly sparse and smaller until they reach the subtlest end;
only then does one produce another *zhuī*. This is the same as the three previous instances of "breaking" (*gài*). (Note: The character *gài* is pronounced *jì*; it means "dense.")
"Xian" (眚) is pronounced *jing* (景) with the *qie* (切) [classifier].

It refers to an eye disease; it should properly be written as "jian" (見). "Xian" (現) is pronounced *lian* (練) with the *qie* (切) [classifier]. It means "to manifest. It refers to the manifestation of jade-like radiance.

In the scriptures of our Śākya clan, this character is frequently used for the term "xian-jian" (顯見—manifestation and perception). Although this was done for the sake of phonetic convenience, the meaning and intent...
This is entirely contrary [to the truth]. Students should recognize this. *Pierqi* (瞥起):
pronounced with the *pǐ* and *miè* finals; it means to catch sight of something as it passes before one's eyes.
The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states: "If one who maintains the precepts directs their mind toward the pleasures of heaven, such a person..."
It defiles the pure precepts, like water mixed with poison. Since celestial pleasures are impermanent and one must inevitably fall when one's lifespan ends, one will undergo great suffering;
therefore, one should seek nirvana.
"Yǎo" (窈) is pronounced *jiǎo* (皎); it means "deep.
Regarding the transformation of reflections (*bìngyǐng*), those who explain them based on the analogy of a forest often cite the *Zāpì jīng* (Sūtra of Various Similes), which says:
A husband and wife were about to take wine from inside a grape-wine jar when both husband and wife said they saw a human shadow. The two looked at each other... [text continues].
Jealousy (*īrṣyā*). This refers to two people hiding inside a jar and beating one another until death, never ceasing. At that time, there was a practitioner who broke the jar open;
when the wine was exhausted, neither of the two people was there. Understanding this as a reflection and feeling ashamed, the Buddha used it as a metaphor:

it illustrates how those within the three realms do not recognize the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the four elements (*catvāri mahābhūtāni*) as suffering and empty, yet their bodies harbor the three poisons (*triviṣa*), leading them through birth and death.
It is not severed. I have observed that Fazhan’s titling of the subject differs significantly from this explanation;

however, upon carefully reading the verses of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, they accord with the intended meaning of the title established by Qingliang. Thus, the *Vijñaptimātra-kārikā* states: "When one posits a small object before oneself..."
This refers to the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*). Because there is still something apprehended, one does not yet truly abide in consciousness-only. Furthermore, a verse says:

"In meditative concentration and wisdom, the Bodhisattva contemplates that the reflected image is nothing but mind. Once the conceptualization of objects has been eliminated, he scrutinizes that which is of the nature of self alone."
Abiding thus within the inner mind, one knows that the apprehended object does not exist; subsequently, the apprehending subject is also absent; finally, one touches upon non-apprehension.
The student should carefully contemplate the meaning of this verse; they shall thereby understand the principle of suchness (*tathatā*).

*Zhòuzǔ* (咒咀): The first character (*zhòu*) is pronounced with the *jiù* rhyme; it means "to curse. The second character (*zǔ*) is pronounced with the *zhuāng* rhyme; it refers to causing someone to act by obstructing them with words.
In the *Gānyīn Pǔmén Pǐn Zhòngsòng* (Verses of the Universal Gate Chapter of Avalokiteśvara) from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, Master Kumārajīva did not translate this term.
Various masters all claim that it exists in the Sanskrit original. Xùkē says: "This too has not yet fathomed the profound intent of Master Kumārajīva. (*Xùgāosì*) [End of entry].
The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Sengzhuan*) states that this verse was translated by Jñānagupta. At the time when Zhiyi appeared, this verse had not yet been circulated.

According to the *Gantong zhuan*, General Wei remarked: "Master Kumārajīva’s rank reached the stages of the bodhisattvas; he profoundly understood the principles of the Buddha and was skilled at the Qin language.

Yet, even when translating the *Lotus Sūtra*, he still omitted the verses on the Universal Gate. Furthermore, the *Fashi yishu* (Commentary on the Meaning of the Dharma Master) states: "In general..."
Regarding the casting of spells and poisons: one employs demonic arts (*bhūta-vidyā*) with the intent to harm another person. That person will only suffer the harm if they harbor wrong thoughts;

if they can maintain right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*), the spell returns to the practitioner themselves. In the *Piyū-jīng* (Sutra of Similes), there was a lay follower of pure faith who initially observed the five precepts.
Later, as he grew old, he forgot much of what he had learned. At that time, a thirsty Brahmin from the mountains approached him.

He begged for a drink. Because the household affairs of the farmer were busy, [the farmer] had no leisure to attend to him. He then departed in resentment. The Brahmin was able to raise corpses and command spirits;
he summoned a killer and commanded him, saying, "That man insulted me; go and kill him. A *arhat* in the mountains knew of this and went to the farmer’s house.
He said to him, "Tonight, light your lamps early and diligently practice the Three Refuges, reciting them aloud:"

"Guard your mouth; let not your body commit transgressions; cherish all sentient beings with compassion, and you shall attain peace and security. The man followed these instructions, becoming proficient in the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha and the recitation of the precepts.
When the ghost arrived at dawn, it sought out his vulnerabilities, yet it was utterly unable to cause him harm. Such is the law of ghosts and spirits.

When people ordered him to kill [the ghost], he was about to do so; however, because that [ghost] possessed the quality of being "unslayable," he instead intended to kill the messenger who had sent it.
Thereupon, the ghost became enraged and sought to harm the brahmin. The Arhat shielded him, causing the ghost not to see him.
The farmer realized the Way, and the brahmin was saved. The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) quotes this, stating: "This is precisely from the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*."
It returns to the text of the person himself.
*Zhao* (朝) is pronounced with the initial *zhī* and the final *qiè*. It means "morning.

*Zī* (緇) is pronounced with the initial *chí* and the final *qiè*. It refers to black silk; it denotes the vestments of the Śākya [Buddhist] community. The *Biographies of Monks* (*Sengzhuan*) states:
Senghui and Xuanchang were both paragons among those in black robes (monks).
"Qi" (to beg) takes the same phonetic component as "shàng" (upper); it is also used in this sense.
"Wāngwāng" (汪汪)—the second character is pronounced with the *wū* and *guāng* initials—describes a state of being deep and vast.
*Nào* (鬧) means to stir up or disturb; it is synonymous with *náo* (閙). It is pronounced with the initial *qǐ* (女教切) and the final *yè* (四夜切).
*Xiè* (卸) refers to unloading a carriage or unyoking a horse. It is pronounced with the initial *wù* (烏貫切) and the final *yè* (四夜切). *Wàn* (腕) means to grasp or clench.

The *Qiu jie wubai wen jing* (Sūtra of Five Hundred Questions on Seeking the Precepts) states: "If one who has left the household life is not permitted by secular law or by their parents, will they obtain the precepts?

The answer says: "They shall not obtain them. The *Wufen lü* (Five-Part Vinaya) states: "All those with physical disabilities or deformities, and those who bring disgrace upon the Buddha-dharma, shall not be ordained."
The *Sāhasrika-pratimokṣa-saṃvara-vinaya-sūtra* states: "The practice of those who have left the household life has its beginning and its end.
Regarding the three types of action—superior, middling, and inferior—the inferior consists of taking the ten precepts as the foundation and upholding them for as long as one lives.

Although one has abandoned domestic ties, one still engages in manual labor just like a layperson. The middling consists of abandoning such labors and fully receiving the eighty-four thousand causal conditions for advancing toward the Way."
The actions of body, speech, and mind have not yet become fully pure; the fetters of the mind still persist, and one has not yet attained liberation.
Those of superior faculties and sharp roots should abandon the bonds of the fetters and defilements; through the power of meditative concentration and wisdom, the mind can achieve liberation.
Purifying body, speech, and mind, one departs from the household of conditioned affairs and afflictions to dwell forever in a quiet, secluded, and refreshing chamber.
Rāhula is here translated as "obscuration" or "that which obscures the moon. In the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra, the Buddha addressed Rāhula:
“Rāhula, go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness. Rāhula replied, “I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness.

I recall that in the past, when the sons of the elders of Vaiśālī came to where I was, they prostrated themselves before me and asked, ‘O Rāhula, you are the son of the Buddha; having renounced the sovereignty of a universal monarch, you have gone forth...’”

"The household life is for the sake of the Way; what benefits are there for those who leave the household life? I then explained to him, in accordance with the Dharma, the merits and benefits of leaving the household life.
At that time, Vimalakīrti came and said to me, "Rāhula, you should not speak of the merits and benefits of leaving the household life.
Why is this? To have neither benefit nor merit—this is what constitutes leaving the household life."
That which pertains to the Dharma may be said to possess benefit and merit. However, for one who has gone forth, it is for the sake of the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
Within the unconditioned dharma, there is neither benefit nor merit. Even if one can act in this way, that is true renunciation.
Thereupon, Vimalakīrti said to the sons of the elders: "In accordance with the True Dharma, you should all go forth together."

"Why is this? Because a Buddha appears in the world but rarely. The sons of the elders said, "We have heard the Buddha say that one cannot leave the home life unless one's parents give their permission.
Vimalakīrti said, "Nevertheless, you should immediately resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; this itself is leaving the home life, and this itself is full ordination."
According to the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*: "Just as when I point with my finger, the Sea-Seal emits light; yet the moment you raise your mind, worldly afflictions (*kleśa*) arise first.
The *Tri-karma-saṃgraha-śāstra* states: "The Bodhisattva precepts take the three karmas of body, speech, and mind as their essence. [In contrast,] the Śrāvaka precepts..."
It takes as its essence the two wholesome karmas of body and speech.

It comprises the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*): first, the integration of giving (*dāna*), because it benefits sentient beings; second, the integration of kind speech (*priyavāditā*), because it guides others through skillful means;

third, the integration of beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*), because it acts for the benefit of others; and fourth, the integration of common purpose (*samānārthatā*), because one’s activities are shared with others.
The bhikṣu Aśvajit entered the city to beg for food; his majestic deportment was so worthy of contemplation that flying birds circled above him and galloping horses halted mid-stride.
*Jīngshè* (pronounced *zhìshè*): the appearance of losing one's breath from terror.
*Tǐnjiàn* (pronounced *túdian*): to exhaust; to bring to an end.
*Zhēnzuò* (phonetic transcription of *zhēn* and *zhuó*): *Zhēn* means to distribute evenly; *zhuó* means to pour wine and serve the cup.

The character *míng* (名) is pronounced with the upper radical *miǎo* (邈) and the phonetic *zhèng* (正). It refers to all things. The lower part should be read as *mào* (貌), pronounced with the phonetic *jué* (覺).
It means appearance. Since it denotes the appearance and form of things, it is called "name and appearance" (*míngmào*).

As for the Elder’s current desire to realize that all things are oneself, it is because within the great earth not a single dharma can be seen. He further instructed him, saying:
"Do not let your time be spent in vain. Previously, he told the Elder: "It is sufficient simply to act in accordance with the season and the moment. If one were to shift...
At such a time, to miss the opportune moment is to waste one’s life in vain; it is not to interpret form as form.
But tell me, is it appropriate or not to interpret form as non-form? If you, the Elder, understand it in this way, there is no connection at all.
This is precisely what is called "running headlong between delusion and madness"—what use is there in that? The Elder should simply maintain his station and pass the time according to the seasons.
Excellent.
*Zuting shiyuan*, Scroll Six;
*Zuting shiyuan*, Scroll Seven.
Compiled and Corrected by Mu’an (Shanqing).
*The Recorded Sayings of Lianhuafeng*.
Lianhuafeng is an alternative name for Mount Tiantai; it is the place where National Teacher Shao entered nirvana. The National Teacher was born... [text continues]

He was from Longquan in Chuzhou and belonged to the lay surname Chen. At the age of fifteen, a foreign monk saw him and marveled at his extraordinary qualities, subsequently encouraging him to leave the household life.
He received full ordination in Xinzhou. During the Tongguang era of the Later Tang dynasty, he traveled to various regions to visit Touzi Datong, Longya Judun, and Shushan Benren;
he visited these masters a total of fifty-four times, yet in every instance, he had not yet realized the ultimate meaning.
In the evening, he visited Wenyi of Chongshou Monastery in Fuzhou and sat in summer retreat with the assembly.

Suddenly, hearing a monk ask, "What is a single drop of water from Cao’s Spring? Wenyi replied, "It is a single drop of water from Cao’s Spring. At this, the Master attained sudden enlightenment regarding his place of return.
Later, while traveling to Tiantai, he visited the traces left by Zhiyi; they appeared as if he had lived there before, so he built a dwelling there. Everyone said:
The wise one was Houshi. Later, at Bore Monastery, he ascended the hall to preach the Dharma.
A monk asked, "What is it like when both oars and rudders have been set aside? He replied, "I congratulate you on your life. The monk asked, "What are the three types of sick people? He replied:
Just as he was about to ask, he asked: "What is the mind of the ancient Buddha? He replied: "This question is no weak one. He asked: "What is the Buddha of No-Sorrow? He replied:
"It makes people die of grief. He asked: "What is the eye of the śramaṇa? He replied: "Black as lacquer. He asked: [The Master] asked.
"How is it when all news and communication are cut off? He replied, "Thank you for pointing this out. "What is the phrase that is free from leakage? He replied, "Your mouth is like your nostrils.
Later, the King of Wuyue treated him with the etiquette due to a teacher and inquired about the essentials of the Dharma.

The Master was by nature fond of seclusion and did not frequent villages; he spent his entire life among forests and springs. Kings and ministers held him in high esteem. This is the *Chanyuan zhuquanji duxu* (General Preface to the Collection of the Source of Zen).
For this reason, I have titled this work *The Recorded Sayings of National Teacher Śāra at Lotus Peak*.
The Master passed away in the fourth year of Kaishi at the age of eighty-two.
As for the Dharma of the Western Regions, the National Teacher was esteemed by both high and low alike; he was honored by both the heterodox and the orthodox. Thus it is said:

Because the state took refuge [in the Dharma], this title was manifested. As the influence of his teachings gradually spread to the East, only the Northern Qi monk Fachang was honored by the sovereign as National Teacher (*guoshi*);
thus, the title of National Teacher originated with Master Chang.

During the Chen and Sui dynasties, Tiantai Zhiyi served as the Bodhisattva Precept Master for Emperor Xuan of Chen and Emperor Yang of Sui; therefore, he was titled National Teacher at that time. Under Empress Wu of the Tang...
During the Tang dynasty, Shenxiu was summoned to the capital; he served under four successive emperors—Zhongzong, Ruizong, Xuanzong, and Suzong—and was titled National Teacher by all of them.
Later, Huizhong entered the imperial palace during the reigns of the two emperors Suzong and Daizong to preach the Dharma, and was likewise titled National Teacher.
During the Yuanhe era, an imperial edict conferred the title of National Teacher Wudao upon Zhihuan. As for the case of a semi-autonomous state, it was the Later Ruler of Shu.
Guangye was bestowed the title of National Preceptor for Protecting the Holy (Yusheng Guoshi) as the Right Street Registrar of Monks. In Wuyue, Deshao was honored as National Preceptor;
this is seen in Zanning’s *Monastic History* (*Sengshi*). "Jian" is pronounced like "jian" [in the sense of] flowing in.
*Chuǎi* (upper radical *shàng*, initial *wěi*; lower radical *xià*, initial *tuó*): to test; to measure. *Cuǎn* (initial *guǎn*):
to collect; to assemble. *Xuán* (initial *chāng*): the pivot;
the fundamental principle. *Shū* (initial *zhū*): the hub; the core.

The character for "branch" (qí) should include the radical for "mountain" (山), as it refers to a branching path. The character for "branching feet" (qí-zú) refers to having many toes; this is not the correct meaning.
As for "tortoise" (guī) and "mirror" (jiàn): the tortoise is used to resolve hesitation, while the mirror is used to distinguish between the beautiful and the ugly.
The *Anāviladharmanirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā* states: "Aniruddha" means "Non-extinction. He was the son of King Śuklodana.
Because he slept excessively, the Tathāgata rebuked him; from then on, he practiced with such diligence that he did not sleep for seven days, whereby he lost his sight.
The Buddha instructed him to cultivate the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), focusing his mindfulness upon the pure matter (*rūpa*) derived from the four great elements within half of his head.
He emits [light], seeing through both internal and external obstructions; he beholds light and darkness alike, viewing the trichiliocosm as if looking at a fruit in the palm of his hand.
Thus it is said that those without eyes can see.
The Dragon Bāḍananda (translated here as "Worthy Joy") and the Dragon Nanda constantly protect the kingdom of Magadha and send down rain.
The marshes were replenished in due season, and the kingdom suffered no years of famine. King Piṇḍola held a great assembly annually to repay the kindness of the dragon;
all people rejoiced, and from this it derived its name. As for its being subdued by Maudgalyāyana, hearing without ears, and the detailed account of the origins—these are not yet fully known.
*Ba* (跋): pronounced with the *pu* and *mo* initials combined.

The goddess Gaṅgā—also called Ganga, which here means "Coming from Heaven"—is the river that flows from the Silver Elephant Mouth on the southern side of Lake Anavatapta and enters Eastern India. The presiding deity of this river is a female.
It is not with the nose that one smells fragrance; its causal conditions have not yet been seen. *Geng* (其陵切).
*Kauṇḍinya* (驕梵鉢提), correctly rendered as *Guḍapattri*, means "Ox-Aspect" (*Gośṛṅga*) in this language. Thus the Sūtra says: "I possess karmic activity of speech;
because in past lives I mocked śramaṇas, in life after life I have suffered from the disease of rumination (*cchardana*). *Cchi* (呞).
As for "the ox": after eating, it habitually performs the act of rumination; thus, people of the time called it a "cow-chi" (an ox that ruminates). Regarding "different tongues":
no specific reason is seen [for this term], though perhaps since it possesses the characteristics of an ox, it refers to an ox's tongue.
Yet, because it is able to discern the flavors of what humans eat, it is said that "a different tongue knows tastes. *Chi* (呞) is pronounced *shi*.
