Shuikong succeeded Shitou; he was a brother of Dadian. The Master Qinghua’s name was Quanfu.
Born in Kunshan on Zhuzhou, he followed his father as a merchant to Yuzhang during his youth.
Passing through Qingping, he wished to follow [the master] into the monastic life. After receiving full ordination, he traveled to Yangshan and paid homage to Nanta Guang.
Master Yong’s single word accorded with the principle. He subsequently traveled to Anfu in Luling, where the local magistrate ordered him to reside at Yingguo Chan Monastery.
His disciples became very numerous, and his reputation reached the imperial court, leading to the bestowal of the plaque "Qinghua" (Pure Transformation).

Later, Qian Wenmu Wang of the Southern Tang dynasty opened up Yunfeng Mountain and constructed a separate vihāra, inviting him to dwell there; consequently, it was named Qinghua after the original monastery.
A monk asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Master replied, "A wooden crane flies while a flower-tablet hangs from its neck.
Later, when Emperor Zhongxian bestowed upon him a purple robe, he firmly declined it; consequently, the Emperor granted him a Zen cassock and the title Chan Master Chunyi.
He passed away during the Kaiyun era of the Jin dynasty at the age of sixty-six.
The master Shao Shan’s name was Huanpu; he was posthumously titled Chan Master Wuwe (Fearless).
When [Wuzhuo] approached Zun, he seized him by the collar. Originally, those four characters did not exist there.

To explain in detail from where these words were made: "Wei" (尉) is pronounced "Yu" (鬱). "Weichi" (尉遲) was originally a multi-syllable clan name of the Ruru (虜) people.
"Xiaonei" (宵內) was originally "Xiaolu" (霄路).
"Que'er" (雀兒) was originally "Que'er" (鵲兒).
Lú Bān (魯般) is the same as Bānshū (般輸).
"Yùlòu" (玉漏) should be read as "yùlóu" (玉耬), referring to the *lóulí* (耬犂), or seed-drill plow. Farmers use the *lóu* to sow seeds.
What is referred to in the Chan records as "looking at the plow and striking the plow" refers precisely to this. The *Wei lüe* states: "Huangfu Yin served as the Governor of Changguang.
As the local people did not understand how to cultivate, he taught them to make the *lou-li* (plow), which saved more than half their labor."
However, the *lǒu* (seed drill) is an implement for sowing on dry land; many people in the south do not recognize it, and therefore it is explained here in detail. Its pronunciation is *lóu*.
Regarding the character *háng* (in *hángjiā*), the first radical is *shàng* and the phonetic component is *huàn* (simplified as *shān*).
In the original text, Luopu is written as Leipu. The Master’s name was Yuan’an. He was the son of the Tan family from Linyou in Fengxiang. He received tonsure and full ordination in his hometown.
Initially, he studied under Cuiwei and Linji, receiving their seals of approval each time. Later, he established a hermitage at Jia Shan in Liyang;
as their spiritual affinities matched, he became a preeminent disciple of Master Hui. He sat in meditation at Luopu.
Mount [Shan]. Not long after, he moved to Suxi in Langzhou, where his Way spread throughout the world. Wuya and Qingfeng were both his dharma heirs.
On the second day of the twelfth month in the second year of the Guanghua era of the Tang Emperor Zhaozong, he manifested parinirvāṇa.
From the *Hòngmén Jiàn Huáichán Shī Hòulù* (The Later Record of Master Huáichán’s Visit to Hòngmén):
Master Yúnjū’s name was Dàoyìng; his secular surname was Wáng. He was born in Wǎngtián, Yōuzhōu. Having left the household life, he studied the Vinaya.
Subsequently, he said, "How can a great man allow himself to be shackled by the constraints of the monastic code? Thereupon, he went to Cùwēi.
Finding that his questions were not met with resonance, he heard that Master Dongshan’s Dharma assembly was very flourishing and consequently went to visit him.
Dongshan asked, "What is your name? He replied, "Daoying. Dongshan said, "Speak further beyond this. He replied, "To speak further beyond this would no longer be named Daoying.
Dongshan said, "Your responses are no different from when you were with me at Yunyan. One day, Dongshan asked, "I have heard of Sita..."
"If one were born in the land of Japan and became its king, what of it? [Zhaoqing] replied, "If one is a Mahāsattva, even a Buddha would not be made;
how much less a king? Dongshan agreed with this. The Master first resided at Sanfeng and later established Yunju, whereupon his profound teachings spread widely.

The Zhong family of Nanchang held him in especially high esteem and veneration. This was on the twenty-eighth day of the twelfth month in the first year of the Tiānfú era of the Táng Emperor Shàozōng.

He manifested illness on a certain day. On the third day of the first month of the following year, he passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture. He was posthumously titled Great Master Hongjue (Hongjue Dashi).
The character *wēi* (倭) is pronounced with the *ū* and *huó* (禾) initial;
*tiánkù* (田厙) should be read as *tiánshè* (田舍). For details, see the "Verses on Ancient Cases" (*Sònggǔ*).
*Yán* (沿) and *tái* (臺): *yántānpán* (臺盤) should be treated as a compound term. It is pronounced with the *zhuān* (專) rhyme. It means to follow or conform.
Regarding the story of the *língyáng* (麢羊) sheep, there is a monk who says, "It has become so difficult to understand. This section is erroneously included [in the original text].
According to the *Chuándēng lù* (傳燈錄), in the biography of Yúnjū (雲居), a monk from Silla asked, "What is it that makes it so difficult to explain? Yúnjū replied: [as recorded in the text].
"What difficulty is there? [Zhaozhou] said. "Then please, Master, speak. Baizhang said, "Silla. Silla.

The master Tong’an’s name was Chángchá; he succeeded Jiǔfēng Qián. His original name was Chù, which is an error.
"Fùjí" (負笈) is pronounced jí; it means to carry a book-box.
"Gōngwén gōng" (公文公) should be read as gōng, meaning to cultivate or govern.
Do not practice indolently. "Infant" (ying):
for a female, she is called an *ying*; for a male, he is called an *er*.
"Ni" (ni): pronounced with the *ku* and *hua* finals, it means to cross over. "Yue" (yue) means to transcend.
"Jingyang" (Essential Yang) means "substantiality. The essence of the Great Yang possesses the blazing essence and the virtue of Yang; therefore, it is called "Jingyang.
The character for "tu" (merely/to stride) should follow the radical for speech and be written as "kuā" (boast); it means to boast or to marvel.
Regarding the Hu people’s practice of drinking milk, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "For example, there was a king who was dull-witted and lacked wisdom.
He had a physician who was by nature stubborn and ignorant, yet the king did not discern this and granted him a generous salary. This physician treated various ailments using only milk as medicine.
Later, another physician arrived who was proficient in the eight branches of medical science and skilled at curing all diseases; he then explained the various [medicinal] methods to the king."
He prescribed various medical formulas. Upon hearing these words, the king finally realized that his former physician was foolish and lacked wisdom.

The king issued a decree throughout the kingdom stating that no one with an illness was permitted to use milk as medicine; instead, they were to be treated using a combination of various other medicines.
Not long thereafter, the king fell ill again and immediately summoned this physician. The physician diagnosed the king’s illness and determined that it required—
Regarding the medicine of milk, the king said to the physician, "Are you now mad? You speak of consuming milk! Previously you called it poison;
why do you now say it should be consumed? The physician replied to the king, "Your Majesty, you should not speak in such a manner. It is like insects eating wood."
There are insects that possess written characters. These insects do not know whether these are characters or not.
When a wise person sees them, he never proclaims, "This insect understands characters," nor does he treat it with alarm or contempt. You should know that the old physicians were likewise;
they did not distinguish between various diseases and administered milk-medicine to all. This milk-medicine is called both "poisonous harm" and "ambrosia. O King!
Upon hearing these words, he immediately took them, and his illness was cured. He then issued a proclamation throughout the entire kingdom:

"From this day forward, you must once again take milk as medicine. When the people of the country heard this, they all felt resentment and anger, saying, "The Great King has now been possessed by a ghost; has he gone mad?"

When Yangyou saw Xuedou’s verse on an ancient case, he noted that "tiánguā" (田蝸) should be read as "tiánshé" (田[書-(土/曰)+(一/((巨-匚)@一)/昍])—the second character being pronounced with the *qie* rhyme "wūguā" (烏瓜). It refers to a shrimp or a toad; "guā" (蝸) is pronounced like "guā" (瓜) and means a small snail. This [original reading] is incorrect.
"Yín-bū" (夤晡): The upper character should be "yín" (寅). The lower character is pronounced with the *qie* "bēn-gū". It refers to the early and late parts of the day.
"Pū-shǒu" (撲手) should be "rǎng-bì" (攘臂).
Táo Yuánběn (陶淵本) is originally Táo Qián (陶潛).
*Chèng* (尺證切) means "to measure.
It appears in the *Taìmìào* (太廟) section of the *Lúnyǔ* (論語): "When the Master entered the Grand Ancestral Temple, he asked about every matter.

Some said, 'The son of a man from Zōu knows the rites, yet he asks about everything when entering the Grand Ancestral Temple. When the Master heard this, he said, 'This is precisely what the rites require.'"
"His axe should rot away like his woodcutter's handle. The *Yiyuan* states: "The woodcutter Wang Qi entered the mountains and saw two elders playing chess within a cave.
He watched them and forgot to return. Suddenly, the handle of his axe had rotted away."
In "Wangyang" (Forgetting the Sheep), one sees the names Zu Ying and Chisongzi.
"He" (赫) should be written with the radical "mouth" (口); it is pronounced as *he* (呼格切). This is because [the character] is not composed of the "person" (人) radical.
"Yang" (漾) should be written with the radical "wood" (木) as "yàng" (樣), meaning "method" or "standard. To use "yàng" (漾) in the sense of "the appearance of water" is not the correct meaning.
*Pēng* (with the initial *míng* and final *qiè*).
The master of Dongshan was named Liangjie. He was born in Kuaiji Commandery and surnamed Yu.

In his youth, he left home as a monk under Chan Master Mo of Wuxie and received the precepts at Mount Song. He traveled extensively to study under various eminent masters and received the Dharma from Yunyan Cheng.
He was the direct descendant of Yaoshan. At the end of the Dazhong era of Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty, he propagated the Way in Xin’feng;
later, he moved to Dongshan. He established the five positions of partiality and correctness (*bianzheng wawei*), being the first to do so at that time.
Having practiced the Way in these two locations for barely ten years, during the Xian Tong era of Emperor Yizong, he manifested his passing without illness. His disciples called him...
Muzhe followed him. The Master turned back, looked at him, and admonished him, saying: "For one who has left the household life, the mind must not be attached to things;

only then can one enter the Way. Why do you now feel such grief? Summon the administrators to prepare a 'foolish' feast (yuchi zhai) for me. Stay for another seven days, and then I shall depart forever."
He was posthumously titled Great Master Wuben.
One monk was the "Paper-Clothed Wayfarer" (Zhīyī Dàozhě); his story is found in the *Guǎngdēng*.
After the Master had remained silent for a long while, he said by mistake, "It should be 'The Master says: What about the men and women of a family of great icchantikas?'"
It can be saved; see the *Yaoshan Zongpai Lu*.
"Suyu" (粟畬)—the character "shê" is pronounced as "shìchē" (式車)—refers to large-scale slash-and-burn fields.
"Wújiàn" (無間) should be understood as meaning "without interruption."
The master of the Fu-ship Monastery was named Hongjian; his posthumous title was Grand Master Shaolong.
This is recorded in the *Prior Record* of Chan Master Jinjian of Yan.
The character for "drone" (蝃蚋): the upper radical is pronounced as *zhuó*, meaning a spider; the lower radical is pronounced as *ruò*, meaning a mosquito.
The character "sān" (蠶) is incorrectly written as "zào" (燥). Its pronunciation is "sǎo. It means "dry. The vulgar form "zào" is an error resulting from the similarity of their shapes. [蠶].
This character does not exist in the dictionary.
"Niáo" (鐃) should be read as "náo" (撓), pronounced with the *niǎo* (尼交) rhyme, meaning to stir or agitate.

Master Deshan’s taboo name was Xuānjiàn; he was a native of Jiànnán who left home to become a monk in his youth and attained a profound understanding of the Sūtras and Vinaya, being most skilled in them.
Regarding Jingang (Vajra): his secular surname was Zhou, and he was thus known as Zhou Jingang.
Hearing that the Chan school was flourishing in the south, yet unable to fathom its origins, he disbanded his assembly and traveled south carrying the scriptures.

He visited Longtan Xuanjian, where he attained the Way upon seeing the master extinguish a candle. The following day, he took up the scriptural commentaries and showed them to the assembly, saying: "Exhausting all profound dialectics, if..."
To place a single hair in the vast void and exhaust all the world’s pivotal mechanisms is like casting a single drop into a great abyss. He then burned [his books].
He roamed freely through the Zen groves, and his Way spread throughout the realm. He lived in seclusion at Linyang for nearly thirty years.
During the hardships of the Huichang era, he took refuge in a stone chamber on Mount Dufu. At the beginning of the Dazhong era, he was [summoned] by Deshan.
The second generation was Ming. In the sixth year of the Xiántóng era, he manifested illness and said to his disciples: "To grasp at emptiness and pursue echoes is to weary your mind and spirit.
When one awakens from a dream, it is seen to be unreal; in the end, what event has truly occurred? Having finished speaking, he sat upright and passed away.
This was the third day of the twelfth lunar month. He lived to the age of sixty-eight and was posthumously titled Great Master Jiàn xìng (Realizing Nature).

The Master was born toward the end of Emperor Dēngzōng’s Zhēnyuán era and passed away during the reign of Emperor Yìzōng. By the time of the Huìchāng persecution, his Way had not yet been fully realized;
however, when the Buddha-dharma was restored during the Dàzhōng era, the Master was already sixty-seven years old. These are the details regarding those who transmitted his teachings.
"Life is like a thread suspended from a string—is this not so?
Master Jingqing, whose name was Daofu, was the son of the Chen family of Yongjia. From birth he abstained from meat; he shaved his head and received full ordination.
He went to seek the Way in Minchuan. Upon first seeing him, Xuefeng asked, "Where are you from?
He replied, "I do not dare say I am a man from Wenzhou. Xuefeng said, "In that case, are you a native of Yisuo Jue?
He asked, "As for one who is Yisuo Jue himself, where is he from? Xuefeng said, "A bed-wetting ghost! He deserves a good beating! And so it was.
He was pardoned. After the Master realized the Way, he was held in high esteem by all, who all referred to him as "Little Tufu the Patch-robed Monk.
He soon received an invitation from the ruler of Yue and resided at the Jingqing Chan Monastery. The Vice-Governor Pi Guangye once sought instruction from him;
Guangye was the son of Pi Ri. The King of Wuyue, the Qian family, paid him great honor and bestowed upon him the title:
The Grand Master Shunde was invited by the two temples, Kaitian and Longce. He passed away in the second year of the Tianfu era of the Jin dynasty.
His body was cremated at Mount Daci, where bone śarīras were obtained; a stupa was subsequently erected on the southern slope of Mount Longmu.
Jingqing was the one whose monastery title was bestowed by the imperial court as "Jingde.
*Chengti* (pronounced *chí*) refers to carpets and mats.
Xuan Sha saw the bottom of the abyss when he beheld the waterfall at Xuedou.
"Sier" (上音斯): This refers to one who follows a messenger. According to the *Fāngyán* (Dialectal Dictionary), it is pronounced with a final checked tone (*rùshēng*).
"Jiè" (楒) is the name for a tree; "Shī" (師) is the abbreviation for "Huì" (慧).
Luzu, Luzu, taught the Master; he transmitted the lamp and succeeded Guankui Xian.
[The character] *èi* (餧) is pronounced with the initial *qiè* (切);
"to overcome" (*kè*) should be read as *kè* (剋). What kind of name does he bear? To "overcome" (*kè*) means to kill; it is not righteous.
*Pián* (pronounced *pián* with the *biàn* and *tián* finals).
Once, when Master Láng was playing the qín, Duke Píng of Jìn said to him, "That which I, the humble ruler, love is music.
I wish to hear it. Master Kùang, having no choice, took up the qín and struck it. Upon the first performance, two dark cranes appeared.
They entered and gathered at the outer gate. The music was played a second time; they extended their necks and cried out, spreading their wings and dancing. Lord Ping was greatly delighted;
he rose and offered a toast to the longevity of Master Kuang. (Recorded in the *Shiji*).
When Emperor Gaozu of Han was enfeoffing his meritorious ministers, some remarked that Zhang Liang had never performed any feats in combat.
The Emperor said, "To devise strategies within the curtains and screens, thereby securing victory thousands of li away—this is the merit of Zi-fang."
In some editions, "Zhou Xia" is written as "Zhou Ke. When the state of Chu besieged the Han King at Hengyang, the situation became urgent.
The Han King escaped and left Zhou Ke in charge of defending Hengyang. When the Chu forces broke through the city of Hengyang, they sought to have Zhou Ke take command.
Zhou Ke rebuked them, saying, "If you wish to surrender to the Han King, do so quickly; otherwise, you shall now become captives! Xiang Yu was enraged and had Zhou Ke boiled alive. This was Zhou Ke.
The character "xià" (下) is pronounced with the *qie* (切) "kě" (可). The district of Zhèn (鎮) is not far away. On the twenty-fourth board, line six, the character "bù" (不) is missing at the bottom.
The character "sǎng" (磉) is pronounced with the *qie* "lǎng" (朗); it refers to the stone base beneath a pillar.
*Mingding* (酩酊) means "drunk to excess.
As for Chan Master Fēngxiáng Shānqiáng, his secular name was Huìqiú.
He was born in Pútán, Quanzhou, and received his monastic precepts at Guīyáng. He studied under... [he went to study with...]
One day, Xuansha Shibei asked, "What is the first moon? Xuansha replied, "What use is there for a moon?

The Master (Zhimen) then attained his realization. In the second year of the Kaiping era of the Later Liang, Xuansha passed away and left instructions with Wang Shi of Min, requesting that he reside at Wolong as the second patriarch;
he was also called Zhongta. Five years later, he died without illness.
He passed away and was posthumously titled Chan Master Jizhao. A master from Min once asked Xuansha, "Who will succeed to your Way?
Xuansha replied, "Qiuzi has attained it."
Master Yantou, whose name was Quanhuo, was the son of the He family of Quanzhou. After shaving his head and receiving full ordination, he studied the sutras and the vinaya for a long time.
Later, he traveled among various monastic assemblies; together with Xuefeng and Qinshan from Yuhang, he discussed the matter of visiting Linji. It happened that Linji had passed away by then.
Because Yangshan had studied under Deshan, their temperaments and dispositions were so well-matched that they were like two halves of a tally fitting together.

In his later years, he built a thatched hut on Mount Wolong by Lake Dongting, where students gathered around him. During the Huichang persecution of Buddhism, he donned a formal robe and a scholar’s bamboo hat and traveled among various villages.
He eventually moored his boat at a secluded inlet of Lake Dongting and established a dwelling on both banks.

There was a wooden board. Whenever anyone wished to cross, they would strike the board to summon the Master. The Master would then dance with his oar and ferry them across. Not long after, he was led back to his former residence.
In the third year of the Guangqi era of Emperor Xizong, bandits invaded the Central Plains and the four seas were thrown into turmoil. The Master remained seated calmly as if nothing had happened.
Suddenly, he was struck by a blade; he let out one great cry and passed away. Emperor Xizong posthumously conferred upon him the title Qingyan (Pure and Austere).
"Da Shi" (Great Master): *zhi* (pronounced with the second tone), *ze* (cut by *li*), *ca* (cut by *zi* and *mo*).
The master Xiangyan’s name was Zhixian. He was born in Qingzhou and studied the Way under Guishan Lingyou, yet his spiritual resonance did not yet accord with the Master's.
He went to rely upon National Teacher Nanyang. One day, while he was weeding in the garden, he suddenly struck a bamboo stalk, which made a sound;
he then suddenly realized his former errors. He prostrated toward Mount Mushi from afar and said, "Had the Master explained this for me, how could there be a 'today'?"
He then composed a verse, which, in brief, says: "With a single blow, all that is known is forgotten; there is no further need for cultivation.

From that time on, he excelled at composing *gāthās*, which are still recited by the world today. After his parinirvāṇa, he was posthumously honored with the title Dashi Deng Dashi (Master Successive Lamp).
There is an old master for whom this anecdote should be compiled into the *Linji Lu*. Furthermore, one should not say "there was an old master";
rather, "night-seal" (*yemíngfú*) should be rendered as "night-illumination seal" (*yèmíngfú*).
Qiào (峭): The upper radical is *qiāo* (七肖切), the lower is *zhí* (直里切). It means steep and precipitous.
Dǐng (頂): The phonetic is *nú* (奴頂切). It means the summit or peak.
*Nian* (釅) is pronounced with the *qian* (欠) rhyme; it means "rich" or "intense" flavor.
Regarding the "Silver City" (*Yincheng*) attributed to Huo Guang, a Han dynasty official: the historical records and commentaries contain no account of him selling a city to trade for horns.
This story likely originated from the casual chatter of commoners in back alleys. That Zen practitioners often use it as a source for their discourse—is this not a great error?

The character for *jū* (居) when used as *mǔ* (牡) should follow the radical *zhuāng* (爿). It is pronounced *zhuàng* (側亮切), meaning "great. *Mǔ* (牡) is pronounced *mò hòu* (莫后切); it does not carry this meaning. *Zhuāng* (爿) has the phonetic value of *chuáng* (牀).

Master Zhuxi Qian of Zhuxi later resided at Doushuai and passed away there.
"Chān" (攙) is pronounced with the initial *chán* (銜切); it means to assist or support from the side.
"Mángrán" (忙然) should be read as "mángrán" (茫然), meaning bewildered or stunned.
Zen Master Hōken (Hira-tendai) of Hōken-ji was born in Hongzhou.

He received the Dharma from Baizhang Hai and traveled south to visit famous sites, eventually settling in a thatched hut on Mount Tiantai. The fourfold assembly relied upon him with devotion, leading him to establish a monastery named Hōken Zen-in.
The imperial court later bestowed the name Shōkō-ji upon it; he was the founding patriarch of this mountain. Once, he...
He addressed the assembly, saying: "Divine radiance is never obscured; it is a magnificent legacy for all ages. Having entered this gate, do not harbor conceptual understanding. He further said:
"The Great Way is vast and empty, the eternal, singular true mind. Do not contemplate good or evil; let the spirit be pure beyond all things.
Following conditions to eat and drink—what more is there to do? Later, he passed away at this very monastery, and a memorial pagoda remains there to this day.
The Venerable Baoshou Zhao studied under Linji and attained his realization. He did not travel elsewhere but remained at Baoshou, serving as its first patriarch.
As the Master was about to pass away, he asked his disciples, "Do you know where I have trodden?
They replied, "For your entire life, Master, you have sat upright and never lain down. The Master said, "You are not my kin. Having spoken, he passed away.
The world says that Baoshou did not cross the river; this refers precisely to this master. Master Xitang’s name was Zhizang.
He was the son of the Liao family of Qianhua. From his youth, he followed a teacher, and later followed Daji to inquire about the Way, becoming one of Mazu’s eminent disciples.
Daji entrusted him with a *nàkaśā* (monastic robe) and instructed students to draw near to him. This was during the Tang dynasty...

During the Zhenyuan era of Emperor Dezong, he opened his hall at Qianzhou. On the eighth day of the fourth month in the ninth year of the Yuanhe era of Emperor Xianzong, he manifested his passing at the age of eighty.
Master Yangshan’s name was Huaiji. He was the son of the Ye family from Zhenchang County in Shaoshan. From his birth, he displayed many extraordinary signs.
While still a young child, he followed Anhetong at Panyu Anhe Temple to leave the household life. At the age of fourteen, his parents sought to thwart his resolve;
he consequently severed two of his fingers as a vow and thereby underwent tonsure. Anhetong repeatedly bestowed [precepts] upon him...
He was received as a disciple, yet the Master offered him no further instruction. At the age of eighteen, his father passed away, so he went to visit Luyuan.
Subsequently, he visited Chuwai of Junzhou, Xingkong of Jizhou, and Tanyuan of Yashan, but found no resonance with any of them.
In the third year of the Dahan era, he went to attend upon Daoyou of Daguishan. When You raised the anecdote of Xingkong regarding "a man in a well," Daowei called out to him, saying, "Ji! (Silence!)

"Disciple," the Master said. "You should respond. Dongsan said, "You have already emerged. Thereupon, the Master attained realization. Dongsan instructed him to go to Dabe Monastery in Xiangyang to receive the full precepts.
The Master said, "Huiji has never uttered a falsehood in my life.
Dongsan said, "You simply follow the dharma of a śramaṇa. The Master complied; he was thirty-three years old at the time. He then returned to Mt. Gui to serve as the *zhidu* (rectifier).
In his later years, he led the assembly to Mount Wangmang in Chenzhou. Subsequently, he moved his staff to Yuanzhou to reside on Mount Yang, where the community grew to over several hundred members.
One day, a foreign monk carrying palm leaves arrived at the Master’s dwelling. The Master asked, "Where have you recently departed from?
He replied, "I left Western Heaven early this morning. The Master said, "That was too late. He replied, "I was traveling through the mountains and enjoying the scenery. The Master said, "..."
"Your supernormal powers are not non-existent, but you have not yet dreamed of the Buddha-dharma. He said, "I came here to pay homage to Mañjuśrī, yet I encountered a minor Śākyamuni.
Having finished speaking, he vanished. The Master resided at Mount Yang, where his divine wonders are detailed in his separate biography.
In the thirteenth year of the Dazhong era, the Vice Minister Wei Zhou established Guanyin Monastery in Hongzhou for the Master to dwell in. During the Xiantong era, he returned [to his home].
In the eastern plains of Shaozhou, on the thirteenth day of the second month in the third year of the Zhonghe era, he gathered the assembly and spoke a verse.
He then sat upright with his two hands clasping his knees and passed away in solemn stillness. His remains were returned for burial at Mount Yang.
Throughout his life, the Master received three imperial honors: Emperor Yizong bestowed upon him the title Zhi-zong; Emperor Xizong bestowed Chengxu; and Emperor Zhaozong... [bestowed]... [upon him].
His posthumous title was Zhìtōng (諡智通). Zhēn (湞) is pronounced zhēn (貞). Pányú (番禺) is pronounced fānyú (藩禺). Chēn (郴) is pronounced with the *chǒu* and *lín* initials.
The master Lóngjì’s name was Shàoxiū; he succeeded Dìzàng, who was none other than Luóhàn Chén.
Master Xuefeng’s name was Yicun. He was the son of the Zeng family of Annan in Quanzhou. From birth he abstained from meat and strong flavors.

As a youth, whenever he heard the tolling of bells or the chanting of sutras, or saw flowers and banners, his countenance would invariably move with reverence. At the age of seventeen, he received the tonsure under Vinaya Master Xuan of Yujian Temple in Putian and received full ordination in Youzhou.
He traveled extensively among the monastic communities for a long time, attaining realization under Deshan. He eventually arrived at Ao...
Shandun (Shan-dun) was certified [in his realization] at once. During the Xiantong era of the Tang dynasty, he thatched a hut on Mount Xuefeng in Fuzhou.
Later, it developed into a great monastery, for which he served as the first patriarch. Emperor Yizong bestowed upon him a purple *saṃghāṭī* robe and the title of Great Master Zhenjue.
His disciples were very numerous. He practiced the Way for over forty years until the second day of the fifth month in the second year of the Kaiping era of the Liang dynasty.
He passed away without illness at the age of eighty-seven.
Master Mingzhao, whose name was Deqian, had already attained the essential meaning under Luoshan and traveled abroad. When Zhiyi of Wunü summoned him, he was appointed to the first seat.
Whenever the master performed the ritual of sprinkling water for purification (*diǎnjìng*), the master would invariably refuse to accept it. The administrative monk said, "The Head Seat..."
He did not recognize that it was the pure vessel. The Master descended from his seat, picked up the vessel, and asked, "Is this pure or defiled?
The attendant had no reply, whereupon the Master smashed it to pieces. He lived on Mount Mingzhao for over forty years. One day, he asked his attendant:
"When the World-Honored One manifested his parinirvāṇa, he extended his two feet and emitted a hundred jewel-lights. Now I am about to go; furthermore—"
"How much light does the Way emit? The attendant replied, "In the past it was Heilin; today it is the Master.
The Master brushed his eyebrows with his hand and said, "Do not let us be remiss. He then spoke a verse and passed away suddenly.
The Master of Shuangfeng was named Jingqin. His birthplace was Yizhou; he received his training at Mount Emei and visited the Dharma seat of Yunmen, where he secretly received his seal of approval.
He subsequently resided at Shuangfeng as its first patriarch.
On the fifth month of the second year of the Taiping Xingguo era, he pointed to the sun and passed away.
The Song of Realizing the Way by Master Yongjia.
His name was Xuangjue; his secular surname was Dai. He left home to become a monk in his childhood and received full ordination upon reaching the age of twenty.

He was extensively learned in the Three Vehicles and practiced the *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight) of the Tiantai school. With an inner mind that was luminous and tranquil, he sought realization at Caoxi.
The Sixth Patriarch was seated in his chamber when the Master shook his staff, circumambulated the seat three times, and planted it upright before him.

The Patriarch said, "A śramaṇa possesses three thousand dignified manners and eighty thousand subtle practices. From what direction have you come, Venerable One, that you display such great arrogance?
The Master replied, "The matter of birth and death is great; impermanence is swift. The Patriarch asked, "How [is this so]?"

[The Master said: "To not grasp at non-arising—how swift is such realization! [Dongshan] said: "The very essence is non-arising; realizing that which is fundamentally non-existent—how could there be swiftness? The Patriarch said: "So it is, so it is.
Only then did he assume the proper dignified demeanor, and after completing his prostrations of salutation, he took his leave to return to Yongjia.

The Patriarch said: "Is your return too swift? [Dongshan] said: "Since it is fundamentally non-moving from the start, how could there be swiftness? The Patriarch said: "Who knows it is non-moving? [Dongshan] said: "..."
The Master said, "Virtuous one, you have conceived a conceptual distinction yourself. The Patriarch replied, "You have very well grasped the meaning of non-arising.

He asked, "If there is non-arising, how can there be 'meaning'? The Patriarch said, "If there is no meaning, who would be making distinctions? He replied, "Even this distinguishing is not itself a meaning. The Patriarch said, "..."
"Excellent! Excellent! Stay for one night. This is why he is known in the world as "The One-Night Awakened One" (Yi-su-gak).

Having returned home, he loudly proclaimed his Way, and the *Song of Realizing the Way* (*Jungdo-ga*) he composed spread throughout the land. Two months later, on the seventeenth day of the tenth month of the second year of the Xuantian era, the Sixth Patriarch passed away.
Emperor Ruizong posthumously conferred upon him the title of Great Master Wuxiang, and his stupa was named Jing.
Guang. During the Chūn-hua era of our dynasty, an imperial decree was issued to repair the grotto and stupa.

The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are: form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). That which is subject to change and obstruction is called form; that which experiences is called feeling; that which grasps images is called perception; that which constructs is called mental formations;
and that which cognizes is called consciousness. They are also termed the five *skandhas*. The term *skandha* carries the meaning of accumulation.
"Skandha" (*skandha*) is used here to signify "covering" or "obscuring.

The "three poisons" refer to greed, hatred, and delusion. The *Catuḥsmṛty-upadeśa-sūtra* states: "The three poisons bring about the three miserable realms: hatred and anger result in the realm of fire;
stinginess and greed result in the realm of knives; and folly and delusion result in the realm of blood."
*Avīci* means "uninterrupted. Those born into this realm experience the retribution of suffering without any interval.

The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* states that there are four kinds of dhyāna: the dhyāna practiced by fools, the dhyāna of examining meanings, the dhyāna of focusing on reality as it is, and the Tathāgata-dhyāna.
What is the Tathāgata-dhyāna? It refers to entering the stage of the Tathāgatas and practicing...
The characteristic of the noble wisdom of self-realization consists of three modes of dwelling in bliss and accomplishing inconceivable deeds for the benefit of sentient beings;
this is called Tathāgata-dhyāna.
The six perfections are: first, generosity; second, ethical discipline; third, patience; fourth, diligence; fifth, meditative concentration; and sixth, wisdom.
Wisdom (*prajñā*). To "cross over" means to reach the other shore.
The *Wanxing qingliang* states: "The myriad phenomena do not depart from one's own mind. In a single thought-moment, the practice of the myriad phenomena is complete.

That the mind does not arise is *śamatha* (calm abiding). Knowing that it does not arise is *vipaśyanā* (insight). Not being conditioned by the myriad objects is *tyāga* (renunciation). Stopping so that delusion does not arise is *śīla* (precept)."

To settle the mind in the principle of truth is patience (*kṣānti*). For the mind to be without interruption is diligence (*vīrya*). For the essence of the mind to be free from thought is the Dharma (*dharma*).
The original enlightenment of the mind is the Buddha (*buddha*). That the essence and its attributes are devoid of a person is the Sangha (*saṃgha*).
The six destinies: 1. The destiny of hell (*naraka*). In Sanskrit, it is called *niraya*, which translates as "instrument of suffering.

It is termed "hell" because this destination lies beneath the earth; thus, it is called "earth-hell. There are eight cold hells and eight hot hells, along with their subsidiary realms, numbering in the infinite.
For those of heavy karma, there are eighty-four thousand births and deaths within a single day. 2. The destiny of animals (*tiryagyoni*).
They are also called *tiryañc* (animals). Clad in fur and bearing horns, or possessing scales, shells, or feathers;
having four legs, many legs, or neither legs nor feet—they devour one another, suffering endlessly. Three: the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*).
Those with merit become deities of forests, mountains, or burial mounds; those without merit dwell in impure places, unable to obtain food or drink, and constantly suffer the lash.
4. The realm of the asuras. This term translates as "those without wine," or "those without comeliness," or "those without gods.
They dwell either on the seashore or at the bottom of the ocean; their palaces are magnificently adorned, yet they constantly delight in combat and experience boundless fear.
5. The realm of humans. The four continents differ from one another, and all are characterized by an alternation of suffering and pleasure. 6. The realm of devas. There are twenty [subdivisions].

The eight heavens are not uniform: six in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), eighteen in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and four in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). These constitute the six destinies (*ṣadgati*).
"Awakening" refers to the subsequent sound-teachings; it means to be enlightened.
The "trichiliocosm" refers to the great trichiliocosm world system. One set of four continents constitutes a small world system.

A thousand sets of four continents, a thousand sets of six classes of desire-realm heavens, and a thousand Brahma-heavens are called a small chiliocosm. A thousand small chiliocosms [constitute a medium chiliocosm]. A thousand medium chiliocosms [constitute a great trichiliocosm].

One thousand heavens of the Second Dhyāna constitute a medium chiliocosm (*madhyama-sāhasra-lokadhātu*). One thousand medium chiliocosms, together with one thousand heavens of the Third Dhyāna, constitute a great trichiliocosm (*mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu*).
As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 456: "It is like a skilled artisan, or..."
For the sake of some purpose, a disciple may construct various mechanical devices—whether female or male, or elephants, horses, and so forth.
Although these mechanical devices perform actions, they have no conceptual discrimination regarding those tasks. Why is this?
Because it is the inherent nature of mechanical devices to be without discrimination. The profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also like this.

Because there is something to be accomplished, one establishes it. Once established, although one is able to fulfill what is to be done and what is to be said, within that there is no conceptual discrimination at all, because by the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), there is no discrimination.
The *maṇi* jewel is here translated as "Stainless Light" (*vimalaprabha*), also as "Free from Defilement" (*vimala*), and also as "Increasing" (*vardhana*). The treatise states:
"The *maṇi* jewel is mostly found within the brains of nāgas; sentient beings with merit naturally obtain it.

It is also called the "Wish-fulfilling Jewel" (*cintāmaṇi*), which constantly produces all manner of precious objects—clothing, food, and drink—all of which are obtained according to one's wishes. One who obtains this jewel...
Poisons cannot harm it; fire cannot burn it. It is said that when Śakra wielded his vajra in battle against the asuras, fragments fell to Jambudvīpa and transformed into this bead.

Furthermore, it is said that in the distant past, after the relics of a Buddha had been lost and the Dharma had completely vanished, these were transformed into this bead for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
The Tathāgatagarbha is the accomplishment of the Tathāgata, surpassing the sands of the Ganges, endowed with the inconceivable dharmas of liberative knowledge;
it is designated as the Dharmakāya. World-Honored One, this very Dharmakāya, when not yet free from afflictions, is called the Tathāgatagarbha.
This Tathāgatagarbha is the wisdom of the emptiness of the Tathāgata, which has never before been realized by any Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
It has never been seen, nor has it ever been attained; only the Buddha fully knows it and is able to realize it.
Furthermore, this wisdom of the emptiness of the *tathāgatagarbha* is of two kinds: the empty *tathāgatagarbha*, which is free from all afflictions that are not liberated by wisdom;
and the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*, which possesses the inconceivable wisdom of the liberation of Buddhas, exceeding the sands of the Ganges in number.

On the Discussion of the Dharmas: The *Wuyan zhilun* (Treatise on the Wisdom of the Five Eyes) states: The fleshly eye sees what is near but not what is distant; it sees what is before but not what is behind;
it sees what is external but not what is internal; it sees by day but not by night. Because one obtains these [limitations], one seeks the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). The divine eye sees all.

Things that arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions are merely conventional designations; one does not perceive their true nature (*dharmatā*). That is to say, they are empty (*śūnya*), signless (*animitta*), wishless (*apraṇihita*), and without arising or ceasing.
As it is before, so it is in the middle and at the end. For the sake of the true nature, one seeks the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*) and attains the eye of wisdom.

With this, one perceives sentient beings as having utterly extinguished all marks of identity and difference (*ekatva-anyatva*). One abandons all attachments and does not grasp at any phenomena (*dharma*). This is wisdom.
Wisdom that is extinguished from within is called the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*). However, the wisdom-eye alone cannot deliver sentient beings, for it lacks the capacity for discernment.
For this reason, one seeks the dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*). The dharma-eye causes these people to practice this Dharma and attain this Path;
it knows the various skillful means for each and every sentient being so as to lead them to the realization of the Path. Yet, the dharma-eye cannot know all things universally or deliver all beings.
This is the path of skillful means for sentient beings; for this reason, they seek the Buddha-eye. There is nothing the Buddha-eye does not know.
It is free from obscuration and concealment; there is nothing it does not see and know.
The five powers are faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. 1. The power of faith: To believe that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions;
that they are born of the mind through inverted and deluded views, like a whirling firebrand, like a dream, and like an illusion. 2. The power of diligence:
Day and night he constantly practices diligence. He eliminates the five hindrances: sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt.
He guards the five faculties. Desiring to obtain, desiring to know, desiring to practice, and desiring to discuss the profound sūtras and teachings, he possesses the three powers of mindfulness.
Always with single-minded mindfulness, one desires to be complete in generosity, ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, and liberation.

One desires to abide within the knowledge of the arising, ceasing, staying, and changing of all phenomena pertaining to the actions of body, speech, and mind, maintaining constant single-minded mindfulness. Fourth is the power of concentration:

skillfully grasping the signs of concentration, one is able to give rise to various profound states of meditative absorption. Fifth is the power of wisdom: for the sake of the noble wisdom that brings an end to suffering, one achieves perfection.

This is wisdom. It leads to the departure from all Buddhas [i.e., attachment to them] and toward Nirvana. By means of wisdom, one contemplates the impermanence of the entire triple world. As for power:
it is the ability to destroy afflictions, to deliver sentient beings, and to attain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas; this is called power.
Furthermore, because neither celestial Māras nor non-Buddhist paths can obstruct or destroy it, it is called "power" (*bala*).
*Nirvāṇa* is here translated as "perfect stillness" (*yuánjì*) or "perfect permanence" (*yuáncháng*).
The character *cuì* (悴) should be written as *cuì* (顇); its pronunciation is *cuì*, and it means "withered" (*jiāocuì*). To use *cuì* (悴) in the sense of "sorrow" (*yōu*) is incorrect.
The three bodies (trikāya) are the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Transformation-body. The Dharma-body is Vairocana, which means "pervading all places.
The Reward-body is Rocana, which means "pure and full. The Transformation-body is Śākyamuni, which means "Able Sage of Silence.
Within the bodies of sentient beings, these correspond to tranquility, wisdom, and function. Tranquility is the Dharma-body; wisdom is the Reward-body.

By means of this transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), the five consciousnesses—eye-consciousness and the others—preceding the four wisdoms constitute the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*). The sixth mental consciousness is the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇa-jñāna*).
The seventh manas is the Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*). The eighth ālayavijñāna is the Great [Mirror-like Wisdom].
Regarding the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*): when one is among sentient beings, wisdom is weak and consciousness is strong, so it is merely called "consciousness.

When at the stage of Buddhahood, wisdom is strong and consciousness is weak, so it is merely called "wisdom. The sixth and seventh consciousnesses transform during the causal stage, while the fifth and eighth transform at the level of fruition.
This is what is meant by the transformation of names without the transformation of their essential substance. From the *Chuan deng lu*: Zen Master Zhizhong of Zhitong read the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.

He recited it more than a thousand times, yet he did not comprehend the three bodies (trikāya) and four wisdoms (caturjñāna). Consequently, he went to Caoqi to visit the Sixth Patriarch to seek an explanation of their meaning.
The Patriarch said: "As for the three bodies: the pure Dharma-body (dharmakāya) is your own nature;
the complete Reward-body (saṃbhogakāya) is your own wisdom; and the thousands of millions of Transformation-bodies (nirmāṇakāya) are your own practice. If you depart from your original nature..."

The teaching of the three bodies is what is called "having a body but lacking wisdom. If one awakens to the fact that the three bodies have no self-nature, this is called the Bodhi of the four wisdoms.
Listen to my verse: "The self-nature inherently possesses the three bodies; Through their manifestation, the four wisdoms are perfected.

Without departing from the conditions of seeing and hearing, One transcends and ascends to the stage of Buddhahood. I now speak this for you; Believe it with earnest faith, and you shall never again be deluded."
"Do not learn from those who run about in pursuit; they spend their whole day speaking of Bodhi. Tong said, "May I hear the meaning of the four wisdoms?
The Patriarch replied, "Since you have already realized the three bodies, you must clearly understand the four wisdoms. Why ask further? If one is separated from the three bodies,"
Setting aside the discussion of the four wisdoms, this is called "having wisdom but no body. That which is here termed "having wisdom" actually results in "no wisdom.
Furthermore, a verse is spoken: The nature of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is pure; The Wisdom of Equality has no affliction in its mind. The Wisdom of Wondrous Observation sees without effort;
The Wisdom of Accomplishing Tasks is identical to the Perfect Mirror. Five, eight, six, and seven are fruit and cause.

They revolve; yet they employ names and words without possessing any real nature. If one leaves no trace of inherent nature at the point of their revolving, then amidst the profusion of activity, one dwells eternally in the *nāga-samādhi*.
Regarding the eight liberations:
first, the liberation of those with internal form who perceive external forms; second, the liberation of those who, having no perception of internal form, perceive external forms.
1. Liberation. 2. Liberation through the perception of impurity. 3. Liberation through the perception of pure forms, having personally realized it with the body and dwelling therein.
4. Liberation of the sphere of infinite space. 5. Liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness. 6. Liberation of the sphere of nothingness. 7.
Liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. 8. Liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling, having personally realized it with the body and dwelling therein.

The six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) are: first, the power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣur-abhijñā*); second, the power of the divine ear (*divyaśrotra-abhijñā*); third, the power of knowing the minds of others (*paracitta-jñāna-abhijñā*); fourth, the power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-abhijñā*);
fifth, the power of psychic transformation (*ṛddhi-abhijñā*); and sixth, the power of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*).

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra on Good Spiritual Friends* states: "One who can expound the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, and non-cessation, as well as the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), causing people’s minds to enter into joy, faith, and delight—this is called a good spiritual friend.
Furthermore, the *Huashou jing* states: "There are four dharmas that constitute a good spiritual friend: first, the ability to cause people to enter into goodness."
Within the Dharma: first, it is able to obstruct all unwholesome dharmas; second, it is able to cause people to abide in the True Dharma;
third, it is constantly able to accord with and transform them through teaching.
*Shàn* (pronounced with the *yàn* rhyme) means slanderous speech.
Regarding the power of loving-kindness and patience, there are fifteen benefits to cultivating loving-kindness and patience: first, peaceful sleep; second, peaceful awakening;
third, protection by devas; fourth, protection by humans; fifth, having no bad dreams while asleep; sixth, constant joy upon waking; seventh, being unable to be swept away by water.
8. Fire cannot burn them. 9. Swords cannot wound them. 10. Poison cannot harm them. 11. They are always reborn in auspicious places.
12. They constantly experience happiness. 13. As their primary retribution, they attain the Brahma-world. 14. As their residual retribution, they become kings of men.
15. As their ultimate fruit, they become Buddhas. All of these are the fruits of loving-kindness and patience.

Regarding the phrase "Mastery of both doctrine and exposition," Qingliang (Zongmi) said: "Mastery of doctrine refers to one's own cultivation; mastery of exposition refers to instructing those who have not yet awakened.
In the "Preface to the Diagram of the Lion Roaring and Striking the Elephant" by Sengbing, it is recorded that Li Boyu recounted what the śramaṇa Shi Sengji had told him:
"Once, while traveling from India toward Daqin (China), he suddenly heard [the sound of something] some tens of li away."
He roared and snorted, "Huan-huan," startling the heavens and terrifying the earth. After a short while, one saw only the hundred beasts fleeing en masse, trampling the ground in their haste;

meanwhile, four giant elephants arrived with a roar. They coiled mud with their trunks and smeared it over themselves several feet thick, repeatedly spraying water from their trunks as they stood at the corners.
Suddenly, there appeared three-headed lions, shedding blood like gushing springs, as massive as great trees.

Cǎoyǎn (草偃): [咸*欠], pronounced with the initial *xū* and the rhyme *jiàn*, meaning "to separate. Cāng (蹌): pronounced with the initial *qī* and the rhyme *liàng*, meaning "to run. Xiāo (虓): pronounced with the initial *xū* and the rhyme *jiāo*, meaning "the roar of a tiger."
The story of the Bodhisattva Kṣāntivādin and King Kali as found in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
Regarding "araṇya" (translated here as *lán'è*): in Sanskrit it is called *araṇya*; this means a "place of tranquility. *Cényín*:
the first character is pronounced *chú zān qiè* (approximating the sound *tsien*) and the second has the phonetic *yín*; it denotes a high, rugged appearance.
*Kǐ* (闃): pronounced with the *kǔ* and *xī* initials; it means "stillness.
Regarding the *Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom* (Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra), fascicle 3, which states: "Giving with material wealth is called inferior giving;
giving with one's body is called middling giving. Among all forms of giving, that in which the mind is unattached is the superior."
Regarding "Buddhist charity" (dāna):
Master Yingliu of the Yingshan Temple stated that one may add the character *fei* (吠) or the character *bi* (毗).
He further remarked that it is called *vaidūrya*, named after a mountain; it is a treasure from the distant mountains. These distant mountains refer to Mount Sumeru. This treasure is blue.
As for color: all jewels are indestructible; they cannot be melted or cast by smoke or flame, and can only be destroyed by ghosts and spirits who possess supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).
It is further said that the eggs of the *garuḍa* (golden-winged bird) are obtained by spirits and ghosts, who then sell them to humans.
The *Weilüe* states that the country of Daqin produces [jewels] that are red, white, black, yellow, blue, green, pale blue, crimson, and purple.
There are ten kinds of *liuli* (lapis lazuli). This is indeed a natural substance; its luster and gloss surpass those of all other gems. Its color is not constant.
What is currently used by the common people is all produced by smelting stone dross, adding various medicinal substances, and pouring [the mixture] to form it.
It is particularly hollow, brittle, and lacks solidity; it is not a genuine article.

The *Boluobenxing jing* (Sūtra on the Original Acts of the Dragon-Taming Alms Bowl) states: When the Buddha first turned the wheel of the Dharma, he subdued the three Kāśyapa brothers at the Hall of the Fire God (*Agnideva*).
He emitted a majestic fire that extinguished the poisonous flames of the fire-dragon.

While the four directions were simultaneously ablaze with intense, raging heat, only the place where the Tathāgata sat remained tranquil; no flames were seen there. Upon seeing this, the fire-dragon gradually approached.
He immediately leaped into the Buddha’s almsbowl. At that time, the World-Honored One held the bowl in his hand and went to where Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa was.
Furthermore, during the eleventh year of the Jianyuan era of Fu Jian, there was a great drought in Chang’an.
The eminent monk Shi She of the Jin dynasty was requested to perform a ritual to summon a dragon; in an instant, the dragon appeared within She’s bowl, and the rain soon became sufficient.
Regarding the resolution of tigers: The High Monk Chou of Qi was practicing meditation at Mount Wangwu in Huai Prefecture when two tigers began to fight.

The Master went there and resolved the conflict with his *khakkhara* (monk’s staff); the tigers then departed separately. Furthermore, while traveling through the mountains, Dhyāna Master Tanxun encountered two tigers fighting;
they did not cease for a long time, so Tanxun took up his *khakkhara* and placed himself between them to separate them.
He said to the tiger, "We dwell together in this forest thicket; there is no great cause for conflict. It would be fortunate if we each took our separate ways.
The tiger lowered its head, accepted his command, and dispersed with its breath held. Furthermore, a stone inscription by Chan Master Chou at Cizhou states:
"In the past, during the time of Emperor Gao Huan of the Qi dynasty, Chou lived in seclusion one hundred and twenty li northwest of the capital on Taoyuan Mountain."
Jin Rock. Beneath the rock is a temple called Junqing. The rock is hollowed out and rises high enough to cover the temple.
At a height of about a hundred feet from the ground within the rock, a precarious pavilion was constructed to house a meditation seat. A ladder made of a single log provided access;
this was the place where the Master spent his days in tranquil seclusion. One day, the Master heard tigers fighting at the bottom of the stream, continuing for many days without ceasing.
He then went there and untied them with his staff. Thereafter, the two tigers constantly followed the Master at his side.

The Master consequently inscribed a verse upon the cliff wall, which said: "Originally I sought not fame, Yet fame insistently sought me. Before this cliff I untied two tigers, Thereby obstructing the attainment of the third fruit.

"He clarifies the mind-source of the Buddha without the slightest error; when practice and understanding correspond, he is named a Patriarch. He then composed a verse, saying:
"Neither observing evil while giving rise to aversion, Nor observing good while diligently striving, Nor abandoning the foolish while drawing near..."
The worthy one neither discards delusion to pursue enlightenment; he penetrates the Great Way beyond measure and masters the Buddha-mind through transcendence.
Unbound by the entanglements common to ordinary beings or sages, he is loftily termed a Patriarch.
In the *Sūtra of the Questions of the Devaputra Susthitamati*, the devaputra asks Mañjuśrī:
"What kind of bhikṣu is entitled to be called a 'dhyāna-master'? Mañjuśrī replied: "Regarding all phenomena, one contemplates them with a single mode of practice, namely, non-arising.
If one knows in this way, one is entitled to be called a dhyāna-master; furthermore, there is not even the slightest phenomenon to be grasped."
What dharma does he grasp? That is to say, he does not grasp this world or the future world; he does not grasp the three times.
This extends to not grasping any dharma at all—namely, that all dharmas are entirely devoid of a sentient being. One who does not grasp in this manner is called a Chan master.
There is no slight grasping, no non-grasping, and no grasping at all. Regarding all phenomena, nothing whatsoever is apprehended.
He has no recollection; if he does not recollect, he does not cultivate; if he does not cultivate, he does not realize. Therefore, he is called a Dhyāna Master.
The term "Elder" (Chang-lao) used today by those who preside over the Chan school must necessarily refer to one who, as defined in the *Dīrgha Āgama*,
is among the three types of elders— specifically, a person who has thoroughly realized the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), possesses internal wisdom and virtue,
and leads and instructs students.

The *Preface to the Translation of the Patriarchal Verses* by Yang Xuanzhi, the Governor of Yumen, briefly records that during the Xinghe era of the Eastern Wei, the eminent monk Yunqi traveled to the Western Regions to seek the Dharma.
Upon reaching Kucha, he encountered the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas, who intended to transmit the Dharma to the Eastern Land (China).
Yunqi said, "The Buddha-dharma has not yet [flourished] in the Eastern Land..."

Zhen said, "It would be appropriate for you to remain here for now. Yaśas then produced the Sanskrit text of the patriarchs’ verse on the transmission of the Dharma and presented it to Huiqi for translation.
Subsequently, Huiqi traveled to India. Yaśas then took the newly translated Chinese version of the patriarchal verse to the Western Wei.
Encountering times of great turmoil there, he entered the Northern Qi. Emperor Wenxuan of the Qi invited him to reside at Shikusi Temple.
Because the Qi dynasty was just then receiving the abdication of the Eastern Wei, there was no leisure for translation.
Guṇabhadra then transmitted the ancestral verses translated in Kucha to the layman Wan Tianti.

Tianti heard that in the Wei there was the *Dharmatāla-śāstra* (Fu fazang zhuan), translated by the Tripiṭaka Master from the Western Regions, Jikaya, and the Śramaṇa Tanyao of Zhaoxuan Temple, which was incomplete regarding the Buddhas and patriarchs.
The verse on the transmission of the Dharma was subsequently transcribed and presented to the Northern Wei.
When Emperor Jianwen of the Liang dynasty heard that a copy existed in the Wei, he dispatched the envoy Liu Xuanyun to the Wei to transmit it back to Jiankang.

During the Zhenyuan era of the Tang dynasty, the śramaṇa Huiju of Jinling, together with the Tripitaka Master Śīladhara from Western India, compiled it into the *Baolin zhuan*. Yunqi—also known as Tanqi—[is the author].
Kucha (also transcribed as Quésuí; the pronunciation is *qiūzī*). Chán (the pronunciation is *shàn*). [Note:

Regarding the first [patriarch] Zhú Dàlì, the second Zhìgōng, the third Dámó, and the fourth the Sixth Patriarch: although they are recorded in the biographies, their origins are rarely known.
I have heard that Yǎngshān’s annotated commentary is quite detailed, yet in the end I was unable to see it.
Later, within the records of the Chan Master Yúnmén Yuào, I obtained eighteen verses annotated by Yuào; as for Prajñātāra, there are only three.
The preface is found in the commentary; it is now recorded here as well. The Chan Master’s name was Chongyao; he was the dharma heir of National Teacher Shao of Tiantai.
His fame resounded throughout his time, and he was held in high esteem by the Qian family. The hand-copied annotations of his prophetic verses (*chan*) still exist in their original state;
they are currently enshrined in the Shadow Hall of Yongxi at Yunmen in Kuaiji.
In the past, Prajñātāra transmitted eleven gāthās on the "Five Non-attainments" to Bodhidharma while in India;
three of these have commentaries. The first says:
Traveling along a road, one suddenly encounters a sheep crossing the water; All alone and weary, one crosses the river in the dark. At sunset, how pitiable are the pair of elephants!
"Horse. "Two sprouts of young cassia flourish long and prosperously. This prophecy concerns the beginning and end of Bodhidharma’s coming from the West.

When Bodhidharma first arrived and met Emperor Wu of Liang—the Emperor's name was Yan (衍)—the character *yan* is composed of the radical for "to walk" (*xing*) and the radical for "water" (*shui*). Thus, it is said: "walking on the road, he spans the water.
Since the Emperor did not attain accord with him, the Patriarch subsequently traveled to Luoyang; hence, it is said: "he encountered sheep. Sheep (*yang*).
The "yang" (sun) and "sheng" (sound) are phonetically close. The Patriarch did not wish for people to know his movements;
that night he sailed westward on reeds, hence it is called "crossing the river in the dark. When the Patriarch came from the West, he met the two emperors of Liang and Wei;
this refers to the "two auspicious horses beneath the sun. He sat facing a wall at Shaolin for nine years; hence it is called the "two young cassia trees. Long ago.
Regarding the proximity of the nine sounds, the second says:

"Though China is vast, there is no other path; one must rely on walking beneath the feet of the descendants. When the golden cock can peck up a single grain of rice, it shall provide sustenance for the Arhats of the ten directions.
This was a prophecy that Master Ma would receive the Dharma from Upādhyāya Xiangruang.
There is no other path; their Way is one. Thus, the Great Master’s name was Dao-i (One-Way).
His descendants are his rightful heirs who walk upon his footsteps—what is called "a single colt that tramples the world underfoot. The golden rooster holding grain:
this refers to the Venerable [Huineng], a native of Jinzhou. The rooster knows the time and crows to awaken those who have not yet woken. Luo... [text ends]
A Chinese monk. Mazu was born in Shifang County of Hanzhou. He received the teacher’s Dharma and the offering of food from his master.
The third [verse] says:

"Though auspicious within the mind, it is inauspicious on the outside; the name of the monk's quarters by the river is not appropriate. Because he encountered a venomous dragon, he was born as a martial man.
"Son, suddenly encountering a small mouse—'silence without end. This prophecy refers to Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou, whose name was Yu (邕).
He destroyed Buddhism, but it was restored in the *gengzi* year; hence the mention of the 'small mouse. 'Silent' (*jimo*) refers to Yu."
The first of the eight poems in the *Weijian Zhu* (Unseen Commentary) says: "Unexpectedly meeting deep waters upon the road, Casually seeing a tiger and then encountering a pig.
Though the little calf has horns, When the dragon emerges from the green stream, it must all yield.
The second says: "In the eighth month, the Honored Merchant flies with a sound; Great fortune arrives, and the flock of birds is not startled. In its breast, it carries a single chicken."
He comes to attend the assembly, holding dragons and snakes in his hands between the two pillars. The third [verse] says: "The public seat is entrusted;
power is relinquished for the time being. The mosquito insect feels ashamed of its small form. The elephant from the Eastern Sea returns to don the right robe.
In both places one receives grace; neither is slight. The fourth [verse] says: "Sun and moon move together, yet the Sovereign remains unmoved. The official lacks a crown as he ascends the mountain."
[He] went. He further bestowed a peak to add to the verdant mountains; it was only when the King commanded his men to identify it that its name became known.

The fifth [verse] says: "When meeting people on the high ridges, one again sheds their clothes; though the small snake is venomous, it can do nothing. One may look at the sky from the bottom of a well to see how near it is;
a tiny novice monk possesses great spiritual capacity. The sixth says: "Though the great waves are high, they are not worth noting; a hundred..."
The years pass like common trees growing toward the heavens; one bird flies south, yet returns to the north; two people head east, yet turn back to the west. The seventh verse says:
"Pitifully, the bright moon alone occupies the sky; the four dragon-children each depart for their own way.
They rush about to the east, west, south, and north, while the sun rises level above, shining boundlessly. The eighth verse says: "A bird comes and perches..."

A lofty hall is about to be raised; white clouds enter the earth, their color returning to azure. The golden dragon in the heavens makes the sun and moon bright. Is the seawater of Dongyang clear or not?
First held aloft, the vermilion wheel is heavy, yet again light. Though it lacks eyes and heart, it turns ever more alert.
One does not see ears or eyes, yet it is skilled at observing and listening. The body is originally non-existent, yet it has a hollow form. It does not speak its name or clan.
He merely verified the names, yet his mind searched through the scrolls, opening the sutras in error; his mouth spoke of favors and blessings while his heart was devoid of feeling.
Whether departing or arriving, his body found no rest.
Yaśanālīyaśa composed thirteen prophetic verses and conferred the five precepts upon the upāsaka.
Ten Great Auspicious Signs. The first says: "The *Vajraśekhara* treasury is hidden from both past and present;
it is armless, yet it possesses arms. When the Dragon arrives, it shall receive the treasure; yet upon receiving the object, it again loathes its name.

This verse was a prophecy concerning the Second Patriarch. He who honors and upholds superior matters has kept them hidden throughout the past and present; when he encounters a Great Sage, [he reveals them].
He was able to give rise to insight. Since the Patriarch had severed his left arm to seek the Dharma, he was indeed the "limb" of Master Bodhidharma.
When the Dragon and Elephant came from the West, it was precisely the day the Patriarch obtained the Treasure of the Dharma. Upon offering the object, the master changed his name to Huikē;
as for the taboo name Shenguang, it need not be discussed further. The second [point] says:
"At first he did not state his name; he was like one driven mad by wind and had a strange voice. When people came, he took no pleasure in seeing them.

'The white jewel is initially level'—this verse prophesied the Third Patriarch. When the Master first went as a layman (*avadātavasana*) to visit the Second Patriarch, he ultimately did not state his name or surname."
He manifested a wind ailment and came to succeed to the patriarchal position; this was not welcomed by others, who called him "Red-Headed Can.
Baibao says that the Master’s name was Sengcan. At first, he was ordinary; although the Master had already transmitted the Way of the Second Patriarch, he did not initially manifest great brilliance.
This was already during the time when the teachings were being suppressed by Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou. The third [section] says:

He arose seeking freedom from obstruction. The Master said, "I shall not bind you. On the road he encountered a monk and prostrated; six sprouts grew from his feet—this was the prophecy concerning the Fourth Patriarch.
When the Patriarch first met the Third Patriarch, he immediately sought the Dharma of liberation, which refers to the Dharma of non-obstruction.
The Third Patriarch asked, "Who has bound you? which means "Do not bind yourself. "On the road" refers to the Way. "Encountering a monk and prostrating" refers to faith.
The Master’s name was Daoxin. Six branches grew from his feet; one branch branched out as a lateral offshoot under the Fourth Patriarch.
This lineage continued for six generations, namely Niu-tou Lanrong. The fourth [lineage] is as follows:

"Three or four, entirely without self; receiving the lamp of mind across the water. His honorable title transcends all measure; from anger, no hatred arises"—this was the prophecy concerning the Fifth Patriarch.
"Three or four" refers to seven. At the age of seven, the Master met the Fourth Patriarch, and their questions and answers were in perfect accord.
He attained the Dharma of non-arising and non-self. "Separated by water" means that the abode of the Fourth Patriarch was divided by a single stream.
"Lamp of the mind" refers to the torch of the Dharma transmitted [to him]. "Venerable title" refers to the Buddha. "Transcending all measures" refers to the Patriarch. "Not giving rise to aversion."
The master’s name was Hongren. His fifth [verse] says:
"Offerings—when have they ever been offered? Diligence in speech—is it not also a lack of diligence? Only by writing this four-line gāthā shall one face the person of the Auspicious Field.
This was a prophecy concerning the Sixth Patriarch. "Offerings—when have they ever been offered? Diligence in speech—is it not also a lack of diligence? The master’s name was Huineng.
This refers to the four-line verse composed by [Huineng] in response to Bei (Shen)xiu, through which he transmitted the robe. "Ruìtián" is Shenxiu.
Its sixth line reads:
"The mind can harbor matters; let them be told by the banks of the Hán River. Probing the moon in the lake waves, it shall illuminate two or three people."
This prophecy concerns the Venerable Huairang of Nanyue. "Holding things within the heart" refers to Huairang. At the banks of the Han River, his disciple Mazu was born in Hanzhou;
he "probed for one month," meaning that the Master [Huairang] had painted the moon at Caoxi. There were two or three people [involved].
The Master once said to his disciples: "All six of you have realized my own person together. Chang Hao has obtained my eyebrows;
he is skilled in dignified demeanor. Zhida has obtained my eyes; he is skilled in looking and glancing. Tanran has obtained my ears; he is skilled in listening to principles."
Shenzhao [understood] my nose; he was skilled at perceiving the vital breaths. Yanjun [understood] my tongue; he was skilled at discourse and explanation. Daoyi [understood] my mind;
he was skilled in matters of antiquity and the present. The seventh said:

"Receiving the precious and diligent words; departing from one's home day by day they unfold. Moving the beam to the nearby road; the remaining breath follows the path beneath the feet. This is a prophecy concerning Mazu.
"Precious and diligent" (Zhenqin) means that he obtained the Dharma-treasure of Master Xiangru and applied it with diligence.
Some versions read "Mile" (Maitreya), but this is incorrect. "Departing from one's home" (Liqing) refers to the south. "Day by day" (Riri) refers to prosperity. Mazu propagated his teachings there.
"Nanchang. Some editions read "Sun and Moon" (Ryōgetsu), which is incorrect. "Moving to Liang" means he went there to save sentient beings.
"Coming to the nearby road" refers to his entry into the city at the request of Lu Sīgōng, the regional commander of Hóngzhōu, to preach the Dharma. "My breath" (*yuqì*)—this is my respiration;
it signifies that the heirs who transmit the Dharma shall continue my work as I do while traveling throughout the world. The eighth [section] says:
"The earth of *gen* (艮) gives birth to the profound principle (*xuanzhi*). 'Tong' (通) and 'Zunmi' (尊媚) are also honored.
Sharing the same rank as the three and nine clans, a single hair on the soles of his feet divides this prophecy. This refers to Shenxiu of the Northern School. "The earth of *gen*" is the northeast;
Shenxiu branched off from the Fifth Patriarch at the Northern Capital. "'Tongzun'" is the title of Great Penetration (*Dàtōng*) bestowed by the state. "'Miyi'" is also Shenxiu.
39. From Xiu downward, there were twelve successive generations in total. Your reverence belongs to the lineage of the Fifth Patriarch;
you are but a single hair’s breadth [of that tradition], yet you are designated as the "Northern School. Its nine branches are as follows:
"Liṅjí (Spiritual Collection) feels ashamed before the Heavenly Grace; twenty-six people have grown teeth. Within the Dharma there is no flavor; merit is established upon stone.
This prophecy refers to Hézé Shénhuì. "Liṅjí" was his former name. "Heavenly Grace" refers to Hézé.
The "twenty-six" refers to the twelve disciples of Shenhui. They lacked any true flavor of the Dharma; they were what are known as masters of intellectual understanding.
As for those who established merit upon the stone, it was because at that time there was Pujì, a disciple of Beishou, whose preaching flourished in the capital.
Relying on his power and status, he claimed that Shenhui’s teachings were heterodox and deluded the masses.

By right, he should have been expelled. However, because Huì was traveling to Nanyang, Zhìjì destroyed the grand monument of Master Dōngnèng and erected a separate inscription for Shénxiù’s life, proclaiming himself the Sixth Patriarch of the Dharma transmission and making himself the Seventh Patriarch.
In the fifth year of the Tiānbǎo era, Sīláng Sòng Róng recognized his former error and again petitioned the throne to summon Huì back to Luòyáng, where he resided at Héshàng Monastery.
At Zeshi Temple, they demolished the stele of [Xuan]zong and erected a stone inscription for the Sixth Patriarch. Its tenth line reads:
"Originally a great tiger-man, he turned back to discourse as a lion; the Imperial House conferred upon him the title 'Ma-ling' (Horse-Neck), together with the details of the thirty-three.
This is the prophecy concerning the Venerable Master Yin-zong, who was originally a lecturer on the sutras and śāstras—a tiger of the Teaching—and later became a proponent of the Mind School.
"Siṃhaputra" (Shizi'er) refers to the official seal. "Maling" (Malingshan) refers to the lineage.
"Thirty-three" means that from the Indian patriarchs down to the Sixth Patriarch, there are thirty-three individuals; Yinzong succeeded the Sixth Patriarch, making eleven [generations].
"Nine daughters depart from human relations; eight pairs sever marriage ties. An old bed gains six legs; the Patriarch of the Mind is the most honored among the multitude.
This prophecy refers to the Venerable Master An of Mount Song. "Nine daughters" refers to Shaoshi (Lesser Shao), for it was at Shaoshi that An resided.
The eighth daughter was named An (Peace). "Rotten bed" refers to the aged An. "Six legs" indicates his extreme peace.
As the most honored among the multitude, Empress Wu paid homage to An and appointed him as National Preceptor. This is the twelfth.

*Zǒu wù* (Walked to Wu) and *zhāo lín* (Dawn Neighbor). *Míng wū zǐ* (The Míng-owl Child) leaves his body behind. Although the Two Heavens have their resonance, the Three Transformations are silent and free of dust.
This refers to the National Teacher Zhōngguó. *Zǒu wù*: the Six Teachers were people of Yuè. *Zhāo lín*: the second of the two [directions] of the East. *Míng wū*: the owl.
This is precisely Goose Island (Ezhou). It is Zheji of Yue; it was formerly called Goose Island, the place where the National Preceptor (Guoshi) was born.

Regarding the "Two Emperors," it refers to the two sovereigns Suzong and Daizong who offered their reverence. Regarding the "Three Transformations," on the third occasion he asked the Tripitaka Master "Big Ears" (Dairi), "Where is the old monk?
The Tripitaka Master was utterly bewildered; this is the state of "Silent Non-dust" (Jiwuchen). "Wu" refers to King Wu’s military expedition.
Qiè. Mín. (Third tone, yúnqiè). Thirteen.
To speak of "few" means how could it ever be few? Words flow yet do not flow. If the mountain were to remove its weeds, the three or four successive gateways would cultivate this prophecy.
This refers to the Venerable Master Xituan of Shitou. To speak of "few" is to mean "rare. How could it ever be rare? The Way is entrusted to...
This person—his words flow; [Dao]qian does not flow; Xi[qian] also does not flow. "The mountain has its weeds cleared" refers to Shitou.
As for the three or four who succeeded the lineage, their cultivation is not detailed. The thirteen verses above are the prophecies of Nālandayaśas.
One scroll of the *Dharmapada* was bestowed upon Yang Xuanzhi, the Governor of Qicheng. Regarding the circumstances of his taking poison as foretold by the prophecy:
"The river raft divides the jade waves; the pipe-torch opens the golden lock. Five mouths travel together; for ninety years there is neither 'other' nor 'self.
This refers to how Paramārtha and Sengguang secretly administered poison to me, which resulted in my reaching the age of ninety.
One verse by Zhu Dalü: The mandate of the Ruler of Wu, Emperor Sun Quan, shall last for twelve years.
Eating a meal under the azure heavens; running and racing amidst the clouds. Twelve years: when one encounters the pig, he closes his mouth.
Eating a meal under the azure heavens—this is the "Heavenly Mouth. "Mouth" above "Heaven" (*kǒu tiān*) forms "Wu" (*wú*). Running and racing amidst the clouds: each vies for the empire. Twelve years.
