The years shall total only fourteen. When the Pig year arrives, the mouth shall be closed; by the Year of the Boar (Hai), it shall come to an end. Master Zhi’s verse:
Looking up at the rain on the fan, he holds a hook at his waist. The nine suns are all shot down, leaving but one head.
"Arriving yet not arriving," "needing a blade for what is required. Meeting the dragon, he does not stay; encountering water, he flees. This is a prophecy.
No commentary has been seen [on this point].

However, the *Lengqie jing bao lin zhuan* (The Jewel Forest Biography of the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra) and the *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) both state that Bodhidharma transmitted the four-fascicle *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* to his disciples.
How, then, can the Chan school claim it to be a "separate transmission outside the teachings"? Answer: This is likely because of Huìnéng...
This was the general outline compiled by Jù; later readers did not examine it closely. In the *Chúndēng*, Dànmó said to his disciples:
"I have observed that in the land of Han there is only this scripture. If you, virtuous ones, rely upon and practice it, you will naturally attain liberation from the world."
It is because these are expedient means used to guide and receive beginners, causing them to give rise to faith. Thus, Mazu addressed the assembly, saying:
"The Great Master Bodhidharma came from South India to China to transmit the Dharma of the One Mind, so as to cause you all to attain awakening.
He also cited the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* to seal the minds of sentient beings, fearing that you might fall into delusion. It was not that he... [did not... provide further instruction.
I am confident that each person possesses this Dharma of the One Mind within themselves. Thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
"The Buddha’s words take the mind as their essence; having no gate is the Dharma-gate. How could it be that the Patriarchs exclusively transmitted this by means of a single sutra?
This is a failure of later generations to examine the matter carefully. Furthermore, this sutra was intended only for those such as Mahāmati.

Regarding the discussion on the meaning of Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), its intent is to inspire those of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) to abandon the Lesser Vehicle and aspire to the Great Vehicle;

how could this alone suffice as the essential path of the Patriarchal Gate? Furthermore, this sutra was translated during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra from India.
How could it be that a Song-period sutra was instead brought [to China] by Bodhidharma of the Liang dynasty?
Examining it by these standards, fallacious arguments are refuted of their own accord without even requiring investigation.

As for the saying that the Chan school’s stream of tradition transcends words and precedes the essence of the Way, how could it involve verbal explanation? Nevertheless, when the ancients engaged with others and responded to circumstances...
There is no comprehensive treatment here; I have merely set forth several conditions to demonstrate them to those who study.
Regarding the account of the words realized by the *dhāraṇī*-holding nun from the land of Akṣobhya:
the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 22, states that when the Buddha manifested supernatural transformations before the great assembly, the entire multitude saw the Buddha Akṣobhya.
The land was perfected with various kinds of merit. When the Buddha withdrew his supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), all these things were no longer seen;
they no longer appeared before the eyes. The Buddha said to Ānanda, "It is so, Ānanda. All dharmas do not appear before one another.
Dharma does not accord with dharma; dharma does not know dharma. The land of the Buddha Akṣobhya is also like this. Why is that? Because..."
All phenomena are without cognition or vision; they are without action or movement, ungraspable, and inconceivable.

Like a phantom person, they are without sensation, without perception, and without reality. When a bodhisattva practices in this manner, they are practicing the *prajñāpāramitā* (perfection of wisdom), yet they do not become attached to any phenomena.
*Dhāraṇī*: This is a title. Her taboo name was Minglian. She was the daughter of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty. [She] served...
Bodhidharma was a disciple [of the Buddha]. Having awakened to the Way, he manifested his passing away. His stupa is said to be about five *li* from Shaolin.
The details of this matter are fully recorded in the stupa inscription written by Chu Xunwang.
Regarding Maitreya preaching the Dharma, the *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) states: "The Bodhisattva Asaṅga, together with his younger brother Vasubandhu and his disciples..."
The two virtuous sages, Siṃhabuddhi and Jñānabuddhi, used to say to one another: "In our practice of the path, we vow to behold Maitreya.
If either of us should first relinquish his life and succeed in fulfilling this long-cherished wish, he must inform the other. Subsequently, Siṃhabuddhi was the first to relinquish his life.
When three years had passed without word from him, Vasubandhu Bodhisattva also gave up his life. Six months elapsed, yet still there was no news of his fate.
During the first watch of the night, while Asaṅga was instructing his disciples in the methods of meditative concentration, a great light suddenly appeared in the sky.
A celestial rishi descended through the air and entered the courtyard, prostrating at the feet of Asaṅga. Asaṅga said:
"Why have you come so late? What is the meaning of your assigned name?

He replied, "Since departing from this life, I went to the Tuṣita Heaven and was born within a lotus among the inner assembly of Maitreya. As soon as the lotus flower opened, Maitreya said, 'Welcome, Viśālamati!
Welcome, Viśālamati! I circumambulated him just once and have now come to report my arrival. Asaṅga said, "As for Siṃhabuddhi, he is now..."
"Where are you? he asked. He replied, "While I was circumambulating, I saw Śākyamuni among the assembly outside;

he was so deeply attached to sensual pleasures that he had no leisure to look back, so how could he have come to report this? Asanga asked, "What were the marks of Maitreya? And what Dharma did he expound?
He replied, "The marks and signs of Maitreya are such that words cannot describe them. The sublime Dharma he expounded is in meaning no different from this. However—"
The Bodhisattva’s wondrous voice is pure, resonant, harmonious, and elegant; those who hear it forget their weariness, and those who receive it never grow weary.

According to the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, when King Aśoka assembled the holy assembly and asked about the Buddha, the Arhat Piṇḍola raised his eyebrows with his hand and said to the king: "The Buddha is like a mountain of gold—majestic and towering."
The Hall is difficult to name;
it is the place where the Many-Son Stūpa gazes upon Kāśyapa with its blue-lotus eyes. According to the *Pratyekabuddha-śāstra*, there was once a great elder in Rājagṛha whose wealth was immeasurable.
He had begotten thirty sons and thirty daughters. Once, while he was out wandering for recreation, he [encountered the Buddha].
He arrived at a grove and saw a man cutting down a great tree; its branches, twigs, and leaves were so dense, beautiful, and luxuriant that many elephants could not pull it out.
Next, he cut down a small tree that had no branches or twigs; a single person pulled it out without any difficulty.
Having witnessed this, he immediately spoke these verses: "I see them cutting down a great tree with its branches..."
The leaves are exceedingly numerous; the dense forest branches entwine and hang together so that there is no way to escape. The world is likewise:
men, women, and all kinsmen bind the mind with increasing craving, such that within the dense forest of birth and death, liberation cannot be attained.
A small tree without branches cannot form a dense forest. Observing this, I have awakened and severed [the bonds].

O beloved one, having spontaneously attained liberation within the dense forest of birth and death, he immediately became a pratyekabuddha at that very spot and entered parinirvāṇa by manifesting supernatural powers.
At that time, his kinsmen constructed a stūpa for him; because of this, people of the time named it the Bahuputra Stūpa.
Regarding the transmission of the lamp through the stages of faith and practice: one attains the stage of faith, but not yet the stage of practice.
In the *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra*, the Buddha says: "From the mind of an icchantika up to the Tathāgata, the true reality (*tathatā*) of the Tathāgata abides in five successive stages.
The first is the stage of faith: one believes that the seed of *tathatā* within this body is obscured by delusion, and thus abandons the deluded mind."
The mind is pure and clear, knowing that all objective spheres are merely mental verbal discriminations (*manojalpa-vikalpa*). Second is the stage of reflection (*cintā-avasthā*):

"reflection" means observing that all objective spheres are nothing but mental verbal discriminations appearing according to the mind; the objective spheres thus perceived are not one's own fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*).

One knows that this fundamental consciousness is neither phenomenon (*dharma*) nor meaning (*artha*), and is neither the grasped (*grāhya*) nor the grasper (*grāhaka*). Third is the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

Position. As for cultivation, it is the constant arising [of wisdom] that is capable of causing [realization], because the arising occurs simultaneously. First, one guides with wisdom to dispel all obstacles and difficulties, and to emerge from the entanglements of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).

Fourth is the stage of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*): the practitioner leaves behind the stages of conditioned activity; the mind has nothing to discard; the faculties are extremely pure and sharp; the mind is immovable and like space;
and one realizes the definitive true nature, which is Great Parinirvāṇa—merely the greatness of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).

Fifth is the relinquishing of the stages (*pada*). "Relinquishing" means not abiding in the nature of emptiness; it is the flowing transformation of right wisdom, the mark of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), and suchness (*tathatā*).
Suchness does not abide in marks; *samyak-saṃbodhi* is like empty space and is not realized as an object. The mind has no boundaries and no location can be perceived;
this is reaching the state of the Tathāgata. Good son, these five stages are a single awakening. One enters from the fundamental benefit. If one transforms sentient beings...
Birth. From the original source, one nurtures the noble embryo.

In the *Benevolent Kings’ Sutra for the Protection of the State*, the Buddha said: "Good son, at the stage of the first subduing patience (*kṣānti*), one gives rise to the nature of the seeds of practice (*śikṣā-bīja*) and cultivates the ten stages of conduct (*daśa-caryā*).
Regarding the characteristics of the initial arousal of the mind (*prathama-cittotpāda*), there are sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges who behold the Buddha."

Regarding the Dharma and the Sangha, there are the ten levels of faith: namely, the mind of faith, the mind of mindfulness, the mind of diligence, the mind of wisdom, the mind of concentration, the mind of non-retrogression, the mind of precepts, the mind of vows, the mind of protecting the Dharma, and the mind of dedication.
Possessing these ten minds, one is able to transform sentient beings to a small degree and surpass all the wholesome stages of the two vehicles. This constitutes the initial growth of a bodhisattva.
Because nurturing the mind constitutes the "sacred embryo" (śrī-garbha).
Regarding the Divine Continent of China (Zhōngguó), when Bodhidharma first surveyed it, he saw that the Great Vehicle’s spiritual potential was established there.

The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (Vibhāṣā-piṭaka) states: "Each of the four great continents is surrounded by eight sub-continents. Among these, the eight sub-continents to the south are called the "Ox" (Go).
There are the continents of *Zhōuzhōu*, *Yángzhōu*, *Yāozhōu*, *Bǎozhōu*, *Hóuzhōu*, *Xiàngzhōu*, *Nǚzhōu*, and *Shénzhōu*. Zhang Heng’s *Lùtú* states:
"To the east of Kunlun lies the continent of Chixian, where wind and rain occur at their proper times and cold and heat follow their seasons.
Were it not for this land, the south would be excessively hot, the north excessively cold, and the west excessively dark. Therefore, the sage-kings [did not dwell there]."
It is located there. Furthermore, in the *Shiji*, Zou Yan’s writings state: "China occupies but one part out of eighty-one parts of the world.
China is named Chixian (the Red County). Within it are the Nine Provinces; these are the Nine Provinces described by Yu."
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Suppose there is one who throws a clod of earth at a dog; the dog chases after the clod, and the clod does not stop.
Suppose there is another who throws [a clod] at a lion; the lion chases the person, and the clod stops of its own accord."
"Drawing legs for a snake": The *Zhanguo Ce* states that when Zhao Yang went to Chu to attack Qi, the King of Qi sent Chen Zhen to see him and said:
"I shall offer you a parable. The King of Chu once held a sacrifice and bestowed a single cup of wine upon his attendants."
The attendants said to one another, "If we drink it among several people, it will not suffice; if one person drinks it alone, there will be enough.
Let us draw a snake; whoever completes the snake first shall drink. One man finished first and, taking up the wine to drink, said with his right hand holding the cup, "I can add feet to this.
Before he had finished, another snatched the goblet from him and said, "A snake naturally has no feet. Now—"
To attack Qi is merely to draw legs for a snake.
"Entering the water and seeing a tall man" is found in the *Yunmen lu*, lower volume.
"Looking at the tower and striking the tower" is found in the *Bafang zhuyou ji* and the *Wanglou*.
Ji Xin feigned surrender, and Xiang Yu immediately launched a fierce attack on Ziyang. King Han was greatly distressed by this.

General Ji Xin said, "The situation is desperate. I beg to deceive the Chu forces so that you may escape through an opening. Thereupon, Chen Ping led more than two thousand women out of the eastern gate at night;
the Chu troops consequently attacked from all four sides, and Ji Xin then mounted the king’s carriage.

From within his yellow carriage, with the *zàodǎo* banner on the left, [Xiang Yu] cried out, "The provisions are exhausted! The Han King has surrendered to Chu! As everyone in the city called out "Ten-thousand-year-old!
from the eastern gate to watch, the Han King was thus able to escape through the western gate with several dozen horsemen. When Xiang Yu saw Ji Xin, he asked, "Where is the Han King?
Ji Xin replied, "He has already departed. Enraged, Xiang Yu had Ji Xin boiled alive.
Li Guang went up to Baqiao Bridge; having been captured alive by the Xiongnu and surrendered to the Han, he was due to be executed, but was instead ransomed as a commoner.
He lived among the southern mountains of Lantian, hunting with his bow. Once, at night, he set out with a single horseman and drank with some people in a field.
They returned to the Baling Post Station. The Baling Commandant was intoxicated and stopped Li Guang, shouting at him. Li Guang’s horseman said, "He is the former General Li.
The Commandant replied, "Even a current general may not travel at night; how much less so a former one? He then allowed Li Guang to stay overnight beneath the station.
Before long, the Xiongnu invaded. The Son of Heaven then summoned and appointed Guang as the Grand Protector of Beiping.
Guang requested that the Commandant of Baling accompany him, intending to execute him upon reaching the army.
In the *Biṇḍulur-bhikṣu-udāyana-rāja-dharma-deśanā-sūtra*, it is said: "I shall now briefly explain a parable for the sake of the King;
may Your Majesty listen with a sincere mind. Long ago, there was a man traveling on a desolate road who encountered a massive, fierce elephant.
Pursued by the elephant, he fled in frantic terror, finding no one to rely upon or protect him. He then saw a dilapidated well."
He sought out the roots of the tree and entered the well to hide within it. Above him were two mice, one black and one white, gnawing at the roots of the tree.
On the four sides of this well were four venomous snakes, intending to sting the man. Beneath this well, moreover, were three great poisonous dragons.
On his sides he fears four snakes; below him he fears a venomous dragon. The tree upon which he leans has its roots shaking.
Three or two drops of honey from the tree fall into his mouth. At that moment, the shaking tree knocks down the beehive, and the swarms of bees fly out in all directions to sting and bite the man.
A wild fire breaks out and further comes to burn the tree. Great King, you should know that such is the plight of that man.
The suffering and distress are beyond measure, yet that man obtains very little flavor while his afflictions are immense.
Great King, the wilderness is a metaphor for birth and death; that man is a metaphor for an ordinary person; the elephant is a metaphor for impermanence;
the well is a metaphor for the human body; the roots are a metaphor for human life; and the white and black rats are metaphors for day and night.
The tree roots are a metaphor for the moment-to-moment cessation of thoughts. The four venomous snakes are a metaphor for the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
The honey is a metaphor for the five sensual desires (*pañcakāmaguṇa*). The swarm of bees is a metaphor for evil discursive thoughts. The forest fire that burns it is a metaphor for old age.

The three venomous dragons below represent death and falling into the three evil realms (*durgati*). Therefore, one should know that the flavor of desire is extremely slight, while its suffering and affliction are vast.
It is very much so.
When the moon is full, the oysters and clams are filled; at other times, they are empty. Thus, the *Xuanxue* says:
"The pearl embryos of oysters and clams correspond to the waning and waxing of the moon."
The *Lunheng* states that the theory of the rabbit’s gestation is as follows: the rabbit becomes pregnant by licking its own fur, and when it gives birth, the offspring emerge from its mouth.

Another account says that when northerners catch rabbits and flay their skins for use as brush-hair, if this occurs on a mid-autumn night free of clouds, it indicates that there will be many rabbits that year; it is said that the rabbit conceives by facing the moon.
Gong Luo’s cup fell [into the wine]. Jin Yue Guang, courtesy name Yanfu, was skilled in discourse. The assembly of worthies praised him, saying: "This man is like a water-mirror;
seeing him is like being made clear and bright, as if one had been amidst clouds and mist and now beholds the blue sky. Once, there was a close guest.
Having heard for a long time that he had not come, [the King] questioned him extensively as to the reason. He replied: "Previously, while seated here, I was granted wine.
Just as I was about to drink, I saw a snake in the cup. My mind felt great aversion toward it. Having drunk it, I fell ill.

At that time, there was a horned bow painted with lacquer to look like a snake hanging on the wall above my ear; what appeared in the cup was simply the reflection of that horn. He then set the wine aside.
In a previous instance, he asked a guest, "Is there anything else you see within the wine? The guest replied, "What I see is just as it was before.
Guang then explained the reason for his inquiry, whereupon the guest’s mind was suddenly enlightened and his long-standing ailment was instantly cured.
Thus, I borrow this anecdote to resolve your doubts and clarify what remains uncertain.

Regarding the fact that there were no worthy men in Qin during the Spring and Autumn period, the *Zuo Zhuan* records this in the thirteenth year [of Duke Zhao]. A Qin grandee named Rào Cháo said to Tǔ Huì:
"Do not say that there are no worthy men in Qin; it is simply that my plans were not adopted."
Regarding the *huábiǎo* pillar, the *Gujīn zhù* states: "Yao established the 'trees for slander' (*fěibàng zhīmù*), which are the *huábiǎo*.
A transverse beam was placed across the top of the pillar so that it resembled the shape of a flower, like a well-sweep (*jígē*). These were installed at all major thoroughfares and crossroads.

Some say the 'tablet trees' (*biǎomù*) were intended to symbolize the ruler’s receptivity to remonstrance, while others say they served as markers for roads. The Qin dynasty subsequently abolished them. This continued until later times.
The Han dynasty renovated it.
The *Mùquèfēi Sōushénjì* (Record of the Flying Wooden Crane) states: Outside the gate of Liaodog City, there was a stone pillar (*huábiǎozhù*).
Suddenly, a white crane alighted upon its head. At that moment, a young man raised his bow, intending to shoot it; the crane then flew away into the void.
From within [the tomb], it spoke, saying: "There is a bird, there is a bird, Ding Lingwei! Having left my home for a thousand years, I now return.
The city walls remain as they were, but the people are no more. Why not learn the way of the immortals? [Look at] the graves, piled one upon another! Thereupon, it soared up into the sky.
People nowadays fashion a wooden image of it and place it atop a pestle.
The "Cock Crows" (Jinji Ming) section is found in the *Preface to the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Huihai*. ● Regarding the *Zazhi* (Miscellaneous Records):

it is a record. Because it accumulates records of various matters, it is called the *Zazhi*. It is like the secular works on calligraphy, calendrical science (*li*), food and wealth (*shi-huo*), and the five [classics].
All practices possess an underlying intent.
The Chan school (Zongmen) maintains that among the three studies, there is none that does not take this gate as its foundation; thus it is called the "Gate of the Source" (Zongmen).
The *Zhengzongji* states briefly: "In antiquity, the Chan Gate was called the Zongmen; this also reflects the intention of the patriarchs such as Nanyue Huairang and Mazu Daoyi."
It is also said that our School is the primary and correct direction of the great tradition of Śākyamuni’s single Buddha-dharma.

However, because the meaning of what is called the "School" (Zongmen) is scattered throughout the various scriptures and remains concealed, it has not yet appeared clearly before the world as it does here.
Generally speaking, all those who enter our teaching must take this as their task.
The secret ultimate realization is precisely what constitutes right view. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"I now entrust all my unsurpassed True Dharma to Mahākāśyapa; he shall serve as a great refuge for you all.
Does this not mean that from this day forward, one may rely upon Kāśyapa’s unsurpassed, wondrous, and subtle esoteric Dharma?
Is this not to provide a standard for it? Those who have transcended the world rely upon these wondrous mind-essence and esoteric words as authoritative proof for future generations.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the Prajñāpāramitā is not a secret teaching, its underlying intent likewise lies in the profound intention of the Great Sage:
he regarded the wondrous, subtle, and esoteric Dharma as the very core of his teaching.

This is the essence (zong). For those who wish to cultivate the three trainings throughout successive lives, they rely upon this as the seal of verification for entering the Way and the standard for rectitude.

Thus we know that when the ancients designated our Chan school as the "School of Essence" (Zongmen), it was because they held it in high esteem beyond the mere traces of the teachings; this is indeed correct.
Since the arrival of Bodhidharma from Liang, Chan practitioners have lived in seclusion within the Wei region.
From the time of the Sixth Patriarch down to the era of Daji (Mahākāśyapa), more than two hundred and fifty years passed without the existence of a formal Chan monastery.

It was only during the reign of Emperor Fazu that the Great Wisdom Chan Master Huaihai of Baizhang first conceived the idea, establishing a system that did not restrict itself to either the Mahayana or Hinayana, but instead took the sutras, vinaya, and dharma as its central standard.

He established regulations and models: long beds were laid out in the hall as furnishings for meditation, banquets, and rest; high hanging racks were installed to hold towels, bedding, water flasks, and alms bowls.
He moved the Buddha Hall and constructed a Dharma Hall to clarify that the transmission of the Buddhas and Patriarchs was received through direct lineage.

In the present age, the practice of honoring the Dharma is paramount. Regarding the communal labor (*pǔqǐng*), those of high and low station alike contribute their strength. All monastic affairs are assigned according to specific offices.
At the two times of rice gruel and the main meal, both guests and hosts participate equally, demonstrating the equality of the Dharma-food (*dharmāhāra*).

In later generations, each followed what was appropriate for them and established separate regulations. Alas! The establishment of Zen monasteries has been of extraordinary benefit. Now, it should be...
As for those who act as stewards, if they truly cannot observe their duties and instead seek personal gain for themselves, what kind of heart is this?
What kind of heart is this? *Yi* (clothes-stand) has the pronunciation *yi*; *ping* (screen) has the pronunciation *bing*.
Zhuzhi’s disciple Qianzi said: "The teachings speak of the 'abbot' (zhuchi). What does this mean?

To be an abbot means to rely on a person to uphold the Dharma, causing it to endure and not perish. Now, the precepts, meditative concentration, and wisdom are the instruments for upholding the Dharma;
the monastic garden and its affairs are the resources for upholding the Dharma. As for the Dharma itself, it is the Great Sage..."
This is the way of humanity. Provisions and implements must await the right person before they can be employed.
It is not possible to have excellent implements while lacking the right provisions; nor is it possible to have excellent provisions while lacking the right implements.
Only when both are excellent can one maintain and abide in them. Formerly, the abbot of Vulture Peak was governed by Mahākāśyapa, and [the abbot] of the Bamboo Grove...
The abbot (zhuchi) has taken the corpse of the son of Śāriputra as his model; thus, the teaching of the Sage flourished and the Dharma of the Sage endured for a long time.
Since the Sage withdrew from the world, the succession of generations has been lost, and a vast period of confusion has passed.

We people have relied on mere fortune, yet we still employ the name, the power, and the profit of the "abbot. The whole world has become accustomed to this, crowding together in a chaotic clamor until it nearly forms [a new order].
When customs are formed by the winds [of precedent], and no more sages emerge, who shall rectify them?
If those who guard the exterior do not observe or discern, and yet wish for the wind of our sage’s teachings not to decline and the laws of the sage to flourish ever more, it cannot be achieved.
How tragic! What can I hope for?

The "Opening of the Hall" (kaidō) was the formal ceremony of the Translation Institute. On each annual anniversary of the Emperor’s birthday, newly translated scriptures were invariably submitted for imperial inspection to offer prayers for the longevity of the Sovereign.
Two months prior to this date, officials from the two central ministries would assemble to observe the translation process;

this was termed the "Opening of the Hall. One month prior, the Translation Commissioner and the Literary Editors would also assemble to present the newly completed scriptures. This was termed [the Submission of New Scriptures].

Regarding the opening of the hall (*kaitang*): when a patriarchal master is now appointed as an elder-abbot (*chángzhǔ*) to preach the Dharma for the first time, this is also called "opening the hall.

This refers to expounding the Treasury of the True Dharma-Eye of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; it is performed to offer prayers for the longevity of the Emperor and to bring blessings to all living beings throughout the four seas. For these reasons, it is also termed "opening the hall."
Regarding the offering of incense, the secular classics state: "If a person lacks faith, it is not known how they can be effective. It further says:

"If a large carriage lacks the crossbar for the yoke, or a small carriage lacks the curved pole, how can they proceed? For this reason, when followers of the Śākya tradition perform Buddhist rites, [they offer incense].
There has never been a case where incense offering was not performed first; this is the means by which the incense is commemorated and faith is manifested.
As the Sūtra says: "Faith is the source of the Way and the mother of merit; it nurtures all roots of goodness. This is its meaning.
That the Elder who opens the hall must personally offer incense is because the Dharma he has received must necessarily have a source. The [incense]...
Regarding the Way of Practice: its external protection must rely upon the sovereign and his ministers to ensure that both merit and wisdom are fully supported.

One must surely plan to repay this kindness on this very day; how could it be a mere coincidence? Nevertheless, when patriarchs and masters of antiquity and today offer incense, they mostly speak of "a single瓣 (bàn)."

*Bàn* (瓣): pronounced with the initial *pi* and rhyme *xiàn*. It refers to the segments of a melon. Because the incense resembles this, it is so named. Sometimes it is written as [片*分] (*biān*), pronounced with the initial *bù* and rhyme *huán*, meaning a "slice" or "piece.

Subsequent generations have followed this tradition and all use these terms. Why must it be so? One should rather say "one piece" (*yī piàn*) or "one stick" (*yī zhù*), so as to avoid the ridicule of the shallow customs of later times.
Regarding the formal proclamation (*pai-chui*) for the World-Honored One’s Vinaya regulations: when one intends to perform a Buddhist rite, it must first be preceded by a formal announcement;
this is the method for maintaining order among the assembly. Now, in the Chan school, the formal proclamation must be entrusted to a venerable elder (*zunsu*) who is proficient in the Dharma.
As soon as the Elder takes his seat, he makes the formal announcement: "O assembly of dragons and elephants at this Dharma feast, you should contemplate the primary truth. Thus speaks the Elder.

Observing the capacities [of the assembly], once the mutual chanting at the Dharma assembly had concluded, he again held up the white staff and said: "Observe clearly the Dharma of the Dharma King; such is the Dharma of the Dharma King.
This is truly the authentic standard of the former worthies, all of whom did not fail to accord with the Buddha’s intent.

Furthermore, we see that in many monasteries they cite the World-Honored One ascending the seat and Mañjuśrī striking the gavel. Yet, even if one were to search thoroughly through the entire Tripitaka, one would not find its source."
As for the ritual procedures for the formal announcement (*bai*), since they have already been established by the Sage’s own composition,
why do you persist in seeking out the words of Mañjuśrī to indulge in such profitless discourse?
Ascending the hall, someone asked: "In the Buddhist sutras, whenever the fourfold assembly is gathered, they have never failed to sit.
Why is it that in the Zen school, when ascending the hall, one must stand while listening to the Dharma? He replied: "This is the profound intention of Master Baizhang.

Furthermore, when the Buddha preached the Dharma, the fourfold assembly gathered like clouds; the meaning of the Dharma he taught was not restricted to the schools of *dharmatā* (nature) or *lakṣaṇa* (characteristics)."
As for the duration of the time since we have met, it is unknown whether it has been long or short.
Now, six hundred years after the Buddha’s teachings first flowed eastward, the Patriarchal Master Bodhidharma finally arrived in the land of Han.

He did not rely on written words, but transmitted the seal of the mind alone, pointing directly at the human mind so that one might see one's nature and become a Buddha. He led his students to suddenly realize the unconditioned beneath a single word.
The assembly that has gathered is not permanent but temporary; therefore, they do not wait for him to sit before standing. Baizhang said:

"When ascending the hall to the seat, the administrators and the disciples stand in a line like geese to listen closely. Through the exchange of questions and answers between guest and host, the essentials of the school are stimulated and elevated.
This demonstrates abiding in accordance with the Dharma—this is its profound meaning."
Regarding "entering the room to inquire," the *Transmission of the Patriarchs* states:

"The Great Master of the Fifth Patriarch, during the night, secretly ordered an attendant to summon the Practitioner Lu to his room at the millhouse, whereupon he transmitted the robe and the Dharma. Furthermore, the *Lotus Sūtra* says:
"Don the robe of the Tathāgata and enter the chamber of the Tathāgata. And the *Āgama Sūtras* state: "The Buddha told the bhikṣus: 'I wish to remain in meditative seclusion for two months.'"
"You need not inquire or question [the Master]. You may only approach when delivering food or when sprinkling water on the ground.
Through this, one should understand that at that time, there was a formal ritual for entering the room to inquire with the Buddhas and Patriarchs."
The *Sengqiji* (Saṃghāvaśeṣa) states: For five reasons, the World-Honored One inspects the monks' quarters once every five days:

first, to prevent his disciples from becoming attached to conditioned affairs; second, to prevent them from becoming attached to worldly discourse; third, to prevent them from becoming attached to sleep; fourth, to attend to monks who are ill;
and fifth, to allow junior bhikṣus to observe the Buddha’s dignified deportment so that they may give rise to joy.
The practice of inspecting the quarters in the Chan school is intended as a model left by the Great Sage;
today, among those throughout the land who serve as masters of the monastic communities, there are none who do not follow this precedent.
In the Zen school, ascending the hall at dawn is called the "morning *sōn*"; chanting at the decline of the day is called the "evening *sōn*";
and preaching the Dharma outside of the regular times is called the "small *sōn*. Now, why is it that all of these are termed "*sōn*"?
It is said: The term "cán" (assembly) signifies that which is vast and great. It means that both the hidden and the manifest gather together, and divine dragons arrive side by side.
Since there is no distinction made between the holy and the ordinary, how could one ever differentiate between the monastic and the lay? For this reason, it is called an "assembly.

Those who preside over the Dharma, with a mind of universal equality, should diligently cultivate all classes of beings so that the Dharma may endure for a long time. How could this be described as...?
A Minor Supplement. Some take the *xiǎo-cán* (informal discourse) as their family precept; this I have not heard of before.
The *shǒuzuò* (head seat) is the ancient equivalent of the *upādhyāya* (elder). In Sanskrit, it is *sthavira*, which here is translated as "Elder.
There are three types of these: the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* states: first, one who is senior by years of birth; second, one who is senior in worldly wealth and reputation.
Regarding the noble class: third, those who first receive the precepts and realize the fruits of the Path.

Throughout antiquity and the present, this rank has been established to be filled by those of mature years, virtue, and administrative capability. The person currently known in the Chan school as the *shouzuo* (head seat) is precisely such an individual.
One must select those who have already completed their duties, whom the community respects and obeys, and who are fully endowed with both virtue and professional competence.
The *Sengshi* (History of the Sangha) states: "The three administrators (*zhishi*) and the three pillars (*sangang*) are like the great ropes of a fishing net;

if they are pulled up, the hundred meshes will be set right. The Sanskrit term *karmadāna* is translated here as "abbot" (*sizhu*), which refers to the current position of the *jianse* (superintendent).
To examine the history of the abbot: it originated with the White Horse [Temple] of the Eastern Han. Once a temple was established, there must necessarily be one who presides over it.
Although at that time there was no formal title of "abbot," there were nevertheless those who managed its affairs. This continued until the Eastern Jin dynasty.
This office has flourished extensively. Now, our Chan school has internal and external administrative officers, with the *jian-si* (superintendent) at its head;
this is simply due to long-standing tradition. Scriptures such as the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* state: "The property of the Saṅgha is difficult to manage, for the Buddha-dharma has no owner.
I permit only two kinds of persons to manage the property of the Triple Gem: first, Arhats; second, Srotāpannas. What is meant here...
For these reasons, other bhikṣus are not fully qualified; their minds are not impartial, and thus they should not be appointed to administrative duties.
Furthermore, there are two types of persons who are suitable: first, those who can maintain pure precepts and recognize the retribution of karma;

second, those who fear the offenses of future lives and possess a sense of shame and remorse. Now, in my Chan school, we must select those whose minds have attained penetration of the Way of the Dharma.

"Yet they do not cling to various states of existence. For one who has forgotten personal gain and offerings to manage the affairs of the Saṃgha, this is the bequeathed intention of the former worthies.

The *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* (Record of Buddhist Practices Sent Home from the Southern Seas) explains that "Weina" combines both Chinese and Sanskrit terms: "Wei" (維) means "to uphold" or "to govern," which is the Chinese term; "Na" (那)... [is the Sanskrit].

This is an abbreviation of the Sanskrit term, having deleted the three characters *jiemo tuó* (羯磨陀). This is translated as "one who pleases the assembly. Furthermore, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"Because there is no one in the monastery who knows the time, the hour is announced by a fixed proclamation and the *gandī* is struck.

Moreover, there is no one to plaster, repair, sweep, or sprinkle water in the lecture hall or the dining area; there is no one to continuously arrange the beds; and when the assembly is in disorder, there is no one [to manage it]."

When people clapped their fingers [to signal him], the Buddha ordered that a *vinaya-dhara* (disciplinarian) be appointed. Furthermore, the term *śabda-vidyā* (phonology) is translated as "sequence," referring to one who knows the sequence of administrative affairs.

Nowadays, the Chan school requires this office to manage the monastic registers (*saṃgha-pustaka*) and the duties of the *pratideśanīya* (proclaimer), and one must certainly select a person of appropriate talent for the position.
According to the *Sengshi* (History of the Sangha), the term "Dianzuo" (Director of Seats) refers to one who oversees nine matters concerning beds and seats;
here, however, it is used to encompass all miscellaneous affairs. This name has been adopted by the Chan school as a conventional designation handed down through tradition.
According to the *Sengshi* (History of the Sangha), the term "zhisui" (year-steward) refers to one who oversees the affairs of a single year; thus, this office was established.
Although the Chan school today does not strictly limit the duration to a full year, the name itself is modeled after ancient regulations.

Regarding the "Discrimination of Robe Colors": the *cān* (chan) family wears the *dàn* (dark/soiled) robe. According to the *Bǎolín zhuàn* (Treasure Forest Tradition), this is the *quxùn* (qūshùn) robe transmitted by Bodhidharma;
it is called "first-grade cloth" and is a deep blue-black color. This likely follows the original system established by the patriarchs.

As there is no textual basis for it in the Vinaya, many have criticized it. However, the Sanskrit term is *kāṣāya*, which here means "not a primary color"; furthermore, the Buddha prohibited [the use of] dyed colors.
The form and color [of the robe] are indeed intended to differ from the secular, yet one must possess a sense of shame and modesty.
The dark, dingy colors used today are not those employed by the laity, nor are they primary colors; thus, for practitioners of the Way to wear them is precisely appropriate.

Furthermore, since forest-dwelling meditators are far removed from cities, even dyeing robes is difficult; these pale, faded colors are neither cumbersome nor wasteful, and thus follow the principle of simplicity.
As Master Cheng said: "The Vinaya specifies three types of dyed colors: blue, black, and madder (mōlán). The *Chao* states: "Blue refers to verdigris;
black refers to mixed mud; madder is tree bark. The commentary notes: "This explains the colors for dyeing miscellaneous robes;
what is now called 'dyeing' likewise does not exceed these three. Now, examining the matter, Zen monks mostly wear black.
If the dark-colored robes (*cai yi*) are dyed, they are subsumed under the "blackish-purple robes" (*zao hei yi*) mentioned in the Vinaya;

for their application of ink, indigo, and various clays is not far removed from that description. If they are pale, blue, or white, they are subsumed under the "blue robes" (*qing yi*) mentioned in the Vinaya;

for they are made by using copper-green (*tong qing*), wooden edges, and various inks for dyeing. This precisely accords with the intent of the Vinaya. How can it be said that there is no scriptural authority for them?
Incorrect. Regarding the vestments of the Western regions, following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, they likewise varied according to different schools.

Those of the Sarvāstivāda school, who were broadly learned, possessed quick intelligence, and benefited others through the Dharma and its transformation, should wear saffron-colored robes. Those of the Sautrāntika school, who upheld the weighty precepts and adjudicated legal matters, should wear black robes.
Those of the Sthavira school, who were diligent in making definitive judgments and protected sentient beings, should wear wood-colored [robes].
The Mahīśāsaka school contemplates the subtle and penetrates the profound; they may wear robes of purple-blue.
The Mahāsāṃghika school diligently studies the various sūtras and expounds their meanings; they should wear robes of yellow.
The *Sengshi* (History of the Sangha) states that during the Later Liang dynasty, there was the Dharma Master Huilang, who wore a green *nāṃsa* robe. Master Zhigong had previously predicted:
"At Xinghuang Temple, there shall be a lay bodhisattva (*kāpālika*) dressed in green who will widely propagate the Mahāyāna. When it came to Huilang, the prophecy proved true.

Toward the end of the Tang dynasty, there was the Chan Master Guanyin of Yuzhang, who observed that many Chan practitioners from the south were wearing white *nāṃsa* robes and frequently [commented on] them...
He placed dye in a jar and urged [the monk] to dye it. Today, throughout the world, this is called the "Avalokiteśvara patched robe.
Recently, there have been those who wear white robes; this is an extreme error. The Buddha prophesied that the kāṣāya would turn white and no longer accept dye.
Is this not what you have attained? There may be sentient beings who possess consciousness in accordance with the Dharma, yet they seize [this] and destroy its form;
truly, such a one is a superior man of great power. Now, Elder, you wear a large robe of crimson color, which the world calls "red silk."
As for the green-colored robes, many practitioners of the Way in the West wear them. As the *Xiyuji* states:

"Śāṇakavāsin’s nine-strip robe was crimson; at the time of his parinirvāṇa, through the power of his wisdom and vows, he left it behind to remain until the end of the Dharma, at which point it would naturally decay.
Xuanzang remarked that it has already suffered some slight damage. Examining this, one sees the kind of robe worn by such great masters of the transmission of the Dharma.
The crimson-colored robe represents the tradition of succession and transmission; what is called a "Dharma robe" (hōe) is a robe that accords with the Dharma.

Regarding the emerald-green robe, some say that Empress Wu once took the robe of Caoxi into the palace for veneration and wrapped it in emerald-green silk, and thus those in positions of authority in later generations came to honor it.
Furthermore, the *Hōgen Dentōki* states: "The patched robe..."

Regarding the robes: some were made of blue silk, while others had their seams reinforced with patches. This began when the National Teacher of Nanyang was summoned into the palace by an imperial decree of Emperor Suzong of the Tang dynasty;
as his *nà* robe (patchwork dharma robe) was worn out, the palace ladies reinforced it with blue silk and patched the seams with purple silk.

The National Teacher wore these frequently, and from this they have been handed down in succession. *Dìàn* (靛): pronounced *diàn*, refers to dyeing with indigo. *Pǒu* (瓿): pronounced *pǒu* (蒲口切), refers to a small jar.
Furthermore, regarding the regulations for robes: the World-Honored One ordained that bhikṣus should possess six articles. Three of these are garments:
first, the *antarvāsa*; second, the *uttarāsaṅga*; and third, the *saṃghāṭī*. The *saṃghāṭī* is the great outer robe; it begins with nine strips.
The eleven-striped and thirteen-striped robes both consist of two long strips and one short strip; these are termed the "inferior grade.
I have observed that many practitioners of dhyāna fashion nine-striped robes without regard for the number of long and short strips.

They merely seek what is square, neat, and pleasing to the eye, disregarding the Buddha’s regulations—this is truly lamentable. Recently, I have also seen those made with dark ink-dyed short returns; this appears to be an attempt to...

In the *Xuanchao lüshi gantong zhuan* (Biographies of the Miraculous Responses of Vinaya Master Xuanchao), there is an inquiry regarding the account of the celestial being Huang Qiong. It states briefly:
"Recently, I have observed that many monks coming from the Western Regions wear robes made of sewn leaves. Why is this? The answer was: "This was two hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
A monk from Northern India lived together with non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). The non-Buddhists were jealous of him and secretly placed sharp blades within the layers of his robe."
They went together to the king’s presence. The non-Buddhist practitioners informed the king, "The Śākya śramaṇas have hidden blades within their robes and intend to harm the king.
Consequently, they were searched and caught. Because of this, all the bhikṣus in the kingdom were executed. At that time, there was the arhat Yaśas.

He ordered the bhikṣus to temporarily sew them closed to avoid the danger of losing their lives; this was a provisional regulation established due to specific circumstances in the north and was not something permitted by the Buddha.
Now, there are bhikṣus in the south who all likewise sew them closed, and even those lacking understanding have learned to sew them as well.
Huang Qiong further remarked that the bhikṣus of the Western lands wear the kāṣāya, yet for the most part they do not...
[The robes were] too large. The Licchavis criticized them, saying, "They have no dignified deportment; the garments they wear look like those of a courtesan, resembling the trunk of an elephant.
For this reason, the Buddha ordained that hooks and fasteners be attached at the top.
He further said, "Now, let the corner of the robe reach the left arm and be tucked beneath the left armpit; it must not hang down as was the case with the aforementioned fault. Thus he proclaimed.
He said: "I have fully heard your elegant discourse. Even if the preceding and succeeding regulations did not provide for such a demonstration, my sentiments would have expanded upon them.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that in other regions, what is considered impure is not practiced despite being proscribed; based on this, it may serve as a standard to rely upon.

How much more so when it was bestowed by a Heavenly Man and promulgated under the Zhou dynasty? It is a pity that I learned of it so late. Having read it with careful attention, I, the fool, [reflect upon it].

Lord Xuan propagated the doctrine of "Heaven and Man" and composed an elaborate treatise, intending to alter the ancient regulations so that the corner of the robe would reach the left arm and be placed beneath the left armpit. Alas!
Suppose one were to fold the right corner properly so it is not exposed and place it upon the left arm while walking through this region—why would this not be pure?
Furthermore, it is said that the bhikṣus of the South sew together the patches of their robes, which they claim contradicts the Buddha’s regulations because those who practice this are ignorant.
Now, since they place the corner of the robe beneath the left armpit, how can it be said that this too contradicts the Buddha’s regulations?

Those who study and follow this path must surely be considered possessed of discernment. Furthermore, the reason Yaśas fashioned robes by sewing together cloth pieces was to avoid the calamity of death;
it also demonstrates that in the past, the preservation of cloth fragments was not done for the sake of creating an object [of attachment].
Even though they were sewn together, they did not lose their character as fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). Now, if one were to hang them...

Regarding the placement of the robe under the arm: what is the underlying reason? To place the color of the robe under the arm, one takes as a standard the textual passages that, though established, were not put into practice.
While sewing "leaves" (patches) on the robe serves to prevent difficulties, the statement that other regions do not consider this pure—how could it be otherwise?
The Tang monk Xuanyi said: "The realms of heaven and humanity are entirely [different]."
They are distinct. It is not only that there is a difference between the pure and the defiled; indeed, their languages are also different.

Even regarding written characters, they are still considered superior; thus, these matters are vastly separated. For the languages of various regions change according to the land, such that beyond ten thousand *li*, their sounds do not communicate with one another.
How much more so for the various heavens, where the phonetic tones are certainly distinct! Now, do practitioners of meditation not inquire into whether this is so or not?
However, [you] have simply made this garment for the sake of convenience in wearing it. How can you be so utterly lacking in discernment? *Yì* (嶷) is pronounced with the *è* and *lì* initials.
Regarding the name "guàzǐ" (挂子), Master Chéng says that it is sometimes called a "luòzǐ" (络子). This was likely the name used by former generations of monks.

It was first established [by him], and later monks imitated it. Furthermore, as the name "robe" (cīvara) had been lost and one could see only a net-like garment (kaṭhina) worn upon the body, it was thus named.

Nowadays, Zen monks in the South wear this for all manual labor; however, because its appearance is not in accordance with the Dharma and no such name exists in the various Vinayas, it has nearly been criticized by the exegesis schools.
Consequently, while reading the tenth fascicle of the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-ekottara-karmavācanā*, I [observed this].
The scroll states: The five-strip robe has three grades. The superior grade is three cubits in height and five cubits in width;
the inferior grade is half that size. Those between the two are called the middle grade. Furthermore, the Buddha said there are two types of *antarvāsa* (inner robe):

first, three cubits in height and five cubits in width; second, two cubits in height and four cubits in width. These are known as the robes for formal possession (*dhāraṇīya-cīvara*), representing the final measurements.

It is limited in size: the three circles [of the garment] cover the navel above and reach down to conceal the knees below. Upon detailed examination, its dimensions are roughly equivalent to those of the modern *guazi* (a vest-like garment).
If one makes it, using five panels—either one long and one short, or with pleats or patches—it is called an *antarvāsa*.

This is not subject to the fault of violating the rules regarding color; it may be worn in all circumstances and is entirely consistent with the Vinaya. Indeed, it is superior to being naked. Whenever I observe this...
This statement further reveals the public consensus of the Dharma masters. Yet, alas, when it comes to the compositions of those in the Zen monasteries, they have never taken this as a model;
furthermore, they do not even adopt the name "guàluò" (掛絡). What could be their intention?
Even the secular classics state that names must be rectified—how much more so for the followers of Śākyamuni! [The character] zhé (襵) is pronounced zhé (摺).
The *Vinayakṣudrakavastu* states: At one time, a bhikṣu had finished making his three robes and, placing them upon his shoulder, traveled along the road.
They subsequently became damp with sweat and soiled by dust. The Buddha said: "They should be kept in a bag."
The bag may be three cubits in length and one and a half cubits in width. As for the robes placed within it, those used daily should be on top, while those not in regular use should be below.
Although the waist-bags of modern Chan practitioners differ slightly in their construction, they nonetheless follow the regulations established by the Buddha.
When those who travel to various regions bind their bags, they should likewise reflect upon the virtuous legacy bequeathed by the Buddhas and Patriarchs.

This is important; do not treat it with negligence. Regarding the mention of "cubits" (*zhǒu*), this is based on the Buddha’s cubit. As for the "foot" (*chǐ*), the standard used is that of the Jī-zhōu (Western Zhou) foot.
A human being is eight feet tall, whereas the Buddha is one *zhàng* and six feet tall. What is now referred to as "three cubits" is thus equivalent to six feet.

"Traveling on foot, traveling on foot" means to distance oneself from one's native village and travel across the land on foot, casting off worldly attachments and abandoning burdens to seek out teachers and friends, seeking the Dharma and realizing enlightenment.
Therefore, one studies without a fixed teacher, making it a priority to travel everywhere.
Sudhana sought in the south, and Sadāprarudita requested [the Dharma] in the east; such was the manner in which the ancient sages sought the Dharma. This is what Yongjia meant by "wandering."
Crossing rivers and seas, traversing mountains and valleys, seeking teachers and inquiring after the Way to practice Zen—is this not so?
As the verse of Śakra in the *Madhyama Āgama* says: "I pay homage to those who have rightly gone forth from the household life; their eyes are fixed as they travel through all directions."
He did not concern himself with whether he was traveling or staying still; when he went forth, he sought nothing. He found joy in the practice of non-action (*wuwei*).

Furthermore, the eminent monk Hui-cheng served his grandfather Qiang as his teacher. At the age of sixteen, he petitioned Qiang, saying, "To be more than a thousand li from home yet still bear the name of a lay śramaṇa is not right.
I request permission to travel far to the capital and its outskirts in order to broaden my knowledge and experience. Qiang then complied with his wish. Such was this journey.
How extensive is the utility of the staff!
When a bhikṣu travels to the Western Regions, he must carry his staff; it possesses twenty-five rules of decorum.
Whenever he enters a room, he must not let it touch the ground, but must hang it upon the wall-bracket. This is why it is called the "monk's place of residence" (*seng-so-zhi-zhu-chu*).
Hanging up the *śikya* (monastic robe). The twenty-five modes of deportment are detailed in the *Śalākā-śāstra*.

Regarding the spreading of the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*), the *Monastic History* (*Sengshi*) states: "In the past, when Indian monks arrived here, they would all spread their *niṣīdana* and perform prostrations upon it.

Later generations, seeking to avoid inconvenience, [neglected this]. Only then did the Venerable [Daoxuan] permit the use of the *niṣīdana*, immediately putting a stop [to the previous practice], and then proceeded to exchange pleasantries."
"Liáng. Furthermore, "zhǎn" (展) is synonymous with performing a prostration twice. The Venerable One stopped him from doing so;

henceforth, one simply uses the *niśīdana* (seating mat) as a substitute for the ritual prostration, which is what is called the "stepping-back prostration" (*zuo-bai*). To perform such an expression of reverence—would it not be too simplistic?
Nevertheless, those who seek purity according to their respective traditions cannot help but practice it. Even today, the venerable masters of the monastic communities likewise [do so].

When performing this rite, if the one who is not yet ready to receive it—such as a monk—first spreads his sitting mat (*niṣīdana*) and then returns a single prostration, this is truly a reversal of proper order.
It often happens that people claim that once the mat is spread, two prostrations should be made; they do not know on what basis they make such a statement.
What is called *zuo* (蓌) is "fraud" (*chā*). When an inferior person performs a fraudulent prostration while the superior person actually responds to it, the gravity of the offense is diminished.
If these distinctions are not maintained, what standard will future generations have to follow?
From this day forward, be careful not to speak of the etiquette of returning a bow, lest you incur the ridicule of onlookers. *Zuò* (蓌): pronounced as *zǔ* and *wò*.
While the Buddha was staying in the Deer Park at Śrāvastī, a certain bhikṣu went along carrying his alms bowl in his hand.

On the road, he tripped and fell; the bowl dropped and was broken. Because of this incident of the broken bowl, he reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "A bhikṣu should not carry his bowl in his hand.
He then wrapped the bowl in the corner of his robe and went on his way, but the same difficulty occurred as before. The Buddha said, "One should..."
He made a bowl bag to carry it in, and the bhikṣu held it in his hand. This incurred the same fault as mentioned above. The Buddha said: "One should not hold it in the hand;
one should instead make a loop and carry it by hanging it over the shoulder. If one acts otherwise, one incurs an offense against the Dharma. (The character *dié* is pronounced *tuō*.)
*Huàn* (襻). Pronounced *pǔ huàn* (普患切).

Regarding the *kamaṇḍalu* (淨缾), the *Caturvargika-vinaya* states: There was a bhikṣu who encountered a place without water; as for the water that was available, it contained insects, yet he died of thirst.
The Buddha, knowing this, established a precept requiring him to carry two flasks—one for ritual purity (*śuci*) and one for contact (*spraṣṭavya*)—for the sake of protecting his life.
The *Vinayakarman-mūla-kṣudraka-vastu* states: When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, a bhikṣu wished to cut his three robes (tricīvara) but tore them with his hands, thereby damaging the fabric.
The Buddha said, "One may use a knife to cut them. The group of six [monks] then adorned it with various jewels and made it excessively long.
The Buddha prohibited this, saying, "This is a large blade; it is not a knife."
You should know that there are three kinds of knives: large, medium, and small. The large may be six finger-widths long;

the small, four finger-widths; and those between the two are called medium. There are two shapes for them: first, curved like a bird’s wing; second, resembling a chicken feather. They should not be pointed or straight.
The *Sengshi* (History of the Sangha) states: "When a bhikṣu possesses a knife, it is called a 'precept-knife' (*jie-dao*). This is because the Buddha did not...
It was permitted to cut down all grasses and trees for the purpose of destroying the groves of spirits; yet even grasses and trees were held in restraint, let alone anything else.
Once, while the Buddha was on Vulture Peak Mountain, an elderly bhikṣu was ascending and descending the mountain when he tripped and fell to the ground.

The Buddha said, "You should keep a walking staff. Having heard the Buddha's permission, the group of six monks immediately carved and decorated their staffs with gold, silver, variegated silks, and other materials.
Laypeople looked upon them with disdain and contempt. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who said, "Bhikṣus, there are two circumstances under which you should keep a walking staff:
first, for those who are aged, emaciated, or lacking strength; second, for those whose bodies are afflicted by the suffering of illness."

Furthermore, it was regulated that the thickness must not exceed that of a coarse finger. This is just like the walking staff (*zhuzhang*) used by Chan practitioners today when traveling through mountains;

because the tail of the staff is thin and weak when crossing dangerous heights or treacherous terrain for the sake of support, a small branch-like section is left at the end, often with an iron ring threaded through it.
Wanderers and eminent scholars mostly carry staffs made of thick, heavy, and hard wood, using them as a means of self-display.

Furthermore, it is said: "This is sufficient to ward off robbers and protect one's person. Often, the ignorant and vulgar will surely claim that such is indeed how things ought to be for those of the Chan school.
Does this not slight the bequeathed teachings of our Buddha?
The *Vījanī* (Whisk): The Buddha was staying in the High Hall by the side of the Monkey Pond in the city of Vaiśālī.
At that time, the bhikṣus were being bitten by mosquitoes; their bodies itched, and they scratched them incessantly. When the laypeople saw this, they asked:
"Noble one, why is this so? he asked, and the other replied with full details of the matter. He said, "Noble one, why do you not carry an object for brushing away mosquitoes?
He replied, "The Blessed One has not permitted it. [The monk] reported this circumstance to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "I now authorize the bhikṣus to keep objects for brushing away mosquitoes.
At that time, having heard that the Buddha had granted permission, the group of six [monks] immediately [prepared] them from various jewels.
The handle was made of *mṛgaśṛṅga* (yak-tail), which served as its whisk. When a layperson saw it, he asked, "What is this object?

He replied, "The Buddha has permitted bhikṣus to keep whisks as a means of warding off mosquitoes; therefore, I carry one. The layman said, "Venerable sir, although you have shaved your head, your greed and defilements have not been removed.
He reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "There are five types of objects for warding off mosquitoes. The first is..."
1. Made by carding wool; 2. Made from *zhoulin* (a type of coarse cloth); 3. Using finely split *die-mao* (woolen) cloth; 4. Using old materials; 5. Using the tips of tree branches.

If one uses precious objects, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing). *Mao* (in *máoliáo*) is pronounced as *mao*; *qū* (in *máoliáopǔqū*) is pronounced as *xū*, meaning "to lift" or "to raise."
When the Buddha was at the Anāthapiṇḍika Garden, there was a bhikṣu who slept naked, failing to protect his bedding and mats.

People all criticized and disapproved of this. The Buddha said, "You should require them to wear sleeping garments (*śayanapatta*). This is precisely what the Chan school uses today as a *miandan* (sleeping mat).
The *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* states: "Prostrating and spreading out sitting mats are things not seen in the Five Indies."

As for what is required: it is intended solely for protecting others' mats and bedding while sleeping. If one uses another's belongings, both new and old items must be provided with a protective layer to prevent them from being stained by sweat or damaged, thereby not defiling the offerings of the faithful.

The *Zhēnzǐ jìguī chuán* (Account of the Return of a Pillow) states: "In the ten islands of the South Sea and the five regions of the Western Kingdoms, wooden pillows for supporting the head are not used at all;
this practice exists only in the Divine Land (China). The style of the pillow-covers in the West is similar to our own."
One may take silk or cotton cloth and dye it, then sew it at will into a straight-sided pouch one and a half cubits long and half a cubit wide.
As for the contents, they should be whatever is locally available: perhaps wool, or hemp-cotton, or reed-pith and willow-down;
or perhaps *kṣavaka* seeds, hemp, or beans. These should be adjusted according to the season’s cold or heat and the practitioner’s own discretion as to height. This is...
Taking what is suitable ensures physical well-being; truly, there is no affliction more solid than this.

However, because wooden pillows are coarse and hard, and the area beneath the head is exposed to drafts, many people of the time suffer from headaches. Consequently, soft materials dispel the wind, while hemp and beans clarify the eyesight.

Furthermore, it is beneficial and, when used with sincerity, is never misleading. Moreover, those from cold regions often suffer from wind-induced ailments and nasal congestion during the winter months;
this is its failing. Nowadays, many practitioners of Chan keep wooden bridge-pillows, likely because they are convenient for traveling monks and easy to pack and carry;
thus, they serve a practical purpose in the present time and cannot be abolished. (The character *wūn* is pronounced *yùn*.)

The *jiaobi lü* (foot-binding robe) is what is called the *zhuan-yi* (calf-protecting garment). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "My disciples wear the three robes (*tricīvara*), which are sufficient to ward off the suffering of cold.
If one is by nature unable to endure the cold, they may, according to their own preference, layer on additional worn-out garments. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: [as above].
The three robes, the undergarment, the upper robe, the rain-bath robe, the thigh-protector, the ankle-protector, the calf-protector, and so forth—all these serve to ward off the cold;
therefore, their possession is permitted. However, these garments are the most humble and inferior; it is sufficient merely to obtain them so that they do not tear.
Yet now I see practitioners of meditation traversing paths of fine thorns, which constantly disrupts their schedule, while moreover the sultry heat is like being consumed by fire.

Wearing high skirts and performing tight prostrations, they claim this is in perfect accord with the rules of Chan meditation. Yet they fail to realize that the Buddha established these garments specifically to ward off the cold.
*Zhuǎn* (pronounced with the initial *chǔan* and final *-ian*) refers to the calf muscle. *Bǐ* (pronounced with the initial *bù* and final *-li*) refers to the thigh.
The *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra* states: "When a donor purchases an item for the purpose of giving, one does not see the act of killing.
For example, if a donor’s ox dies and he sells it to a butcher, who then buys its hide to have leather sandals made and gives them as a gift, it is permitted to accept and wear them.

The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "Those made from hide are called *li*; those made from hemp are called *ju*. The sandals (*xi*) were fashioned by Yuze, a minister of the Yellow Emperor. *Soqi* (the phonetic gloss for *xi*).
Qiè. Jù. (The pronunciation is jù).
*Zútíng Shìyuàn*, Scroll Eight (End).
Composed by the Venerable Mù'ān Qīng. *Zútíng Shìyuàn*.
Zhengzong composed a preface for it, in which his exposition is extremely detailed.

The Chan traveler Daosong of Jiuyang, who has traveled extensively through the monastic communities and possesses firm faith in this Way, presented this book to me, desiring that it be transmitted to the world. Upon reading it, I marveled at its excellence.

However, as for those who sit upon a curved-wood meditation seat while this book is being produced, yet harbor a mind that hangs on words and phrases, uttering even a single character—how can they avoid shame?
If you truly do not understand, then for now look into the tangle of complications.

Written respectfully on the twenty-seventh day of the eighth month in the second year of the Da Guan era by the Commander of Jianwu Army, Acting Director of the Imperial Clan School, and Marquis of the Upper Pillar Rank.
Re-engraved and published again in the late summer of the Jiaxu year of the Shaoxing era.

When Bodhidharma came from the West, he directly received those of great capacity; yet the assembly of monks did not study, and as a rule they claimed that no words or texts were established. How foolish!
To lack self-awareness and perish from hunger is truly pitiable. The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time began as learners and ended as those beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*).
